COMMODORE *S COLUMN A Happy New Year to you alli It won't be long before we are sailing again, although some of our hardier members started the year by "Catching a Crab" in the Maldon Rowing Race (see Brenda Tate's report). Your enthusiasm and support for this event was so good that it could well develop into becoming the high spot of our Winter Programme. Some very useful work was done by those who braved the very cold weather at the Christmas Working Party. Fortified by Soup and Rolls from the Galley, a "Rustic" Stile and Refuse Collection Area were erected, trees tended and fencing strengthened. A number of jobs remain to be done, so please watch out for the next "Call to Arms" How about this for your New Years Resolution? "Contribute to Navigans"! Committee/Official reportage is important, but it can be very dull if not interspersed with rays of sunshine. CRUISER FLEET NEWS It was good to see a very good turn out for the RNLI Sponsored Rowing event on New Years Day. With a good entry and excellent support the club was well represented. It proved to be a good way of celebrating the occasion and working off hangovers. May I remind everyone that Jack Pateman, our President, will be at the Generals Arms on the first Wednesday in February (6th), relating his adventures sailing off the coast of Maine. Hope to see you all there. Russ Fuller Cruiser Fleet Captain Tel: Home [redacted] SPONSORED ROWING RACE New Year's Day was bright, sunny and frosty with a light easterly breeze, providing ideal conditions for the Annual Rowing Race in aid of the RL NI, organised by the Maldon Little Ship Club. A large crowd of Marconi supporters gathered on the quay at Maldon to cheer on the five club entrants in the field of over 30 boats that were participating. There was a staggered start and Vic Crisp was the first competitor away, resplendent in full 18th century naval uniform, complete with periwig and tricorn hat, a fine sight rowing his infPatable down towards the end of the prom. Jackie Hall and Ian Manning were in the next batch, they were well prepared with a full picnic basket on board in the Manning's new Bumble Bee dinghy built in Jack's study over Christmas specially for the race. Close behind, keeping an eye on things was Pete Hall and Jimmy Campbell in a revamped Queen Mary sporting a new coat of shiny red paint and a lot of fibre glass filling. Jim Coy and family were there too rowing their converted Mirror, centre box well covered with sticky tape, although I did think they were a little low in the water at the stern! In the last section to start there was Peter Clayton and crew in the Fisherman, sporting a modest burgee, 3 foot square, Pete, Ian Lindsey, Graham Mead and Danny Lumley with Pete Foreman as Cox made a fine sight as they rowed(?) down the river on the five mile course. Down to the end of the prom, back to the Full Bridge, back down to the port hand marker buoy by the end of the Fun Fair, and then back to the quay just before the Queen's Head. Many people took a brisk walk along to the sea wall to give support to their favourite boat, others less hardy gathered in the pub for a reviving glass of Scotch. Less than an hour after the start at 1030 and the first boat was home. The Fisherman came in fifth with Pete Hall and Jimmy Campbell not far behind. Half an hour later Captain Hornblower Crisp returned to uphold the honour of the club and take first prize in the fancy dress section. All the other competitors finished the course and had the satisfaction of knowing that through others generous sponsorship of their boats over £1,500 had been raised for the RNLI. The occasion was celebrated in customary drunken style by competitors and spectators alike in the Queen's Head. Brenda Tate

sa A me CHANGING FORTUNES The 1979 Rum Tub and Bung race, organised by Maldon Yacht Club and raced from our Club was, like the three previous years, raced in very light variable conditions. At least for the long line start, in misty conditions, there was sufficient wind to enable competitors to stem the tide and we elected to start at the Stansgate end, our plan being to tack down stream on the Stone side to benefit from the main ebbing tidal stream. The misty conditions made sighting the Nass difficult, but at that point of the race, having used the tide and the weight of our GP 14 "Lotus Blossom", we were well placed, relative to other dinghies. The sea mist thickened and we had a guessing game on our hands for the next mark, the Bench Head, visibility became almost nil and all the fleet seemed to be taking fairly short tacks, in what we hoped was the main streem, occasionally sighting opponents such as Ray Smith, last years winner, in his Enterprise "Tomatiga", Snipes and 420's from Maldon YC and our Commodore who being a Marconi man would have, we hoped, built in radar that would guide us to the mark. All around us Yacht Fog Horns were sounding off and we could hear our opponents calling at them to ask if they had seen the Bench Head, was this outside assistance we wondered? We seemed to be sailing for an age and felt that sooner or later the answers to the calling would be in a foreign language?! Suddenly the mist cleared and there we were cross tacking with our arch opponent, Ray Smith from Saltcote, who had not got away from us after all, we were not far from the buoy, now this was when our fortunes changed for the worse, we thought the tide was still ebbing and that Ray Smith taking the port tack was doing the wrong thing, he was right and reached the Bench Head easily, we were wrong and took at least 30 minutes longer to round the mark against the tide with the breeze going lighter. Once round the buoy we hoisted the spinnaker, still hoping the catch the leading 420's etc, but alas! no wind to even fill it, but yet not far away was a Hunter from Blackwater SC, with her spinnaker full, Orang Utan was also not far from us and having just as much bother. My crew was getting thoroughly irritable and furious with the spinnaker, spitting blood because the Enterprise was so far in front, sending shivers straight up the mast, which emptied any air nurtured in the mainsail. Was it poor visibility that made the fleet led by Hornets go inshore to the Power Station?, or did they go that side for breeze?. By then my crew had completely given up, we took the spinnaker off and he stretched out on the starboard side and went to sleep; to my annoyance too far aft, which meant that in order to lift the transom, I sat forward for ages, still, very still, with my arm stretched straight out aft, but we were moving on the tide, fortunes changing again? Yes! On my cheeks there was a little breeze. I awakened my crew, spinnaker up? Yes! It filled and we were in the main stream, the mist lifted and there in sight was the main fleet, including the Enterprise that we were most anxious to catch, seemingly huddled in the lee of the Power Station, motionless. Indeed, our fortunes had changed and my crew was getting his enthusiasm back, but we still had a long way to go, and a National from Maldon YC and Orang Utan from Marconi were behind us with a breeze, would they catch us? If the breeze got stronger they surely would, this breeze which carried us up to the main fleet reached all of them, but they were not in mid-—stream and we were, our furtunes held, and we finished well ahead of the Enterprise and most of the fleet which gave "Lotus Blossom" and the Marconi SC this very nice trophy, "The Rum, Tub and Bung" — the message must surely be that ina long race, keep on trying, never give up, fortunes do change like the fickle conditions. Phil Kenworthy

MIRROR NEWS Shortly before Christmas I was asked by John Weedon if I would take over the Captaincy of the Mirror Fleet. As you may know, Malcolm Gandy has sold his boat and I am selling my Solo and will be left with a Mirror in which to concentrate my efforts this year. I hope that this coming season will see many more Mirrors out racing. Out of 51 boats registered last season, only 5 indicated that they would not race, yet only about 4 of the remainder appeared to compete regularly. I'm sure more of you would like to race, but do not want to show your ignorance of the rules. Well, join the club. Most of us who race regularly have read them but promptly forgot all but numbers 36,37 and 42. Well don't worry too much about that, get on the water and start competing. It's surprising how a near collision can improve your memory of the racing rules. That's once you get back to the club and have time to think what you (or the other chaps) were doing wrong. We have a new Cadet Fleet Captain this year, and I feel it is part of my duty, especially as Mirror Fleet Captain to work with him in encouraging the new and younger members of that fleet. So I hope that fathers and mothers who are owners of Mirrors will dust them off, and get their offspring on to the water this season. elde NAVIGATION SIMPLIFIED? Picture the scene if you will: the boat is on a broad reach, hissing through the water with the skipper at the helm, keen eyes searching the horigson all around, every nerve, every sinew in tune with his environment, the hand transmitting the message from the brain to correct the CourS€ececsccccccccceseccess DUt what course ? ‘Tis easy me dears. Harken and all will be revealed. The skipper knows where he is at all times. He knows this because he knows where he isn't. By subtracting where he is from where he isn't (or where he isn't from where he is, whichever is the greater) he obtains a defference or deviation. Deviations are used to generate corrective commands which will cause the boat to be moved from a position where she is to a position where she isn't. She arrives at the position where she wasn't, consequently, the position where she was is now the position where she isn't. O K so far? Now, in the event that the position where she is now is not the same as the position where she originally wasn't, the skipper acquires a variation, this being the difference between where the boat is now and where she wasn't. *(Variations are caused by various external factors and the discussion of these factors is not considered to be within the scope of this discourse). If the variation is considered to be a significant factor then it too may be allowed for and correction applied by the skipper; but he must know know were he was. His lightning thougtt processes are as follows:- Because variation has modified some of the information which he has obtained, he is not 100% sure where he is. However, he knows where he isn't and where he wase He now subtracts where he should be from where he wasn't (or vice versa) and by differentiating this from the algebraic difference between where he shouldn't be and where he was, he is able to obtain the difference between the deviation and it's variation, this difference being called error. It is this correction which causes the hand to move positively at the helm bringing the boat on course, the whole process being known by kindly professionals as a comedy of errors. I told you it was easy. ae YEAR BOOK CHANGES One important change in the 1980 Yearbook is the deletion of rule 5 - Anchors This was the decision of the Main Committee and the Sailing Sub Committee. The carrying of anchors in dinghies has been a "bone of contention" for several seasons. New designs such as Lasers, Sailboards etc do not make provisions for carrying anchors nor do some Class Associations require their members to carry anchors in their boats. So it is left to the individuals choice, but helmsmen are advised to check their insurance policies and Class Association rules just to be sure. CAMPING DAYS As a club we are only allocated a certain number of camping days each year. These are allocated to various events throughout the season. Therefore it is very important that tent#caravans are not placed at Stansgate before the day and date stated in the Yearbook, and must be removed by the last day of each stay. . Stan Oaker Sailing Secretary |) 1980 MOORINGS Cruiser Owners will be pleased to know that their fleet has grown with 12 new members. This results in pressure on both mooring positions and allocating spaces in the boat park. It is regretted that without a mooring position, a space cannot be allocated in the boat park. At the moment we have 5 cruisers "Stored in the boat park" with no mooring position. Will owners please arrange to move them. Will you please make sure all your mooring ground tackle is as specified on the chart in the club house, and also that it is laid in the correct position by 1 June and has Row and Number painted on buoy. The Mooring Committee has ruled that moorings shall have large buoys to float scope and short 6' pick up buoy or warpse No long trailing warps to catch dinghies or propellers. Visitors mooring will be laid for sole use of Visitors to club. The bad habit of cruiser members using it will result in their position not being re-allocated next season. With mooring positions now at a premium will all cruiser owners please observe the above so as to guarantee their allocation for next season. a THE MOORING COMMITTEE MEMBERS: R Greygoose R Fuller G Pewter F Savill M Bates P Clayton V Tate

sah be HORNET FLEET NEWS As there was a Hornet on the front of Navigans the other month (and this - Ed$) I thought I had better write a few words and tell you that we will soon be out on that wet stuff again. The first races this year start with the Easter Handicap Series. Most of you know that Pete Clayton has stood down as Fleet Captain and delegated his responsibilities to yours truly. I would like to say on behalf of the whole fleet, thanks Pete for all the work you have done in the past for the fleet at Marconi's. After another successful meeting at the Horse and Groom, I would like to mention a few points again for our absent followers. As you know the Hornet on the front of the January Navigans was not from our club, or did you?? Well to help rectify this the Hornet Association nationally have suggested an "Open Day" to promote our class, not only within the club but also the surrounding area. This is to be held on the 14 June. It is to try and attract people to join our fleet and find out what sailing is all about. So all you cadets the Marconi Hornet Fleet invite you to a sail on that date, where you can sail a class boat. The intention is to let people have an hour or so trying out the boat, helming and crewing in order to get the feel of a Hornet, then later to have a short race in the afternoon. This invitation applies to everyone, so please don't hesitate to ask me for more details and I will help to convert you. At the meeting we talked about Fleet sweaters and we hope to have some in the near future. It's good to let people know where we are from when we go to open meetings. The last thing is the Dinghy Exhibition to be held at "Pickets Lock"on 22 and 23 Marche I can give you directions if you contact me in advance. We also have a stand at the show. Well, thats all for now, hope to see you soon, on the water early this year. oe, Se COMMODORE 'S COLUMN Sailing is under way again. The weather is fine, the Easter Eggs have been eaten and everything looks set fair for the season ahead. Unfortunately however, we have already had report of a trolley wheel being stolen from the dinghy park, and I hope it does not mean that we are in for a repeat of the petty thieving we had last year. Although Stansgate is such an exposed and isolated site there are precautions we can all take to minimise the risk of theft and increase the likelyhood of eventual recovery. Close gate behind you everytime. uWBHFY Lock Clubhouse on leaving. Mark and clearly identify all items of equipment and clothing. Take home with you all items of value which are not securely stowed away. Don't leave valuables in the changing rooms when sailing. I believe that most of the thefts are committed by outsiders, but not alle A Club can only thrive on mutual trust and support, anybody who cannot keep this trust is not welcome. THIS IS MARCONI RESCUE = ZZJW So by knowing what May Day call to send out if the Mariner founders on the rocks 10 miles SE of the Needles and the answers to 14 other equally relevant questions, I passed the competency exam for the use of a V H F radio link, and all members in the club are now assumed to use the Radio having had instruction from me. For Race Officers and other members using the base station the instructions posted near the handset should be followed. Rescue boat drivers who have access to the multichannel] set will be advised separately. Please remember that as more clubs get radio the channel is getting busier, so please keep it brief, follow the instructions and NO chatting or Christian names. Our new call sign ZZJW will only be used at the start of a session and for calling the Coastguard so only drivers need worry about it. Malcolm Gandy has joined the regular drivers Ken Hughes, David Ormerod and Albert Fuller and I'm sure his experience as a former sailer will prove invaluable. We are very fortunate to have so many in the club who don't sail regularly. My annual reminder to OOD's and others who may deposit petrol cans at or collect from the garage that the OIL IS ADDED FIRST to the empty can. Drivers will usually supervise this operation. Finally congratulations to Ken Hughes and his young assistant for a skilful rescue of the Stone Past-President following an accident in his motor cruiser. By all accounts it could well have been fatal had they not assisted so ably. -_ 2 = COMMODORE 'S COLUMN It hardly seems possible, but our Annual Regatta is only a few days away. Elsewhere in this issue are the necessary calls for assistance with the many activities which are essential to ensure the smooth running of this event. I should like, however, to make a personal appeal to new members, and to those established members who have not participated before, to come along this year - Enjoy the atmosphere of the big occasion and while you are there, spend a few minutes helping out with one of the many and varied tasks to be done. If you can, please give a firm commitment before the day. I must also remind all members and friends that it is imperative that we demonstrate to our neighbours and the Local Council Officers that we can control all aspects of this event in Camping, Trespassing and Nuisance, to their complete satisfaction. Please report any infringements of good behaviour immediately to me (Regatta OOD), or to any other Club Official, so that it may be dealt with promptly. Ron Greygoose Commodore STANSGATE SITE Over the years there has been some uncertainty in our Committees concerning the true situation regarding the authenticity of footpaths in the vicinity of our Club and its approaches. Recently in our endeavours to secure our boundaries against the trespass of animals from neighbouring properties we entered into discussions with the Essex County Council Planning Department to obtain permission to place a stile on the sea wall at the western boundary of our property. During the course of these discussions a considerable amount was discovered concerning the local footpaths and for the information of members who may be asked for guidance by the general public a summary is given here. In general there are footpaths round the whole of the Essex coast between Maylandsea and Burnham, with a notable exception in the Stansgate area between the top end of Steeple Creek, which is near the second bend after coming through the gates at the entrance to our approach road and the concrete wall seen to the west of our boundary along the sea wall. The footpath leading to the gap in the sea wall at the Club starts at the Sun and Anchor Public House in Steeple Village and crosses the fields to emerge and join our road at the second bend. It then proceeds along our private approach road and through our gate to the sea wall at the flood board gap, where it divides; the main path then running along the sea wall to the east towards Stone. The other spur goes along the wall to a dead end approximately where the sea wall, after crossing our neighbours property, is blocked by the concrete wall to the west. If one wishes to proceed further round the corner this may only be done along the foreshore below the highwater mark until one comes almost to the end of Steeple Creek where the official footpath can be rejoined. It is also interesting that there is no public right of way between the gates at the end of the public highway leading to our road and the second bend where the footpath from the village joins the road. Although it is shown on some maps there is now no other recoanised footpaths to the Steeple Creek sea wall across the fields from our approach road, We must emphasize that it is essential that members, their families and the general public keep to the footpaths when not on our property, especially when going west to watch activities in the Maldon direction as it is important that we maintain good relationships with our neighbours and that damage is not caused to their property.

a 2 w= CRUISER FLEET NEWS From time to time, many of us have the opportunity of helping another member in some small way, by tying down a loose cover, securing a loose rope or some such similar act. Sometimes the help is anonymous, sometimes otherwise, but always it is appreciated and is one of the things that makes a Club worth belonging to. Recently however I was privileged to turn up in time to see the later stages of a very heroic rescue by several of our members who spent over an hour in the water in very bad conditions, holding a cruiser from being damaged against the sea wall after it had broken its moorings. Very ably assisted by Pete Clayton in the work boat they eventually got the boat back to a secure mooring, with I understand, no damage to the cruiser. When I say that onlookers were driven away by the force of a hail storm during the time that the lads were in the water it will be appreciated just how great their efforts were. Well Done Everyone Concerned$! When overhauling moorings and rope strops in particular, it is essential that metal eyes are fitted and that tubing or some other form of chafe prevention is put over the rope wherever rubbing could occur. As some people may have heard there is a certain amount of feeling, particularly from the owners of certain Maldon based boats, that our outside moorings are ina vulnerable position. In view of this I must remind everyone of the need for A row boats and those at each end of B and C rows to show mooring lights — it may be a bore, but as someone has said before "You know it makes sense". Once again another Regatta is over and done with and I believe a good time was had by all. Unfortunately this year I was unable to attend any of the proceedings due to alternative arrangements (Cub Camp!) The next Social Function this year will be the Barbecue, on Saturday 19 July, Tickets will be available nearer the date from the usual ticket sellers. I have been asked to remind you that Osea Island is privately owned and that anyone landing on the island and crossing the High Water Mark is TRESPASSING. Another reminder, this time regarding Rubbish! We have a Waste Disposal problem at Stansgate, and would appreciate it if all members could take home their rubbish. Any rubbish left at Stansgate must be put in the new bins, which are located around the site. By the time you receive this months copy of Navigans, I shall be sunning myself on the sandy beaches of Ibizae See you in July3 Ann Allen Editor LAST DATE FOR JULY NAVIGANS Saturday 12 July 1980 FRONT COVER Chris Denny receiving the Garrett Memorial from our Presidents Lady.

a en COMMODORE 'S COLUMN My overall impression of the Regatta was of small, well organised groups each efficiently managing their own areas of responsibility. The members of each team were all very busy, but nobody appeared harassed or in bad humour. I am sure the fine weather helped but you, the members made the event one of the most successful and enjoyable for years. Many visitors complimented our Club on its facilities, organisation and friendly atmosphere. Once again we are indebted to our neighbouring clubs for their assistance with race facilities and for restricting their own sailing programmes. Finally I should like to offer my personal thanks to all who worked so hard before, during and after the event. It made my final Regatta OOD Duty so pleasant and memorable. Ron Greygoose Commodore REGATTA REPORT Let me start by thanking all those club members who supported this years Regatta, whether by sailing, or working or both. My own job was made easy by a fine team of people all knowing exactly what was needed and just getting on with the job. Thank you very much. We had a total of 210 dinghies entered this year, of which 38 were Marconi Sailing Club entries. Saturday morning started with fairly strong winds, but this reduced before the start of the Pennant races giving flat water conditions for the 78 starters. These lighter conditions were maintained for the Sunday and Monday, allowing all races to be sailed without mishap. = 5 = THIS IS MARCONI RESCUE = OVER I must use my space this month to put in a few words of thanks to certain people for their help when the throttle/gear control on the Mariner packed up during the week before the Regatta. John Chisnall braved a two foot swell on the Wednesday evening removing it, whilst I just stood and watched, feeling worse by the minutel. Then John Witter gave up his lunchtime on Thursday and his Friday night camping to deliver it to and collect it from Shoreline, who themselves did us a great service with a quick turnround. We had a quiet time over the Regatta, but nevertheless with boats on loan from Maylandsea Bay, Steeple Bay and Harlow SC's we gave an extensive coverage should we have been needed. The need for vigilance was demonstrated on a relatively calm day, during the National Canoe Championships held at our club recently. Called out in our lunch break to check on a safe but drifting Solo we found two Canoeists in Stansgate Bay clinging to their waterlogged craft, both of whom were very very pleased to see us. Pah ae BEWARE -— THIEVES ABOUT! We have all been warned recently about personal items disappearing from the changing rooms, but there now seems to be another hazard. On Sunday 13 July, the racing having been abandoned due to light (or lack of) winds, I washed my boat and took it to the Dinghy Park, as usual. On returning to my car I put a 40 foot coil of new anchor rope by the rear of my car whilst bones 2abakeyte several friends parked two cars away. Five minutes later, the Several cars had pulled away in the meantime so it could have been one of their occupants. Whilst showering, washing the boat etc, I think most people leave their sails, rudder and other equipment by their cars for short periods -— In future DON'T, I lost a relatively inexpensive item — yours may not be! a ae COMMODORES' COLUMN As I shall be on holiday when the last date for copy for this issue of Navigans is reached, I have to write these notes early this month. So early in fact that I shall not know of the discussions and the decisions of the September Committee Meeting. This is a very busy and important time of year in the life of the Club, particularly with the approach of the Laying Up Supper and the AGM. The Committee will be considering weighty problems such as rule changes, budgets, fees and next years officers and committee. There is always something in need of repair or replacement such as a road, outboard motors and clubhouse decoration, to mention just a few. If you would like to see any improvements in facilities or changes in policy, now is a good time to speak up so that an accurate budget forecast can be prepared and fees set at the appropriate level for the next couple of years. For those who did not attend the MASC AGM on 22 July you may read elsewhere in this issue the address given by Tony Mayhew the Vice Chairman, to the assembly, prior to voting in the increase in basic MASC subscription. On a lighter vein, the Jackpot race, for us over 40's, was made memorable by the dramatic rescue made by one of our members. Louise risked life and limb, on the seawall at Heybridge and by the "skin of her teeth" saved a set of chompers from a watery grave. A startled and anxious looking Solo helm assured me they were not escaping from one of Pat's sandwiches! Sorry Malcolm (and Pat!) There is a nice walk through the woods to Wolvestone Marina and it's 1 mile long. Pin Mill has got a pink pub and 2 little shops, that both sell sweets and postcards. Pin Mill isn't really a good place for shopping though. There's a postbox near the 2 shops so if you liked you could find a hard-back book, some money and a pen, then you could buy a postcard, put it against your book, write a letter and post it. Then if you liked the picture on the one you sent, you could buy another to keep. The pictures on them are mostly pictures of the pink pub but they look very nice. The walk to Wolvestone Marina is also quite pleasant when the sun is shining and it's a nice hot day. Pin Mill's on the River Orwell. Ae te CRUISER FLEET NEWS Laying up time is unfortunately approaching once again and there will be more boats than before in the boat park this year. A new plan is being drawn up and will be on display in the clubhouse. Please ensure that boats are laid up in the correct allocated position, which as far as possible correspond with previously used sites. However, most of the spare spaces will disappear. I must ask everyone to be prepared to park as economically as possible so as to conserve space. It is essential that no one parks other than as directed, otherwise there could be chaos. If anyone is rebuilding their trolley, I would advise use of the largest available wheels and the strongest possible metal work. For starting afresh it is not always realised that the converted lorry chassis such as mine is cheaper than road trailers which are flimsy. Always remove brake shoes and if possible brake drums. These make good mooring sinkers. I hear that several inflatable tenders have recently been stolen from Stansgate. The safest procedure here is obviously to take them home. They will travel safely on the roof of any saloon car, using a boat type roof rack - I carry mine on my Mini without trouble - also this shows how easy their theft is? - 6 = LOOKING TO THE FUTURE: AN ADDRESS TO THE CLUB IN GENERAL MEETING, 22 JULY 1980 The committee thought you would like some idea of our thinking for the future. As a general policy, like most of our predecessors, this committee believes that the Club needs to grow if it is to be healthy: that if it were to stop growing it would start to wither. The most important task for the Committee therefore is to husband that growth: to make sure that it is healthy and desirable and does not over-tax our resources. We feel that we have had your support for our policies during this past year and now we seek your support and encouragement for the future. It is a matter of fact, published in the Club accounts (the latest of which you have received tonight), that in the last three years the Club has made additions to fixed assets totalling over £230,000 Remember? The new bowls pavilion, the re-vitalisation of the lounges and games area, the air-conditioning there and in here, the extra office space and kitchen store, the new car park, the very chairs you are sitting on, and these are by no means all that has been achieve Everything continues to become more expensive, and we think it prudent to plan for perhaps three or even five years ahead. If we do, then the record I have just quoted shows that great things are possible They are possible, all right, but they will not happen unless we work for them. This includes planning them and paying for them. Grateful though we are for the tremendous vast and present support we have had from the Companies (despite our ups and downs, Gentlemen, be sure that we were, and are, very grateful) nevertheless we are very largely a Members' Club. We have consistently agreed here that we wish to remain so and indeed to become more so. Two tags came to mind: "The Lord helps those who help themselves", and "If it is worth doing, it's worth doing well". We would rather do it ourselves, and do it thoroughly. Clutching our binoculars, then,what do we see in this expensive future? (I meant to say expansive, but both words are appropriate). Many of you will be aware that since 1975 we have had planning permission for an extension of the clubhouse, on condition that we provide more car parking facilities. This we have done, so now we can consider expanding:twenty feet towards the playing field for our entire one hundred and ninety feet length. It would be appropriate, here, to pay tribute to our predecessors who obtained that planning permission. They also garnered considerable funds for the future, some of which were used in the programme of improvements that I referred to earlier. They rendered the Club a great service. We might tackle this expansion in stages and the most important one would be to build a full-size properly laid out kitchen, capable of meeting all our catering requirements. Others would provide extra rooms, usable separately or united with the existing hall and lounges a separate toilet suite and perhaps additional foyer for the hall and a lot of much-needed storage space. This is all very valuable in itself, but there is a large spin-off; Tne present kitchen premises would become available for conversion into toilets, adjacent to the bars: a very desirable improvement.

Another project that has been mooted is the building of a changing-room complex, probably incorporated with the squash courts. This would provide more accomodation, keep muddy boots out of the clubhouse and release the present rooms for other uses. We have planning permission for more squash courts. We are considering how we might increase the capacity of the ballroom, because very often our dances and other functions are sold out and many potential customers disappointed, Perhaps we could expand into some of the present changing-room space: we might build a gallery at the back and along the sides. There is a suggestion for expanding our foyer to include cloakrooms, shops etc. If we are to do all our own catering, a lot of equipment will be required. These are by no means all the possibilities and we shall be pleased to hear any suggestions that you may have. (That's not an idle, throw-away, remark. You would want us to be responsive to your Pos ae ging very difficult when we don't know what they are. Please tell us). We intend to provide more changing-room and bar storage space in the bowls pavilion. Apart from this, we have no major proposals from the sections, so we are concentrating at present on the Club head=-quarters. This is, after all, our engine room, our real money- spinner. We are not yet committed to any of these schemes, but will you appreciate that they all involve large sums of money. Those sums will not get any less if we delay. So, if we are to continue to grow in these challenging times, we must make the necessary provisions. The sections, as you have heard, continue to make increased contributions and our trading is buoyant. We have studied very carefully the options open to us and have concluded reluctantly, that we have to recommend yet another increase in subscriptions. Three years ago, subscriptions covered 99.6% of administration costs, the next year 85.7, the next 93.7 and, as you can see, last year 94.4%. It is inescapable that administration costs will be higher this year, although everything possible will be done to contain them. That is the specific reason for an increase. The general case for growth, and the investments which that requires, you have heard here tonight, I urge you all to support the resolution. A.J.Mayhew (Vice-chairman)

Hs: en 'S COLUMN COMMODORE Two very important occasions are approaching fast. These are of course the Laying up Supper and the AGM. a DRAMA ON THE RUM TUB For most of you the annual Rub Tub and Bung jaunt to the Benchhead probably gave some of the best sailing of the year, but I thought you would like to hear the background story of the day. I've never been very happy about the Rescue facilities of this event - organised by Maldon YC = but maybe it's just my fear of sailing! They provide 1 cruiser to go to the Benchhead and their own reccue boat to cover to Bradwell, which we back up with ours. At 1100 there was no wind and no rescue assistant so Rosemary came with me to assist with the expected towing. We. gave Bantam Radios to the two Maldon boats and I arranged for Stone and Dabchicks to relay messages with their Seavoices. As the wind increased to force 1 and then 2 the rain came and despite supplementing waterproofs with double layers by the time we got to Bradwell we were soaked to the skin and starting to get cold. We then picked up a radio message advising that the "becoming force 6 later" which we had been promised five minutes earlier had become "Gale Force 8 imminent" for the Thames area. Ten minutes later another measage "Gale Force 8 approaching rapidly”. I radioed the Club but as half the boats had rounded the Nass they felt cancellation was out of the question. By this time we were both very cold and the engine failed ' but fortunately it was only a fuel line fault soon put right. The Maldon crew agreed to proceed to the Benchhead and I returned to the club at high speed for qualified assistants and a change of clothing. Once there, Murray Bates and John Chisnall downed their pints in a speed which would have been admired by Rick Anstey. Eleanor Witter lent me her wetsuit and in five minutes we were back on the water ready for the affray. You will know what happened then, the sun came out, the wind stayed at a steady force 3-4 and there wasn't even a single capsize! Norman Kerridge Coxswain eoeesrstr#eteeeetee#* # # # ¢« ¢ ¢ * #® # #@ CHOOSING YOUR AUXILLIARY ENGINE I am prompted to write these notes by several comments that I heard recently; "My motor isn't powerful enough, it won't drive the boat against the tide". "I had to sail as the wind was right on the nose and the motor couldn't manage" "We were short of power as a plug kept whiskering up". I know exaggeration can easily occur, expecially over a pint, but obviously we have room for improvement. All things in sailing are a compromise but I believe that most people in our fleet regard comfort and safety as more important than absolute maximum sailing speed. From this point of view there is nothing to beat the inboard diesel with a reduction gear driving a very large propellor. This was my cho ce for Kalinka and I have never regretted it. Consider first the propellor. Large props turning slowly can get a real grip on the water, whereas smaller propellors would "slip" more. However they require a lot of torque at low revs and hence the reduction gear. Kalinka can motor out of the River Ore at half flood spring tide if I really open up the motor, which must mean about 7 knots through the water. The motor is only 10HP however, which the manufacturers say is right for a 26ft boat. A high revving small prop would probably need 20 or more HP due to the inefficiency.

Why do I recommend diesel? Weel the above arrangement with petrol would also make the boat go, and possibly more quietly too, but I feel that the reliability, safety and economy, which means greater range are valuable qualities. I understand that a Stuart 10 uses approximately a gallon an hour of petrol, my Sabb 10 gives me 54 hours from every gallon - yes, I do have an hours meter fitted. Disadvantages? - of course the noise level is a little higher though not objectionable, but it is nice to switch it off and sail in quietness, and of course the diesel costs more to buy when new. Electric starting is normal but I can and regularly do start mine by hand, though if it were much bigger this would become difficult. I once met a fisherman on Walton Backwaters whose engine was identical with mine. He reckoned he'd used it 6-7 hours a day for 7 years and never touched it. It might be a slight case of 'the one that got away", but it must prove a point. I know you wont all go rushing out to buy new engines but the points are worth bearing in mind when looking at different boats. But don't came trying to buy Kalinka — she's not for sale. Apparently he was on passage from Woodbridge to Holland with five crew members in his 40ft Dutch Barge "Vabel" when she was struck by a huge wave which swept him overboard and broke his (13) steel rudder, causing them to be driven ashore on the Dutch coast. Flares and a helicopter came to their rescue but his body was not recovered until a week later. Christopher was a founder member of our Club when he owned a Jewel dinghy "ATA" built at Walton on Naze which he moored near Tollesbury pier, which in those days projected into the Blackwater just down-river from Thirslet beacon, where a concrete pillbox can still be seen on the shore amongst the trees. On one occasion when we held an open day at Heybridge, before the days of Mamgu, Christopher agreed to join us, but when he came to board his dinghy at Tollesbury, it was already afloat. undaunted, he stripped off and swam out to bring the dinghy ashore and then sailed single-handed in time to join us at Heybridge for the party at highwater; after refreshment, he then sailed back to Tollesbury. Christopher was an eminent scientist and those of us who make long distance calls overseas should bear in mind the pioneer work he did in telephone terminal equipment is in no small measure responsible for the high quality of the speech obtained in these calls today. Christopher will be greatly missed by all who knew him; he was much too modest and retiring to have taken office in the Club, but nevertheless, he did a lot to help to get the Club started, and continued sailing to the last. I am sure that we would all wish to extend our deepest sympathy to his wife Stella, his son Andrew who is now in Marconi Radar, his sisters Deborah and Alison and to his elder brother Henry, who is in the Merchant Navy doing Navigational research in the far east. Eric Payne

i CATAMARAN CRUISING Last year you may-recall, I took a: Flotilla Sailing Holiday in Greece, and in company with other friends and other boats, I spent two week's hopping from island to island. ‘ This year I returned again to Greece for a sailing holiday, but this time it was not flotilla sailing. It all started when we learned that some friends whom we had met in Greece last year decided to buy a big catamaran in Poole and sail it out to Corfu. The boat in question is a Wharran Catamaran of the Narai class named "Tinorua". She is 41£ft long and 18ft 6in beam, and for. those who are not familiar with the design it has twin hulls that are not connected by the acccmodation. One hull consists of galley, dinette, and berths, and the other hull is wheelhouse, navigation cabin and more sleeping berths. Having completed their fitting out and provisioning, our friends Peter and Ann set forth from Dartmouth where the voyage began and made their way via Lisbon, Gibralter, Tangiers, Malta and so across to Corfu. They had a difficult wet journey to begin with, but gradually the weather improved as they proceeded eastwards. But to get back to my holiday venture I should explain that three of us were invited to join Tinorua in Corfu fer two weeks sailing as paying guests, this is actually a fine point of law because the Greeks have rules about "chartering" that can be difZicult. The ships company consisted of Peter and Ann (Skiprer end Mate), John, who sailed with me last year on the Flotilla, and Linda, a young woman who is studying to obtain her RYA Certificate, and myself. ~Peter and Ann are magnificent people to sail with, they have utmost confidence in their poat, which is entirely justified, and they are absolutely unflappable. Every action is carried out calmly and steadily and is an object lesson in seamanship. John is big end strong, keen to learn and useful when you need to raise a Kedge anchor weighing 351lbs frem a rocky weedy bottom on a windy night! Linda is a charmer, she could charm the warts off a hegs back, and any cifficultics encountered with Cfficials, eitner at Airports, Seaports or Hotels could be confidently left to Linda to deal with. We never asked how she obtained such results, but whatever she did, it worked!! . We flew cut to Corfu from Gatwick on sunday 6 July on a Dan Air Comet, and I think its true to say that we arrived on a "Gin and 4 Prayer". I thought that Comets had long ‘ gone out of service, but apparently Dan Air still use them. From Corfu Aizpert we took a taxi to Gouvia Marina to find the boat, but unfortunately no one knew of her whereabouts, so we had to return to Corfu Town to find a room fer the night. This was no easy matter, as the season was in full swing, and all the Hotels were full. Eventually we found a rather grotty place that had one room with three single beds in it. We had a cenference with Linda, and tuo her eternel credit she said "Well if I've got to share a boat with you two for the next two weeks, theres no point in arguing about sharing a room", so we 2.1 piled in and sorted ourselves out. Next morning we managed to locate the Skipper and Mate, andwe went aboard Tinorua, and stowed all our gear. After one or two routine jobs we sailed from Gouvia right down the coast of Corfu, to a little place called Petreti, where we stayed the night. Every- one seemed to know Peter and Ann and the Taverna owmer, a man named Stamatis is also a great dancer in the Greek Style, and he soon had the music going and we had to learn a few steps. ‘“e dumped our ice packs in his ice cream refrigerator overnight and collected them next morning when we watered ship. At 1030 we set sail for Paxos. Monday 7 July. We had absolutely no wind at all and eventually we were obliged to start the engine. We motored for about two hours before the wind rose and we managed to set sail. The engine on Tinorua is a 1500cc BMC Diese! and is housed in a pod under the deck. The drive is a "Sonic" 90° retractable leg and we motored easily with this arrangement, albeit a trifle noisily. We had an excelient lunch on board, and with the vast deck space available, we were able to set out a large table and chairs, with food and booze and a sun canopy over tie top just as though we were eating in the lounge! With 16'6" beam it was worth a guinea a box to see the looks on the faces of people on boats as we passed, with all our goodies around us we looked like an advert for Martini: After lunch things got a bit serious, the wind arrived quite suddenly and about force 3 and we had a glorious sail into harbour at Gaios which is the seaport of the islarid of Paxose From Corfu to Paxos is about 30 miles which means you just lose sight of Corfu about half an hour before you sight Paxoss Tinorua is ketch rigged and her normal sailing suit is Main, Mizzen and Staysail with a flying Jib set high above the staysail. ;

On one occasion we had six sails set, main, mizzen, mizzen staysail, fore staysail, flying jib and a large genoa (Ghoster). You really have to experience it, to do it justice. She just picks up her skirt's and runs!. We found Gaios harbour full of flotilla boats and busy, bearing in mind that we needed lots of room to get twin hulls nose on to the quay, we eventually found a spot in an odd corner which other people had considered too shallow, but as we only drew 2'9" we just made it. Lots of people in the harbour were people we had met last year and there were many reunions including the chap who was our flotilla leader last year, he now had a senior position, and his company had given him the use of a Moody 40 to live on. I don't think he really appreceiated it, "She doesn't sail all that well" he said! Once again we were aware that Peter and Ann knew everyone and after a Taverna supper and lots of drinking we eventually retired to our bunks. Tuesday 8 July. Today I arose early despite the previous late night, and had a good wash down with a bucket on deck. Sailing a Wharran cat robs you of all sense of modesty you have to wash and dress on deck and no one seems to take much notice of your hygiene or your private ablutions! It was my job, as first man up, to brew the morning coffee, and I quickly learned the routines Skipper =< Coffee black no sugar Mate - coffee white no sugar John - coffee black 1 sugar Me - coffee black 1 sugar and Linda - NOT BEFORE 9 O/CLOCK Coffee white, not too much milk, not too hot, and 2 digestive biscuits! We made sail and blew down to anti Paxos where we had a grand swim in a little bay with lunch on board and lots of swimming etc. After lunch we were hailed by a local fisherman who knew Peter and Ann, and he tied up astern and came on board. He had Mmever seen a Polynesian cat before and he was duly impressed with the boat. We noticed that both he and his companion were well gone in their cups, and they brought us a gift of some white wine, whicn we of course shared, then we contributed a little more from our stock, and the party got quite merry. I never knew his real name but he was known as "Fingers Spiro", and we soon learned how he earned the nick=-namei He sat on deck next to Linda and started to make overtures to her. Fortunately Linda is well able to take care of these situations, and after two or three unsuccessful ferays, he decided to return to his own boat. At first we thought he might fall overboard, then we suspected he would get his warp around his prop shaft, but eventually he started his engine and roared awaye Most of the Greek Fisherman seem to think that a <C' caique should have a minimum engine of 100 hp and Spiro was no exception. However, at this precise moment, a flotilla of Sadler 32's were sailing into the bay, and Spiro decided to enjoy himself. He roared around the first one in a big circle, singing at the top of his voice and making rude gestures. Then he aimed his bow direct at number two, lunged towards it and when only a short distance away, the threw the engine into reverse and came to a stop about 10yds from the Sadler. Meanwhile the Skipper of the Sadler was having kittens and before he could do anything about it Spiro was off again like the wind. I don't know if Greek fisherman can be arrested for being drunk in charge of a boat, but Spiro should have been. Linda was also very worried, she said "By God, I hope we don't meet him tonight in the Taverna", and truth to tell, so did I. That evening we sailed back to Paxos to a harbour at Mongonissi. It is a very small place, but we were surprised to find a large modern Taverna with tables set out on terraces, and a separate disco to provide the wiggles afterwards. During dinner a woman sitting several tables away started shouting in a very pronounced cockney accent about the lack of service. John, a scotsman who prides himself on his imitation of a cockney stood up and said in the best Lorraine Chase style "Cor blimey gal, where ycu from?", and the whole restaurant collapsed in a roar. The disco was very good and by about midnight the owmer and all the waiters were together on the dance floor demonstrating some really first class Syrtaki Greek Dancing. Later their wives joined in. It was the first time I have ever seen the greek wonem performing the folk dance and it is taken very seriously. As you may have guessed it turned out to be another very late night.

=| Wednesday 9 July. Today we have to make an early start as we have to sail from Paxos to Levkase It is 38 miles to the port of Nidri and it took 84+ hours total passage time, tacking most of the way against head winds. The weather is getting hotter and we have to be careful to avoid burning. Peter gave us our first lesson in the use of the sextant and we all took midday sun sights. We averaged our errors and we were within 0.8 mile of our true position so I think we made a good start! Peter has two sextants on board, an expensive one whose make I do not know, and an EBBCO plastic one. The latter was very good and I preferred it to the posh one, it was easier to handle. Between North Levkas and the Inner sea, there is a canal which was cut through the marshes back in the days of the Corinthians, and as you may know the area is still subject to very active earthquakese Both Levkas and Zante were badly hit in 1953, so the canal probably suggests that Levkas was once part of mainland Greece. By the time we had reached the northern end of the canal we were sailing really well, with lots of canvas aloft, including the ghoster. It is expressly forbidden to Sail through the canal, but we were going so well and the wind was in our favour, that we could not resist the temptation to press on. Unfortunately after about one mile, the wind died and we had to turn.on the engine, but it was fun whilst it lastede As soon as we were clear of the southern entrance, we again raised sail and made for Nidri. We sailed “ast lots of small islands, quite beautiful, Sparti, Moudra and of course Scorpio, were Onassis used to live. Peter and Ann's parents live on a boat at Nidri,so they were waiting for us anchored in Tranquil Bay, and we had a pleasant chat. Later we all went ashore for our evening meal, with Peter's dad towing us in our dinghy behind his inflatable with his seagull outboard. It must have been difficult for him because we yawed all over the place, and when we came alongside the quay I stood up a moment tco soon, in order to grab the jetty. The dinghy lurched, I made a second grab at a small caique that was also alongside and suddenly I felt the dinghy moving away from me. I had thet terrible thought that at any moment I would be sopping wet, including my nice clean shirt and trousers!! But once again I was saved by the strong right arm of Linda She confessed to me later that she was so tempted to let me fall in, that its a miracle I survived. Anyway, I was iucky she relented and I only had a wet bum. Linda is a very strong girl. After a good Taverna supper we all went back on board chatting and drinking local brandy at 70p a litre! In case you think it was fire water, let me assure you it was note. It was so smooth it just knew where to go! Unfortunately brandy Stimutates=me and gives me a lift, so I still didn't get my early night. Thursday 10 July. Up early again, with bucket bath and shave, and a visit to, ell the local boat owners we met last night. I did a grari tour of the bay, and met people “tho were living on a Colvic Watson, and so.ie on a Macwester Wight. Peter also showed we a 26" converted ships lifeboat which he had sailed out from England some years previously. An interesting boat, he had fitted it with Lee boards and rigged it in the style of a Dutch Botter. After breakfast we all went ashore to shop in Nidri for Stores, water and Diesel oil. We bought some ice for the cool box, and by lunch time we sailed for Port Vathy on Ithaca. About an hour later we were just sailing past the island of Sparti, when John lost his hat overboard. We were sailing fast on a broad reach on the port tack, and to my amazement, John jumped overbcard to retrieve his hat. On a monohull we would probably have gybed, but I was not too sure of the cat under these conditions so we luffed her into the wind, and slowly bore away towards him. By now he was 250 yds away swimming strongly, and I was getting worried. Finally we threw hima line and got him back on board. The hat sank, it seems it had a gold pin on it, that had been given to him by a young lady who had given him her all, and ho was very upset at losing the pin. I gave him the biggest rocket he has ever had, and told him NEVER AGAIN to jump over-— board for a THING, you can jump overboard for a person but NOT a thing. Things, we can buy, poeple we can't. I think he got the message.

: Cc Meanwhile the wind had freshened and we were skating along at a steady 8kmts. We arrived at Port Vathy at 7.00pm and moored alongside the town quay. I visited this place last year, its nice to be back, I like this place. It has the minimum number of people, and the maximum number of facilities. It has shops and a Bank, and a good big harbour. Unfortunately it is subject to fierce winds and down draughts, which can be unpredictable so you have to watch your moorings. We re-visited the restaurant where we ate last year, and the owner produced fillet steak and lots of salad etc. Afterwards we retired to a Kafenian for ice cream and coffee and brandy. Another late night. Friday 11th July. Spent the morning ashore in Port Vathy, went to the Bank and changed travellers cheques, bought some nice fresh bread. Back on board the wind had suddenly started to roar, the two large ferry boats ahead of us have both swung, fouled each others anchors and are dragging, they are very large passenger carrying ships and are not suited to charging around in a harbour. This is no place for us, we slipped our lines and got clear before we became involved with them. We set sail for Kioni which is only a few miles up the coast, but the sailing was so good, that we reached back and forth most of the afternoon just enjoying the sail, by now, the wind was about 6 gusting to 7 and Tinorua was flying along on reduced canvas, we were passing several mono hulls making for the safety of Kioni at about twice their speed. The hulls appeared not to ride over the waves in the usual motion, but to slice through them like a motor boat. I laid flat on the deck and took photosraphs of the bow waves. We entered the comparative shelter of Kioni and snugged ourselves down for the night. Went ashore and had spit toasted Eid for supper, it tasted like lamb, it was expensive, well anyway you have to try all these things don't you? Saturday 12th July. 0400 I awoke to the noise of the wind and a loud banging, the dinghy is bumping us. I went on deck and snortened-the painter which seemed to clear the problem, but I noticed that our kedge was not holding:and we were swinging~very close on to some fishing boats. Called the skipper, and he rowed out and laid a 351b Danforth across the harbour into the wind. It didn't hold, we laid it again, this time it held well, back to bed for some beauty sleep. Up again at 0700 hours for T & P. The wind is now force 8 and the local fisherman won't go out at all, big seas outside the harbour all breaking with big white horses and spume being carried off on the wind. We spent the day walking around the area, its a very beautiful island. Linda has found a windmill for sale, she thinks it would make an ideal holiday home and before you can say "knife" she has been to see the local mayor and dignitary and arranged to make a formal offer if the family are agreeable. Actually its not easy to buy land in Greece if you are a foreigner but there ARE ways and means. Late in the evening a flotilla arrived with about eight boats, Sadler 32's and the chap in charge was an old friend from last years trip, so we went aboard and enjoyed his hospitality. Another late night, but before we turned in, we had a council of war about where we were heading now that we had lost a day and a half due tu the weather. Originally we wanted t sail down to Zante (or Zakinthos) its well off the beaten track and its an island that not many cruisers visit, but with the wind in its present direction flowing from the N.lW. we decided it might take another week to get back again so we chose instead to go across to the islands of Kastos, and Kalamos, which gave us a broed reach all the way. Sunday 13th July. Up anchor and eway from Kioni at 0730 am. Had a most difficult job raising the Kedge we had laid the night before. No wonder it held fast, we had tucked it under a fishermans mooring chain. Peter went over the side with his snorkel, and directed operations, eventually are raised both our own Kedge and the fishermans anchor, so we had to re-lay it for hin. Nice steady sailing breeze, breakfast on deck oven freshened bread, egg, fruit etc. This is the life. The theory of broad reaching across the wind has worked out well, we have made one long continuous broad reach almost all the way steering a compass course until we reache. Kastos. We were quite hungry by this time, and the mate had nipped below and put a chicken in the oven whilst we were sailing, so we anchored in a little bay, and ate our late meal chicken, salad, cheese and fruit with nice little drinkies in between. By this time I am really enjoying every minute of this holiday. John is engrossed in a book, the music is playing on the tape-deck, Linda is learning to wind surf (we carry a wine surfer on board) and I am swimming. The skipper is re-varnishing the bow-sprit hope nobody touches it: We went ashore and walled up through a little village. The people seemed very pleased to see us. Not many people call in at this island. We were given almonds from a tree by an old woman who stood bare foot on the wooden ladder to reach them, and she cracked them for us with a rock. We sat around outside the village shop and drank beer and lemonade. The little children spoke excellent english, it was very surprisin,;, but Peter explained

\\ their parents emigrate and return to their island when they have made enough money to .buy land. The children are sometimes born in Australia or United States, and they pick up the language quickly but their parents revert entirely back to their native greek, About seven pm we up anchored and motored around.to Kalomos (the next island). for supper, as there is no Taverna on Kastos. Kalomos has a small harbour, reasonably well protected, but we anchored orf, and rowed ashore. The Taverna was a bit crude but we ate a fish that was probably sea mackeral, the flesh was a very dark colour brown, but it tasted very good, all the dishes we ordered came twice. We ordered five salads and got ten; Also we ordered five plates of chips, and got ten. The proprieter obviously has an eye to business: Its amazing how small the world is, we ran slap into Mona and Bruce from the castaways club in Dartmouth they are on along mediterranean cruise we all sat drinking Retsina and talking till 1.30am and just as we were about to row back on board, Mona fell in the water, she fell between the quay and .their boat and fortunately two lusty lads reached down in a flash, and grabbed her as she bobbed up, rather a sobering thing to heppen!! Monday 14th July. Nice morning, we are riding calmly at anchor, but there has been a very heavy dew. It seems always to be the same, everything sopping wet on deck and slippery, but within an hour its all dry again. The skipper frequently takes his sleeping bag into the forward trampoline, and when I make the coffee he is covered in dew but he seems to survive. : We are taking the boat alongside the quay to get water and bread. We have met up with some friends of Peter and Ann, and we are going to sail off together today to the island of Meganissi, a place call Vathi (last year you may recall my wrist watch finished up at t bottom of Vathi harbour). Our friends are sailing a Claymore and they have challenged us to a race (foolish virgins) but first we have agreed to sail to Port Lioni at the other end of the island for lunch and swim. As we sailed down the coast we noticed someone had bought two windmills and joined them together with a low building designed for luxury living! Linda's eyes popped "Thats what I want she said and we had to sail in close and take photographs so that she could keep a record of the details. The race started quite seriously about tea time, our friends in the Claymore went north about (the shortest route round the island) whilst we went sovth about, and once again had a broad reach all the way, we arrived in Vathi about 19CO hours and iearmed over the radio that our friends had been becalmed in a 2knt southernly so we won easily. We were met on the quay by a customs man who asked for the ships papers, and we paid a small harbour dues. I think my sandals were out looking for my watch, as I saw them drop over the quay into the harbour. There is about 15ft of water there and not too clean either, but Peter fished them out for me next morning. ' The local Taverna owner has been to the United States, and he is mown as "Americnn George", and he maintains that he knows all about food etc, "a la Americaine”". Linda accepted the challenge, he should never have véasted, she wiped the floor with hin, she ordered four different starters, and ther changed her mind, then she ordered three d ferent meat dishes, and each time he asked her what she wanted she quoted different one. By this time George was aghast, he looked across at Linda and myself and said "You want three kinds of NEAT!2" Yes we said, and you can serve them all on one plate. This last riposte was the final touch. We never saw George again till the meal was over, he lurked in the kitchen muttering about good American fsod and the crazy english, but I suspect he had the last laugh, because the bill seemed quite high to me, even for a greek taverna: I hope I never have to face another meal quite like it, but we finally sat down to plates of Sirtiki (yoghurt - Garlic - and cucumber) Taranasalate (cods roe etc.) these are known as dips, because you dip your bread in then, (butter is OX if you have a fridge). Aubergines sliced thinly and fried in batter (delicious) and a plate each bearing one pork chop, one beef burger, one stick of kebabs, and chips, incidentally it took about five bottles of local white wine to quench that lot down. JI think it must be something to do wit: the fresh air and exercise. Linda was triumphant, she is a good looking girl, but after this she glowed: Tuesday 15th July. I walked up to the village at the top of the hill, called Kanto Marin, we are running short of Gin on board and thats very serious, I tried every little place I came to, and each in turn offered Whisky, Rum, Brandy, and 0UZO0 but no GIN! Finally I went back to Vathi and made my peace with American George, and soft soaped him into parting with two bottles that he normally keeps for his bar stock. I suspect he makes it with Kerosine, but it tasted quite good. ; ; Ann and Peter's parents have sailed across from Nidri and we are-all together here planning a really good barbecue with our friends, we are about twelve in all, and every one is busy getting food and drinks and the fire implements ready. We sailed around from Vathi

V2 to Port Atheni which we oped would be a nice quiet bay, and we anchored in a well chosen spots. Linda went of windsurfing, I swam to a nearby wreck of a caique and dived arcund it, , It is laying about 12ft of water and most of it is awash but it is gradually disintegrating. Lots of fish swim around it. John has gone ashore with the lads to start the barbecue fire so that it will be nice and glowing when the evening time comes. Meanwhile our secluded bay has started to fill up, we have some Italians, French and some English Flotilla boats, and we now have the feeling of being watched!, as we are putting on the show. We have two large lanterns for light, a tape recorder to play the music, the food is cooking on the fire, and some variety of punch thet our friends have concocted. We started off with a good sing-song round the fire, and we all took turns to sing, when my turn came I found it hard to remember a clean one, but eventually we ate our food and cleared @ Patch of ground for dancing. After a vigorous country and western with Ann's mun, I began to realise-how important it is to keep fit in order to enjoy ones holiday, perhaps I was just feeling my age. — Wednesday 16th July. Up again early next morning, several people went ashore to make certain thet the fire was out and that we had not left a load of litter around. My recollections of getting back on board last night are very vague. I can remember hearing our friends rowing back to the Claymore, and I heard a most awful crashing noise on board, next moment a youthful voice called out "Dad, the search-light doesn't work anymore." I didn't catch the reply but I can imagine it was quite nautical: We set sail at 10.30am but had no wind and we were obliged to motor. We are still coasting around the Island of Meganissi, and we anchored off the beach in Vahthi Vali. This time we really had it all to ourselves, a long curving golden strand with a few goats grazing in th scrub, with their bells around their necks tinkling as they moved, we had a good swim and lunch, the light breeze had swept Linda and her wind surfer, around into the next bey and she had’ to be rescued by Peter in the dinghy. We are painfully aware now, that every place we stop for the night, is getting further north and we are on the second lap of our trip. We try not to think too much about it, we are such a happy ship, we try to put realities out of our mind. The wind has died again and its mid afternoon and we have set off to motor through the Leyka:=: Canal, and John is at the helm. I think he must be a lorry driver at heart, with the diese] engine going, he steers the boat well, personally:I hate having to motor. By the time we reach the yacht basin in Levkas harbour, the wind has freshened to a strong easterly straight on to our beam as we are trying to yet nose on to the quay. It was quite tricky, with the wind blowing us sideways. Whenever we enter port, we always attract loads of attention. All the sailing types come to look at us, most of them have never seen a large Polynesian cat close up before, and they take it all in. We are all getting washed and changed to go ashore in Levkas town. Its the capital of Levxas istand, but its not very big. The evening is warm and the streets are getting busy and the local people are commencing their evening stroll, (its called a Volta). Perhaps I should explain here that Linda is a very provocative girl, also she dresses very provocatively, her going ashore dress on this sccasion, would have done credit to a west @. cocktail party, it started late and ended early, (the dress I mean). It was to say the least revealing, and it kept reminding me of the old saying about ninon-none on: The effect on the local males can only be described as electrifying. I don't think that they had experience anything like it sinde they grabbed a copy of "play-boys" We sat at a cafe and had cakes and ice cream and Linda enjoyed being the centre of attraction which she always is anyway, she really didn't have to try that hard.. We all went our separate ways, and did our shopping, and met at a Taverna for supper. The people who own the place know Peter and Ann well, and we had a good meal. We were waited on by a cheeky little nine year old boy who spoke good english and took liberties with everyone he served, you couldn't really complain as he was the owners son. I think Linda wanted to mother hin. When we arrived back on board, we were greeted at the quayside by a Frenchman with a Greek wife, who managers a large Hotel overlooking the harbour. He has always wanted to see a Polynesian cat and asked lots of questions, we had a drink, and Linda made future contacts for "business" reasons. Thursday 17th July. We cleared our lines and got under way at 06.30 hours this morning. We have a long way to go today, and we are making up the mainland coast to a place called Parza. The wind was light and a bit fluky, we hoisted every concevable combination of sail to coax her along, with Genoa sheeted out and a big ghoster that Peter had made himself from a parachute, it was enormous, if the wind had really blown, I would have been frightened to death. Eventually the wind died and we hed to motor. By this time we are about half way there and adout ten miles off the mainland coast when we spotted a beach ball floating in the ocean. We altered course and recovered it. It must hav

Y- .- before we turned in for the night, going round in circles trying to anchor near us. r Saturday 19th July. Would you believe it: I've overslept, we've messed it up; We are late getting away, the wind is dying on us, and the Austrian is about half a mile ahead of us going nicely on his main and spinnaker. We will never live this down. ’ Well we've been trying all day to coax the boat along but finally both the Austrian and ourselves have had to motor, he made off to Kaloura and we made for St Stephanos. Tonight will be our last real night ashore together, so we are planning some speectes ete. First of all after we had anchored°and secured the boat, everyone went over the side for a swim, and we played with our beach ball in the water, then we washed and changed and went ashore for our evening meal. ‘Je managed to find a Taverna with room to spare and we had the usual drinking prelimanary. Then came the main speech of the evening from our skipper Peter. Starting with me he awarded me a certificate of merit for eariy rising and making the tea and coffee. I still have-it mounted on the wall in my back bedroom at home, it contains some marvellous inuendos concerning the likes and dislikes of the crew. Then he refered to John who drank the ship dry of beer before you could blink:. And finally to Linda and thanked her for her pornagrayhic place mats, but didn't think he would be able to use them on the next trip, as he was due to take aboard a South African couple with two children! I presented John and Linda with a set of worry beads. All the Greeks use worry beads, they look like very small rosaries, these ones had an "evil eye" medallion and a small metal fish dangling from them. I explained the need for patience in life, and the worry beads to clear the mind, the need for protection against th evil eye, and to keep always "as cool as a fish". We had a great meal, squid, fried liver, Red Mullet - fried chicken, salad etc. m in serious trouble with Linda, in my alecholic haze I told her I thought she weighed 11 stone. I must have been mad: She will never forgive me, especially as I found out afterwards that she only weighs about 95 stone. They say that ladies are like cigars, once they have been put out, they are never quite as nice egain: You great big twit Les, You've done it this time! We were all late turning in tonight dancing on deck with music and brandy, and I gave up at 2.00am the rest were still at it. Sunday 20th July. I gave everyone an early call this morning, with tea and coffee at 07.30 we have to be under way to be sure we are back at Gouvia before midday so that Peter and Ann can clear the boat ready for the next craw. This was our last night on board and we are packing our bits together its a very sad day, I've got a lump in my throzi ‘as big as a pineapple, and I feel all watery eyed. We have to say our goodbyes to Petes: and Ann and thank them for co great trip they are stalwort types. Linda and John and myelf stumble into a taxi — we head for Corfu, we have to fly home - its all over - we talk vaguely about next year, I feel terrible.
