It rapidly increased to about force 4 and we began to sail beautifully, like a great bird. We could trim our sails using the ships speedometer and we were clocking 6kmts. As the wind continued to freshen to abcut force 5 we coaxed the speed up to Stimts and by the time we reached Parga we had really got her tail up and going strong. I was really enjoying this sail, but I asked John to get some canvas off her as we were beginning to head for the beach at an alarming rate: John took down the mizzen sail and by this time I had decided we would have to "go about" and make a fresh approach. I think the skipper was enjoying himself watching my antics: Unfortunatel I discovered that with the mizzen down she wouldn't tack. I had two atterpts and the skipper had a go too but she wouldn't have it. You need the mizzen to swing her stern xound. So we gibed her round much to the skippers’ amusement. Anyway we downed sail, and motored up to the anchorage, which was a wise thing to do as there were so many swimmers and wind surfers in the water, with (would you believe) people water skiing among then: As we motored up to anchor a young lady came alongside on a wind surfer. Like most of them she was topless. (Actually a very poor description). I lost all concentration and the boat went all over the place. She waived and I waived, and the skipper had to grab the helm, oh! if only I were young again: Actually I think that this place has the makings of a future holiday resort on quite a large scale, it may unfortunately become the Costa Parga, it is certainly the most "tourist" place we have visited, but it was quite nice. It has an »ld village with winding streets all up and down steps very picturesque. Having recovered from our sail.i had a swim. We went ashore for supper. Peter and Ann knew the people everywhere we went, and we had a good meal in a Taverna. I tried a very Greek dish, stewed veal with lemon sauce. It was quite nice our host kept up his menu by followaus with various vegetable dishes, we had spinach, and stuffed tomatoes, and an aubergine cooked whole with mince meat and cheese stuffing, the Greek call it a "slipper" it looks like one when its on the plate} But it tastes good. We were quite good tonight we were back cn board by midnight, this must be the early night we've all been talking about. Friday 18th July. This morning we left the anchorage in the bay and motored around to the town quay where we watered the ship, and bought provisions. We have been running a "kitty" for our food on board, and Ann has been shopping for us. We each put £10 in for starters and then topped it up as necessary. It workdd quite Well. I bought the local Brandy, a litre of lemonade bottle full to take home and Linda bought 3 litres (at 7Op a litre). We met a chap who owned a general grocery shop in the village, he was a Greek bouzouki plays: ard he told us that he tours England and Germany with a band. He said that they may be in England in November. His shop wes a good one, bright and clean and busy. I bought some Halva and gave everyone a taste, they had never tried it before, its the food of the God's. Its made from ground almonds, sesame, honey and who knows what, but its delicious. You can find it in Ingland but its expensive, in Parga I paid 17p for about 4ozs. I also bought tins of olives and olive oil to take home, as I am afraid the end is in sight. By about midday we set off for Mourtos, the wind was very light, and we had to motor. We visited an enormous cave on the coast, it was so big, a’jaguar 27 could easily have saile@ in, on one flotillia, one actually did! We were more cautious we motored in slowly in revers its a most eerie sensation, the water is deep and clear, and cold, and the voice echoes around you as you talk. By late evening we were anchored off the village for the night. Its a very small place but the tourists get here so there are one or two shops full of trinkets. Linda bought some modern reproductions of old Greek plates with very sexy scenes on them, I told you she is provocative, I think she enjoyed discussing them with the man in the shop, eventually ehe went back and bought a set of drink mats for the boat as a present for Peter and Ann, these mats were really quite pornograpnic, there was one that I just couldn't understand at all: Once again the Taverna owner was a friend of Peter and Ann and spent quite a long time trying to sell some land to Linda, but sne knows how many beans make five, and I think négotiations cessed when the price rose to about £20,000. He cooked us a special meal with an unusual starter, he fried auborgines,: green peppers, and a thick slice of hard cheese in batter, it was very tasty. Then he presented us with a steak thet nad been grille with large prawns all over it. ‘ell I mean to say, you've got to try these things and I pride myself I have a strong stomach! The local white wine was delicious we sank five or si: bottles at 20p a bottle, and back .on board we had a happening with music, coffee, Brandy| and lots of dancing on deck. I vaguely remember climbing the mast, with the object of tying Johns shorts on the truck, but I was commanded by the skipper to "come down" and I did. I also remembered drinking with an Austrian chap who was sailing a shark 24 he had trailed down through Yugoslavia. It was a fast boat, and he was a very good sailer, he had been eighth in the Finn Gold medal class at Kiel week. The shark reminded me of an achilles 24. ax: 4B we IT'S THERE — SO SAIL ROUND IT OR: THE LONELINESS OF A LONG DISTANCE SOLO SAILOR $ We arrived at Sheppey YC at about 0830 on Sunday 17 August, the club was open so we took the boat up the concrete ramp, over the sea wall and down onto the beach. The height of the sea wall has recently been raised by about six feet, due to frequent flooding of the town of Sheerness, which means the view from the club lounge has been blocked by a concrete wall about ten feet from the windows, but there are plans for another storey on top sometime in the future. The clubhouse is comparable to our own, but it is owned by the coucil, to whom the club pay rent. Launching is quite good, down a wide concrete ramp onto a firm beach. It didn't really start there. It started at Pickets Lock Dinghy Exhibition in April. I was chatting to the people on the Sheppey YC stand about their "Round the Island Race", having read reports about it over the years. I have sailed round Osea, Norsey and Mersea (3 times), but this was the big one — to me anyway. Having been born and bred on the Isle of Sheppey it had added interest for me. Although I moved away from the island when aged about ten, I have been back frequently and roamed over most of it, and seen the sea all round looking outwards, so thought - it would be interesting to sail round looking inwards, and also see what changes had taken place over the years. But I have digressed so lets get back nearer the start of the race. We got the boat onto the launching trolley and rigged, took the car and trailer along to the car park. By this time Janet, John, Gavin and Russell had arrived (my niece, her husband and two sons). John and the two boys were to crew one of the rescue boats, so I knew I was going to be OK. One of those rare situations in Sailing Clubs arose, they had more volunteers than there were rescue boats so they stood down. They plus Vera became my support team, travelling round the island by car to the vantage points to cheer me on. There were four starts, the catamarans started at 1030, by this time it was blowing 4 to 5e Although the north side of the island is sheltered from the SW wind the cats were really moving fast. The other 3 starts were slow, medium and fast handicaps. I was in the slow handicap, 120 and over, with a Europe, a Streaker, 2 Miracles, a Graduate about 6 Mirra and a Solo (me), and we started at 1100. The club has a very interesting starting system which I will try to explain. The race box is on top of the club house with a large window to the front, along the top of which are five spotlights and below the window is a round four foot diameter window, with a flourescent tube which rotates like the sweep second hand of a clock. On the ten minute signal all five lights come on and the hand starts to rotate, as each minute goes by one light goes out, and at the five minute signal they all light up again, and repeat until the off. All this is plainly visible from the far end of the extended start line which was used as it was low tide, The race has to be started at low tide so there is water round the back of the island when one gets there. The tide flows round the island and meets somewhere near the bridge. Anyway back to the start. We started in an Easterly direction to go round the island clockwise, that gave us a reaching start. The wind was south westerly and away we wnet sometimes planing, but moving very fast. The trouble was very shallow water and at times we found ourselves sailing in about 2ft of water and wondering if it was going to get shallower. It was fortunate that we had our centreboards up.e This continued for about 3 or 4 miles until we were off Leysdown (see map). Until now we were sailing about 2 to 300 yds off shore with the cliffs sheltering us, but the cliffs now drop down to sea level and there are beaches, but it is very shallow for about a mile offshore (just like Osea Spit) but about 2 miles wide and 1 mile long) and one has to more or less sail around the edge.

PM, The cliffs which have been sheltering us until now are mainly clay and each winter more erosion takes place. Some of the holiday shalets are on top of the cliff in the autumn and next spring are down the bottom. In one place the road ends at the cliff edge and the next section of road has just slipped down about 50ft complete. I was wondering just how much smaller the island has become after the past 50 years since I have known it. They are now building a concrete wall along the base of the cliff to try to stop the erosion = its going to be a mammoth task. We are now off the eastern end of the island about half a mile off shore, and start to point up a bit to come across, when I saw something that looked like black posts sticking out of the water half a mile away. As I got nearer I saw they were a group of people and the water was only up to their knees although they were about 400 yds from the beach. So I freed off a bit to look for some deeper water, now I am about ? of a mile off- shore and its really blowing — no shelter from the cliffs now. The water is still fairly shallow - the centreboard still touches now and then. I thought to myself "If I capsize I'll be able to stand on the bottom and right it". The water coming into the boat is very muddy. I am now beating and the waves are about 4 or S5ft high, and now and then a bigger one curling over, which toe boat would go right through. I am now about a mile off Leysdown and its wind over tide. Imagine beating through the narrow part at Stansgate for about 5 miles.- We used to go to Leysdown for a day out when we were children. We would get the train from Sheerness, a single track railway — named the Sheppey Light Railway, and on the roughly 10 mile journey there were about ten level crossings, and at each the driver had to get out , drive the train through, stop then the guard would get out and close the gates at each crossing. © There was nothing at Leysdown in those days, just a small community, one Public House, the Station and the beach. I remember the beach seemed a long way from the station, or perhaps it was that my legs weren't vert long in those days, now Leysdown has changed completely, miles of caravans and chalets. I have just managed to get a soggy Mars Bar out of my pocket and eaten it, and as the wet paper blew away it stuck on the sail. Wonder if I'll be disqualified under rule 26 (Advertising )?? I looked towards the shore at Shell Ness and saw 2 or 3 boats near the beach, they must have retired. The nearest boat to me all this time was a Miracle being sailed single- handed, and I was getting annoyed because his handicap was higher than mine and I couldn't shake him off. A cruiser about 30ft.long is sailing parallel to me about 50yds to port, reefed down to about half mainsail. The skipper shouted "Where have you come from" and seemed surprised when I said Sheerness. He said "I've come from Margate and it's been pretty rough, I wouldn't want to be in your place". With that I went about on the other tack. Now a Thames barge is beating in close by so I knew I was OK for water, and the tide was rising. It is now about 1330 and we are past the roughest part, and in the main channel into the River Swale, about level with Seasalter, a couple more tacks and I can free off a bit. Although the first part of the River Swale looks straight the channel winds about quite a bit, and its only 3 hours after low water. The channel is marked by quite big green and red buoys. The first one, | named Sand End was about 15ft high. By now the faster boats that started later where beginning to appear on the horizon. Now the river ahead is divided by a sand or mud bank, a small channel to starboard and shorter, or follow the main channel but lomger to port. I chose the main channel

- 18 - . but some other boats (obviously locals) chose the small channel. I have now reached Harty Ferry, and am now round on to a reache The wind is now clear and the boat is going well. So I managed to have a drink and a few biscuits. Then on the end of the jetty at Harty Ferry were my supporters waving to me. The next 3 or 4 miles of the Swale isn't very interesting, mainly marshes on each side and a few old boats left to fall apart on the mud. It varied between beating and reaching to stay in the channel, but the tide is still pushing me. The Fireballs and Scorpions were now catching me up and passing. A World War II four engined bomber has just flown over, an American Liberator — I think, a rare old sight these days. Although I could see the bridge in the distance it never seemec to get any nearer. Sometimes it was on one side and then the other as the river twisted and turned. Now the river begins to narrow down, about a mile from the bridge. This is about where the tide meets as it flows around the island, and there is still about two hours to high water. There is a large factory on the mainland bank. It looks like a foundry of some sort, there is a tall chimney belching evil smelling smoke, which is blowing right across the river, and a jetty with two large grab cranes on it. Nex on the same bank is the paper mills — Boaater Lloyds - they used to make mainly newsprint, but they probably make toilet rolls and Kleenex tissues now. Quite large ships dock there from the Scandanavian countries with cargoes of wood pulp. Now we come to the bridge, the present bridge was built about 1960 and is a large concrete structure with a lifting centre span which lifts vertically between two towers, and replaced the old iron girder construction, which lifted from one end. This bridge carries the only road and rail link with the mainland, and causes much inconvenience if it breaks down, as the old one was very prone to do, but it won't lift up for every dinghy that comes along, especially in a race with a boat every few minutes. I sailed right up to the bridge and stopped on the mainland bank, I had to jump out quick to stop the boat going onto some very vicious looking rocks. Then one has to lay the boat on its side and push it under, the tide was owing under the bridge, and the wind was like a wind tunnel, but we got through OK. It's about 40yds wide. The river at this point is about 400 yds wide, and there on the far bank was my faithful band of supporters shouting to me, I gave them a ‘ick wave as I was having trouble getting into the boat again. The catamarans are timed to the bridge, then the bridge opens for them, and they are timed from the start again on the other side. The river now widens out again, and this stretch is a water skiers paradise, with dozens of boats and skiers, but they didn't cause us any trouble. It is now broad reaching for about two miles, but the wind is very gusty and the boat keeps on trying to broach. We had one or two planing stretches along this part. The Miracle is now about 100 yds behind me. Now the river goes round a sharp bend and the first gybe of the race, the wind is still blowing hard, and I'm in company with two Lasers, but they wouldn't gybe, they chose to go about in the normal way. They both did it at the same time, it looked more like square dancing than sailing. On the island shore in the shipbreakers is the "Caprice", last of the wartime destroyers which is now down to a bare hull. (This information came from my brother in law, he knows everything that happens on the Isle of Sheppey. It also happens he served on the ship during the war, and he has "borrowed" a few souvenirs from her). Another bend, and gybe on to the other tack and we are at Queenborough. During the war it was a large minesweeper base. One could almost walk across the river on the ships they were so Close. I remember being on holiday there during the war, when the Flying bombs (doodle=bugs) were the in thing and when one came over every ship in the harbour

- 19- would fire at it -— quite a spectacular sight -— and sound. That has all gone now and it's all moorings for cruisers. The river Swale joins with the Medway now and is about a mile wide, and its almost high tides. I'm on a dead run with a fair swell about 3ft high. I don't want to go any faster or I shall catch up on the waves and probably capsize. On the island shore at this point is Westminster (not the one with Big Ben). This one has two large gasholders (not the House of Commons and Lords either). The gasworks and little community has long since been demolished. We used to go round there with my father to see the sailing barges unloading coal, he knew all the sailing barges and some of their skippers. (He was a sailing barge man in his younger days). We are now entering Sheerness harbour, which is very empty now! I remember before the war when Great Britain had a real navy, there would be 3 or 4 battleships in at a time. Rodney, Renown, Repulse etc, plus lots of smaller ships. This would be about 1935-36. My father worked in the dockyard and I've always been interested in boats, even as a very small boy. He would take us to the dockyard on Navy Days and after dark all the big ships would be floodlit. They looked really magnificient - if deadly — creatures. All there is today is one small tanker coming out from the Isle of Grain refinery (BP) and one container ship moored along side a jetty. Over on the Isle of Grain side is the controversial power station standing idle. I am now approaching Garrison Point and I am sailing by the lee on starboard tack and should gybe really, but I'm trying to hang on so I need only gybe once. The two Lasers have just done their square dance routine again. There is a very strong current here and the water literally boils. I thought "If I capsize here I wonder how far back I'll be before I get the boat up again". The Miracle man is quite a long way back now. I have just gybed and I am still upright. Garrison Point is a big formidable looking building of stone and concrete with slats for guns and lookouts, built partly during the Napoleonic War and the first world war to guard the entrance to the harbour. It is now a reach along the seafront to the finish about a mile past the fairground with its big wheel showing above the sea wall, all the construction cranes being used on the sea wall, then we pass the catholic church which looks as if its perched on top of the sea wall, past the stone jetty where Frank Spencer (Michael Crawford) drove the car off the end in "Some Mothers Do Have Them". Now about a quarter of a mile to the finish, the wind is very gusty between the buildings on the sea front. The tide has just about turned now and the water is quite smooth. I wonder if my support team are waiting for me at the finish. Its just after four o'clock as I cross the line. No, they are not there, they are at my sisters house having a cup of tea, they didn't think I would finish so soon. It was about 35 miles and took me 5 hours and it was fairly hard sailing all the way, but I had completed the course without any mishaps and I was quite pleased with that. I might do it again next year. There were about 70 entries in 23 different classes. Stan Oaker

— 2 cae COMMODORE'S NOTES Ten years! ago I decided to build a Mirror dinghy as the family were at a suitable age to start sailing and we also renewed our active interest in the Club. Now the boys are grown up and have gone their own ways J seem to have inherited a much larger family temporarily. It is hoped that this will be another period of mutual co-operation and I will expand on this over the rext few months. In the meantime any constructive suggestions or problems associated with the Club can be raised with myself or other Officers. It is important, in my view, that we operate in the best interests of all the active membership but it may need your help to achieve this. I would like to pay tribute to Ron Greygoose, having just completa his three years as your Commodore, his quiet efficiency and diplomacy ensured a smooth period in the Club's histery, and it is hoped that things do not change too much! The post of Sailing Secretary has now been filled by Murray Bates, in addition Ann Bates has agreed to supervise the galley = both appointments are most welcome. They will be looking for your assistance throughout the next year to ease their tasks. Those with moorings will notice that their fees, payable to Maldon, have risen sharply this time. Unfortunately we as a Club have no say in the amount charged but Only act as agents in their collection. However, negotiations with Maldon Council are currently taking place for a long term lease for the whole Mooring area at Stansgate. Although this is not expected to reduce the total cost payable it should however give members with moorings more security. The Season's Greetings to You All. John Weedon. Commodore. HARD WORK AT STANSGATE The hard is due for some more preventative maintenance at the bottom especially towards the Maldon end, and for this we ask for volunteers with spades, pickaxes, gloves and boots to attend a working partyat 10 am on Monday, December 29th. As this can only be tackled around low water, which is at 11.30 am, the work should last only up until Lunch time. Refreshments will be available at the galley. Johne A.G.M. 1980 = COMMODORE'S REPORT I have been asking myself whether beginning and ending a term of office with subscription increases has any particular significance, I don't think so, except that it highlights the relentless march of inflation and the inevitable effect it has upon us all, Before we come to the proposals and elections tonight, your Officers and Committee are obliged to submit for your approval, reports on the state of the Club, its finances and activities over the past year,

o <= The activities of the Club, as our constitution states, are concerned with the promotion of amateur sailing, social fellowship and the provision of all possible facilities to this end. I believe as a Club we have once again met these objectives, and I should like at this point to thank, on your behalf, the Officers, Committee and Members who have worked so hard to bring this about. The activities of course are divided between sailing and more domestic matters. Stan Oaker our Sailing Secretary will be reporting on the former whilst I must deal with the latter. However, as 0.0.D. at the Regatta I feel entitled to offer my thanks to whoever it was who organised the weather = please do it again next year! Now to the main events of the yeare Two new features were the Inter Social Club's Sports Day, and the use of our Club by the British Canoe Union for the Blackwater Canoe Race. Only one team eventually made the journeyto Stansgate to compete in the Inter=Club event, but it was very enjoyable none the less. Also gratifying was the support given by members to the Maldon Little Ship Sponsored Rowing Race held in aid of the ReNeLeIe I am Sure we enrich the quality of our Club by socialising and joining in events with other Clubs on the TIivere On the more domestic side, our caretaker, Claude Emerson, assisted by his wife Ivy, have once again worked hard to maintain the Club and premises in a clean and tidy condition. The purchase of a vacuum cleaner which can pick up water from the floor has been a great help, The effluent arrangements worked well after repairs and modifications early on in the year. Under the able direction of Cyril Drakeford our Clubhouse Secretary, a number of other tasks were completed — a carpet was fitted in the galley; the rubbish collection point was moved away from the Clubhouse; a stile of unique and spontaneous design was constructed on the sea wall and a flag mast was erected = Mark 3 or is it Mark 4? will feature next year. The trees have again been tended by Bug Bradley and June and Russel Fuller. We are now discovering the species which flourish at Stansgate, so our success rate should gradually improve, The Club has continued to support 8.A.C.S.P.A. and 8.J.R.Ce. AS you could not fail to notice in the local press, 8.A.C.S.PeA. has been in the thick of the controversy over water skiers on the river. I have personally attended a number of meetings on this subject, one with the River Sub-Committee of the Maldon District Council, who are feeling the brunt of the complaints about water skiers. It has been the opinion of most Clubs on the river that there is room for us all, and that with a modicum of common sense and co-aperation a solution could be found. Fortunately this has proved to be the case, and next year the Stone Ski Club have agreed to confine their Club racing to 1 hours duration ina designated area on the northside of the river and at a published time around mideday. They will also operate a voluntary speed limit slsewhere on the river, of 30 mpehe Of interest also is the intention of the Maldon District Council to call a meeting of all river users, at the beginning of each year where ideas and views can be freely expressed and it is hoped that any potential problems can be nipped in the bud. The licence mentioned last year, for us to maintain the concrete apron, mete, groyne and scrubbing posts on the foreshore was formally agreed with the Maldon District Council. We are also currently engaged in negotiations with the Council in order to lease the area of foreshore where our moorings are positioned. The objective here is to give members greater influence and security of tenure over this important aspect of our Club. To this end the newly formed Moorings Sub=—Committee has done much useful work,

~~ 4 - Security has continued to be a problem. Money has been taken from the changing rooms, and wheels, trailers, Even dinghies, petrol and various other items have also been stolen. It is a sad reflection on our times. I can only suggest that we take greater care and take home or lock away the more attractive and valuable items of equipment. On the social side the Barbecue was again lucky with the weather, if a little on the draughty side. The Regatta Disco was as noisy and boistrous as evere The Christmas Dance was a little thin on the ground but was a considerable success. The Laying=Up Supper was well supported = the numbers being considerably up on last year. The Winter Lectures and Cruiser Evenings were interesting and well supported. Russel Fuller, Pat Harper and Social Committee are to be congratulated on their efforts. Ann Allen has done good work as Editor of Navigans = I would however like to see more members contributing to make it more entertaining and newsy, as well as being the vehicle for the Commodores and Committees notices and exhortations. The Galley Ladies have again worked against increasing odds to give us a pleasant and profitable service, It is well to remember that their efforts save us all nearly £2 per head on our subscriptions. The Bar has worked efficiently under the management of John and Mavis Weedon, and Jack & Joyce Reeve have given loyal and friendly service behind the counter every Sunday. Camping has been well supported and trouble free. We must continue to keep this activity well disciplined and controlled if we are to be successful when we apply to renew our Planning Permission at the end of next year, Throughout the year the M.A.S.C. Committee have been negotiating with the larger Sections, to try and find a fair and reasonable formula for arriving at Section contributions for the facilities and services they use. We have insisted throughout, that whatever criteria are arrived at to assess contribution, they must be applicable to all sections and accepted by the membership as being fair and reasonable. I believe we are very near to reaching such an agreement. The rent or contribution we now pay is fixed by our 6 year agreement with the M.A.S.C. at £2,000 per annum. This agreement has 1 more year to run. When it expires however, the M.A.S.C.e have made it clear that they will be expecting an increased contribution from use As a continuation of our policy of self sufficiency and as a gesture of goodwill the Committee have offered in the mean time to pay the insurance premiums on the Clubhouse.=<This item being the only Sailing Section cost currently paid for by the M.A.S.C. Whilst no figures are yet on the table for 1982 it has been indicated that a rental in excess of £3,000 will be expected. The proposals for increased subscriptions contain a provision to cushion a rise in contribution, but I should stress that it is only a relatively small proportion of what we need. The bulk is required to cover other items of expenditure we shall incur over the next 2 years. For example the road will need to be repaired and surfaced again = this alone will cost £2,000 at todays prices. We must replace the Rescue Boat Engine, paint and redecorate the Clubhouse, repair the hard and finish piping the ditch. In all we need to raise an additional £2,000 per annum. As you can see the Committee have chosen this time to allocate most of the increase on to the members who make the greatest use of the facilities, that is, the sailors. The increase proposed is essentially £3 for ordinary members, £4.50 for associates, plus £4 on the Hard Fee. I should stress also that even with these increases our subscription rates will still be appreciably lower than other Clubs on the river. I shall of course be pleased to answer any questions you may have when we come to consider the proposals later on in the proceedings.

—_ 5 -_ As you can see from the Agenda a number of well known members are taking a well deserved break from office. They arez= Cyril Drakeford, Alan Goss, Stan and Vera Oaker, Russ Fuller, Ann Allen, Mick Gray and Margaret Linquwood. I would ask you at this point to join with me in showing your appreciation for their generous services to the Club. Needless to say they are not going to disappear from the scene all together, all have expressed a willingness to help their replacements settle in. We do however have 4 vacancies on the Committee. Two very important posts are going begging — namely Sailing Secretary and Clubhouse Secretary. Please come forward after this evenings proceedings if you would like to offer your services in any waye As one who was coaxed into being Club Bosun more years ago than I care to remember, I can ensure you it is a great team to belong to. John, Frank and David will make you most welcome, Finally I should like you all to know that the Marconi Sailing Club is held in high regard by other Clubs and organisations on the rivers; That Mary and I have found it a pleasure and an honour representing you as your Commodore and Lady and that we wish John and Mavis every success and hope that they derive the same enjoyment and satisfaction as we have done, Ron Greyqoose. POLICE REGISTER OF YACHTS The police are compiling a register of yachts in order to help owners who are unfortunate enough to have their boats stolen and also, no doubt, with the idea of taking proceedings against those who offend the law of the sea, Members should therefore, in their own interests, and to collaborate in this commendable scheme, complete and return the forms which are available from clubs and police stations. Care should be taken to ensure that the numbers of items which are specially liable to theft, such as, outboard engines and inflatable dinghies, are entered an the forms, It is also important to display clearly the names of our yachts, their port of registration or the letters indicating their home club. The same applies to tenders and inflatable dinghies carried uninflated on board, Where is your yacht? An amusing incident happened to me towards the end of the season. The Customs in London telephoned me to say that a yacht called Hullabaloo had suspiciously turned up at a WesteGerman port. From the Lloyd's register of Shipping they found that I was the owner of a yacht bearing this name and where was it? After checking, I was able to assure them that my Hullabaloo was indeed safely at her moorings. To date, I have not heard the sequel. No doubt, other owner's yachts have an equally frivolous name, although, perhaps in my case, some people might consider it appropriate! Eric Payne. CALLING ALL RADIO OPERATORS I am attending an operator's course of lectures at the Maldon Little Ship Club, which is proving very educational and entertaining.

— I have suggested to the lecturer that the growing army of radio users in the MeSeCe Could warrant running a similar course for use He would be prepared to come along if there is enough demand. About 15 to 20 people are needed to make a course worthwhile. Basically, all skippers of vessels fitted with VHF radio are required by law to hold a certificate of competency (issued by the Post Office). The course consists of five weekly lessons on radio procedure (largely practical work using two Seavoices on closed circuit). At the end of the course there is an examination by a P.0. Inspector, who issues the certificate of competency (hopefully). Current cost of all this is £5.00 for the course, with an examination fee of £17.00 to keep Susby in bird seed. If you already own a radio, or are thinking about fitting one, or are just interested, then I am sure you will find the course interesting. You never know, one day it could prove to be the best investment you ever made? Please give me a ring on Chelmsford [redacted], and I will take it from there. John Smith. 1981 WINTER MEETINGS PROGRAMME AT MTM.A.S.C. As members will be aware I have stood down from the Committee after thres years service, and that includes the work of organising these meetings. It is now time therefore for someone else to consider taking on the task, and now is also a good time to start thinking about next years programme. Anyone who feels they can help please contact either me or Pat Harper. I shall of course see through the programme which I have arranged for 1981 which is as follows:= Thursday 15th Jan. 8 pm. Mr. Stewart Platt, local representative of the Cruising Association will be showing a film and slides of a Spanish cruise he made recently. This meeting will be in the new lounge. Wednesday llth February. 8 pm. A further visit from Cathy Foster, Not certain yet of her subject, but those who saw her last year will, I know, come again regardless of what she sayse Meeting in the main hall. Thursday 12th March. 8 pme John Torrence = Enterprise Champion, Nimbus Winner, current E Boat World Champion =— coming to talk, hopefully with film of some of his events. Meeting will be in the new lounge. Please support these speakers with a good turnout. EARLS COURT BOAT SHOW I am organising a coach trip to the Boat Show for Sunday llth Jan. leaving The Vineyards at 9.30 am. It is expected the cost will be about £3 per head including admission to the Show. Please telephone me at [redacted] to book a seat on the coach. Russ Fuller, CRUISER FLEET NEWS At the meeting held at The Generals Arms on 3rd December discussion took place concerning the future of these meetings. It has become apparent that there seems to be a decreasing interest in monthly meetings. However, it was not felt to be wise to reduce to alternate months since those wha only go occasionally would not be so sure what to expect.

i Rl In principle therefore the meetings will continue on a monthly basis. Members will be grieved to hear of the passing of our good friend Colwyn Stone in December, after a long period of heart trouble. In November, I had a long conversation with him when he seemed so much better that he was contemplating a return to work, when the relapse came on December 9th. The funeral was held on December 17th at St. Stephen's Church, Chatham, when as evidence of his popularity, there was a large attendance of friends and colleagues, Colwyn had visited Stansgate on many occasions and also several of our laying=<up suppers, where he was a very popular figure, and he took a great interest in our sailing activities, in fact, he organised the annual Rochester visits. He was a member of The Institution of Mechanical Engineers and was leader of a team which developed the TSR2 flightecontrol system, subsequently becoming Research Consultant to The General Manager of Marconi Avionics at Rochester. Our Club has sent a donation to the National Heart Foundation, which was requested in lieu of flowers, I feel sure that all members would wish to join with me in expressing to his wife, Joan and his sons, Richard and David, our heartfelt sympathy. We shall all miss him very much at the Rochester visit to Stansgate, which this year, is due to be held on July 18th/19th. Eric Payne. The season got away to a fair start with the Easter Series, in spite of the reluctance of crews to get wet and cold, when even decorating the house seems a preferable pastime. The Spring and Summer Points Series had a reasonable turn out all through the season, although, sadly, the Enterprise Fleet has declined, Very few races have been sailed by them this season. Well done Dennis$ All the other Club Trophy Races were well supported, and one thing I noticed when looking through the Dinghy Challenge Cup Results, out of eight entrants wha made incorrect starts, six were Marconi members, who should have known better, and one of the six was "Guess Who", Perhaps this trophy also will be won by a Marconi member next season, as it nearly always seems to find a home away from the Club = only once since 1971 has it been won by a Club Member. The highlight of our Sailing season must surely have been the Regatta, for a change we were blessed with good weather, and not too many problems = on or off the water. - 6 loll RNLI ROWING RACE 1981 Sunday January 4th was crisp, sunny and cold = fair conditions for the annual rowing race in aid of the RNLI organissd by the Maldon Little Ship Club. This year competitors had a choice of course from the start, which was at the lock side at Heybridge Basin. Several chose the outside routs, down river and around Hilly Pool Point and then back up river into Colliers Reach and past Herring Point, with the finish at the quay side by the Queen's Head. This was by far the quickest way, taking some a mere twenty minutes to cover a distance of approximately 3 miles. However, the majority opted in favour of "the pretty way", along the canal past Bentalls up to Beeleigh Weir, then into and down the river, under the Full bridge and back to the quaye Marconi were particularly well pepresented. The Fisherman immaculately turned out by Claude Emerson, with a new coat of varnish, dazzling white painted rubbing strake, and a pristine white burgee fluttering from the bow. Her crew, Pete Clayton, Grahem Mead, Ian Lindsey and Danny Lumley with Sarah Cant as coxswain soon sorted out a little problem with timing during the early stages, and although because of handicapping were one of the last boats to start, they were one of the first competitors to finish. Pete Hall and Jim Campbell did well in the Queen Mary working off the excess's of the festive season, while there were two new "faces" on the scene, Steven Hodges and Nick Nice resplendent in war paint and pheasant feathers handled their canoe with flair and panache, and "bravely" paddled their way round the bend and up the creek. Following at a more sedate pace Vic Crisp and colleague were obviously more interested in viewing the scenery and as the Owl and the Pussy Cat in a real pea green boat they made a picturesque sight gliding up river, Maldon Little Ship Club had a strong female entry with several boats under feminine command, but the most outstanding craft was "Macavon", an inflatable gaily decorated with balloons, crew and helm sporting full tartans, complete with low slung sporran and tape recorder giving us all the "thrill" of the pipes. The onlookers had a choice of vantage points, from the canal side at Heybridge Basin, then after a quick drive up the road to Langford Water Works, one had a pleasant view from the bridge just below Beeleigh Wein, watching the boats being carried from the canal across to the river. MLSC supplied the porterage, which seemed to run chiefly on rum. Then back in the car again to see if you could beat the boats back into Maldon and alongside the quay to celebrate their arrival in traditional style, in the pube A very worthwhile exercise, which deserves more public attention and raises a considerable sum each year for the life boats and life boat men, Make a note in your diary, the next race is on Boxing Day 26th December, 1981. -_ 3 - CRUISER FLEET NEWS A record number of members turned up at the General's Arms this month and were rewarded with an excellent slide show and talk by Dennis Byatt. The Saronic Islands really came to life and looked most inviting = everyone afterwards was saying "When we can get thereee...--etc". Afterwards a spontaneous collection was made in aid of R.NwL.I. which raised £5 for the lifeboats. Thank you Dennis, and thank you Audience. For mext month I have arranged a visit by a member of the local River Police. He will be talking about the history and operation of the Service and showing slides of some of their activities. I hope we shall get a good turn out. Those concerned will certainly remember the fiasco at the commencement of our Boat Show trip. While you were all waiting in the cold I was frantically making phone calls, and it transpired that the firm concerned had got the wrong date in their diary. My apologies to all, but as they say "It is an ill wind that blows no good", I deducted an appropriate amount from the bill, which leaves me now with a small surplus = again the lifeboats can benefit, Cruising Trios We have a tradition of cruises in company where many friendships have been made and great times had, often over a pint or three. It has been suggested to me that some of our members would like to do some short cruises in company, perhaps with a quiet creek as an overnight anchorage. I suggest that anyone interested in cruising in company, who does'nt already do sa, should let me know their interests and I*ll put them in touch with sach other and see what we can come up with. Finally = the Surleigh Telephone Exchange has been pensioned off = not berore time from my recent experiences of frequently being out of order etc. = anyway please nota my new numbder. COXSWAINS REPORT It doesn't seem possible that I've now done three seasons as coxswain, but no doubt it probably seems longer to you! Once again thanks to Ken Hughes, Albert Fuller, David Ormorod and to newcomer Malcolm Gandy for their efforts. We blotted our copybook once when a driver failed to turn up, but in defence I am on the phone and could have been at the Club in 15 minutes. Oh, yes, we did'nt cover the Hornet Meeting either = but then no one told us about that event! At the start of the year I passed the compet€ncy exam for use of V H F Radio, and I hope other members will take up John Smith's offer of organising the course. It is important to remember that dozens of people on the Blackwater and Crouch are listening to every conversation. The Mercury 40 HP engine became very sick during the latter part of the season, and the drivers nursed it through to the end, which then enabled us to do some end of season bargaining for it's replacement, and we've finished up buying a Yamaha 55 for next year. Our two big events = the Regatta and Open Weekend presented no problems as the weather was so kind, but nevertheless I was grateful for the support given by Maylandsea Bay, Harlow (Slackwater), and Loughton Steeple Bay Clubs, and for the tolerance shown by Stone Sailing Club over the radio. COMMODORE'S NOTES The River Blackwater being an important area of natural beauty, is used extensively for varied recreational purposes during summer weekends, and additionally having other commercial pressures it is inevitable there could be conflicting interests. To protect these interests there are a number of organisations and authorities acting as advisory or in executive capacities. The Essex County Council are currently publishing a report "Coastal Water Recreation in Essex", and this will be studied with interest by the Club committee. Maldon District Council who has immediate authority over the majority of the Slackwater has recently initiated occasional regular meetings to bring together representatives of all the river organisations to discuss matters of mutual interest, and Dennis Byatt will be our representative at the inaugural meetings An organisation formed some years’ ago, to act mainly in an advisory capacity towards preserving the environment of the river consistent with the interests of sailino, is 8.A.C.S.P.A. (Blackwater & Colne Sailing Protection Association). The local Sailing Clubs, Power 8Boat Clubs and the R.¥.A. are all gathered twice a year in discussione A recent topic has been concerned with the Stone Water Ski and Power Boat Club activities on the river. The Stone Sailing Club, particularly, were very concerned with increasing use of the river by fast power boats including organised races in an area already used by racing and cruising yachts. After negotiation the Ski Club agreed to limit their practice and racing to a stretch of the river between Thirstlet Spit and Tollesbury Creek on the north side of the fairway. Their race dates this year are programmed for May 10, 24, & 25, June 7 & 21, July 5, August 16 & 31 4 September 13, between 1 = 2 pm, except May 24 which is all day. Therefore it may be sensible to avoid this area if peace and quiet relaxation is desired at these times, John Weedon, SOCIAL NEWS Fitting Out Party 4th April. Savill Spring Points 5 and 6 CRUISER FLEET NEWS Our next programme at The Generals Arms will be presented by John Todds. John spent a considerable time on business in the Caribbean recently and took the opportunity of doing some travelling and photography. We can look forward to an interesting evening. Last month P.C.Winter, a member of the crew of Alert visited us and Qave a very humorous account of the history and work of the Marine Police. He was also interested to hear of our relationships with other users of the river. Concerning the saffety aspect of our moored boats, P.C. Winter endorsed our club recommendation of using mooring lights on all the outer and end boats, as bright as possible on the end positions. He also emphasized that permanent use of a radar reflector was to be encouraged, Since these recommendations come from the River Police we would do well to attempt to observe them. It was pleasing to hear, on the other hand, that, at least at present, the new lighting regulations are not the subject of any great interest to them. However, in the event of any insurance claim I'm sure that importance would be attached to compliance with the rules so it is still wise to have approved lights, which must be fitted by July. HAVENGORE CREEK "Tt has been drawn to our attention that yachtsmen have, on occasions in the past, had difficulty in obtaining information on access through Havengore Creek. This difficulty may stem from the fact that the Bridgekeeper is only on duty from 2 hrs. before high tide until 2 hrs. after. Because of the nature of our work and the responsibility for public safety, the Range Planning Officer must be the authority for granting permission to sail Havengore Creek during firing times. Any yachtsman seeking advice on access through Havengore Creek snould telephone Shoeburyness 2271, inform the operator that he is seeking information on the use of Havengore Creek and ask to be connected to the Range Planning Officer on Ext. 211. If the call comes at a time when the Ranae Planning Office is not functioning, the operator will connect the caller to the Duty MOD Police Officer who will have been briefed to deal with such calls. oe ae COMMODORE'S NOTES At last we have reached the time of year when members are starting to use the facilities for going afloat and it will not be very Long until the Spring Bank Holiday weekend, when our big event of the year — the Regatta = is here. The programme of events is similar to previous years with a practice/pennant race on the Saturday afternoon and points races on the Sunday and Monday. we will be having a marquee again for the bar and social events on Saturday and Sunday evenings. There will be an evening, Wednesday 20th May, for preparing the site, and further setting up on the Friday. To try to ease the load we would like as many members to help with this. Over the holiday weekend spotters will be needed at the race box, servers at the galley and bar, and receptionists and results assistants at the Clubhouse. Camping will be available at Stansgate from Friday 22nd until the following weekend 30/3lst May. Why not help us over . the holiday weekend and then relax during the following week after all the visitors have gone. There will be some friendly social events in the eveninas — a cheese and wine party, darts tournament, and durino the day why not....sail? : A rather laroe number of old yachting magazines were collecting in the lounaoe at the Club at Stansgate, and it was decided to only keep the more recent copies (1980 onwards) or any with articles of special interest. The remainder I am holdino, and if the person(s) who donated them would like them back please contact me. If not claimed would any other member like them? Jonn Weedon, Tel. Harry Ide, however, only joined recently. Our condolencies go to their families. John Weedon. Prizes for the most original dress were won by:= Mr. & Mrs. David Thomas and Mr. & Mrs. Brian Court. I would like to thank all concerned for their help with preparing and serving the food. Next social function will be the Regatta Disco on Saturday 23rd May. Hope to see you there. Pat Harper. Social Secretary.

od CRUISER FLEET NEWS Our final meeting for the winter at the General's Arms was marked by an excellent presentation of slides by John Todds, mainly showing shots of the Carribbean. As John commenced with items from his Ocean Youth Club trips we began to wonder whether the navigation had gone astray. However with suitable encouragement from Stan Campbell we made it eventually, Launching time is with us again and I would like to make two points for everyone to remember. First = is that ground tackle good enough for its job? If in doubt, inspect it. Secondly = those trolley modifications which you want to make during the summer to make laying=up easier = remember to take all essential measurements before launching the boat. During the sailing season it would be a nice idea if cruising people would get together in the Clubhouse on Friday evenings. It is too easy to just see each other in the distance, or not at all, but a little while spent in the Clubhouse before setting off would enable ideas to be swopped, opinions sought on weather suitability, cruises in company to be discussed etc. Remember — we are a club = and no one really does all their sailing independently of others, so let's try a bit harder to act as a Club. Russ Fuller. Cruiser Fleet Captain. Tel. Maldon [redacted], CRUISER FLEET DINNER = MARCH 14th 1981. On Saturday March 14th the cruising fraternity downed tools, left their paintbrushes to soak, discarded their dungarees and wellies, and repaired to the Clubhouse for an informal fleet dinner. And what a dinner! The flowerebedecked tables were decorated in a suitably nautical theme with little boats of flowers each with a candle mast, blue sail and minuscule M.S.C. burgee. All these were concocted by Sylvia Crisp and won "oohs" and "ahs" of admiration. And then the food. Just to remind those of you who were there, | and make the rest of you green with envy, this was the menu: Spring Vegetable Soup with Roll and Butter, Roast Beef Salad with Jacket Potatoes and Coleslaw, Chocolate Gateau, Cheese and Biscuits, Coffee. all superbly cooked and efficiently served by ladies of the fleet, and all for £2 per head, which astonishingly ended in a profit for fleet funds of £12. Other fleets could well follow our example. Our thanks go to Anne Smith, Brenda Tate, Joan Thomas, Shirley Pearce, the organising committee, and their helpers, Jackie Bowsher, Jackie Manning, Margaret Campbell, Sylvia Crisp, Christine Bingley and Bea Pewter. Also = a special vote of thanks to Stan Campbell who did the washino-up! June Fuller

-_— 4 - THIS IS MARCONI RESCUE After a few setbacks we've installed our Yamaha 55 and I must thank John Weedon, David and Peter Sayer for their help in fitting it durino the Working party and also Murray Bates who made a special journey the week after to help me with the control cables. Phil Grey did a grand job in replacing the Mariner's orab rope and he assures me it's strong enough to pull even him aboard! With the closure of the Jet Garage in Latchinodon we've opened an account with the 8.P. Garage in Mayland. A fuel log will be kept just inside the clubhouse door, and no cans should be filled without oil being added and logged by the coxswain (except the upright green can which is petrol only). Empty cans may be left in my garage at any time. (From the Club lst right and right again after the garage). Now my yearly reminder about the use of the Radio. No fewer than 16 clubs are now equipped with it and many have attended the operators! courses during the winter, and I would like to feel that our procedure is heard to be as good as anyones. Please read the instructions which are by the set, but in short the message from Race Box officials should be " MARCONI RESCUE THIS IS MARCONI BASE =— OVER" for the initiating call and " MARCONI RESCUE FROM MARCONI BASE" for the rest of the conversation. Please, no idle chat, enquiries about the bar etc. and please LISTEN first to make sure the channel is clear. Remember, 15 other clubs can hear you! Not beino slim enough to get into the wet suit advertised last month I am now the proud owner of a High Visibility Oranoe Thermotic Flotation suit. (Rescue assistants need dark glasses!!). The first day of sailing was as cold as we can expect (especially with the lack of activity due to the non appearance of Murray Todd's promised fleet!) and it certainly did its job well. However I think they are more suited to Cruiser people rather than dinghies. Finally, three of us attended a seminar for Rescue Boat Personne] at the Burnham Sailing Club. A very useful day = it covered the use of flares, VHF radio, first aid including the treatment of hyperthermia and the kiss of life = and the role of the coastguard, Norman Kerridaoe, [redacted], Maylandsea. -_- ? _— COMMODORE'S NOTES It is good to see the Club coming alive at the weekend and starting to be used for sailing, but let us hope for better weather than has been common recently. For those who are inexperienced it is important that you do not take risks, particularly during the early part of the season, as the cold Blackwater is very uninviting and can be dangerous. If in doubt ask the Officer of the Day's advice before setting sail. One last caution, for this month, is directed at reckless car drivers. The owner of the cottage next to the gates to the approach road to the Club has pointed out that every year there are several accidents or near misses on the blind corner by these gates, and apart from the annoyance, he is concerned for the safety of his children and animals. There has been one collision already this year, so please drive carefully and avoid any more. There is a good reason for the 15 mepehe speed limit, Let it not be forgotten that the main purpose of the Club is to help everyone enjoy their sailing. John Weedon. a 4 eal REGATTA WEEKEND CAMPING I, together with a number of other people, have expressed concern about the fire hazard created by disorganised and too dense camping in the clubhouse field: especially during the Regatta weekend. The other field tends not to lead to a problem. In an attempt te improve the safety aspect I will be placing a drawino, showing a suggested layout, on the notice board and would ask our own camping members to look at this and pitch their tents or park their caravans accordingly. Please encourage our visitors to do likewise. I know that we have not had a fire accident yet, but there is always a first time. The result of an exploding gas cylinder in a field packed with tents, caravans and cars and with inadequate clear space would be devastating. Let us hope that the fine spring weather, surely due, arrives in time for the Regatta Week. Enjoy yourselves. Jim Coy, Camping Marshall. MIRROR NEWS At this time of year I have a fellow feeling with the hedgehog who lives in our garden, We have both come out of our own form of winter hibernation, he (or she) to do those things hedgehogs like best and I to do what I like best = racing/sailing our Mirror at the M.S.Ce I don't suppose the hedgehog has experienced the thrill of racing other hedgehogs around the garden =— come to that I haven't had the thrill of racing other Mirrors around the Blackwater yet this yeare As the only Mirror to have actually entered a race (time of writing Sunday 3rd May) we find it a bit lonely doing battle with the 'bio boys' and playing with the 420's, It reminded me of the day our dog met the hedgehog ir the garden. Both dog and hedgehog seemed eager for a contest of some sort, but a worthwhile competition between the two wasn't forthcoming since dog and hedgehog are of different design. Similarly with the Mirrors and the 420's, etc. What a pity the hedgehog hasn't got other hedgehogs to play with: what a pity the Mirrors are conspicuous by their absence from the races. I'm sure we'd all have a lot more sailing enjoyment if we Mirrors got together more often. However, hope sprinos eternal and I'm naive enough to believe that the 16 Mirrormen who said they would race really mean ite Wouldn't it be marvellous for the Club if they all actually turned up (more or less regularly) and re-established the Mirrors as a fleet to be reckoned with on the water, My first duty as Mirror Fleet Captain this season has been to make out the Mirror Fleet Duty Roster. " The Marconi Hornet Fleet turned out in force at the ‘Easter Eqo! open meeting held at the Royal Corrinthian Yacht Club, Burnham over the four day Easter Holiday. Five of our boats went along, which was very encouraging for an event so early in the season. Good Friday came with winds of about force 4 = 5 with occasional gusts of 6+ 3 This year the Hornet has a new larger rig and many of the competitors were worried about trying out the new ‘set up* in such conditions and subsequently the number of starters was only about 10 out of a fleet of 19, /continued.

ae Murray Todd and Mike Shipsey in ‘'Kyle' were one of the first teams to retire but the claim from the Todd camp was that Mike had forgotten his sailing shoes and was unable to get any grip on the gunwales. (A highly suspect excuse, probably carefully planned to avoid further embarrassment) (sorry Murray). By the time Ii capsized there were only 5 boats left in the race but I was only half way up the first beat $!$ Christopher Denny, in his first ever race in a Hornet was doing exceptionally well, until he unfortunately fell off. Once we had capsized we had great difficulty in righting the boat, and eventually had to drop the main and sail in under genoa alone. Soon after 3 more boats retired leaving just Malcolm Goodwin from Brightlingsea and our own Graham Mead and Danny Lumley sailing Ultimate to fight it out. Malcolm managed to get round the course with no problems at all, but unfortunately Graham and Danny capsized some 10 times, before finishing 2nd, totally exhausted. Saturday brought better weather with not so much wind (about 3—4), and the morning race was again dominated by M. Goodwin. Graham and Danny kept the pressure on however with another second, and I managed 9th place, In tr afternoon the wind died and Murray turned up with a new crev, Ian Stott, but they unfortunately capsized and were the last boat to finish. Graham and Danny were fourth in this race and Mike Williams sailing ‘Special Care’ was 6th. we did not compete this race because the helm contracted a severe stomach disorder (sounded reasonable at the time anyway). The winner of this was predictably perhaps M. Goodwin, with Mr. & Mrs. Bennet from Sussex Y.Ce and Richard Barnes from Stone taking 2nd and 3rd places. Sunday came and so did the wind, but we were pleased to see that the Easter Bunny had not forgotten us as he had put some Easter Eogs in all of the boatse Murray Todd capsized 50 yards from the start, Mike Williams and I both retired after capsizes, and so it was left once again to Graham and Danny to produce the goods. They did well to finish 4th after capsizing on a spinnaker reach. Malcolm Goodwin clinched the meeting with his fourth win in four races and he came ashore and put his boat on the trailer and took it homee The Bennets and Richard Barnes once again came in 2nd and 3rd. In the afternoon the wind became too strong, and the exhausted competitors decided unanimously against sailing the Sth race, Monday morning was exceptionally windy and only 4 boats sailed of which only 2 finished. Graham and Danny decided not to sail and therefore forfeited their chance of second place. Instead they had to be content with 4th. A very good effort. The event gave good experience of sailing in tough conditions, but the water was very congested with moorings, and the exceptional tide prevented much tactical ‘windshift' sailing on the beats. The courses set were too long for the conditions, but an enjoyable weekend was had by all the Marconi boats. Colin Harper, Hornet 2100. - TFT = LOCH NESS & MORAR PROJECT Supported and approved by The Scientific Exploration Society PATRONS: NORMAN COLLINS THE HON. SIMON FRASER, MASTER OF LOVAT. THE RT. HON. LORD GLENDEVON, P.C. DAVID JAMES, M.B.E., D.S.C., M.P. SIR ROBERT McEWEN, Q.C. 61, Bramfield Road, SIR PETER SCOTT, C.B.E., D.S.C. Clapham, Field Leader: Adrian J. Shine F.R.G.S. London. Sw 11 6RA, Dear Sin, We are writing to seek the support of your club in inviting your members to participate in a new phase of research at Loch Ness. Shore based surface surveillance has been discontinued owing to the very small proportion of body revealed by the films shot during the sixties. Underwater photography, on the other hand, is largely thwarted by peaty water and the fact that we simply do not have enough behavioural information to place cameras in such a vast body of water. It should be borne in mind that Loch Ness is scarcely explored biologically and would be capable of comfortably immersing every man, woman and child on earth; and the Post Office Tower for that matter. The only search method producing repeatable results is sonar. All adequately equipped sonar expeditions have so far recorded targets larger than salmon and having behaviour very different to fish shoals. These include Oxford and Cambridge, Birmingham University and Vickers Oceanics. The problem lies in interpreting the results since a sonar record alone can only indicate the presence, strength and behaviour of the target. The Project is now undertaking a major sonar monitoring programme in order to resolve the ambiguities of sonar contacts made at Loch Ness. We now need to know what they are. We have been fortunate in acquiring sonar equipment with greatly superior detection, assessment, tracking and recording ability to any so far used, We should now be able to hold contact for long enough to glean real hints as to a target's identity from its speeds and diving rates. A methodical study of the times, places and depths of contacts will also allow us to place underwater photography on a truly active basis. But if our results are to mean anything, we shall need more than the equipment. In order to bring back valid results, a very protracted operation will be necessary. The search must be pressed at different times of year, day and night until a pattern emerges. This is far beyond the capacity of a single volunteer crew. We shall need manpower and seamanship. /continued.

The work will be conducted from a specially constructed 40ft. inflatable catamaran with cabin requiring a crew of six. The vessel is powered by a combination of engine and square sail for silent patrol, A staff is responsible for administration, training and maintenance, but the main work of the expedition is to be carried out by volunteer crews of six including a suitably experienced skipper. It is hoped that three crews shall be maintained at any one time in order to allow the following cycles: One day will be spent as crew of the sonar search vessel which includes night patrols, one day running the base camp and one day shall be left free, during which members may stay on camp or visit the surrounding area. The Project has a base camp at Ballachladaich Farm near Dores off the B 852 on the south shore of the loch. The Project is therefore in need of volunteer crews of six including a competent skipper and preferably already known to each other, For this reason we hope our proposal may be of interest in a club context. we emphasize that such a group would be treated as an entity within the expedition. After training, the crew would be entirely responsible for the conduct of the work and would naturally merit a great proportion of the credit for success. Individual applicants contribute £32/wk. towards tentage, food, fuel and other running costs but in the case of a complete crew, this is reduced to £25/person/uk. Volunteers should provide themselves with a sleeping bag, waterproof gear and are advised to bring warm clothing. They may also wish to bring their own tent. There is a minimum age limit of 18 years and from 16 years if accompanied by an adult. Individuals and potential crews should write to the above address stating preferred dates (20/7/J%e- 344/Yiu,—). Skippers of crews should have at least inland cruising experience. For the first time ever, we are in possession of the means to do a good job at Loch Ness. Now we need the men (and women). we hope that you may be able to find room for this invitation on your notice board. Yours faithfully, fly at she Adrian J. Shine (Project Leader). - ) _ CLUBHOUSE Days spent at Stansgate are times enjoyed by the whole family. The sailing facilities, the comfort of the Clubhouse and the uncrowded grounds provide the freedom for all the family to relax and follow their own interests. The sailing and the Club facilities are organised and maintained by the small band of hard-working Officers and Committee Members who put in a large amount of voluntary time for the benefit of a membership of about 400 families. To keep the Club operating smoothly and to ensure that all the facilities are available, it is essential that the responsibilities for various activities within the Club are spread as widely as possible if the voluntary basis on which the Club operates is not to break down. These arrangements have worked well in the past, but this year the Committee is experiencing a particular problem, in that it has so far not been possible to find a volunteer to take on the job of Clubhouse Secretary. This is an extremely important post on the Committee and one which it is very necessary to have filled, if we are all to continue to enjoy the facilities at Stansgate, and to ensure that everything continues to work. For the last three years this position has been filled by Cyril Draleford who is now taking a well deserved rest after ensuring that the Club operated smoothly durinag his term. We feel sure that from our membership there must be someone who could be and would be willing to undertake this role, and so that the requirements of the job can be better understood here is an outline of the main responsibilitie, 1. Provision of all consumable supplies, i.e. soap, disinfectant, paper towels etc. 2e Monitor the working of the Clubhouse services, and arrange for repairs and replacements, ieee light bulbs, tap washers, hoses, gas appliances etc, 30 Arrange for maintenance of the fabric of the building and the furnishings, ieG@e Painting and decorating, window repairs etc. 4, Arrange for maintenance of the grounds. The job of the Clubhouse Secretary is not so much doing the work, but organising it and arranging for tasks to be undertaken by other members who have the relevant skills. Much of the work is undertaken by Claude Emerson our hard= working Caretaker. The old proverb "Many hands make light work" is particularly true in respect of the tasks associated with the Clubhouse, and to enable the work to be spread more widely the Committee is going to experiment with a scheme to attract more volunteers. The basis of this experiment is that a jobs register will be created and a copy will be available at all times to the Officer of the Day. It is then hoped that anyone at Stansgate who is for any reason at a loose end will approach the 0.0.0. to see if there is anything that can be done to assist the Club. It is surprising how many times peaple come to Stansgate, and, for various reasons outside their control, are unable to pursue their intended activity, and if people finding themselves in this position could use the time profitably to the benefit of the Club a great deal could be achieved towards maintainino the facilities. This is not intended as a substitute for volunteers, who are always welcome and for whom there are elways tasks. From this it may be seen that the role of Clubhouse Secretary is primarily one of determining the needs of the Club and co-ordinating the activity. The job is made easier if the post is filled by a practical person who can undertake some of the tasks and show others what is required. /continued.

If, as a result of reading this, anyone is willino to consider taking on the job, or there are any volunteers to undertake any of the outstanding tasks, please contact John Weedon who will be very pleased to hear from you. John Witter. ALTERNATIVE SCORING SYSTEMS (or "The Best Man May Win"). The Sailing Sub=Committee are sometimes asked to consider, or suggest, an alternative scoring system for a Class Points series, or the special series such as Ladies, Cadets, and Helmsmen of the Year. Behind such a request often lies the desire to encourage larger turnouts or give more incentive to less expert helmse With small fleets e particular problem is the ever present threat of a class race being abandoned because fewer than three boats sail. t temporary bolt hole of the Handicap Fleet will be less than satisfactory unless the whole series is sailed. Even then we have the problem of how best to extract Class results from Handicap points. Having set out some possible problems with the established system of scoring we reach the difficult part of suggesting a viable alternative. A major problem with many alternative systems is that they require times to be recorded. Possible in the Handicap Fleet, but do we wish to burden our Race Officers and Results Secretary with more number crunching? In recent years we have combined Ladies and Cadet Fleets to avoid the ‘less than three boats sailing' problem, and by moving the Enterprise Class into the Handicap Fleet we have giventhe Class breathing space to regain its former glory. Soth the actions have worked with some limited success, but we may be able to do more in these and other directions. Looking back over the Club's history one can see the evolution of new Dinghy Classes and the disappearance of others. A Fleet may rise out of the Handicap dinghies and fall back in over a period of years, or we may suddenly find ourselves with a new class. (Either way we should accept change and frame our scoring system to allow for it. A points scoring system inevitably produces a winner, the prize sometimes going to the "best" helm. No system can guarantee that the "best" helm will win, some indeed are designed to make this more difficult by personal handicapping, by creating a "second class division" or by givino extra points for performance above normal standard. The Sole Fleet are this year playing with a personal handicap system suggested by John Rutherford which gives the lesser mortals a chance to catch him up. A nice thought here is that if they used their personal handicap in pursuit fashion J.R. would have to sail through the rabbits dirty wind. Not so far fetched, this suggestion, it is used regularly by IeP.C. Yacht Club. A particular example of a scoring system designed to make your Fleet champion sweat blood for his points series cup is "The Ostroboqulous Leaque" as described by Eric Twiname. It attempts to hold interest in a points series to the very end by counting all races for the helms who compete in them, and awerding points to each helm only for beating helmsmen of similar standard to, or better standard than, himself. It works like this = you get one point for starting and not subsequently being disqualified, so if you retire you get one point. In the first race of the series you get a point for every boat you beat, so that if you won the first race when the turnout was ten boats you'd get your starting point /continued.

- ll - plus 9 = 10. All very straightforward so far, but then what happens is that if you win the next race you score only your starting point plus a point for every boat you beat which was within a fixed, critical number of points of you before that race. For example, if the critical number (which is the same for everybody and decided before the start of the series) was 6 then you'd only score points for boats that had 4 points or more (the 10 points you had before the race minus the critical number, 6, equals 4). In practice this means that no-one can streak away into an unassailable points lead by the middle of the series, for as soon as they get more than 6 points clear of the second boat they can only score their startino point, though anyone beating them will score a point. The scheme works a little like a squash ladder, in that merely by looking at the scoring sheet you can see where you are lying at any time during the season, but it has the merit that to build up a good position you have to sail well in a fair number of races, The beauty of this system is that a Club, or even a Class within a Club, can decide exactly where it wants to strike the balance between Harry Flyer who pops in occasionally and wins and Plodwyn Round who is almost part of the furniture and doesn't — except when the experts are away. A biog Critical Number emphasises success, while a low Critical Number emphasises frequent attendance. In the light of experience gained from Clubs using the system a Critical Factor of about 14 to 2 times the expected average turnout for a series of 10 to 30 races is recommended. As an example of how the system would work, the 1980 Sole Summer Points are reproduced with our standard scoring system and as an Ostrobogulous League. It is interesting to note that despite nine wins out of fifteen races sailed S.2862 fails to win the League using a Critical Number of 10, However in practice had we been operating the League and displaying accumulated points each week on the notice board our S.2862 may have put aside his dreams of H.e2100 and won both Cup and League. Finally, please don't take this too seriously — I'm not all that good at adding up. Malcolm Stuart, (Points Table on Page 12) Results Secretary. JUST LOOKING SV I do not often get the opportunity of racing in close company with other boats and consequently rarely have to bother about applying the racing rules. I suppose the most often used rule at the Club is Rule 36, Opposite Tack = Sasic Rule, which tells me that port tack gives way to starboard. Even the start of our races do not offer too many opportunities since, by the time it is the turn of the Mirror Fleet, there is so much room and so few Doats that the rules are just never invoked. Therefore, whenever I'm watching other boats racina, I ‘practise’ the rules on the situations that occur. It was whilst watching from the rescue boat that I observed the following event. Two boats P (on port) and S$ (on starboard) were converging on the beat from A mark to Noe le I glanced away and looked back in time to see what appeared to be a very hurried tack by P from port to starboard and an equally rapid luff by 5 to avoid a collision. This made the boats overlap with P just ahead butto leeward of S. Hai Hag I says to myself, says I, this ought to be good for a protest — but to my surprise both boats appeared to be sailing happily onwards (at least I did'nt hear anythingsS). I thought it was a clear case of Rule 41 in which the tacking boat P had failed to keep clear of right-of-way boat S and forced S to alter course before P had completed her tack. After all, at the time S was luffing, the crew of P were not in their 'normal' position for a beat and looked to be in a bit of a shambles. Since nothing came of the incident, I looked up the rules and their interpretation when I got home. It seems to me that P%s obligations to keep clear of S under Rule 41, and S's obligations as windward boat to keep clear of P under Rule 37 once the tack is completed, depends upon how you define the ‘completion of the tack’. For this beating situation, the definition of tacking is that P is tacking from the time she is "beyond headetoewind' until she has ‘borne away to a close=hauled course’, I read in a yachting magazine that it is an established principle that when beating to windward, a boat is considered to have ‘completed her tack' when she is heading on a close=hauled course irrespective of her movement through the water or the sheeting of her sails, Although in my eyes P was not sailing ?mormally' and her crew were not in their 'normal' position for beating, she was "heading* on a close=hauled course parallel to that of S and had therefore completed her tack = hence S's sudden luff to keep clear. Perhaps the acid test of whether P has completed her tack isse (a) if S hits P"s transom, then this proves P has completed her tack, and (b) if S hits P*s side, this proves P had not completed her tack. Maybe those with more experience of applying the rules would like to comment on this = in the meantime I'1l carry on just looking. Mike Boreham.
