a) Sw CRUISING WITH THE OQCEAN YOUTH CLUB. l6the23rd flay, 8l. The Ocean Youth Club maintains a fleet of seven 72ft ketches at various points around the coast. Whilst they are mainly for the use of 15=21 year olds, during term time adults have the opportunity to sail aboard them. On 16th May I arrived at the Old Customs' House at 8rightlingsea and, finding no-one around, I went to the nearest pub. In one corner was a group of people who turned out to be the Skipper, lst and 2nd mate, and Bosun of "Master Suilder". B8y about 2100 hrs a total of 14 people were assembled and we left for the tender and the trip out to the boat. During Sunday morning with typical British sailing weather of rain and too much wind, we provisioned the boat with water and fuel, despite the various thick heads. By lunch time the wind had begun to moderate, and the mooring was dropped at 1400 hrs with the intention of heading for Harwich. However by 1600 hrs the weather had improved sufficiently that course was set for Ijmuiden and Amsterdam. Four hour watches were set and by 1200 hrs on Monday with no wind, the more hardy types (all female) went for a swim over the side before the engine was started, Sy 1600 hrs the lock at Ijmuiden was entered and we travelled up the Noordzeekanaal to Amsterdam, Monday evening and Tuesday morning were spent exploring the city and avoiding the cyclists. We left at 1630 hrs to go through the lock into the Ijsselmeer (Zuider Zee). As the average depth here is only 8 feet and the draught of the boat was 7.5 feet there were a few interesting bumps eccompanied by the skipper's cry “i'ts a bit thin here". Sy 1900 hrs. we were moored alongside a Dutch barge in Muiden on the Southern edge of the Ijsselmeer. After a visit to the local pub, some people decided to sleep on deck as the weather was very warm. On Wednesday we motored to Enkhuizen to visit the Zuider Zee Museum and also to watch the U.eE.F.A. Cup Final in the local with a number of Dutch supporters, Again the weather was hot and clear enough to sleep on deck which helped relieve the "snoring" problem. An early (relatively) start was made on Thursday for Den Cover, the locks and open sea so that we arrived at Qudeschild on the Friesian Island of Texel at 1530 hrs. After showers in the local yacht club we all visited a restaurant for a meal of eels, mussels, fish or steak before setting sail for England at 2330 hrs. This crossing is 140 miles but due to S.W. winds the best that was achieved initially was a course down the Dutch coast. By 1200 hrs on Friday the wind had started to turn southerly and freshen so that we could head for Harwiche During the 2400 — 0400 watch we passed the sunken lLightvessel at about 10 knots with No. 2 jib, mainsail and mizzen set. However the weather was now becoming English again and at 0400 hrs. we handed over to the other watch as the rain started. By 0630 hrs. on Saturday anchor fad been dropped at Srightlingsea after a sail of 190 miles in 31 hrs. All in all it was a marvellous week of sailing and cruising with that memorable night sail on the return journey. /continued over

TREATMENT OF HYPOTHERMIA Reported deaths due to Hypothermia regularly make the headlines in our National Press every winter, Victims include elderly people dying of the cold in their own homes and healthy younosters unexpectedly overtaken by bad weather whilst tracking in organised parties across exposed country within normally easy reach of urban communities. All this happens in a temperate climate. ' Now you sailors are going to ask what the above paragraph has to do with us! It has an awful lot to do with us. Just a few minutes in the Blackwater doesn't do some people much good, so imagine what half an hour would do to a sailor (not properly protected) after capsizing = the rescue boat could be unaware of your trouble because he is helping another sailor elsewhere on the river?! If you are called to a hypothermic casualty this is what you are likely to find. The patient will bes 1, Blue with the cold. 2e Stiff with the cold. 3. Immobilised with the cold. 4. Unconscious or semi=conscious with the cold. Possibly able to nod his head weakly in the affirmative to the question "Can you understand what I am saying to you?" He is likely to be irrational. Se His respirations will be shallow, slow and irregular. 6. His pulse will be weak, slow and difficult to feel. 7. His rectal temperature is likely to be below 31°C. 8. His blood pressure, if you could record it, would be very low. 9. Since he is exposed to the cold and long past the staqe of shivering his deep core temperature is likely to be below 31 CC. I am not suggesting that you should stick a thermometer up his anus to find oute In any event, unless you take immediate action his temperature will accelerate downwards to death by heart failure, What you should dos l. Treat him very gently. Rough handling may precipitate heart failure in a dangerously cold man. 2. Get him into the warm, out of the cold and away from the wind. 3e Keep him horizontal. His heart is weak and his blood pressure is low. Blood supply to the brain must be maintained at all costs to avoid irreversible brain damaoce,. 4- If local conditions permit, get him to the nearest shelter and stop his heat loss. Remove his wet clothes = dry him — put on warm clothes - wrap him up in warm blankets with a warm human being beside him. 5- Do not waste time giving him hot drinks unless you are sure he can swallow. If he cannot swallow you may drown hime Unless he is getting warm and beginning to shiver do not give him alcohol. Alcohol dilates surface blood vessels and increases heat loss. 6.¢ Trained mountain rescue teams carry special breathing apparatus capable of administering heated, oxyaen enriched, air. /continued.

7. Take him to the nearest available HOT BATH. 8. The water should be at 42—44°C, Test it oy putting in your slbou, If your elbow will accept it — so will the patient. 9. Lower the patient gently ine If sufficient help is available attempt to keep his upper and low limbs out of the water, It is his trunk that needs reheating. The limbs have a larger surface area in relation to their mass than does the trunk. If immersed, it is possible to reduce markedly an already low blood pressure by inducing vasodilatation over the skin of the limbs and to make matters worse excite the return to the heart of a pool of very cold blood in the extremities. This could prove to be the last straw that broke the camel's back and arrest cardiac function by lowering still further Deep Core temperature. 10. Do not foroet to_top the bath up with hot water to maintain the temperature at 42—@44 C, ll. The first sign of positive recovery to look for is the onset of shivering. At that moment, the patient will start dynamically to reeheat his own body. Continue to reheat him passively with the bath treatment. His bodily functions will begin to return. wWhen you are sure he can swallow in spite of severe shivering, this is the time to give him hot groge Alcohol is good fuel and quickly absorbed from the stomach. 12. You have now saved a man's life. Hopefully, by this stags, the patient is in hospital or medical help has arrived. Hand over, for the patient is not out of the wood yet. Lots of complications could occur = for instance, a common one is pneumonia. Yourpatient is ooina to need expert medical care and devoted nursing. The practical aspects of survival training will now be considered under the Following headings in decreasing order of importance. l. Protection. 2 Location. 3. Watere 4, Food. As we now have a large number of boat trolleys of the four wheel steerable type, I think it is appropriate to give some quidelines on their handlinge For moving in the forwards direction the automatic steering works well provided care is taken not to try to steer too tight a circle. wheels can in some cases go "over centre" and require manhandling to get them back, so always restrict the steering angle as much as possible. Manual steering will limit this and the possibility of bent steering arms, but pedestrians must be very aware of the weight of the tow and avoid finger accidents. A supply of wheel chocks is advisable, For reversing a different set of problems arise. It is not generally recognised that it is impossibie to reverse any great distance with the draw bar coupled in any way to the towing line. Trolleys being reversed down the hard must be steered entirely by hand until the trolley reaches the water; the draw bar may then be secured to the tow: line to assist removal from the water, It is always preferable to secure the winch wire or towing rope directly to a strong part of the trailer chassis. Steering bars are not normally as strong for taking the pull of the heavy load. It is strongly recommended, and at club sailing times essential, that a recognised tractor driver or winch supervisor be called in to help. The list of these names is displayed on the Club noticeboard. It is not the duty of an 0.0.0. to help here = he is too busy with other duties and may not be qualified to do the job anyway, so, out of season, please make prior arrangements. No other person may drive the tractor, it is not the same as a car and needs to be properly understood. The qualified operator will satisfy himself that the load appears safe, the gear appears fit for the job, and that the working team is sufficient for the job in hand. Onlookers are normally willing to help if asked but if not involved may become critical observers, All persons concerned with launching boats must be sure that no-one is infon the water in the immediate vicinity. Dinghy owners approaching the shore don't like to see lifeboats approaching from the shore! Less seriously but worth a thought, it would help if steerable wheels could be locked in the straight ahead position, just for when the trolley is in the water — they always slew round a bit otherwise. Trolley wheels should be as large as possible to assist rolling and as for conventional jockey wheels, they Frequently jam in the gaps between the blocks on our hard. How about engineering up a Mini wheel, non steerable, to replace it, /continued.

STANSGATE, JUNE 27th. Ths: Boothby Cup is now held annually for two competing 420 teams. Although originally held for G.P.14 team racing at Maldon, with the demise of the G.P.14 Fleets, the cup is now contested between Osea S.C. and ourselves. This year it was hoped to include a third team from Maldon S.C. but due to previous commitments this was not possible. In future, however, it is hoped to increase the number of competing teams. Enough of the history = what about the sailing! The first race started in force 3/4 winds with the promise of some Dlaninge At the first mark Marconi boats held 3 of the first 4 places, and using local tidal knowledge these positions were consolidated by the time the windward mark was reached. Places began to change over the following beat and broad’ reach, with an Osea boat moving into second place with the remainder looking menacing. It was noticeable that during the broad’ reach some Marconi boats were having considerable trouble with their spinnakers. At the mark at the end of the reaching leq more positions were lost and at one point Ron Greygoose, who had been in a favourable position was seen heading for the shore still carrying full spinnaker. The visitors steadily improved during the second lap and were gaining in confidence. Generous distances between boats reduced the use of team racino tactics and Osea finally gained 3 of the first 4 positions. The second race started in light winds and by the first mark it was obvious that the visitors were well placed. On the first leg it was pleasant to see tactics being employed when Colin Harper literally luffed an Osea boat off the water without loss of his own position. Positions remained fairly constant during the beat up Goldhanger Creek, the reach back to Noe 1, and another reach to Noe 2e The wind was steadily drooping and by the time all boats were homeward bound even the telletales were dropping. Race tactics were abandoned and all efforts concentrated on maintaining forward movement against the tide. As the fleet edged imperceotibly closer to the promontory Peter Chrystis and Colin Harper seemed well placed, but Pete averdid his search for thermals and was last seen sailing backwards towards Maldon. It was Ron, however, who scored by putting in a tack almost through the farm's front garden to get second position with Colin third. /continuede

420 NEWS Although August is a difficult momth for flset sailing I am happy to report that the number of boats competing has remained constant during the month. This can be attributed in part to the summerelike weather we've had. On a personal note, the camping week was undoubtedly the highlight of the year and although there was little wind for sailing I belisve we all benefited from living in close quarters for a week (sorry about the noise, Lou!). The main event of the week started in what can only be described as unbelievable weather, with the Blackwater resembling the Meditteranean. The central theme was to have a 'tuneeup! session starting with some basic measurements on the boats, followed by a number of short races where helm and crew by a rota system sailed each participating boat in turn. The boat measuring aspect of the afternoon was intended primarily to establish a data base against which rig alterations and performance can be measured in the future. Oue to the difficult nature of some of these measurements (e.9. spreader deflections) some time was taken over them, and due to the high ambient temperatures it was noticeable that everyone except the fleet captain and John Chisnall disappearsd for a swime However, the exsrcise was worthwhile and the details will be kept in a book which we can hopefully add to and upedate. Those not present at the session can have their own boats measured by prior arrangement. Six boats were raced in very light airs, in what turned out to be a mammoth racing session of about 34 hours duration. In fact, after the fourth race, several helms and crew were seen disappearing over the sea wall by the race box presumably to irrigate the cruiser park! The lady crews tightened their harnesses and managed to "hang ont (sorry about that Pete!) until the end of the session. All the race results were duly recorded by Robert Weedon (now affectionately known as Robitehead) in the race box for later analysis in the bar. The one thing that the session produced was a lively discussion of the results and the way in which future sessions could be organised. Several useful points emerged from the discussion:= 1. Since the aim was to quantify boats and helm/crew combinations, spinnakers were not used since they represented yet another variable in the analysis. Although this was falt to be reasonable at the time the consensus of opinion was to include them next time. 2e Since all racing was conducted in light airs the results are only applicable to those conditions. 3e Some participants infringed the sailing rules at times during the races without recourse to alternative penalties, (sorry about the green stripes, John and Murray!) and although these were overlooked at the time, future sessions will have to be more strictly controlled. 4e Awkwardly placed or dangerous fittings wers pointed out by helms and improvements to centre board and kicker fittings suggested. To my knowledge these aspects were acted upon the following day = (yes, my boat is safe now!). Se 8y discarding the worst result the analysis showed that the best helm/crew partnership on the day was that of Janet Chisnall and John Weedon. The best tuned boat was found to be 41106 = "Wishful Thinking" (shortly to be renamed$), followed closely by 36372 = "Zoot", 29379 = "Boobs", and 27858 = "Blackbird", After further discussions it was felt that the next session should be held on a course that embraces all the aspects of sailing — due to the conditions, available time and courses, little or ma tacking took place. Finally the overriding observation and admission by some helms was their inability to start

well and get clear wind. The only answer to this problem is to get out and practise, watch those who do it well and try reading Chapter 6 of "Start to Win" by Eric Twiname (I have a copy for loan). Hi -— de — Hi It started with a casual remark after dinner one night, as these things often do. "Darling, there's an article in the local rag about the Maldon Little Ship Club running a Radio course for Yachtsman", "You should do that", replied the skipper. "Why me?", said I, thinking of the sails and the anchor, the galley and all the rest. "Well, I*m too busy holding the bit of wood, and in an emergency, it would be you using the radio, and, anyway, it's all good experience", The result of this profound logic was that I attended the six week course and am now certified by the Home Office, to be competent in the use of a VeHeF.e Radio, I hasten to add. The course was held in the M.L.S.C. Clubhouse on Maldon Quay for two hours on Wednesday evenings starting at 7.30 pm. Our tutor, Cyril Mansfield, a college lecturer and member of the Slackwater Sailing Club was the instigator of these short courses, an off shoot from when he was lecturing for Yacht Master Courses and had been asked on many occasions to go into V.H.F. Radio orocedure in more detail. The outcome is that over 300 people have attended the lsctures, many taking and passing the Home Office examination for the Certificate of Competence. The six lectures cover basic standard procedures, which channels are used for what etc., how to make a link call through a coastal radio statisn and how to contact your friendly neighbourhood Coastquard. Ample opportunity is given to practise as Mansbrite Electronics of Maldon provide two radio telepnone sets, which are placed at gach end of the lecture room and calls can be made and received. Each week, Cyril asked for a script concerning the procedure on making a certain type of call, Mayday, Pan, Pan, stc. The following session we would present our scripts using the radios and trying to be as realistic as possible. Imaginations ran riot and some hilarious situations were invented. At the end of six weeks we attended ane sunny Friday afternoon for the examination. The course is cheap, cost £5., the exam isn't, the fee being £17.50p, but if you pass the Home Office send you a pretty certificate with your picture on it, that you can keep. The paper was a written one, there was no verbal test, and consisted of a selection of 20 questions from a possible 60. It took. about an hour, and as we finished, the man from the Home Office sat down and marked them, thers and thens; not normal procedure, so I have been told. Twelve people out of sixteen passed, several being Marconi Sailing Club members. If you are interested in taking a Radio Course, the man to contact is Derek Steel, Commodore of M.L.S.C. Telephone Maldon [redacted] as they will be organising another series of lectures in the near future. If you would like to know more about Marine Radio, what is available on the market, how difficult they are to install etc., then come along to the November Cruiser Meeting at the General's Arms, Little Baddow, when 8rian Ash and 800 Donaldson from Mansbrite Electronics will be there to show us their range of equipment, give advice and answer any questions you may nave for them. Srenda Tate. 3/9/81.

Mirror FLEET NEWS What a lovely week my family and I had camping at the Club during tne August Sailing Week. In contrast to last year's excess of wind, this year nad wind just right for experiencing the joys of meandering around by the simple means of wind upon sail = not going anywhere particularly = just sailing. I enjoy cruising in the Mirror just as much as I enjoy racing and I hope I'm never tempted to become so devoted to one that I forget the other, Now, you might ask what all this has got to do with Mirror news, and [I must admit = not a lot. However, during the week the mideweek handicap race saw six (yes =— SIX) Mirrors taking part. Our regular mideweekers of Alf Cottam and P.Collis were joined by Robert Coy, John Stringer, myself and David Green in his new Mirror which looked to be quite fast. It proved to be an interesting race and, for me at least, provided a number of lessons on how NOT to deal with the tides. BP, Collis had the right answers and I'm told by those watching on shore that he made up at least 150 yards on the leading boat between No. 1 and A mark by intelligent use of the tide. However, although first Mirror over the line, he came second of the Mirrors to Robert Coy on handicap since he was single handed. The Summer Points racing was resumed on Sunday 6th September and although the morning race was a bit of a drift (Vic Sraybrooke won after sailing for almost three hours — whilst I got fed up and retired for an early lunch), the afternoon race was very enjoyable with Vic and myself swopping the lead until the last beat when Vic pulled ahead to win by a few yards, You may get the impression that Vic and myself were the- only Mirrors racing and this is almost true. The third Mirror in the races contained my wife Margaret trying her novice hand at helming with Marie Dear as crewe The morning race saw them towed back from Osea having run out af wind, whilst the second race saw them sail throuch the moored cruisers and finally retire (in embarrassment for fear of hitting one. They needn't have worried since L manaoed to run full-tilt into a mooring buoy (cruiser attached) and come to a surprised halt. My crew innocently asked why I'd done that and I replied I didn't know — or words to that effect. The lesson is = don't be afraid of making mistakes = we all do it sometimes and we can only improve. Anyway, let's hope Margaret and Marie have another qo. I referred earlier to the very enjoyable August Sailing Week and was most impressed by the 420 fleet who organised a "tuning! session for S or 6 of their boats and then raced them in a series of short races with the helm and crew swopping boats for each race. Their aim was to determine the effects of tuning on boat performance. I don't know what their conclusions were but the effort was impressive and I would love to see the Mirrors adopt a similar fun=sailing session next year. I propose to call a meating of members of the Mirror fleet, say in November, so that they can discuss what they would like to see happening with the Mirrors. For example, we could encourage each other to race and so improve our boat handling skills. We could hold a "racing rules session" before the start of the 1982 racing calender and perhaps try to arrange for a quest speaker to tell us the secrets of "go faster" Mirror handling. Perhaps we could arrange for a Mirror fleet "gathering" one day during next year's August Sailing Week. Older members of the Club who enjoyed happy times at Heybridge when the barge=yacht Mamgqu was our headquarters will be sad to hear that she has finally reached the end of her useful life and lies derelict at the end of the Maldon promenade adjoining The Maldon Yacht Club. In 1957 our Clubhouse was a shed on the seawall at Heybridge Sasin and we were seeking more adequate accommodation when we heard that Mamgu was up for sale, the asking price being £2,000 which, at that time, was far beyond our means. However, the owner who had been living aboard whilst she was moored alongside the quay at Maldon, had taken up residence ashore, was anxious to sell the barge and we heard the whisper that an offer of around £500 would be accestable, After prolonged negotiation, towards the end of 1957 we finally bought her and started Fitting her out as our new Clubhouse, During this time we laid moorings at Heybridge Basin outside our shed on the seawall, /continued.

as ee On April 20th we arranged with Cecil Stebbens Senior, the Pilot and River Bailiff, to tow her round from Maldon quay to Heybridge, some of us taking the wheel during the voyage. Sy choosing suitable states of wind and tide, we managed to manoeuvre her bows=<on to the beach outside our shed, adjusting the Bow moorings on the seawall and the stern moorings which we had already laid. Access to the Barge from the seawall proved to be quite a problem and we Finally constructed a pier at seawall height extending to the bows of Mamgu, the final section being hinged to allow for the rise and fall of the tide, a matter of some 4 metres. We then proceeded to fit her out to suit our requirements as a Clubhouse, with changing rooms, saloon and galley, not forgetting the motor pump which was essential for keeping her bilges reasonably dry, and from time to time, caused us some anxiety. The barge served us very well for some five years but our main limitation was that we could sail for about only two hours on either side of high water, so we scoured the river for a more suitable site, After a considerable search, we finally decided on a site adjoining the summer residence of Tony Senn at Stansgate Abbey where there was a concrete hard which extended right down to the water's edge at low tide, thus permitting sailing at all states of the tide. A lease for the site was obtained and we bought a hut which we found right in the centre of Braintree, which we dismantled and transported to Stansgate, where it was reassembled and made into a very nice clubhouse. This was in April 1963 and it served us very well until we were treated to a permanent bricke built premises which we now enjoy. In the meantime, Mamgu was sold to the London borough of Newham for the same price we had given for her,and after a refit, it was used for training young people from that borough in the ways of the sea, However, the condition of Mamgu deteriorated to the extent that she had to be abandoned and another barge substituted, which is still giving excellent service and giving London youths a taste of the sea. me Q = COXSWAINS REPORT 1981 As I write this, there are just two weeks to go to the last race and I'm glad I invested in a Thermotic suit: Looking back, it's been a season of ups and downs. The new 55 Hp Yamaha engine has been a delight to use but we were very unfortunate to have a major breakdown at the same time that the work boat was having its overhaul. A lot of nice things were said about our coverage of the Regatta and a lot of this good work was the result of cooperation with other clubs. Having just a few regular drivers means we've come to know the other drivers and recognise their voices over the Radio. Our Regatta has become a sort of club for us all to meet. We also had the help of the Police this year (at last they now have our Radio Channel) and they turned up in their new Even inflatable (still wearing peak caps!) Rescue crews get a lot of thanks when the weather is bad but I would like to thank all my drivers for turning up and for their patience during all the quiet days of July, August and September. Waiting for that last Mirror in a Force 2 when everyone else is in the bar is no fun. We did have one or two critisisms and these were discussed fully at Sailing Sub-Committee meetings and hopefully we learned from the episode. One example is that we now carry two 20 Metre floating lines to cut out the need to approach fragile dinghies in rough weather. In conclusion we are fortunate in having our small band of non-sailing drivers and I hope they will carry on being available. NORMAN KERRIDGE COXSWAIN P.S. The Commodore recently asked how we could quieten the enthusiasm of the Saturday night Regatta. Ray Harvey tells me that at the last Maylandsea Bay open meeting, they showed the film "Jaws 2" and the effect was quite interesting !!

15 8] COXSWAINS VIEW OF THE PILOTS CUP The sailing sub-committee's decision to run the postponed Pilots Cup race to Mersea No. 5 in October was rewarded with ideal conditions with a Force 3-4 N.E. wind on a flowing tide. No problems for anyone of course but I know from comments from one anxious wife on the shore that they do worry when you leave the haven of club waters and I was out of sight of most of you for the day so here's how it was covered. The course was Mersea No. 5 to port, Marconi No. 4 to port. Entries varied from the fast Dart to the comparatively slow Solos and we weren't even sure if West Mersea No. 5 was still there. So, the-0.0.D. agreed to cover up river from the club when the faster boats returned and we proceeded down river - needing half speed to keep up with the Dart : Problem No. 1] the Solos will soon be out of Sight. "Stone Rescue 2 - this is Marconi Rescue - over " "Marconi Rescue from Stone 2 - Good Morning Norman - over" So contact had been made with Derek on Stone Rescue 2 and their two boats kept an eye on you through their section to Bradwell. We proceeded to the buoy half hidden amongst the dozens of participants in the Golden Cod contest and dropped anchor. My high visibility orange suit came into its own and was seen by competitors long before the buoy!! The Dart rounded 10 minutes before the Hornets and by the time the 420s arrived Stone were reporting the Dart back in their waters and the Solos were only just in sight at Bradwell. We then had a bit of luck. I spotted Steve in the Dabchicks No. 1 Rescue Boat at anchor fishing ! (They weren't racing until 2.30 PM). He agreed to watch the Solos and kept in Radio contact. We caught up the 420s and by this time the fleet was back in visual contact. All in all a good day out and for me at least a pleasant change from the usual triangles. A final message to shore based relatives. If you are at all anxious - get the 0.0.D. to call us on the Radio. We can usually put your mind at rest even if we don't appear to be in the right position. NORMAN KERRIDGE COXSWAIN Note from Ed. SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT -— 1981 The 1981 season started on the first weekend in April, with 10 crews competing for the first of the Spring Points, The series, 12 races in all, turned out to be very wet and windy, and provided plenty of work for the Rescue boat. The Summer Points, by way of contrast, were sailed in mainly light conditions. Soth the Spring and Summer Series had increased support this year, with average entries up in most fleets. The Enterprise fleet has recovered some of its lost support and managed to compete in both series, but the Mirror fleet only managed to race a Summer series with an average entry of 3.18. The Cadet Series entry showed a small increase this year, with 5 races sailed, and the average entry was 5.8, Whilst on the subject of cadets I think it worth noting that for the second year running the Helmsman of the Year has been won by a cadet. The Ladies Cup had very poor support this year with only 3 of the 6 races sailed. The major event in the Clubs sailing calendar is the Regatta. This year it attracted 206 entries, which was very good considering how wet and windy the weekend was. The Clubs two open trophy races, the Dinghy Challenge Cup and the Cruiser Cup were both won by competitors from outside the Club, with the Dinghy Cup going to G. Palmer of Stone Sailing Club, and the Cruiser Cup to J. Littlewood of Maldon Little Ship Club. With an average entry of 19 the MideWeek race has proved to be as popular as ever. Indeed, one race had 33 entries, which is better than some SundaySe The Solo, 420, Hornet Open Meeting, held in September, again attracted a good entry, particularly the Hornets. As for open meetings outside the Club, we had no major successes this year, but a party from our Hornet Fleet did travel to Holland for the World Championships. The best placed Marconi Boat being that of Graham Mead and Mike Turner, who finished in 15th place. Finally, my thanks to the members of the Sailing Committee, Rescue Boat crews, Race Officer and all Club Members who have given up their time to help during the past year. st 420 NEWS I must hold more 420 meetings at home. This revelation struck me the morning of the day put aside for a discussion of next year's sailing. Firstly I noticed that the windows had been cleaned (evidence - slight smear bottom left of patio door) causing me to squint at the morning paper because of the high level of reflected light. Secondly, the pile of adult reading material hai mysteriously vanished, Thirdly, my name neatly written in the dust on the bookshelves had been 'siliconed' away. Where will it end I thought, grabbing my coat before I too was polished. Well, unlike Howard Hughes I have survived this cleansing experience and the 420 meeting did take place with 12 of us discussing the following proposalss= le The general feeling o* the meeting was that the 420 flset would support any move to select the helmsman of the year from preeselected points races. This would hopefully free race officers to select courses of a reasonable length according to class. In larger fleets (or fleets with a large turn-out) it was felt that perhaps more than one boat could be selected for the H. 0. Y. finals. This selected could perhajs follow the same set of rules that are presently applied to the number of prizes awarded in points series. Although this move would require changed in che H.0.Y. finals format the event could perhaps become a club event held on a Sunday rather than held on a Saturday as at present. This latter poiit will require further debating by the Sailing Sub- Committee (as wil! all thes points mentioned here) and will depend largely on the arrangement of next year's sailing programme. 2. Useful discussions weve held on the arrangement and scheduling of points series. The concensus of opinion was that most fleet members would welcome a third points series as it is felt that at present there is a six week spell around August uwtere points series are dropped. It was proposed that these series could be called Spring, Summer and Autumn, with probably more emphasis on the Summer Points (i.e. more races). Since at present the end of Spring points occurs at a natura! break in the racing calendar (the week before the Regatta), this series is best left as it is. If the proposals are adopted then the end of the Summer Points could conveniently be arranged for the week before the August Bank Holiday. The meeting also supported a move towards scheduling the afternaon races for 1400 hrs. The main justification for this move was that less time would be spent sitting around getting cold (or drunk!) between the morning and afternoon races. One problem with the proposal is that race officers might set very short courses in the morning to make sure of starting the afternoon races on time. The meeting then launched upon discussions concerning the abilities or otherwise of race officers to which various points emerged. Firstly, since not all race officers sail 420's it was proposed that more fleet representation be made when courses are being set. It was felt that this could best be achieved through ~he fleet captain. Secondly, concern was voiced that perhaps more course guide!ines could be issued to novice race officers, these guidelines to be based on existing race records. This information, however, could be difficult to coliate and may well be a complex task since the time to cover a given course is a function of tides, wind strength and wind direction. Furthermore it was not known how well the race officers sheets are filled in} (I expect Malcom can tell us#!). As an aside, Ron Greygoose is organising race officer instruction for those interested, as part of the winter meetings. Finally on this point there appeared no resistance to the proposal that the order of class starts be reversed in order to reduce the time on the water for the rescue crews. /continued.

3. It was proposed that next season the fleet should hold two or three team racing sessions. It was felt that our team racing tactics and skills are non- existent at present and that if we are ever to win the Boothby Cup we must do something about it. The format of these meetings is at yet undecided, but they will almost certainly be held on a Saturday since the normal sailing programme is usually full. On a personal note I think that these sessions could be a boost to getting a firm commitment to team racing from the more active crews. Remember that being a good team racer does not necessarily mean having the fastest boat —- so those of you that are interested in joining these sessions please let me know. 4. The holding of a 420 Open Day was briefly discussed. It was decided that having a single specified day would not necessarily reach the largest number of possible converts and could wastefully occupy crew's time and boats unnecessarily. A better solution would be to advertise through Navigans, that anyone interested in sailing a 420 could do so by contacting the fleet captain, who would arrange a suitable time and helmsman. Several boat owners at the meeting pledged their support (thank you Pete and Anna!). 5. Finally, the meeting discussed tuning sessions for next season. This year's session was held during the August camping week and although the benefits were difficult to quantify, it was felt that much experience in the running of the event was gained which could be used to produce a better organised and more beneficial (and more fun of course!) session next season. To summarise the discussions it was felt that perhaps two days were needed and that time should be given to boat tuning adjustments. This would necessitate two or more boats for instance, sailing parallel courses (but each in clear wind), at the end of which the slower boat alters boat tuning in a attempt to increase boat speed. If this is successful, then the initial fast boat may well have to alter her rig if she is now the slower. To obtain any reasonable conclusions from this approach, all points of sailing will require covering. This of course will require considerable organisation and monitoring! Some of these points have already been discussed in the September .Navigans so will not be laboured further. There will be a "weightlifting" sessionWJanuary at some suitable hostelry so we can formulate some ideas then. Well it's been a memorable year and I will be sorry to see John and Murray and Dave Harper leave the 420 fleet to join the Hornets, It would seem that the main qualifications required for joining the Hornet Fleet (apart from a Hornet that is) are that you are ‘slightly overweight, can drink enormous quantities of beer, know the words to countless rugby songs (if not be able to hum in a deep tone) and, as Kate Nicholson puts it, be 'mental', Of the first two qualities John and Murray rate highly and of the latter two only time will tell! Dave, I think, will have no problem in making the transition. Kate and I will miss John and Murray whose victories on the water are only surpassed by their repartee before and after races, I*m happy to report however that John and Murray's boat will still be seen on the water as it has been bought by Russell Jeffries who, through the Marconi Grapevine and thin office walls, is prophesying spectacular victories next season. Well, good luck John, Murray, Dave and Russell. Russell's boat has been bought by Nick Pavitt, so I hope we shall see him racing next season, and I wish him the best, Phil Gray. Fleet Captain.

~ 5 —_— ENTER!RISE FLEET NEWS Last season was a much better one for the Enterprise Fleet with most of the Spring and Summer Points races being sailed, and because of the increased turnout and keener competition it was extremely enjoyable. At a well attended fleet meeting held recently, representatives from eight boats wishing to race regularly next year were present. This may not sound many to the 'big fleet' sailors in the Club but it does show a steady increase in interest within the fleet. The main topics of discussion at the meeting were prompted by she report of the Solo Fleet meeting. The Enterprise Fleet basically agreed with the proposals listed with the exception of the rescheduled start time after lunch. It seems that the only occasions any excessive drinking times occur are after Helmsman of the Year qualifiers, if these are rearranged as suggested, the present afternoon start times could be retained. It was agreed that a lot could be learnt from having a ‘tune up’ day, perhaps on the Saturday following the Regatta when the benefits obtained could be proven over the Summer Points Series. A suggestion was made that some of the more experienced helmsmen could give some ‘on board’ experience to any novices wishing to start racing by holding some ‘teach ins! If anyone would like to start racing next season and has any problems do not hesitate to get in touch with me as I am only too willing to help. I would like to thank everyone who assisted in fleet duties last year - it makes my job very pleasant to have willing volunteers? One final thoug!it prompted by Mike Boreham asking about catching fish in spinnakers, I did manave to catch two winkles and a crab whilst capsized off Osea on one of these blustery October days (just testing the buoyancy). = 6 = GUR TROPHIES For a Club which has been running for some thirty years, members must have looked with pride on the handsome trophies arrayed at the Laying- Up Supper and some of them may have been intrigued at the names given to theme The President's Cup was presented by one of our founder members, and first President, the late Sir Eric Eastwood, who intended it for Fleetwinds, a class originally favoured by us. We adopted this class because of its ease of construction and good all-round performance 3; also we knew its designer, Alan Eckford from Stanstead Abbotts who helped us and gave lectures at the Clubts winter evenings, which, at that time were held at The White Hart in New Street, before we had the use of our present fine premises at Beshive Lane. The Fleetwind was popular at the time and some of them found their way to Ceylon and are still sailing today. The Pilot's Cup was presented by the late Cecil Stebbens of Heybridge Basin, who was pilot and River Bailiff, and was intended to be awarded for an all- in long-distance race. He was very helpful to the Club and towed Mamgu from Maldon to its moorings and he constructed the access ganqway from the top of the seawall to the bargée Mona's Cup was also presented to us for an all-in long-distance race by Mona Clark, who with her sister, Reena, ran the Jolly Sailor, which was handy for the barge and was much patronised by our members. for the first race we asked her to come aboard Mamgu and fire the starting gun and we also invited them both to our Laying=Up Supper, The Garrett Memorial Cup was presented to us for cadets by the wife of the late Fred Garrett who was our Secretary and because he attended to Mamgu, he was known as the ship's husband. He did a tremendous amount of work for the Club and he owned a cruiser named "Melody". He cycled to Heybridge from his home at Great Baddow each weekend and some evenings but unfortunately he suffered a heart attack and was unable to cycle, but, undaunted, he acquired a scooter so was still able to reach the barge until his heart finally failed. His daughter still works in the canteen at Great Baddow. The Boothby Cup was preented by Bob Boothby, Commodore of the Osea Sailing Club when they built a clubhouse on the seawall at Millbeach and were and still are keen sailors, turning out in good numbers, in all weathers. In their early days their membsrs joined our Laying=Up Supper which was held in the New Street canteen, when some 60 of them occupied one complete spur of the top table, making an attendance of some 450 = an all-time record! The Mamgu Trophy is awarded annually for the best log or account of a member's cruise or adventures during the past season. It is a beautiful model of the sailing barge in her heyday and is correct down to the smallest detail, It was constructed by one of our founder members, Arthur Adam and there is a similar model in the Science Museum at Kensington. The Triple K may be something of a mystery to somes; it was presented by Nic Tovey and Brian Partridge for Enterprises of which they were exponents. Their boats were named Kiora and Kool Kat respectively, and they were all spelt with Ks, hence the triple Ke They seem to have taken it in turns in the early days to win their own cups. Eric Payne.

SCANNER FUND SPONSORED WALK SATURDAY AUGUST 7, 1982 For the past two years several of us have walked along the sea wall from Burnham to Bradwell and have enjoyed raising nearly £900 for the C.A.T scanner in the process. This year, we plan to vary the format slightly and start at St. Peters, Bradwell where we finished last year and walk the south bank of the Blackwater estuary to Steeple, ending up at [redacted]. By starting at 9.30 a.m on a Saturday we should pass The Green Man at Bradwell Waterside, the Stone at St. Laurence Bay, The Marconi Sailing Club and the Steeple Bay Bar all during opening hours (provided you don't linger too long) so the logistic problem of providing refreshments will be avoided. The distance is 14 miles, the same as last year. I hope you will be able to participate and can persuade all your friends to sponsor you on the form overleaf. Attached is a map showing the route and the stage points where there will be vehicles to pick up anyone who wants to drop out. There will also be transport available to get you back to the starting point if you need it. We should meet at 9.30 a.m at the gate leading to St Peters and I recornmend you bring a windproot jacket as well as boots or strong shoes and a spare pair of socks. It is absolutely essential that participants "sign-in" at the start and that no one leaves for home without advising Carolyn or me. I will be the back marker and will not leave the start before 10.00 a.m. Please follow the route precisely as shown on the map, particularly the section from Marconi S.C. to Steeple Bay. IDEAS _ SECTION. As promised last month I will open this section with a descriptian of how to mount the kicker lever under the thwart with little loss in efficiency. The figure (on Page 6) shows how the wires, pulley and lever are positioned. The two wires should be of substantial thickness (2 mm suggested) since the lever generates impressive forces. The upper half of the longer wire, above thwart height should be plastic sheathed to minimise damage to the crew (actually this system improves crew mobility during tacking). The main anchorage point for the system is at the aft end of the centreboard casing. This should be achieved by drilling a vertical hole through the casing and attaching a substantial eye bolt. Ensure that a washer is employed to distribute the load on the casinge Attachment of the wire to the eye bolt can be by shackle or by direct attachment with a thimbled eye in the wire. Sincs the rules allow only two pulleys with a lever, and since one of these pulleys is required on the mast, the second cannot be used to any mechanical advantage. However the length of the lever is not restricted and it is possible to employ a longer lever than is conventionally carried in the classic kicker arrangement. I have not found this to be necessary but for younger helms/crew this is worth considering. All dimensions shown in the figure can be varied by plus or minus one inch without any problems if the boom fixing is variable. If this is not the case the long wire length must be determined to suit your own boom setting. The modern 420 has a fixed gooseneck with sail luff tension controlled by the cunningham. If you have an older boat (eog- Snapir) the gooseneck can be permanantly fixed and the same principals of mainsail tuning applied, To prevent the lever slapping the centreboard casing it: is possible to loosely mount the lever to the casing with a rubber bush. The mounting /continued.

must allow enough movement for the rotation of the lever and should be placed as close to the centre of rotation as possible. Finally the kicker control rape is led out through a cleat on the top edge of the centreboard casing, and here the spare pulley can be used to provide directional variations for the linee If you wish to know more about these last two aspects have a look at K38346 when she's next out. THAT WAS THE YEAR THAT WAS Well, my ears have only just stopped ringing from the calls of STARBOARD!, WATER!, and UWP UP UP!, it seems that if nothing else, Hornet sailors can outeshout anybody on the river or in the barJ But despite my temporary deafness, "mine's a pint of lager", I have survived a very enjoyable year with a new boat in the Hornet Fleet and it's not called Stimulation for nothing, being a largermainedstiffriggedgybing= boardgofastershapedgoodwinhornet$ Steering me round the buoys has been Simon Kenworthy, who has perfected his Jacque Cousteau impersonation despite ‘all sorts of problems depending on the wind(pardon). But as if to confound our sometimes brutal treatment of the boat, due to our unusual sailing techniques, it has proved to be very strong and resiliant. The fleet at Marconi is looking very healthy (boat numbers that is}) under the careful guidance of Murray Todd our Fleet Captain. The Tacing at the club has been excellent and Marconi boats have also done very well in other clubs! open meetings. Along with Colin Harper we competed in the Junior Nationals at Medway Sailing Club. The sailing was good but the social life(?) left something to be desired. The event was won by the Newman brothers with Div Mellor second, we finished Sth. and Colin 8th. We also competed in the Stone open meeting and finished 10th out of 38 boats, This together with a 7th in our own Regatta and a 4th in the Summer Points are good results, we feel, for the first year. We also competed in the Brightlingsea winter series, and although this is a closed event, Colin and ourselves were given temporary membership of the club. In spite of not managing any major success we enjoyed the sailing and our thanks go to the Commodore, Roger Robinson, and everyones at the club for making us so very welcome. The social life has been, and still is, the best of any fleet with great friendship extended by other clubs* fleets, much entertainment being enjoyed both organised and impromptu< "nice one moonie and steady. dickie". So, eagerly looking forward to the new season, which starts for us with the Easter Egg at the Royal Corinthian Club, Surnham, on the 9thel2th April, we hope to sae you there and we'll go ffor it in a really big waye Congratulations must be extended to Dave Harper, Murray Bates and John Chisnall for their excellent taste in joining the Hornet Fleet. MIRROR FLEET NEWS FIRST, THE GOCD NEWS = the Mirror Fleet meeting at my home in Sillericay was well attended by eleven members, with another four members sending their apologies for absence due to illness or other unavoidable commitments. Since the four absentees have all raced and helped with Mirror duties in 1981, then I am encouraged by the response to this meeting and hope the fleet can carry it through to the racing programme in 1982, The meeting was arranged to hear a talk by Dennis Sristowe on Sailing the Mirror. Dennis is a well-known Mirror helmsman of national standard and (to borrow a theme from a well-known advertisement) his talk reached those theoretical parts that the text books cannot. reach. In other words, Dennis avoided the pitfall of merely repeating the standard text—book theory of sailing and instead gave us a more practical approach to solving the problems of mast rake, lee and weather helm, rigging, sail setting, spinnaker systems, hull painting etc. - in fact, all those subjects falling under the more general heading of "boat tuning". The meeting soon took the form of "question and answer" and I personally found the talk just right in: helping to bridge the gap between text=book theory (which I can understand). and practical application (which I can't). Now I'm counting the weekends to the time I can get the boat into the water to see if I can make it all work. One interesting piece of information to come out of the meating is that our own Vic Sraybrooke first introduced Dennis Bristow to the pleasures of sailing. NOW FOR THE GAD NEWS = the Mirror Fleet has unfortunately lost half of its prime dinghy parking space in the Dinghy Park (West) to the 420 Fleet. This has occurred due to the Hornet Fleet not unnaturally feeling a little aggrieved at having to drag their boats a considerable way on race days whilst many Mirrors never move from the park from the beginning of the season to the end, or, if they do move, do so on relatively rare occasions and not as part of the racing programme. The consequent rearrangement of dinghy parking means that part of the Mirror Fleet will be in Dinghy Park (West) and the remainder in the space vacated by the Hornet Fleet in the Dinghy Park (East) i.e. the cruiser park, In order to keep the Mirror Fleet alive as an active group and to encourage a Mirror "awareness" both amongst ourselves and the other fleets, I have asked that the known racing Mirrors be kept together with the other racing fleets in Dinghy Park (West). I would be grateful for the co-operation of all Mirror owners in ensuring that their Mirror is correctly parked in their alloted space and not in any other space. Pat Harper, Social Secretary. DINGHY PARKING On reading the March issue ef NAVIGANS I was concerned to find items which indicate a trend of opinion which cannot be allowed to go unchallenged. The contributions in question refer to the re-allocation of space in. the dinghy park and clearly imply that racing helmsman should be given prioity over those whe do not race. I have no axe to grind as to how people make use of their sailing time whether it is to race, cruise or potter but it has always been recognised that, unlike some other clubs, the M.S.C. is not a purely racing club. It should also be remembered that those dinghy owners who do not appear to sail. very often are still contributing to club funds and are therefore making it possible for the more enthusiastic to organise their racinge Those who spend little time at the club are the losers as they are not making the use of the facilities to which their subscription entitles them. It may be a sad fact to the racing committee but an examination of the club's statistics leads one to the conclusion that the racing members are in fact a minority of the membership. Under these circumstances why should a Tacing helmsman have priority regarding parking position over the next? I have always in the past been reluctant to make criticisms of the club's management as I am only too aware of the valiant work they do and what little contribution I make to their work (also some are my friends?). On this occasion, however, I must point out that such a move constitutes a change in club policy which to my knowledge has not been referred to the membership. All dinghy owners who pay the same subscription must have equal access to the club's facilities. Douge Paynter. Editor's Comment -= I have been advised by the Committee that there has been no change in policy over dinghy parking as could be construed from the item in the /continued.

on 3 ot March issue. The policy has always been to site the heaviest boats closest to the water. THIS IS 22]3W -— MARCONI RESCUE The first week of April always finds me in a cleft stick as the start of the Sailing Season overlaps the end of the Hockey season and so I will have missed out on all the free beer that was on offer on April 4th. My thanks are due to Phil and his 420 fleet for getting the Mariner ready for the water this year and for choosing a weekend when I was away in Francee I'11 try and make up by working extra hard in the season. Now for my Annual Reminder about the use of the Radios Remember that all the other clubs on the river can overhear all that is said. So please = NO C.B. jargon or idle chat and listen first to make sure others are not on the aile During these early weeks please do not underestimate the power of the cold water. You should wear a wet suit as a matter of course and if you've capsized and even just begin to feel cold don't be afraid to call it a day. Remember COLD CAN AND DOES KILL. The rescue drivers rota for the early part of the season has been prepared and will be on the notice board. Jack and I are off for our own spot of sailing - two weeks on the Canberra — on April 17th (hard luck Norman, Ed.) and in my absence Ken Hughes will take over. (Perhaps I could enter for the Mamgu Trophy this year!). Finally may I congratulate Mary Greygoose for the consistently high standard of Navigans which has brought a refreshing break to us during the winter months. -—= 9 os The following article came into the hands of our President, Mr. Jack Pateman, from an unknown source:= "MARINE CASUALTY = A report sighted by Captain G.P. Byth (1940). Dear Sir, I write in haste in order that you will get this report before you form your preconceived opinions from reports in the world press, for I am sure that. they will tend to over=dramatise the affair. We had just picked up the pilot, and the apprentice had returned from changing the 'G* flag for the *H', and being his first trip was having difficulty in rolling the 'G* flag up, I therefore proceeded to show him how, coming to the last part I told him to ‘let go', the lad, although willing is not too bright, necessitating my having to repeat the order in a sharper tone. The Chief Officer overhearing from the Chart room, and thinking that it was the anchors that were being referred to repeated the ‘let go' to the Third Officer on the forecastle. The effect of letting from the the port anchor drop ‘pipe’ while the vessel was proceeding at full harbour speed proved too much for the windlass brake, and the entire length of the cable was pulled out ‘by the roots? I fear that the damage to the chain locker may be extensive. The braking effect naturally caused the vessel to sheer in that direction, right towards the swing bridge that spans a tributary to the river up which we were proceeding. The swing bridge operator showed great presence of mind by opening the bridge for my vessel, unfortunately he did not think to stop the vehicular traffic. The result being that the bridge partly opened and deposited a Volkswagen, two cyclists and a cattle truck on the foredeck. In his efforts to stop the progress of the vessel the Third Officer dropped the starboard anchor, too late to be of practical use for it fell on the swing bridge operator's control cabin. Up to now I have confined my report to the activities at the forward end of my vessel, aft they were having their own problems. At the moment the port anchor was let go, the Second Officer was supervising the making fast of the after tug, and was lowering the ship's towing spring down onto the tug. The sudden braking effect on the port anchor caused the tug to 'run in under! the stern of my vessel, just at the moment when the propellor was answering my double ring Full Astern. The prompt action of the Second Officer in securing the inboard end of the towing spring delayed the sinking of the tug by some minutes thereby allowing the safe abandoning of that vessel, It never fails to amaze me, the actions and behaviour of foreigners during moments of minor crisis. The pilot for instance, is at this moment huddled in the corner of my day cabin, alternately crooning to himself and crying after having consumed a bottle of gin in a time that is worthy of inclusion in the Guinness Book of Records, The tug captain on the other hand reacted violently and had to forcibly be restrained by the Steward, who has him handcuffed in the ship's hospital. I enclose the names and addresses of the drivers and insurance companies of the vehicles on my foredeck, which the Third Officer collected after his somewhat hurried evacuation of the forecastle, these particulars will enable you to claim for the damage that they did to the railings of number one hold. I am closing this preliminary report for I am finding it difficult to concentrate with the sound of police sirens and their flashing lights. Had the apprentice realized that there is no need to fly pilot flags after dark, none of this would have happened. I am Sir, Yours faithfully, MASTER.”

- l]0. REMEMBER = COLD CAN KILL Extract from R.Y.A. Publication = G 16, Hypothermia is the most dangerous of conditions caused by exposure to cald, and is a condition best avoided} Indeed, cold is probably. the main threat to life during prolonged immersion in any waters other than trapical ones. It is therefore sensible to assess the risks befere sailing on cold water and take all possible precautions te avoid becoming chilled. when the water is very cold, say around 5 C (41 F) a man of ordinary build would be hypothermic and helpless in half=-an—hour or less. He would be reduced to the same state within one or two hours if the water were 15°C (59°F) although these times may be doubled by the wearing of conventional clothing and even more if special clothing is worn. Some sailing clubs insist on their members wearing "wet-suits" when water temperatures are below 5°C(41°F) and this is a very wise rule because, quite apart from hypothermia, immersion in cold water can cause sudden death and because the shock of immersion makes it difficult to breathe: normally. Avoidance — Avoiding hypothermia therefore resolves itself into a matter of wearing a sufficiency of warm clothing with a wind=proof and waterprooff outer layer. When in the water it is preferable to float quietly and wear gloves or mittens whenever possible to minimise the chance of cold injury to the fingers. Ignorance — There seems to exist a considerable ignorance about the dangers of immersion in cold water, or alternatively, there is a reluctance to accept that the hazard is important. Measures are taken to avoid ordinary physical injury and drowning and, indeed, most sportsmen and others are familar with the first aid treatment of these conditions. Oddly enough, the universal acceptance of approved life-jackets has probably increased the danger of death from hypothermia, though only because drowning is delayed long enough for cooling to take place. Drowning occurs very rapidly after immersion in cold water because of certain respiratory reflexes and the fact that very few people can swim for more than a few minutes in very cold water, More and more enthusiastic sailors, canoeists and others use their boats all the year round, even when conditions are extremely cold. In general, such activity should be encouraged, but with reservations, because there is no doubt that there is an appreciable hazard, although the risks can be reduced to an acceptable level by sensible appreciation of the simple actions necessary to reduce the possibility of injury by cold, and the reasons for them. Your committee strongly advise all dinghy sailors to wear wetsuits when sailing particularly in the Spring and Autumn Series. WINTER MEETING = VIDEO SHOW = 1980 ENTERPRISE WORLDS. M.A.S.C. LOUNGE. ov 5 oF 420 News I am writing this with sticking plasters on certain fingers — this being a sign that the season is well under way and that excellent winds have prevailed (except for one Sunday that is). Three 420's turned out for Spring Points 1 in force 3/4 winds, but very low temperatures, The race was won by Caron and Heather Stuart even though Heather went for a swim during the race. Well done girls and don't forget that you get a free night out with the Fleet Captain every time you win (Notes— two free nights out with the F.C. for those coming second$$). The Easter Series were held in ideal 420 conditions with winds of about force 4 from the north (hence very cold$) and the water was fairly choppye On the Sunday 9 boats started, of which 3 were 420's. It was obvious from the morning start that it was a 420's day, as the Solos and Laser were left behind in the spray. Russell Jeffries was out with his newly acquired boat and he rapidly discovered new found power that led to a few encounters of the fishy kind$ The race finished with Heather Stuart and myself taking first place with Pete and Dave Sayer a close second. The afternoon was virtually a repeat of the morning with a slightly shorter course due to the extreme cold. Easter Monday arrived with almost identical conditions to the Sunday with the exception that the water was a little flatter. In the absence of Heather Stuart (come back Heather = all is forgiven!) Malcolm Stuart kindly crewed for me. Malcolm and myself went into an early lead after a good start but on the first spinnaker reach the spinnaker pole snapped and we capsized. Malcolm landed on his back on the half extended centre=board waving his legs in the air. How he achieved this position defies logic and in my startled condition I thought he was either signalling to the rescue boat or had assumed his famed vasectomy position! However, by the time the boat was righted Pete and Dave Sayer had taken the initiative and had sped past to win the race. So it was all down to the last race with lots of sailing psychology being applied in the bar at lunchtime. The race proved to be very exciting with Pete and Dave getting away to a good start leaving Malcolm and myself to restart after crossing the line before the start signal. Some lost ground was made up on the leading 420 but no amount of effort could prevent Pete and Dave coming home first and winning the series. Well dorelads, and I hope those two large Easter Eggs make you fat! Fleet Duties. By the time this is published a list of fleet duties up to August llth will have been posted on the 420 notice board. - 3 = The First Time A Nearly True Story. Well, there was I, the owner of a motor cruiser, and suddenly the cost of my trips poodling up and down the river were beginning to get quite frighteningly high. It was then that a friend suggested that what I was doing was not real boating, and offered to introduce me to sailing. He took me sailing in a Wayfarer on an idyllic summer Sunday evening with a puff of wind blowing now and then, and we cruised down to the local hostillery and drifted back somewhat more ballasted than when we went. That was the moment I decided that this sailing was for me. [I decided that I would like to build a popular fibre=-glass dinghy because the local dealer was very close, and I was sure he could advise me if I got into trouble, but to cut a very long story short that was an absolute disaster, because, not only was the dealer an incompetent fool, who eventually delivered to my home enough resin and matt to build two Morning Clouds (the gel of which was the wrong colour anyway), but as the moulds (hired from the imcompetent fool) were being delivered, one half fell off the trailer and was last seen apparently trying to overtake a police car on Blue Bell Hill. After that I decided to look through the magazines, try to find a second= hand boat, and suddenly there she was, an Enterprise, called Wild Times, trolley, trailer, cover, and all go fast gear. What else could I ask for (I didn't even know what size an Enterprise was$) but the owner proudly told me of the races she has won and the thought of getting to the hostillery somewhat quicker than the Wayfarer spurred me one I took delivery on a day that was to be somewhat of an omen. A ; tremendous thunderstorm was in progress, complete with lightning, hail and torrential raine A bedraggled man rang the door bell and asked if this was Mr. Noah's house, handed me a soggy envelope with a "certificate" in it and disappeared into the wettness forever. So Wild Times was mine. That weekend I thought I'd sort out all the ropes and wires and funny looking gear and it took several lengthy phone calls to my friend with the Wayfarer to rig the mast, but finally we made it and decided to hoist the sails — whereupon the boat promptly blew over, and looked most undignified lying on the next doorneighbours car, so we very hurriedly righted her before it was noticed (my neighbour is a very big bloke, and has no sense of humour?). I think it was then that I noticed these silver things in the bottom of the boat. I rang my friend and again "it's okay, those are the elevstrom bailers", "just part of the sophisticated bailing system". Then I noticed two perspex flaps in the flat end, I rang my friend again “what are the windows for", I asked, "just part of the sophisticated bailing system", he said, and this time I detected a touch of impatience in his voice, I then noticed something else which I didn't understand, but decided not to ring my friend as maybe I was straining relationships a bit far. So the big day arrived. Michael Fish said it would be force 3/4 and sunny and warm — and so it was. My wife and son rigged the boat while I took one more glance at my "teach yourself" sailing book. It is at this stage I should explain that the better half of my marriage was not relishing the maiden voyage of Wild Times, and with life jacket, water wings and Rosary at the ready climbed aboard. A good shove from me and we were sailing."Beautiful — now I think the pub is that way", It was then I wished I had strained my relationship with my friend to one phone call more, because there were these two holes in the transom letting in water like the Murda Dam after 603 Squadron had finished. The crew drew my attention to the fact and I informed the crew that it was all right — probably just part of the sophisticated bailing system and when we really got going the stern will lift and the Elevstroms would take the water away", Well, it didn't happen quite like that. In fact the water got deeper and deeper and crew got more and more agitated until I wasn't sure whether it was my blood pressure causing the screaming in my ears or the crew requesting — no demanding = that I do /continuede

mt kk = somethinge Fortunately, just across the river to where we had launched is an island, and we headed like a wounded wallowing water buffalo towards the beach with the finger of the crews glove in one drain: hole and my bobble hat jammed in the other. We landed, and with the crew standing with arms akimbo (the classic mother-in-law pose) demanded I empty the Medway back into the Medway. “What with?", I asked, meekly. "You work it out — you're the skipper", came the acid reply. I looked around for something to bail with — nothing — not a thinge There was only one thing to do — I took off one of my wellies and started to bail. This was too much for the crew who broke into uncontrollable hysterical laughter. Somebody said that being a skipper is a lonely business so I took. no notice. I got the boat relaunched with my hankie ripped in half, and, with a big knot tied in each, rammed into the drain holes. We sailed back to the slip whereupon the crew ran to the parked car, screaming oaths about male chauvenists, incompetent helmsman, and mumbling "that's it, that's it, never again{". So it was that the crew of Wild Times hurled themselves at the delights of sailing. A short time after this we found, and joined, the local sailing club - with all the advice and help one could ever wish for (plus a safety boat on hand). There, Wild Times and both of her crew learned how to sail safely and properly, and the true reason for their existance, which is to continually cut down the amount.of — time that it: takes to reach the pub on the river, , —_ HORNET NEWS A number of Marconi Hornets have done well at recent open meetings. « © = Rule 50 states that a yacht whose entry has been accepted and which sails about in the vicinity of the starting line between her preparatory (i.e. 5=minute) signal and the starting signal shall rank as a starter whether she starts or not. I've always understood that this requirement is satisfied if a yacht is actually in the water at the 5eminute signal, even if merely being held stationary by a member of the crew, and still ranks as a starter even if held after the starting signal or indeed never actually crosses the start line at all. In one race this year, it appeared from the race box that one yacht was still on the hard at the Seminute signal and, in accordance with the rule, did not rank as a starter, In fact the yacht was still on the hard at the start signale The yacht in question then got afloat, sailed up to and crossed onto the pre—course side of the line, and started "correctly" (if that is possible for a yacht not ranking as a starter!}). This rather confused the race officer who was now assailed by doubts as to whethers= (a) the yacht should rank as a starter by the mere fact of having "signed on" ? (b) since the start had been towards the west (ise. towards A mark) and the —_ yacht approached the start line from the course side, should she have been regarded as a premature starter and the class flag left at the dip ? (c) would the race officer be held up to public ridicule had the yacht subsequently "won" and protest ensued ? In the event, the yacht conveniently capsized (no harm done) and "retired", but had she completed the race in a winning position (more=than=likely possibility) then an interesting protest meeting might have resulted. Subsequent discussion indicated the race officer was correct and the yacht did not rank as a starter, Of course, all this can be avoided if you get off your hard and start sailing = or at least "float your boat" = before the preparatory (5S-minute) signal. signed = The Watcher in the Little Wooden Hut. a SAILING TECHNIQUES FOR TIROS — We have members in our Club who have a wealth of knowledge which I feel sure would be of real interest and value to novice or less experienced sailors. Why not use Navigans as the medium to impart your pearls of wisdom! Unfortunately most potential contributors are too busy sailing to put pen to paper but somebody has to make a start = so here goes} There are many excellent books available on boat tuning and the sailing techniques and tactics necessary to win races, but the Tiro can sasily become confused by the detail and get his priorities all wrong, e.g. the finer points of tuning and having the best equipment only marginally effect performance whereas what really matters is Helming Ability, or as it is sometimes said, the nut on the end of the tiller. How does one obtain this Helming Ability? Obviously there is no substitute for hours spent on the water, nevertheless there are bad practises which need to be unlearned and good practises which must be followed at all times if you are to get amongst the race leaders. Probably the most difficult skill to master is the ability to sail to windward. It is here that most races are won or lost. Sailing to Windward Getting to the windward mark first depends on a combination of speed and directiane Direction is a matter of choosing the shortest route by making use of /continuede

a oF mw the wind and tide but it is no good going in the right direction if you are not getting there fast enough. Real improvements in speed to windward may be obtained if certain basic points are understood and mastered. It is the relative trim of the sail and centreboard which determine how well you sail to windward. If the boat is not to slide sideways through the water the centreboard must generate a sideways force equal to that exerted by the sail. NeB. In order to generate drive and sideways force it is necessary for both the sail and the centreboard to be set at a small angle of incidence to the wind and water respectively. Priority 1 — Keep the boat Upright. Both the sail and the centreboard operate at maximum efficiency when the boat is absolutely level and the mast and centreboard are vertical. Centreboard theory. The force generated by the centreboard (F C.) is proportional to the square of the speed of the boat through the water (S) and the angle of incidence to the water (A), ieee F Ce 00 A.S*, The angle of incidence is in fact the angle at which the boat is slipping away to leeward. Every effort must be made therefore to keep this angle to a minimum. Remember Aoof C. and 1/82, If the boat is to be kept upright all the heeling forces must balance. Let us consider a typical situation. (Any resemblance to a SOLO is purely intentional). \ X Centre of Effort alll 2el m 3m Centre of Lateral Resistance If the boat is not to accelerate sideways the force generated by the centreboard must equal that provided by the sail ie@e F Se = F Ce The boat is prevented from heeling solely by the balancing effect of the weight of the crew. It follows therefore that the maximum force that can be handled depends on the ability of the helm/crew to sit out for long periods, ise. F Se = WX dy CcoQe a 12 stone helm sitting comfortably on the side deck (d = .75m) will only manage a driving force equal to that of a 9 stone athlete sitting well out (d = 1m). NOTE SOWESTER LIFEJACKETS OTHER THAN THOSE MADE BY AIRBORNE ARE NOT AFFECTED. TAKING YOUR MOORING To the single=handed yachtsman taking his mooring, every second counts. Having grasped the buoy it still takes several seconds to belay the mooring rope round the bitts, while to haul in the chain to the required length and flick it vigourously to remove most of the mud, may take minutes and a lot could happen in this time. The operation can be facilitated by splicing a loop of strong line into the main mooring rope at about one metre from the buoy. It is then an easy matter to haul in the buoy over the anchor chain rollers just far enough to secure this loop round the bitts. The skipper can then relax and return at leisure to the cockpit to stop the engine or release the sheets, which have an uncanny habit of fouling on these occasions. But don't forget to haul in the chain and secure it before going ashore Incidentally, it is much easier for the boat hook to take the loop rather than the thick strop or the buoy itself. oO 3 = The distance involved is about 40 miles each way which will be sailed entirely with favourable neap tidese This means the fleet will leave Stansgate at 10 am on the Saturday morning. The return trip on Monday will leave at high tide = about 10.30 am. On each of these trips it will be essential to maintain a speed of 4% knots, which will mean use of the motor if the wind is unfavourable. From a comfort point of view the trip as a fleet would be called off if winds were expected to be above force 4. From a safety viewpoint the expectation of fog would also mean cancellation. I did this trip in Kalinka at Regatta time this year and found it an easy one in the conditions we then had. It worked out that I did 50/50 sailing and motoring as breezes came and went. I had about 1 mile of visibility which pressnted no problem and we completed the trip with time to spare before the tide changed. Please let me know if you hope to come then I will give out any final details as necessary. Anyone who would like to come as a crew should also contact me as there may be boats looking for crews. Remember Rochester have been visiting us regularly for several yearse One small detail is worth giving at present. Do not bring rigid dinghies, but inflatables. In my experience these are best towed stern first hauled in tightly to the transom by two warps attached to the outboard mounting points of the inflatable. This prevents flipping in a strong breeze, and if you get something round your prop you have a stable platform from which to work to remove ite In my case recently it was a large piece of polythene that came off easily with the boat hook.
