Beehive and Tijo left Stansgate for Lavington Marina with Margaret Cambell from Tijo stating that as she had six people on board, namely Tan Campbell and his fiancee Kim and Jimmy Campbell and Jackie Hall as well as themselves plus all the extra food stacked quite high, they were going to have a steady sail and were not going to push it too hard. The wind was a northerly force 4 gusting 5, right on the nose and while sailing with wind over tide in the wallet I watched Tijo being thrown all over the place and realised, not just from the Way my stomach was trying to escape from my mouth, that we were doing exactly the same thing. While keeping my back to the bow of the boat and trying to concentrate on what the first thing was that I would do when discarding with my wet oilies Vic kept me informed of the state of each wave in short form, MY. (medium wave) L.W. (long wave) and F.W. ( which he assured me was a freak wave) With wind over tide it took 9 hours to reach Lavington Marina where we met up with Brenda, Vic and Mary Tate of Copernicus and Sandra and Peter Claydon of Peace who should have been in Holland but were held up by unfavourable weather. The following day (Sunday) we were all held up by very favourable weather when the sun beat down on us and the only relief had to be the nearest watering hole at Lavington, so there we were outside the local pub, taking up most of the seats and tables lunchtime and again the evening and what an enjoyable day that was. Mon. Aug. 3rd. Still glorious sun but winds barely force 2. Copernicus and Peace had left very early that morning for their destination in Holland and we set motor for Southwold. According to Mr Trigg, the harbour master, our boats would be able to enter the Southwold entrance at any state of the tide. We approached the entrance at about 7.15 pem. and low tide was about 8 p.m. We saw Tijo who was just ahead of us looking slightly stationary for just a few seconds and when we followed we realised why, we bumped a few times but made it in okay. At least we know now just where the bar lies. On tying up at the quayside we were delighted to find that the pub there was serving fresh fried fish and chips ~ bonus - especially for me wno had ran out of calor gas that day and had been looking forward to a mere sandwich that evening. It was the freshest fish and chips we'd tasted for a long time. Whilst in the town the following day (Tuesday), Tijo's scouts spotted a fellow member, Bill Penkham of Sirius but although we made our way to where the sighting had taken place, he had obviously gone to ground or perhaps we'd passed him on the way, anyway we returned to our boats in readiness for our sail? to Lowestoft the next day. At this point, Margaret discovered that Tijo's loo was completely blocked to which we all discussed the possibilities of the cause of such a thing while Stan, looking a bit down in the mouth knew that he was going to have to do the curing of it. Weds. Aug. 5th. Still hardly a puff of wind, plenty of sun and some fog banks. Vic and I were sitting having our breakfast in the cockpit, marvelling at the still glorious morning when other sounds caught our eare coming from Tijo -

It was Stan, banging and retching whilst clearing his blocked loo = suddenly, up came the forehatch cover and one at a time out jumped the four inhabitants who had been sleeping only seconds beforehand, gasping for air as they came. The job done and up came stan, bucket in hand and proceeded to throw the contents overboard - on our side = oh well, we werent that hungry anyway. Before leaving Southwold we met up with another Macwester called Penelope Jane, the owners were schoolteachers on holiday and had sailed down from Humberside, so before leaving there were hurried inspections of each others boats. The weather conditions were so calm en-route to Lowestoft it was hard to believe that this was the north sea, and it seemed Jimmy Campbell didn't believe it either and leapt overboard to investigate, attached to a warp and a buoy - although we rather suspected that Margaret and Stan had that many on board they'd been eaten out of a boat and a dinghy so they'd cast Jimmy overboard as live bait - but the fish didn't want to know. Reaching Lowestoft, was for me, absolutely wonderful - although our main intention for this holiday was to go to Lowestoft I somehow had the thought in the back of my mind that weather conditions would not allow it in the two short weeks that we had - me of little faith. We had been forewarned that the mooring charges would be £6. a night for our boats in the outer harbour, but if we had chosen to wait until the road bridge was lifted we could have gone up river for a mile or so and the sailing club there would have let us use their moorings for £1.50 a night, but as we did not want to be dependant on waiting for the bridge to be opened for coming out we rafted up in the outer harbour where, with quite a lot of other boats, especially Dutch, spent a few not too comfortable days of snubbing and not too easy times getting onto the ladder up onto the quayside. The Royal Norfolk and Suffolk Yacht Club however was very welcoming and very comfortable, we proudly left a Marconi burgee to be hung amongst the other club burgees in one of the lounges. Fri. Aug. -7the Left Lowestoft for the Butley River, once again hardly any wind but the sea had some nice rollers coming in and when Tijo and Beehive were both in a ‘downer’ we could only see each others masts, In spite of the fact that we were having to motor again it was a very pleasant trip. On passing Southwold the Macwester we had previously met there called Penelope Jane re-joined us and stayed in our company for the following week. — Sat Aug 8th. Left the Ore making for the Deben and Woodbridge Marina. Passed Ron Phillips of Vanellus making for Lowestoft and Ann and John Smith of Freya making for the Ore. We were to meet up with Wendy, Jean and Peter Hall (and one plastered leg) of Jappa in Woodbridge and their guests for the weekend, John and Shiela of Two's Company, where we spent a very pleasant weekend. A very reluctant John and Shiela had to leave Woodbridge by train to go home on the Monday and I dont think that the rest of us waving them off and jumping up and down at the station made them feel any better. Monday night the men had our five gallon water container half filled with real ale in readiness for the bar-b-que the following night. Tues. Aug. IIth. Prepared to leave Woodbridge Marina for the Rocks, weather glorious again and a calm day. Vic had rather a long walk into town to get petrol before we could leave as only diesel fuel is available in the Marina. On reaching the Rocks we walked to Ramsholt and collected wood on the way back in readiness for the much awaited bar=-b=que that night. It was Kims birthday as well so it was to be a celebration, and we certainly had a terrific celebration the singing round the fire that night was pure harmony - well it sounded so at the time although we did start a few wolves howling somewhere in the distance. /to be continued in September.

The distance is 14 miles, the same as last year. I hope you will be able to participate and can persuade all your friends to sponsor you on the form overleaf. Attached is a map showing the route and the stage points where there will be vehicles to pick up anyone who wants to drop out. There will also be transport available to get you back to the starting point if you need Lt. We should meet at 9,30 a.m at the gate leading to St Peters and I recommend you bring a windproot jacket as well as boots or strong shoes and a spare pair of socks. It is absolutely essential that participants "sign-in" at the start and that no one leaves for home without advising Carolyn or me. I will be the back marker and will not leave the start betore 10.00 a.m. Please follow the route precisely as shown on the map, particularly the section from Marconi S.C. to Steeple Bay. Locking forward to seeing you on Saturday August 7. Peter Marshall

Those living in the Maldon area may have seen in the local newspaper a report that a site for tipping rubbish is proposed at Stansgate. The situation is that four sites have been put forward by Maldon and these are to be presented to the Essex County Council for their consideration and they expect to choose one or two of these, when planning permission will be sought. Maldon [redacted], HORNET WORLDS 1982 Highcliff Sailing Club. August lst to 6th. Five Marconi boats entered the World Championships this year at Highcliff Sailing Club. Dave Harper crewed by Murray Todd, Colin Harper crewed by Danny Lumley, Simon Kenworthy crewed by Ian Stott, Graham Mead crewed by Mike Turner and Pat Black crewed by Caron Stuart. After a good journey down to Highcliff, the boats were unpacked, measured, weighed and then entered, this taking all of the Saturday. However, with 70 boats to be done and with nice sunny warm conditions, the wait did'nt seem all that longe All the boats were passed fit, but a little on the heavy side, and we all looked forward to an eventful series on large Olympic courses. Sunday Practice Racee Winds light, Westerly, Variable. The fleet started first time and on time on a very long line start. Colin Harper 2100 sorted out the wind shifts on the first beat to arrive 7th at the windward marke Simon Kenworthy 2093 started late, after being line shy, to reach the mark in the pack with Dave Harper 2078 not far behind. The first reach developed into a run allowing the back of the fleet to overtake the middle of the fleet. Many place changes took place with 2093 and 2070 moving up through the fleet during the following legs. The first 6 boats, led by Malcolm Goodwin 2101, got well clear of the fleet on the second triangle and kept their respective positions till the finish. Colin finished 11th with Simon finishing 17th after a close tacking duel against three boats, Dave in 2078 finished in 24th place, Monday Race One. Winds light, Southerly, Variable. The Sailing Committee decided to run a gate start using the tenth finisher of the practice race as pathfinder. The first start was recalled because the pathfinder's wind was being blocked by early starters and also he did not sail for the minimum of 3 minutes. This meant that the late starters, including 2101, were unable to cross the line. The second start was better and it paid to start late. 2101 arrived first at the mark and held this position till the end of the race. Graham Mead 2108 rounded about 10th with Simon close behind in 15th. The pathfinder did well in this race rounding the mark in 8th place. Places at the front changed on the first reach with 2108 moving up to 3rd which he held to the finish. Simon in 2093 moved up to 10th /continued.

- 5 = and held this to the finish. Both Colin 2100 and Dave 2078 were unfortunately disqualified for failing to ‘sign off*, Tuesday Race Two. Winds light, Southerly, Variable. Pat Black having dashed down to Highcliff and slept in the car, entered as a late arrival in this race. The race was started after a three hour postponement waiting for wind. Simon was relieved to find they were not using a gate start for this race. Both 2100 and 2108 got off to good starts but, unfortunately, 2093 was baulked on the start and unable to tack into clear wind, got left behind. 2101 won this race to put him in a strong position overall in the series, with 2108 finishing llth and 2100 15th. Simon managed 26th, Dave came in 30th and Pat finished 45th. Wednesday Race Three. Winds light, Westerly, Variable. This was a copy of Race Two from 2093's point of view and although the wind picked up later in the race, 2100 and 2108 were too far away to catch. During this race there were many cases of mark violations and protests ensued well into the night. There was a major hiccup at the front of the fleet with Sally Allyard winning the race and 2101 coming 4th. Colin finished 11th, four places in front of Graham in 15th. 2093 came in 26th. Dave Harper had to retire after a capsize at the Gybe mark as also did Pat Black after one on. the reach. Thursday Race Four. Winds medium, Easterly. After a good start 2093 misread the first beat to round the first mark in the middle of the pack. 2108 managed to wriggle through to escape the crush. Colin after a bad start managed to pick his way up the first beat to be somewhere just behind the other two. . Just after the start 2078 staged his spectacular capsize as a ploy to distract the fleet However this proved to be unsuccessful and he found himself last. 2100 overtook 2093 on the third beat along with twenty other boats after 2093 went the wrong side up the beat} Colin finished 20th and after a good run and final beat Simon finished 3 boats behind in 23rd place. Dave Harper, after overtaking 20 boats, finished 42nd and Graham finished very well in 11th place. 2041 was unfortunately well down in the placings. The race was won by Malcolm Goodwin thus ensuring him of overall victory in the series, Friday Race Five. Winds medium, Easterly. As 2101 had won the Championships he did not need to enter this race and so it was left to somebody else to take line honours. After a good start 2093 tacked into clear wind up the first beat to round the windward mark in 18th place. 2100 and 2108 were not far behind in the pack. This race was won convincingly by Stan Sheppard and, after overtaking /continuede

« Cw 6 boats on one of the reaches, Simon finished llth. Graham and Colin finished 15th and 21st respectively and Dave came in 52nd. Pat in 2041 unfortunately retired. So, this meant that Malcolm Goodwin and Derek Gentry in 2101, from Brightlingsea, had won the Worlds, Second was Chris and Andy Stodell, also from Brightlingsea. Marconi boats finished 9th(2108, 18th(2100), 20th(2093), Sist(2078) and 2041 further down the pickings. The social events were excellent, as any Hornet event usually is. The Highcliff Sailing Club managed the fleet of 70 boats very well, sometimes under difficult weather conditions. The Marconi contingent thoroughly enjoyed themselves both ashore and afloat, all vowing to go again to the next championship. Written by Ian Stott on behalf of the Hornet contingent from M.S.C. MIRROR FLEET NEWS CAMPING/CADET WEEK (TWTWTW) = That Was The Week That Was — and what a most delightful time we had at the camping week this summer. Phil Gray worked extremely hard to organise an activity week which both cadets and adults enjoyed to the full = aided and abetted by his brother Bob Gray who gave all those interested a first Class introduction to the art of canoeing. On behalf of the Mirror Fleet my thanks to Phil and Bob and to all those others who contributed to a wonderful week, including Frank Savill who helped us prop up the bar by pulling the pints on the other side. (Mirror) Fleet Cruise = I got my cruise in after all, thanks to TWTWTW during which a combined fleet cruise was arranged to Heybridge Basine A fleet of some 13 dinghies included four Mirrors helmed by Robert Coy, Maggie, Philip Taylor and myself. The wind was, to say the least, a bit patchy and most of us had to hitch a tow from a couple of passing cruiserse However, Philip Taylor (son of Mick Taylor) and Jim Coy (GP 14) both showed they had a nose for smelling out what wind there was and got to Heybridge way before we other poor souls drifted ine After a mild liquid lunch at the local ale house, we had a nice beat back to the Club and finished with a feeling that it was a day well spent. My thanks to Ray Ball and Murray Bates who sailed cruisers to act as guard boats. I must say I thoroughly enjoyed the cruise and wonder whether one or two “officially sponsored" dinghy cruises couldn't be included in future sailing programmes. Racing Backwards = one of the events during TWTWTW was an obstacle race on both land and river. The last time I did anything like this was on basic training at RAF Padgate many years ago = and I think I'm a bit out of practise. Stephen Jeffries (11 years) proved quite conclusively that he can run much faster than I can during the ‘land® part of the race, whilst Maggie proved she can beat me sailing backwards as well as forwards during the "river" part of the race. Considering the times I've managed to sail backwards accidently during normal races, an inability to sail backwards over the finishing line on this occasion was close to being irksome. Racing Forwards = the Mirror Fleet continues to enjoy some good competitive racing even if our numbers are disappointingly smalle In one race, Vic Braybrook and myself were so intent on tactical manoeuvres upon each other that we missed out "Dp" mark and had to sail some considerable distance back to round it correctly. In the meantime Bob Leeder had kept himself well clear of our fun and games and sailed through to take a clear and well deserved wine There must be a lesson there somewheree Although I have not yet seen the official results, Vic has obviously /continuede

om am won the Summer Points Series — congratulations Vic} We now look forward to the Autumn Seriese During the summer sailing John Stringer managed to break his tiller, and the very next week my tiller broke whilst tacking shortly before the start of a race. I actually started using the stub of the tiller but that also gave way after a few tacks and I took the hint and retired for an early shower. Like the fisherman and the one that got away, I'm certain I would have been on a winning streak that day = anyway that's my tale andI'm sticking to it. Capsize Drill - I'm glad my youngsters attended Phil Gray's cadet classes during the winter and the practical Saturday afternoon capsize practise earlier this year. Maggie and I peered over Phil's shoulder as he instructed the cadets and thereby provided ourselves with some useful revision. Consequently, when Maggie and I capsized recently during heavy weather we were able to right the boat without much difficulty. I reckon the capsize was caused by my crew standing up when I called “Gybe Oh" and consequently ending up leeward of the mainsail. Maggie reckons it would help if I gave the commands before the event and not afterwards. Anyway, her cry of anguish and shock as she disappeared below the cold waters of the Blackwater did introduce a comical element into the situation — at least from where I was sitting shortly before I, too, slid into those self=same waters. Helmsman of the Year Qualifier — much to her relief, Maggie will not be the Mirror Fleet representative this year. Although I haven't seen the official results, I believe the Mirror Fleet will be represented by Vic Braybrook. Racing Stop=Press — Autumn Points 1 and 2 have seen the welcome return of Mick Taylor to the Mirror Fleet. He scored two very convincing firsts to present Vic, Bob Leeder and myself a problem to ponder upon until Nose 3 & 4e A warm welcome to his crewedaughter Helen and crew-son Mark. Let's hope more adult/child teams will emerge to join our racing fun. WANTED =— CARAVAN Anyone thinking of selling a 4 berth Mike Boreham, caravan? I'm thinking of buying one and may be interested Mirror Fleet Captain. in yourse [redacted], CADET WEEK I have just calculated that I have spent twenty days under canvas during August. I know this to my cost as I have lost weight, am a mass of cuts and bruises and find difficulty in sleeping in a warm soft bed. Apart from the fact that there are grounds for a divorce in the Gray camp I would not begrudge one of those days. Cadet Week will remain in our memories for some time and whilst we sit by our winter firesides with the snow gently carpeting the landscape, we will harken back to those halcyon days of warm sun, blue seas and insect bites, My fondest memory of the week (apart from a full bottle of whisky brought to my tent at a moment of dire need) is the sight of scrubber Mike Boreham making a fool of himself in the diving competition. I didn't tell you at the time Mike, but I thought you were better than that idiot in a stupid shirt who eskimo rolled off the board} Another fond memory will be the sight of Murray Bates' face when contestants in the treasure hunt kept pestering him for his autograph. Murray didn't_ appear to make as many beers out of this activity as I did from another part of the proceedings$ /continuede

- f° — Congratulations must be extended to the Pete, Bob and Stephen team for noticing that the flags at the racebox were in fact hoisted at the yardarm and not at the masthead. However, it did not help them to win! Further congratulations are also in order for Damian Boreham for producing the smallest crab ever seen on the Blackwater. In fact this very.same crab can be seen through an electron microscope at the Natural History Museum. There was a marked absence of wind during the week (apart from that coming from Kate’s tent that is) and although this curtailed some of the planned sailing activities it appeared at times that we had forsaken sailing for canoeing! My only memory of the canoeing races is that of suffering pains in places where I didn't even know I had places! If the Obstacle Race is ever held again the rules will be changed so that I can win something’ It showed me two things = firstly I do not sail backwards well and secondly that for those intrepid single handed sailors in a two man dinghy who do in fact raise the spinnaker (well done John in the Hornet and me in the 420) - these should be rewarded with a longer spinnaker leg (weather permitting that is!). I observed several things during this epic event. Firstly during the capsize exercise, on leaping over the side I found that Kate had not put the centreboard down$!$ (what are crews coming to these days). Secondly two man (or one man, one girl or one boy, one girl, etc.) lasers came first and second, and thirdly we appear to have an olympic swimmer in the club who can swim from A mark to Osea faster that a dinghy can sail the same distance Anyway, everyone joined in the spirit of the event and I'm thinking of joining the Hornet Fleet to learn how to sail backwards. The innumerable games of volleyball, rounders and football once again brought out the competitive spirit in everyone. The volleyball produced a superstar in Janet Chisnall whose spatial awareness and her dexterity close in to the net was sheer poetry. (Janet — I was a little disappointed that you didn't keep falling on me this year$) The mixed football proved to be very physically demanding with some impressive tackling and dribbling (I had forgotten my handerchief!). Power struggles eventually started between the Gray Brothers and a duo of Robert Weedon/Little John Chisnall and the game was only finished when Lucy Boreham stopped an almost certain winning shot from Bob Gray, with the back of her head. Well done Lucy, and keep taking the pills luv. What a great game rounders is when you have a left hander on your team who can whack the ball. into the ditch and then stroll round for one rounder. Even with this advantage, the final outcome was very close and apart from a few obvious cases of obstruction, (worth half a rounder I believe) very little rule=bending was evident (shame$). Man overboard drill for the Cadets went with a splash with scenes reminiscent of the Marie Celeste. Some cadets were seen re=entering the boat over the stern and this is to be discouraged as even a big cadet like myself can get over the side! (enough of the serious stuff). To those of you: who enjoyed the week, on your behalf I would like to thank the followinge Cheers John and Murray for the support and something like ten man= hours of work (hard work) in constructing the deathslide. Thanks to Bob and Russell for their help on the Sunday and to Bob for all the canoeing instruction and the nightcapse Thanks to the Sailing Sub-committee for their finalcial support and the authorisation of the splashing out on prizes (they haven't had the bill yet!). Thanks to Mike Boreham for the prize=giving ceremony (see list of prize winners at the end) = you lucky devil Mike, I hear you got two kisses from Kate. Special thanks from Bob and myself to all those that so generously contributed towards our second favourite pastime. Finally thanks to all those that joined in the spirit of things and for anyone that may have been bored for the odd hour or two — you had better watch out next year$ /continuede

NATIONALS AT LLANDUDNO The Marconi Fleet and families descended in force on the Brig-y=Don Hotel at Llandudno for what turned out to be a very windy and curtailed event. Of the 49 entrants 4 were from Marconi, and the results were as follows:= 1. Geof Carveth = Littleton S.C.-23. 2e Martin Payne = Salcombe Y.C. —7. 3e Guy Bradbury Dover Y.C. —7. 17. Ron Greygoose -42. 18. John Salmon -43. 25. Roger Smith -55. 42. Geof Josey -118. Tan and Sue Shaw arrived and entered at the last minute, and finished lOth and 20th respectively. Only 2 races were completed in the series. A last desperate attempt was made to run 2 races on the last day, but this was abandoned after the start. Half the fleet managed to get afloat through the surf, but some (me included) didn't make it. Many boats suffered damage and broken tillers were the order of the day. The lack of sailing did have compensations as we were all able to spend time together and make a real holiday of our stay. Other notable items were:-— 1. John managed to up=-end Jack Holt on the promenade! 2. Roger was leading Ian Shaw in the final race before it was abandoned? 3. Geof never stopped eating scones and searching newsagents for a plastic mac. 4. Margaret's hairdrier did not set the hotel on fire, despite any rumours to the contrarye The Hayling Island Club took the team prize = we thought we could be in the running at one stage. The final departure was marred by an unfortunate accident when Caroline was knocked down by a passing care Roger, Wendy and Grandma, had to stay on for a few days until Caroline was well enough to return home. oi EGM MARCONT SAILING CLUB: Code of Practice for Launching and Recovery of Cruisers Large Boats = Boats above 27 ft length will NOT be allowed on the hard when dinghy events are in progress, At other times they should be handled with great care due to their weight. The tractor is more suitable than winches for heavy boats but see below concerning ropes. Tractor - Only to be operated by authorised drivers. It is extremely dangerous for non key holders to operate the tractor. Winches - When Club organised dinghy events are in progress the winches must be under the charge of an authorised operator. Only the East half of the hard may be used, leaving the West half for dinghies. The OOD will be informed and suitable notices must be displayed for information of dinghy sailors, At other times the following code should be observed:= When winding up the slope always use the ratchet. Winching down the slope should be done by use of the brake with the handle removed. Avoid sharp bends in winch cables = shackles should be used for attachment to trolleys. It is the responsibility of the boat owner to ensure that the operation is done safely. This includes providing a sufficiently strom team of helpers, If the tractor is used to pull boats up or lower them down the slope, the boat owner must provide a rope or cable of suitable strength and sufficient length that the tractor may remain on eae level and always clear of loose shingle. Boat If left submerged should be adequately marked to avoid damage to Trolleys = other boats, Work Boat - This may be operated by any club member after obtaining permission from Peter Clayton who will advise upon its use. A team of at least two people is necessary for work on moorings. wo he OUR COMMODORE'S NOTES Having recovered from the annual withdrawal symptoms once again it is time for the autumn activities. The Laying-Up Supper (which we hope is successful) at the Chancellor Hall, and the A.GeM. which is usually well supported, come close together. The committee are very reluctant to put up members! costs but our expenditure over the last few years has been rising and there is no choice but to increase members! contributions. There were no increases in fees last year when the Club made a loss of a few hundred pounds, thus reducing our reserve to just over £2,000. This year we expect this to fall to around £1,000 which is considered to be the lowest acceptable level. With projected increased expenditure we have to look for extra income next year. Increases in our running costs which are mainly rates, rent, fuel and maintenance are continually rising and unavoidable. Unfortunately membership has fallen over the last few years, but this is the trend nationally so we are no exception, which all means increased fees but we hope you will be aware of the reasons and support the resolution. I wish to thank the many members who turned out at the recent working party and ask that you continue your support as I say my farewell as Commodore, and pass you over to Frank Savill, may Frank's team be a happy one. Many apologies to Sylvia Cris p for having to wait until now ¢ of your Summer Cruise 1981, . 0 see the completion Weds. Aug. I2th. Yet another sunny day. We spent the morning re-cooperating Stan organised the cleaning up of the debris from the night before, heard the news that Peggy and Jimmy James of ‘Sonya had sailed past our boats earlier that day while we were all out for the count and only Peter Hall was up and about to hear them..Now as Peter had his leg encased in plaster, the best way for him to get ashore the night before was to put insulating tape round the foot of his plaster and then put his leg into a plastic bag to keep the plaster dry while rowing ashore. The trouble came very early that morning when Peter woke Jean to say he was in agony because they'd bound the tape tco tightly, so while Jean fumbled for the light switch she also unwittlingly put their clock forward one hour, and when later that day we sailed up to the river Ore, Peter was entering one hour earlier than the rest of us, saying to Jean that he was convinced we'd worked the tide tables wrongly, why else was he taking so long to clear the entrance, We made for a mooring at Aldeburgh that evening but being Wednesday it was early closing so we were disappointed about not being able to get fish and chips for supper, Thurs. Aug. I3th. We made our way for Orford where we spent a few leisurely hours looking round the castle before going back to the Butley river. The castle has an old well covered by an iron grid, and with Stan Campbells natural charm with children he obliged them by letting them know how deep it was by daintily spitting into the well and the kids listened intently with their heads on one side waiting for it to land. By evening we were back in the Butley and once more found our feet taking us in the direction of the Boyton Bell and spending another happy evening in good company, besides, Stan was quite dry after all that spitting, Fri. Aug. T4th. Left the Butley for Lavington Marina, Winters Maid and Myth of Mynto were already there after returning from their holidays in Holland. Now I like to think that coming into a marina presents no problem for me as long as I'm not helming, so I didn't foresee any difficulty this time until on reaching the rest of our boats in Lavington, in readiness to go alongside I suddenly realised that we were going to have to back Beehive in and she does do some odd things when in astern, anyway there were lots of hands there to help us and I think that most of us were to our sleeping bags early that night ready for our first very early start the next morning at 5 a.m. The operation by our Marconi fleet, casting off whilst our eyeballs were still protesting at being woken so early was probably done with great skill - I never noticed - it was all done so quickly but I wont mention the boat who was trying to take the pontoon with him with his stern rope still tied onto it = no better not = he might mention the fact that he was too busy noticing that Tijo was trying to motor off and we still had her tied to our bows. Well for Beehive it was back to the mooring at Stansgate and after such a lovely holiday we were quite sad to leave her = I wonder where we will be going next year?

OAVID URRY — I am sure that we were all shocked to hear of the canoeing (This is a change of date). accident two weeks before Christmas, in which David Urry lost his life. The funeral has already taken place but a memorial service is due to be held. Thursday 17th March Third Winter Meeting M.A.S.C. Lounge. 8.00 pm. Like many of our children David was introduced to the club by parents involved in club activities. Later as a cadet he became a Mirror sailor, but was noted most for his hard work both ashore and in the rescue launch. Recognition of his efforts came in 1978 when he was awarded the Garrett Memorial Trophy. Mike Boreham, Mirror Fleet Captain, [redacted], | HORNET FLEET NEWS I am happy to report that my second attendance at a Hornet Get-together (The Ship, Stock, 25th Feb.) was rewarded with a good turnout. Unfortunately I have not yet seen the assistant F.C. at any of these gatherings (mind you, I have only attended 66.66% of such meetings — well two out of three anyway!). A very enjoyable evening was spent disposed about a large round table and the only person who appeared to be missing was — yes you guessed it = Guinevere! Great pressure was brought to bear on Murray Todd, to hold a party on the weekend of the Dinghy Exhibition. Afterseveralminutes Murray succumbed and by the time you read this you*®ll have to "reach" back into your subconscious to remember it! Judging by conversations during the evening, boat preparation is being left to the last minute so let's get our fingers out and get to it lads! The fleet working party (March 6th) was extremely well supported — so well in fact I was reduced to insulting the assistant F.C. (yes, he does exist after all) for lack of something to doe The "greater" half of the fleet (interpret this as you wish) assembled at the race=box to witness a revolution (not the boat design) in the making, whilst the remainder distributed layers of paint (sometimes on the race marks). The revolution at the race=—box was the brain=-child of our new young Race Equipment Officer whose name escapes me for the moment. It involved the fitting of a semi-automatic continuous halliard flag raising system (otherwise known as SACHFRS). The principal of operation was basically sound but the implementation generated two schools of thought. There were those who argued the case for splicing (minority) and those who argued the case for knots and whipping (majority). I myself belong to the whipping school, but I am always open to suggestion. I had not realised that the simple act of tying a few knots and splices could be the catalyst for so many new relationships. Malcolm Stuart and Geoff Josey (once Solos) were caught in flagrante delicto whilst attempting to seal their frayed ends with burning matches, whilst Sarah and the unknown gent in the flares (sorry I didn't rise to the bait Colin) held intellectual conversations. /continuede

Some of the changes this year are obvious and will I hope make it easier for new members to umderstand. Other detailed changes I should like to bring to your attention are:= PRIZES: Recently 2nd and 3rd prizes have been awarded for all races on the same basis so the special arrangement for open and closed races is deleted. ae ae PERSONAL SAFETY: For all races sailed before the Whit Regatta Wet/Dry suits must be worn by all competitors. Failure to do so will result in disqualification. SIGNING ON AND OFF: Much confusion exists between clubs on what to call race sheets. A declaration sheet can be for signing on or off or both. This year you will have new race sheets and all references are standardised on the most direct description, i.e. Signing On Sheet = Signing Off Sheet. COURSES: Although space did not allow inclusion of a map covering the whole of the river the Year Book does now make reference to the long distance courses traditionally used for All-In and Cruiser races, Details of these courses are available on a new "4 double sided map which will be available at the signing-on point in the club house. DESCRIPTION OF MARKS: The new mark at the East end of the outer cruiser moorings is included as Mark Fe Responsibility for this mark may be taken over by the Fisheries Protection in which case its description will change. To avoid last year's confusion and to allow for new courses the description of E mark this year has not specified it by type or position. Therefore any courses using E mark must add the description on the board at the signing on point. Mike Boreham, Mirror Fleet Captain, [redacted], HORNET NEWS I hope this reaches Mary alright as I'm writing at the eleventh hour as they say. Well, things are hotting up in the sailing world (not the weather I notice) and it has been rumoured that people have actually been sailing! This month started with the Dinghy Exhibition at Crystal Palace and Murray's party. Marconi were well represented at the Exhibition in the form of Mike/Colin/Sarah (the pretty one) and company. The pristine Hornet of Graham Mead apart from being a repository for Hornet balloons, attracted many admirers. Some Marconi Cadets (bless their little cotton socks) complained at the lack of helium in the balloons but this was soon solved by attaching a helium filled Merlin Rocket balloon to the cheaper imitation. Also seen on the stand was a Hornet with an automatic (well semi-automatic) spinnaker pole system. This system appealed to my engineering sensitivities as it appeared to be well thought. out and remarkably economic in its use of blocks, fittings and ropes. It's rumoured that John and Murray may be fitting this system this year as they are convinced that the majority of their swims have resulted from the pre=spinnaker launch balancing act that takes place. The system may well suit us helms with lightweight crews (84 stone naked!) so I shall be watching with some interest (other boats that is!). Anyway well done all those who supported the Hornet stand. The same weekend saw the annual Hornet party once again hosted by Murray Todd. Sue and I had heard so much about these parties that we started training several weeks before. I contented myself with evening runs round the estate to build up my stamina and Sue got cracking on the sausage rolls, eventually producing a round one hundred. I bet you all think I am going to make some really cheap joke here at the expense of Murray but as you now know I am not like that. I would like to thank Murray for a very relaxing evening (ZZZZ....) (sorry Murray, couldn't resist that one!) and a stimulating video show. I couldn't actually see one of the video films as David Harper had his face pressed to the screen = I believe it was something to do with Hornets sailing at Stone. Talking about Stone, don't forget our first race with them is on May lst, 10.30 am start. News is trickling through of a Marconi success at the Burnham Easter Eqq and I hope a report appears in this issue of Navigans or failing that, next month. Now it's slap wrist time. Hands up those of you who attended the last get-together at The Ship. I am reliably informed that Murray Bates (not so Rear Commodore) was the sole attendee on this occasion. In recognition of Murray's devotion to duty I suggest all those members who are 35 years or older buy Murray a drink when they next see him. /continuedo

— That's all the gossip for this month, and hopefully next month will see some reports of the Spring Points racing. Cheers, Worried of Chelmsford. (Name and address supplied). HORNETS AT BURNHAM ( ANYONE FOR A G & T?)ccoe Three Marconi Hornets entered the 32nd Easter Egg meeting at R.C.Y.C. Burnham. The event attracted a disappointing turnout of only eleven boats, Graham Mead and Mike Turner in 'Ultimatum' had an unfortunate start to the weekend when, on the first leg of the first race, Mike's trapeze harness broke and he spent quite a considerable time hanging on to a mooring buoy before being rescued by the less than adequate rescue service. There was Marconi success in this race however because Colin Harper and Ian Stott in 'Renaissance’ won the race by a considerable margin from the only other finisher in the severe conditions which prevailed during the race. As a result of the incident in Race 1, Mike Turner sustained an injury to his finger which prevented ‘Ultimatum! from taking any further part in the event. Race 2 on the Saturday was held in winds of about force 3 to 4 northerly, and was dominated by Nick and Tony Smither from Dover who had won the event in 1982. Colin Harper improved from a bad start to finish second, narrowly holding off a challenge by the other Marconi boat 'Gingernuts' sailed by new member Dave Berger with his crew Kim Ridge. Sundays race was held in very light conditions and Colin Harper and Dave Berger found themselves towards the back of the fleet but fortunately the leading group sailed the wrong course allowing 'Renaissance! to round the final mark in 3rd position with 'Gingernuts! not far behind and after a long run against the tide with many changes of position the race was won by Neil Hutton and Margi From Weston S.Ce, Nick and Tony Smither were second and Colin Harper and Ian Stott managed to hold onto 3rd. Sunday afternoon saw the first ever Hornet Open Meeting snowball fight in which the joint team of Marconi and Datchet took on all comers and remained unbeaten, Sarah very skillfully pretending to be with the opposition and hitting people on the side she was standing (or was it really accidental?). We were under the impression that it was a very competitive, lively and go-ahead fleet famed for its massive turn=—outs and bawdy socials. Well readers, I can reveal that this is not the case and I may have to change class (maybe to the Mirrors) if things don't improve. Come on lads, I can assure you the estuary is nice and warm now} Six intrepid sailors made Spring Points 3 and 4, the first Hornet class race of the season. They were Graham/Mike, Graham/Murray (F.C.), and Phil/Kate. The first race was held in wind strengths of 0 to force 1 from a N./NeW. direction. The two Grahams made good starts with "Stimulation" fighting the current armed with the knowledge that all those sheets must do something and eventually making the start line about one minute later. Mike/Graham in "Ultimatum" immediately stamped their authority on the race rounding 'E' mark with the Mirrors and a substantial lead. This lead was maintained throughout even though "Stimulation" forsook the northern route from C to Breezy (very slow run against the flood tide) and opted for a reach to the race box and then a course out of the tide to Breezye This course to be a mistake on the crews part] After a pint and a sandwich, Spring Points 4 was started in even lower wind strengths. The start was with the tide and the first mark = A to port. "Ultimatum" arrived there first only to find the leg back over the start line and then on to Breezy was to be a very protracted affair. All three Hornets were soon involved in a tussle for windward position (albeit out in the wicked tide), but "Stimulation" opted for a shore hugging position and with the help of a foot over the side to avoid a breakwater soon established a small lead. The other boats soon followed this example and an orderly progression made its way to Breezy. Graham/Murray rounded first and established a good lead to Noe 1 with "Ultimatum" moving into second place. After gybing in order to lay "A" mark Graham/Murray Overstood and immediately made a bee line to the shore and out of the current. "Ultimatum" and "Stimulation" stayed out in the current and at 10 yards from the finish all three boats were in line abreast, and despite all the pumping and Flatulence aboard the other boats "Stimulation" creamed over the line followed fractionally later by Graham/Mike and Graham/Murray. THORPE BAY YACHT CLUB -— 30th April = lst May, 1983. Thorpe Bay Yacht Club hosted the annual Two—Pint—Pot meeting for Hornets. The entry of twenty four boats included three Marconi teams. Saturday's race was sailed in medium winds and sunshine and the olympic course was set very accurately which made for some very close racing. Nick and Tony Smither (winners of the faster Eqg meeting) and Sally Allyard dominated the race and soon got well clear of Chris and Andy Bines who were unchallenged for third place, The following Group of four boats contained two from Marconi; "Ultimatum" (Graham Mead and Mike Turner) and "Renaissance" (Colin Harper and Ian Stott). This group remained close together for the whole race (about 2 hours), with Graham making up for his poor upwind performances with very fast downwind legs. Eventually however, both Marconi Boats lost out to the other two in the group and Graham and Colin finished 6th and 7th respectively. The race was won by Sally Allyard who was sailing her last hornet event Since she intends entering the ladies World Championships in which she will sail a laser. After the race most of the younger competitors went down to Southend to the Kursal where great amounts of time were spent arranging group discounts /continued.

on the various rides. We all returned to the club for a ‘Chicken and Chips! supper which some people ate and others ended up wearing. The disco which followed was enjoyed by all who stayed and finished with a rapturous chorus of a few well known songs! Sunday Morning's weather was dismal with torrential rain and very little wind. There was an encouraging forcast however and by the time the race started the rain had stopped, but the wind was still very light. (IDEAL FOR PHIL). Colin and Ian made a poor start and tacked out on port to gain clear winde In doing so they picked up a good wind shift which allowed them to lee=bow the tide on the starboard tack and the whole fleet crossed behind them. Peter Bennet and Giles Weston from Sussex Yacht Club just overhauled Colin by the windward mark and these two got well clear of the following group. Bennet pulled away and Colin and Ian dropped back into the bunch. After this, the race became a little processional until a force 5 squall came through to allow Colin and Ian and Nick and Tony Smither to go from 5th and 6th to 3rd and 2nd in the space of one two sail reach. Bennet won the race convincingly with Smither 2nd and Colin 3rd. Both the other Marconi boats had disappointing results in this race, The gruelling third race in a strong force four to five began soon after the end of race two and Dave Berger and Kim Ridge in ‘Ginger Nuts! from Marconi displayed excellent upwind speed on the first leg, but he was unable to maintain this performance throughout the race. THE MARCH OF THE MIRRORMEN = I read with considerable delight in the May Navigans that a certain Hornet man contemplates joining the Mirror Fleet to get some competitive racing. Rumour has it that one or two others are also getting Mirrors in readiness for encouraging their youngsters to sample the delights of competitive sailing. Who knows, perhaps we'll recruit a few from the 420 and Enterprise Fleets as well, to say nothing of a "comeback" from those in the Solo Fleet. Apart from that, there are a number of the Cruiser Fleet with Mirrors and the younger generation to go with them. What better way of encouraging those skills, of sailing technique and basic boat handling in emergency situations, that we parents wish our children to have than to encourage and assist them to take part in racing. It has one major advantage in that if you/they do get into trouble, there is a rescue boat to assist you to get out of trouble. By racing, you learn to recognise the potential problem situation and how to avoid it. The other particular advantage of the Marconi Sailing Club is that it. IS a sailing club and we don't expect everyone who takes part in the racing to know the racing rules backwards. You don't have to be a diehard racer to be welcome in the fleet = but it's certainly easier to get to know you if you do take part and that surely is part of the function of a club. CADET NOTEBOOK =— 1 SAFETY CAPSIZE DRILL — THE R.Y.A. METHOD — (LEEWARD CAPSIZE), Stage 1 = Crew (c) and Helm (H) fall into the water, each checks that the other is 0.Ke and then they both move towards the transom (Fig.A). Stage 2 = Helm checks that rudder is secure, crew frees the mainsheet. Stage 3 - Helm moves to the back edge of the centreboard using the mainsheet as a safety line (Fig. B).e If the centreboard is not down crew moves into the boat and lowers it. CAUTION = crew should make sure that the helm is not struck by the centreboard! Stage 4 = Crew throws jibsheet to helm who acknowledges its receipt (Fig C). Stage 5 =— Crew lies in the boat facing downward supported by the water (NOT the boat) Fig D). Stage 6 =- Crew informs helm that everything is ready. The helm climbs onto the centreboard using the jibsheet and leans back (Fige E)e The boat will come up slowly (Fig. F) and in doing so scoops up the CTeW. Stage 7 = The boat is upright and the crew uses his/her weight to balance the boat. Stage 8 = Getting the helmsman aboard is achieved in several ways:= (A) The helm might be able to climb in unaided as the boat comes upright, (B) In boats with high freeboard (i.e. 420's) the crew rocks the boat boat towards helm, grabs his/her hands, and rocks back pulling him aboard. (C) In boats with little freeboard it may be necessary to bail out some water before the helm comes aboard, REMEMBER: Do not enter the boat over the transom, Stage 9 = Open self bailer, transom flaps or bail out the water and sail awaye Phil. os 8 — Letter to Editor [redacted], Rayleigh, Essex, [redacted] 22nd May, 1983 Dear Mary, In the 'Navigans' - anf excellent publication, I think; - and for which many thanks to you all the effort you must put in each month - there is one particular point with which I feel I'd like to take issue. May I refer to the article in the March Issue entitled 'Calling Willing Ladies'? As a mere male I have many times been grateful for the care and concern shown by ladies, and it is always very nice to be on the receiving end of such ministrations, — but why is it always considered the 'normal' for men to have their ladies prepare and serve their refreshments, - and wash up afterwards! Surely nowadays there is no discrimination in the kitchen, galley, or what you will - or if there is, what are the ladies doing about it? More to the point, perhaps, what are the men doing about it? Are we incapable of cutting sandwiches, or making tea or coffee - and of washing up afterwards? — Fuex poke eheag? Many ladies nowadays sail with a great deal of expertise, and no one thinks it is strange that they do. No one apparently finds it strange to see a man behind the licenced bar. Would it be too strange to have men working in the refreshment bar? — and notice the word 'working'. That's what happens there - from start to finish with very little respite, respect, or even appreciation, especially at Regatta Time. I would like to suggest that one member of eeth fleet in turn wee- bo made responsible for refreshments = to be aided by a cadet. After all they get all the benefit of tuition and experience from the Club, and they should be prepared to give something back - No doubt they are. If the idea is acceptable, perhaps we shall not again have such notices as ‘Ladies — Don't Forget to Volunteer to Work in the Galley, Will You?' - Why should you? After all, isn't your leisure as precious to you as your male's is to him? Of course, if doing your thing is serving, etc., ... That's great! Best Wishes & Tiianks — Yours, my ee > Editor's Notes=— Well, what about it, all you males} Us ‘'ladies* would be highly delighted to be waited on occasionally by you strong athletic types, The idea of a men's cake competition would also be very acceptable to us, especially if we could be the judges = including first taste. Comments please. Marye

~ 6 - SADLER SHAKEDOWN There we were, George and I, in the middle of the main shipping channel at Harwich/Felixstowe harbour, We were motor sailing intending to clear the harbour entrance as quickly as possible. I had already noticed a floating block of flats being towed by three tugs bearing down on us from our stern. Looking ahead I saw a Townsend Thoresen ferry start to leave Felixstowe, soon a huge white bow wave grew in front of it and was heading our way, then out of the blue, the engine's warning bleeper started, setting my heart racing. Was it the oil pressure?, was it the temperature? was it ???. I called to George to helm whilst I started to check. There were no warning lights illuminated on the console, but not having any gauges I could not check whether it was a malfunction of the bleeper, a malfunction of the warning lights, or prelude to engine seizure. The engine did not smell hot and kept a steady beat. To stop the engine would have been suicidal as the light wind was blowing directly towards the Felixstowe harbour, the very direction that the Floating block of flats was heading. The Townsend Thoresen Ferry kept forging OUr Waye George called to me that a Sealink ferry was just rounding the corner and heading towards us. There was nothing for it but to turn out of the channel and hope the engine would take us out of trouble. With the warning bleeper becoming louder I increased the throttle. The engine responded and we were soon surging out of the main channel and away from being run down by the two ferries. We stopped the engine and sailed on. The floating block of flats was in reality 15,000 tonnes container ship — it was enormous, or seemed to be in those confined waters. Once clear of imminent danger and with the tide under us we sailed up the Orwell towards Pin Mill, JI checked the oil lever, it was correct and the oil was not burnt, I checked the water inlet, it was not blocked. I gingerly started the engine, no warning came from the bleeper, it ran smoothly. I then checked the water flow, the delivery pipes were running full bore, nothing wrong there. In fact there did not seem to be anything wrong with the engine at all, Of course there should not have been, the engine was almost brand neu, having only run approximately 10 hours. We were on the first cruise of my new Sadler 29 = I had just spent the last year building it and did not expect any troubles apart from minor adjustments. I had tested the engine on short trips previous to this cruise, We fetched up at Pin Mill, picking up a mooring buoy. The tranquility of the mooring soon made me forget the near panic situation just a short time ago. We cracked open a couple of cans of beer, I was at peace with the world once again. That evening we were cordially entertained at the Pin Mill Yacht Club, by some of the members of that club. On returning to our dinghy we found it to be a very long way from the water's edge! We had arrived at high tide earlier that evening and now it was low tide. The hard at Pin Mill has a very small rise from top to bottom, consequently the tide recedes very quickly leaving a long hard. We staggered back to the water carrying the dinghy. George stepped off the side of the hard into the mud. We both started to laugh as neither of us could see where we were, (It's very difficult to direct a torch when carrying a dinghy!) covered in mud we rowec back to the boat, Next day we sailed back to Tollesbury, having a very pleasant sail without any drama. Next day I telephoned the engine's main agents. “what age is your engine", the engineer enquired, "When did you buy it"? My reply was that it was /continuede

- Fw new and came with the boat. "Oh yes", he said "your engine is in the series that needs a modification, I will send you one in the post", To my surprise and delight the modification turned up by return of post. It consisted of a new terminal strip with two resistors and a diode soldered on to it. This was easily fitted and the old terminal strip returned to the agents. The fault that had occurred in my installation was that the diode had been leaking a voltage across the terminals and this had operated the bleeper. The fact that this only happened when the engine had run for some time was due to the diode warming upe When cold the installation was perfect, but on running for a period the bleeper would operate, The moral to this tale is that although warning lights and bleepers bring one's attention to a fault in the engine, they do not tell the full story and only a set of engine gauges can be used to actually know what is happening inside the engine. Needless to say, I am now fully instrumented, the little bleeper will not worry me again! : D. Field. THIS IS THE 420 NEWS In the absence of Peter and Anna (you remember them, they are the ones always seen low down on the horizon) who have temporarily deported (sorry departed) to Australia in search of didgeridoos, I thought I might emulate Phil Gray's inimical prose and write a load of old rubbish on the 420 sailing events. First, the Summer Points - John Weedon immediately stamped his authority on the series and left no chance for anyone else to win the series. We had him worried at times though as occasionally we were almost close enough to see his sail number. This left second place to be contended between myself and the indomitable duo of Alan Mack and his ace crew Julian Brown. With equal points and one more race to go I used my secret weapon (my wife as crew, not wings on the centre board) and had a really exciting race with Alan, narrowly beating him by a mile at the last mark (sorry Alan). Julian was seen to be heavily bandaged after the race. Seriously though, Alan and Julian had an excellent mid-week win, storming ahead of the fleet and intimidating Phil Gray into retiring. The Mona's cup was won by John Weedon and Damian Boreham. Damian also crewed for John in some of the Summer Points races. Are these two really invincible? Phil Gray ex=420 only came second! Those 420 sailors who have not sailed lately will not have experienced the new hazard to blissful 420 sailing. It's called the blue peril. A certain type of boat seems suddenly to ap;ear to windward creating massive holes in the wind leaving the poor hapless 420 sailor bemused, sails flapping, spinnaker collapsed, speed zero and spray kicked in ones face, (enterprising sailors will have guessed the class by now)e The only known cure for this malady is for more 420s to sail and regain our oun fleet start, The real highlight of the season was David Hall's visit. 420 sailors who missed this really must kick themselves. David instructed us on the theoretical and practical handling of the 420 and imparted many useful ideas and tips on topics such as rig setting, spinnaker handling, barbar hauling and tacking. I will not go into further details as I feel sure that Peter on his return from holiday will want to write a separate report on David's visit. I would like to thank David on behalf of the 420 fleet for sharing his valuable time, knowledge, and experience with us. As I work in the same office as Phil Gray — no violins please - I have instructed him on some of the techniques learnt from above, so the next time you see him on the water, keep clear, he's still learning. I apologise for numberous references to Phil (who is this guy anyway) and assure you that it won't happen again as the next 420 news will be in the erudite hand of our intrepid pommy fleet captain ably assisted by his Sheila.. (you remember, she's one of the prettier 420 crew/helms). RF. Jeffries. PeSe Rumour has it that Sue Gray is to be our next Editor. Sue, who has a classical bent (it is left as an exercise for the reader to work that one our) will bring a new dimension to satorical editing. This change was necessary in order to censor the numerous insidious innuendo's about Phil's inability to keep a Hornet upright. I am able to say that this is the real reason he may join the Mirror fleet and not the one reported in an earlier Navigans. 420 FLEET NEWS I am writing this only 24 hours after a harrowing 35 hour return trip from the Antipodes so if it seems a bit more garbled than usual please put it down to jet lage First of all the 420 fleet would like to wish Louise Greygoose and her husband all the best for a happy future together. This may seem a bit late, but they are getting married tomorrow (at time of writing). Next —- a reminder. There are two important dates coming up. These are the Osea Open Meeting on 24th and 25th September, and our own Open Meeting on the foilowing weekend (lst and 2nd October). These are both very easy meetings to enter (involving no trailing) and it would be great to see a good turn out = especially for our own so do please make an effort to attend. This will also give us an idea of how much of David Hall's race training we have retained. Now to strike a sour note — it has been brought to my notice that whilst I've been away at least three times people have not turned out for their duties. [redacted], ee CADET WEEK 1983 Now that the cuts, bruises and scars have healed (all except Neil Pembleton's that is!) we can look back and reflect on this years' cadet week. The Sunday evening treasure hunt supplied the usual surprises, one of which was that a live crab can survive ina pint of beer! I was disappointed that no-one produced an octopus (although one was seen alive and well later in the week?), although there were a lot of poor imitations. By the way, the answer to the last question was any number between 20 and 25. It's unbelievable but one team wrote 35 and another wrote "very ancient", To reduce the fire risk due to long dry grass the cadet skipper arranged for a moderate fall of rain during Sunday night! Monday dawned with more rain and high winds which proved to be a realistic background for capsize drill, Malcolm Stuart kindly offered his services as a proving ground for potential 420 crews wishing to learn the art of trapezing. I use the word ‘art' loosely as many aspiring crews appeared to spend a large amount of time under the water. These crews I should add were mainly parents and the mirth they caused was only topped by Malcolm's demonic laugh as he dunked one after the other in the soup — well done Malcolm! Tuesday saw an improvement in the temperature and a lessening in the wind strength. The morning was well spent in learning and practising how to start a race, Four practice starts were made and each one was video-taped from the racebox by Pat Stuart. The tapes were later played back in the lounge and proved to be very constructive. It was plain from the tapes that most boats got a good start once but no-one got it right all of the time. However, it was noticeable that the three Mirrors taking part showed considerable and sustained improvement throughout, In fact, so good was the general improvement that when the Cadet Skipper made his final run for the start line in the Wednesday evening race he found the line blocked with Mirrors$ Race 1 for the Cadet Series was held on Tuesday afternoon in fairly light winds. Ten (yes, 10) cadets took part which in itself must be a record judging from the last few years' performances, The race was won convincingly by Damian with Kate second. Race 2 was sailed on Wednesday morning in very light airs and with the /continued.

crew of 420, K.41106 looking slightly the worse for wear. Conditions were difficult because of a tight leg to No. 1 against an ebb tide. The faster boats made agonisingly slow progress whilst the Mirrors were slowly drifting seaward. 41106 retired with sun-stroke and hangover (the boat was also sinking — yes, honestly!) and the race was abandoned after 1 hour 55 minutes to allow Bob in the fisherman to rescue the tailenders. As the abandon flag was being raised a zephyr of wind appeared and Penny (crewed by daddy) who was by now virtually on the northern shore of the estuary began to move and eventually finished the course. Well done, Penny - hope you enjoyed the "After-Eights" luv. As a bit of light relief and because of the rapidly rising temperatures, on Wednesday afternoon a Super Teams competition was held. This involved the various skills of cycling, dribbling (with a football that is!), running, tug-of-war, throwing the welly, throwing the ball, cartwheels and canoeing. The dribbling produced a play-off that resulted in a draw between Robert Weedon and Robert Gray. The cartwheels were included when it was found that there were so many budding gymnasts on site and Damian showed us that he can do other things besides sailing. The cycling race required stopwatch timing to 1/100th second and it was during this event that Adam Bloomfield decided to audition for the next James Bond film by arresting the motion of a bike and rider doing Mach 2 by merely placing his body in the path of the machine. Well done, Adam - hope the hand, arm, leg etc. are better. The canoeing event provided its usual thrills and spills with something like a span of eight years separating youngest and oldest. The event was won by Steven Gray (youngest) whilst Andrew Sharp (oldest) canoed three quarters of the course and then decided to swim the remainder. If you can remember whose team you were in then the final winners were team C captained by Robert Weedon. Cadet Race 3 was sailed Thursday morning and this time a fairly old looking cadet called Frank (or Uncle Frank as he is now known) sailing a Solo (sail number withheld!) joined in, and in fact managed to win} Now seriously the winner was Keith Boyles followed 34 seconds later by Alec Pembleton. Alec by this stage in the week had ditched Dad and his "Graduate" for a slightly up-market boat and a younger crew (that will cost you a pint Malcolm!). The final Cadet race was sailed on the Friday morning and once again the wind was very light. The windward mark (S8reezy) was reached quite quickly by virtue of a strong ebb tide but the beat to C was to leave only three boats in contention. They were Keith, Kate and Alec. Alec showed very good boat speed (and sailing skill) and when he rounded C mark the other two boats were 400/500 yards ‘yw behind in lightening winds. The duel for second place raged over the next two legs with Kate easing past Keith on the Osea shore and then making a late break for A mark with the tide. Alec was first home with a 22 minute gap before Kate with Keith a close third. In the final reckoning Alec won the series with Keith second. Uncle Malcolm can now boast that he has crewed a winning boat in a series (give me a call sometime Malcolm). About 20 participants tried Phils walk along the seawall on Thursday evening and made it to Steeple Bay sailing club where they were picked up by the Mariner, a Leader and a cruiser for the return journey. Those lucky enough to join Lynn (I hope that's how it's spelt!) in the Mariner experienced a brisk and damp sea passage home with the golden orb of the setting sun kissing the world goodnight (good stuff eh!). Well, what a change Saturday was! Winds force 4 and where had the sun gone? The plan had been to cruise up to the "Jolly Sailor" at Heybridge, get outside of a few Cokes, have a spot of lunch and cruise back — but it was not to be. However, a few intrepid souls did manage a picnic on the lee shore of Osea Island with a little help from Malcolm and Lynn in the Mariner. One final event (I used this word loosely) was the paper chase held .in. an attempt to clean our site of rubbish. If there were any rules at the start then /continued.

they disappeared as soon as the bin-liners were handed out. At one time I saw Claude looking resignedly skyward as bag after bag of rubbish turned up. Some of these bags had been stuffed full with inflatable dinghies, tenders and for all I know, dinghies out of the park’ To all those that took part you can rest assured that you have performed a civic function for the good of your club. Well, that's about it for this year except of course for the list of prize winners, Well, throw me to the sharks I nearly forgot to mention the Friday evening fancy dress party. — CRUISER FLEET NEWS There will be a Fleet Meeting at the General's Arms, Little Baddow on Wednesday Sth October, at 8.30 pm. The main business will be to elect a new Fleet Captain as I have decided it is time to stand down and let someone else bring in some new ideas, John Wade has kindly agreed to take over but other suggestions or offers are welcome up to the time of the meeting. The business should be quickly over when we will continue with a slide show, so whatever you may have taken recently, please bring it along. It has been necessary to reearrange the winter lay-up plan for cruisers in order to reduce the risk of heavy boats damaging the boat park. The new plan is shown in the Clubhouse, It is not easy to be precise in planning a major change so members are asked (a) to park as economically of space as possible (b) to follow the spirit of the plan rather than the letter if necessary. (c) if anyone gets squeezed out of their allocated space to use the marked overspill area. Please note it is essential that neither boats nor lowered masts obstruct ad the access area which will be used initially by the tractor and possibly later by the river board for sea wall maintenance. Remember — if the wall is breached urgent action will be needed. Finally, I would like to thank everyone who has helped me during my term as Fleet Captain whether they be fleet members or other club members and especially Mary, Anne, Shirley and Brenda who have put me into Navigans quite a few times. — Thank you all, Russ Fuller. The request for the use of our premises was made at short notice, but since the event was organised in aid of the R.N.L.I. the committee agreed that it should go ahead. Maintenance costs have continued to rise. This year maintenance for our tractor and rescue boat engine has been particularly expensive and next year we are predicting significant costs for clubhouse maintenance. In addition, as the size and number of boats in our cruiser fleet increases, we shall need extra equipment for mooring maintenance. For these reasons, as well as normal inflation, it has been decided that an increase of approximately 10% is required in our subscription rate for 1984, Final details willbe published next month, however, it is intended to place the major burden for the increase with boat owners since they will see most direct benefit. Only minor changes are required for next year's committee since most members have agreed to stand for re-election. However we will require one or two ordinary committee members. It is important that we continue to inject new blood in order to provide a strong committee in the future. One post that has not been filled for two years is that of Clubhouse Secretary. This puts an additional burden on club officers with the inevitable result that standards reduce. Please help Find someone to fill this post. See you at the Laying—Up Supper. This was all easy going with not too much wind at any of them, but it was a different story when we arrived at Mounts Bay for the Nationals, At the beginning of the week it wasn't blowing all that much so I just had to sit around and watch the kite and all those other things crews have to do. 420 FLEET NEWS First of all I would like to say a big "thank you" to the Hornet Fleet for the way they organised the 420 Open Meeting. Everything went very smoothly - apart from some completely unfounded mutterings about the competence of the Race Officer (thanks Phil, moving E mark to the opposite side of the river was a really good idea, we should do it more often). Thanks to Ann Bates for chasing up those notorious entry fee dodgers as receptionist and to the ladies who organised and ran the galley. Luckily somebody volunteered for the arduous task of running the bar =— thanks Colin. The Open Meeting itself was very well attended, attracting 18 competitors (six from M.S.C.). Saturday dawned Foggy, grey and drizzly with practically no wind at all. However, it soon improved to be foggy, grey and drizzly with some wind. As the wind was southerly it was very difficult for the R.O. to arrange a beat, and, in fact, by the time we had reached what should have been the windward leg the wind had shifted and it was a reache The visitors soon showed the Marconi Fleet their heels reflecting our lack of practice against good opposition, and this is shown in the positions of the Marconi entry of llth, 12th, 13th, 14th, and 16th out of 16 entries, Paul Springett won this race closely followed by Dave Hall after the lead had changed several times during the race, Sunday was much better from the point of view of the onlookers (in that the sun was out, the water was blue and visibility was well over the 100 yards of the previous day). However, the wind strength was less and dropped gradually throughout the course of the first race. The wind was now straight out of the west and so the first leg was a beat with everyone trying to keep close to the shore to be out of the tide. This made for an exciting beat up to the corner off the Club with the air ringing with shouts for water at the shore, at cruisers and for starboard boats. Much to my surprise we didn't hit anything! After the point, however, things eased off as the visitors pulled away again. Springett and Hall again tussling for lst and 2nd places. Unfortunately they were both disqualified for being over the start line and so first place went to Geoff Lynch from Hickling Broard. Marconi men again bringing up the rear, The final race started in very light airs and was really a repeat of the morning race as far as positions went, with Paul Springett and Dave Hall monopolising the lead between them. Despite the fact that Paul spotted the new position of 'E! mark first and made a long leg on starboard tack to reach it first (we thought he must be on a really good wind shift) at the finish line Dave Hall took first cannon with Paul taking the second. Again the Marconi entry maintained their positions. These results meant that there was a tie for lst place between Paul and Dave as they both had identical results (one lst, one 2nd and 1 disqualification) and Geoff Lynch was 3rd. The final position of the Marconi entry are recorded as follows:- 12th J. Weedon and Damian Boreham 13th P. Chrystie and Anna 14th A. Mack and J. Brown 15th Le White and L. Graves l6th P. Sayer and Novice Crew 17th R. Jeffries and Vic and this is out of 18 entries. In spite of the positions I think that everyone enjoyed themselves, and after all it's not winning that matters but taking part (what else can I say}). The comparatively large turnout shows that this event is popular with the open meeting crowd and I believe that it is the best way to improve our own standard — to race against these people who are, after all some of the best in the country. /continuede

DAY TRIP JO FRANCE After getting up at 5.30 am, we managed to be ready at 6.30 am and were waiting for Ron and Mary Greygoose who arrived about 6.45 am. Our coats and bags were put in the car boot and we were off. Less than two hours later we arrived at Dover's booking hall and bought five tickets to Boulogne. Mum and Mary got their Identity Cards — they both hated their photographs. We got back into the car and drove to the dock entrance, where we gave the officer our tickets. He tore a bit out and gave them back, then we drove along to the passport office. The officer was reading a book, and when she saw our car arrive she opened the window of her office, took our passports, looked inside them and gave them back, without looking at us at all. She just closed her window and carried on reading. We then drove off again towards the ferry, where another officer told us to park next to the two coaches. We had plenty of time to go to the cafe to have a drink, returning to the car at 9.30 am to find more cars in the queue. A few minutes later we drove onto the M.V. Tiger, a P & O ferry. We were one of the first cars on the boat, and, having parked close to the exit, went upstairs where we found five seats in the lounge before looking around the ferry. At just after 10.00 am we left for Boulogne. After reading for awhile Dad and I went for another walk and had a look at the radar. It was fairly rough and when I sat down again I began to feel travel sick. I had one of Mary's tablets and went with Dad to stand on deck and look at the horizon, which by now was the French coast. Half an hour later we were told to go to the car, and after about ten minutes the front of the ferry opened and we were let out. Before we left the dock we had our passports checked again. Leaving the dock we turned onto the road (on the right-hand side). The second car we saw we all thought was a mad driver. We drove through the town to the old part of Soulogne, and had a look in a small shop. Then we found a nice restaurant. We were taken upstairs and saw at least a dozen people all eating at one big table, but they were English. I think we hoped they would be French. It took two hours to eat our meal. The ice cream at the end was the nicest part. On the way back to the car I bought a Boulogne doll from the small shop we had looked in before, Leaving Boulogne we drove to Calais, and from the road we could see the white cliffs of Dover. When we got to Calais we went to a hypermarket. Dad, Mum, Ron and Mary bought all the wine they were allowed and I bought chocolate, chewing gum and some other sweets. At about 6.00 pm we drove back to Boulogne. We were just in time to catch the ferry, and were the last car on. It was a 7.00 pm sailing and as soon as we drove on the boat we started moving. lt was dark, so we could see both sides of the channel because of the lights. We arrived at Dover just before 8.30 pm and were let through customs. wWe all slept a little in the car on the way home, except Ron, of course, who was driving. /continued.

o« OF =m We were dropped off at home at about 11.00 pm, and I went straight to bed exhausted and drifted off to sleep, thinking about what had happened during the day.
