22 June 1983 - it = SAILING ETIQUETTE It was one of those rare hot, sunny Sunday afternoons and we were having a lovely run-back up the Blackwater with the tide under us. We had anchored for lunch in a sheltered spot in the mouth of the estuary and, with a fresh NE blowing there was no point in hoisting more than the working jib for the return trip. It would also give a chance for my non-sailing friends to take a turn on the helm since, in the morning it had meant hard tacking down river into very short lumpy seas. My MacWester 27 didn't quite look like a carnival float but with two families plus a friend on board, Blucette's foredeck and cockpit were groaning under the weight of 5 adults, 3 growing children and good lunches. Hardly in racing trim! We had manoeuvred safely through two legs of a dinghy race and: were managing to leave plenty of room for a stream of racing cruisers to pass with spinnakers flying when, uh-ho! The upwind leg of that race? Here he comes, hard on the wind, crew way out on the trapeze, going like the wind and he has us on starboard! I'm standing on the companion steps and my wife calls from her reclining position on the foredeck. "See the one to Port?" "Yes" I say. He'll pass ahead of us I had decided, so best leave the hehksman alone as he had been steering a good steady course. Now what's happening? The approaching craft had altered course and was now aiming to go clear under my stern. I was secretly glad I hadn't gone to port to cross under but I still came back into the cockpit, stepping over the maze of legs, and reached behind me for the tiller. That was the best move I had done all day as - you guessed it - he altered course yet again and, with a very few yards now separating us was obviously aiming at my sink outlet 6 inches or so above the waterline just abaft the after chain plate! At that moment he called "STARBOARD" and I hauled the helm hard over and 4 tons at 4 knots did a reasonable impression of turning on a sixpence. "Not that way, you stupid B----r!}"; "Oh, B------ y hells"; "Who taught you to B------ y saili"; "Oh, -------!". They went down my starboard side with 6 to 8 feet to spare shouting all sorts of abuse, something about rules and parentage and the number af arms and legs I didn't have, which continued way into the distance... Now, turning as I did to Port mean't I only had to turn 45° or SO; reduced the time to pass; kept the jib flying (it was out to starboard) and didn't knock my helmsman overboard (he was standing to port of the tiller). Turning to starboard - I suppose that was what he mean't, or was it reverse - would have mean't 135° of turn; an increase in the time to pass, thus allowing the tide to set me across him; backing the jib, reducing directional control, and would have given my helmsman indigestion, with a stout tiller in his stomach so goon after lunch. Maybe I could have argued that the almost inevitable. I a se

ao 12 = ae would have been his fault as he was then the overtaking craft Needless to say I had a barrage of questions from my guests. Of course we should not have got into such a tight situation but he could have held his initial course and passed clear in front of us with room to spare. In the ideal world we wouldn't need any collision avoidance regulations, (I won't bore you with the chap who tacked in front of me in the morning and I just avoided using his towed inflatable as a fender). In fact one of my friends was SO impressed with the day out he's now talking of taking up sailing! Sailing is fun, and most of the time very friendly. In my six years of sailing I have never been shouted at like that before, except when I've been racing as well. Then if I catch you on starboard -plug your ears - unless of course you are just out for a cruise. Those that attended the race training session this year will know most of it as it is basically going to be a summary of what Dave Hall told us. (Not necessarily in order of importance). The first item concerns the jib sheets. I expect this is old hat to a lot of people but it was new to me this season and, having tried it, I've found it an improvement. The basic idea is that, instead of fixing the centre of the rope that forms the jib sheets to the jib, both ends of the same rope are attached, so forming a continuous systen. When I was shown this my initial reaction was that the rope would not now be long enough for the crew to go out on the trapeze. In fact, this is not the case. Using this system means that the crew always has the jib sheet to hand instead of having to reach across the boat. This is particularly useful should the jib need adjustment when the spinaker is being flown. « B= COMMODORE'S REPORT 1983 This report for the 1983 season is my first as Commodore and I start by thanking my Committee for the support given to me during the year. Our Sailing Secretary, Malcolm Stuart, will report on the year's sailing activities; however, I must make some comment about our Regatta and Open Meetings. Although we will remember 1983 for the glorious summer, you may need reminding that the weather prior to the Regatta was generally wet and cold. This resulted in a lower than average turnout of boats and an even lower than average turnout of camperse Income was down and this was particularly noticeable in the Regatta bar. In an effort to overcome the problems caused by bad behaviour, it was decided to cancel the disco and in addition arrange for the Police to be on site for the Saturday evening. Unfortunately, plans for an alternative entertainment fell through, with the result that we still had a minority causing problems. However, we believe that we must find a way to combat these problems, because there is no doubt that the majority attending events like our Regatta are well behaved and we cannot allow a minority to spoil this great event. We also had a behaviour problem at the Disco evening held during our September Open Meeting, but, again, it is our intention to continue with these events. For our Barbeque we also provided additional security cover following a threat of trouble, but, in the event, there were no problems and I hope everyone enjoyed the evening. My own sailing activities were over very quickly this year. Having made a late start, within a few weeks I managed to trap a nerve in my neck, which put paid to my activity. Qur colleagues from Rochester visited us as usual this year and two of them returned with their families to camp with us later in the season. For once we planned a return visit. 1 went along as one of Dennis Byatt's crew, enjoying my first cruise out of the Blackwater. Later you will be asked to vote on a proposal to increase subscriptions. ‘The aim of the suggested subscription increase is to increase our income by approximately 10% in order to keep our income end expenditure account in the black and increase our reserve to cover future replacement of capital equipment, (radio, tractor, rescue boat, etc.) as well as provide the large sum that is needed every few years to cover road maintenance. The proposed increase has been added in such a way that members making the most use of the Club, i.e. the sailors, will bear the major share of the increase. Your Committee feel that this is not only fair but necessary in order to encourage new non=-sailing members. I do hope you will support this Committee proposal. We started the season with no one nominated to organise the Galley. My thanks go to those involved in keeping it going during the early part of the season and, of course, to Maureen Ball for later accepting the post of Galley Organiser. I am glad to see that most of the team have accepted nomination for the coming year, and at the same time I thank the retiring members: Vic Crisp, our Treasurer, Mike Cerey anc Tony Cockrell, for their past effort. Two junior Officers retire this year: Phil Gray, our Cadet Captain, who has done a magnificent job motivating our youngsters, and Mary Greygoose, who ends her second term as Editor of Navigans. Sue Gray (Phil's wife) has offered to take on this job and I wish her every success. Finally, may I say to all who have in some way helped the Club run smoothly during this year, thank you. Frank Savill Commodore

« 10 = SAILING SECRETARY's REPORT 1983 INTRODUCTION I will outline this years sailing activity drawing special attention to a significant reduction in the numbers of boats sailing. But first I will take you back to this time last year when we started to put together the 1983 sailing programme. SAILING PROGRAMME The sailing year starts with the appointment of officers at the AGM. By that time details will have been collected on tide times and dates agreed through the BJRC on the major sailing events for the following year. The December Committee meetings then put together the basic sailing programme, allocating duties and trying to avoid conflicts with other sailing events and social activities. Inevitably it proves impossible to avoid all conflicts but the aim is to produce a balanced programme from the beginning of April to the end of October. The 1982 season had seen the successful introduction of an Autumn Points series for dinghy racing but a lack of support for the Ladies and Cadets series of six races spread throughout the year. It was decided therefore to perpetuate the Autumn Points series and replace the Cadet races by a series to be run during Cadet Week. The Ladies series reverted to the original formula of a single race and it was planned to extract results from a new Figure of Eight race to be sailed round Osea and Northey. The basic sailing programme for 1983 was therefore constructed round the three points series taking notice of suggestions made in previous years that racing should continue through the summer since not everybody took their holiday during August. Also all points races were programmed as morning and afternoon pairs since complaints had been received when only one points race was scheduled. Although a Spring Points series was introduced as far back as 1969 it was not until this year that the change from one premier series was fully recognised in the Year Book. It was anticipated that the new format for displaying the Clubs awards would encourage fleets to present new trophies to fill the now obvious gaps on page 2 of the Year Book. Did you all notice that this year saw the last vestage of male chauvenism removed from the Year Book. Now we are all Helms together in eager anticipation of one of our ladies carrying off the Costain Cup. DINGHY POINTS SERIES The season has been an unmitigated disaster for the three dinghy points series. An overall reduction in points racing of 36% compared with 1982 affected all fleets as the statistics show:- FLEET TOTAL ENTRIES 1982 1983 Change Mirror 89 71 - 20% Hornet 149 72 - 51% Solo 194 140 - 28% "420! 122 50 - 59% Handicap 125 85 - 32% Enterprise 79 48 - 35% Dart i oe = Totals 58 488 - 36% Notes 1. Handicap excludes Enterprises and Darts (1983 only) 2. 34 races scheduled both years but one Abandoned in 1983

Activity seems to have fallen off after the Regatta:- POINTS SERIES Average Number Boats/Race 1982 1983 Change Spring 18 13 - 26% Summer 26 17 - 34% Autumn 23 13 - 45% Overall Averages 23 15, = 34% Having presented the bald and unpromising statistics the next step is to seek some convincing explanation. Club membership fell this year and was reflected in a 20% reduction in boats entering any race in the points series:- FLEET Boats Entering Any Race 1982 1983 = Change Mirror 11 7 - 36% Hornet 12 9 - 25% "420! 16 La - 32% Solo 18 13 - 28% Handicap 10 6 - 40% Enterprise t 6 - 14% Dart cy) 8 N.A. Total REY 60 - 20% The basic sailing programme changed very little and in both 1982 and 1983 there were 34 points races scheduled. A superficial examination of the number of races sailed in each month appears to show a difference in the distribution of races in the Summer months until one remembers that a month can have either 4 or 5 weekends. At this point the exercise becomes too difficult and one is tempted to say that comparison of statistics from only two consecutive years is a mathamatical nonsense. Afterall we know what a difference weather conditions can make to our sailing. 1983 one argues was a classic balmy English summer and we all opted for a lazy year. Whether or not this is true, and who is hoping for bad weather next year to prove it, the fact remains that the average entry for a points race was only 15 dinghies. (By conincidence entries for Wednesday evening races also averaged 15) Fleet as opposed to handicap racing remains remarkably popular at our club and runs against the trend at other local clubs. However when you consider that we currently try to support 7 fleets each needing at least 3 boats on the water to make a race, then our average entry of 15 dinghies doesn't indicate a healthy state of affairs. To support this mini-armada of 15 dinghies on race days we have to organise about a dozen volunteers acting as duty officers looking after the clubhouse, the race box and the rescue launch as well as assisting with the Galley and Bar and totting up the results. Then there is Claude Emerson who clears up behind us. We have often debated the organisation required to run our Regatta, but this, for some 200 dinghies, seems well worthwhile compared with the effort we put in each weekend for a meagre 15 boats. One aspect not considered above is the National trend in dinghy racing. It is claimed that the advent of Sailboards has reduced the number of dinghy sailors and there is some evidence from attendances at National events that this is true. More optimistic forcasters reckon that the total sailing activity will increase with Sailboarders turning to dinghies as they get older or wiser. There are few sailboards registered at our Club and there has been no demand for organised racing, but we may have an artificial barrier to sailboard membership in the way in which we make up our fees when one considers the minimum facilities required to launch a sailboard.

a 32 ws So long as sufficient people come forward each year to pay their membership fees the Club will remain financially viable, but can we continue to gain respect as a sailing club with so few sails on the water. REGATTA Although the total entry was 30% down this year, this was largely due to the atrocious weather preceeding the weekend, which discouraged camping. Marconi entries remained steady at 24 dinghies but we didn't get any nearer to the prizes. The event remains remarkably popular with our visitors who this year had to put up with light and variable winds which played havoc with our starting and finishing procedures. As a result the Regatta Sailing instructions were altered after the second race to allow for a committee boat finish, and this facility was used in the final race to stop the Mirrors and Toppers at Breezy. The detailed procedure will have to be refined somewhat for 1984 because the assistant race officer who was hastily conveyed to Breezy got her wellies full of water. OPEN MEETINGS The three Autumn open meetings were well supported and actually showed a small overall increase on last year. Entries FLEET 1982 1983 ‘420! 20 18 Hornet 26 29 Solo dé 13 Totals 58 60 The Hornet open meeting was particularly successful being the best attended of the meetings in their 1983 Calendar. SAILING MATCHES The only successful match of the year was the Rochester visit when the BP/MAV contingent brought six dinghies and took away both the individual Colwyn Stone Trophy and the team win, albeit by a small margin of 872 to our 882 points. Perhaps the most remarkable feat was that despite light winds and flaming June weather a Shearwater Catermaran made the sea passage from the Medway without the assistance of the infernal combustion engine so beloved of the 43 knots or bust approach. The other sailing matches planned this year failed to materialise. No Boothby Cup since neither Osea or ourselves could raise a '420' team. No Solo team matches with Fishers Green, although we did support each others Open meetings. Finally plans to sail joint fleets of Hornets with Stone SC got no support. CLOSED RACES Overall statistics show support for the closed races was poor but despite the failure to sail for the Pilot Cup or Ladies Cup some encouragement can be gained from the continued success, despite reduced numbers of Hornet Buoy and Jackpot, and the undoubted success of the Cadet Week series. CLOSED RACES Contd Jackpot was as enjoyable as ever this year. The racing up to the Jolly Sailor at Heybridge and back with the tide is always interesting, but the added spice comes at lunchtime. It is invariably sunny and one sits on the sea wall quaffing ale, trying to give the leader of the morning race a special handicap for the return leg, but basically just sitting around and waiting for someone to provide the entertainment. This year the prize went to a lady who appeared out of nowhere to create havoc in our moorings. The poor innocent lady, who owned the large wreck that our geriatrics had tied their dinghies to, was overwhelmed with male helpers, one of whom managed to capsize his Solo in his eagerness to display his gallantry. In the best Jackpot traditions said gallant helm was awarded the trophy, despite the fact that he won. This years Hornet Buoy was sailed in very strong winds and despite many spectacular capsizes there was no expensive damage. This event consistently generates some of the best Hornet sailing of the season. The organisation of a 4-Race series for the Payne Cup sailed during Cadet Week attracted 10 dinghies and showed itself to be a great improvement on the previous formula of a six race series spread throughout the season. It was impossible this year to organise sufficient Mirror's for all helms and with a very young batch of helms on our hands at the moment some were still handicaping themselves with geriatric crews. With this years winner being only 10 years old, I think we can look forward to a Cadet fleet growing in Significance for the rest of this decade at least. TRAINING I have mentioned the promise that our Cadet fleet shows for the future and much credit must go to Colin Leveridge who again took on the Winter instruction sessions which attracted 20 cadets. Phil Gray put a tremendous effort into organising the Cadets this year particularly during camping week. Having seen his sailing performance deteriorate after Cadet week, I propose that all future Cadet Captains should be able to claim average points for the rest of the season. The use of video equipment to help training on starting technique was so successful that we wondered at the time how long it would be before all our starts came under the close scrutiny of a camera. In order to keep ahead of these fledglings some of the older members also had training sessions. The '420' fleet had a very successful day organised by Dave Hall and until the Autumn Open meeting, the whole '420' fleet were convinced they were going faster. Although no formal training took place in the premier fleet the friendly and persistent instruction of Solo tail enders continues relentlessly. POT HUNTING The Hornet, Mirror, Solo and Dart fleets went out into the wider world for a little pot hunting this year. Most successful being Robin Smith (Dart 2606) who brings to the club its first National and European championship since Roger Hance won the Enterprise Nationals in 1973. Neil Salmon crewing for Dave Sherwin of Leigh on Sea SC (Mirror 64203) helped him come 2nd in the National Cahmpionship and then mopped it up by winning the Mirror Worlds. Colin Harper (Hornet 2100) did the round of Hornet Open meetings winning at Weston Sailing Club and coming 4th overall in the Hornet Travellers series whilst Graham Mead (Hornet 2108) came 16th in the Hornet World and National championship.

POT HUNTING Contd Three members of the premier fleet entered the Solo Worlds at Hayling Island but as in previous years their final positions were still into double figures but then standards are so much higher in this fleet. CRUISING Some 80 cruisers are laying up at Stansgate after a year which indicated once again that there is little demand for organised Cruiser racing. The three Barnacle Points races organised for Saturdays were abandoned, no cruisers entered the club all-in races and we had only one entry in our own Marconi Cruiser Cup. Next year it is proposed that we extract results for Barnacle Points from Mona'S Cup, Pilot Cup and the Cruiser Cup. Dinghy sailors may be forgiven for gaining the impression that cruiser activity is limited to scrubbing, painting and launching. To dispel this myth I will chronicle this years epic voyages. John Todds notched up a Marconi first by taking "Chimo" to the Baltic via the Kiel canal. Joan and Dave Thomas did 800 miles on their Channel Islands trip taking in Belgium and Holland en route. As for the rest of the fleet, a company of eight cruisers went up the East Coast as far as Aldebugh during August. Finally we must not forget the two Marconi Cruisers who made it round to the Medway to sample Rochester's muddy reception. CLUB BOATS We now have a total of eight club boats:- Working Boats Pleasure Craft Mariner Rescue Launch Brazil Rowing Tender Idle Vice Fisherman Cadet Work Boat Graduate A mooring raft is to be added to this fleet over the winter to release the Work Boat from handling increasingly heavy mooring gear. The cost of running club boats is high both in financial terms and the effort expended in routine maintenance and emergency repairs. We are indebted to those members who take responsibility for a particular boat since any boat which was merely club property would soon deteriorate. It remains to be seen next year what use will be made of our four pleasure craft particularly by the Cadets. After some major repair work on the Mariner Mitsui outboard this season, the engine should be good for a few more years. However we are aware of the Mariner's limitations as a rescue launch and it is felt that we should start looking round for a more satisfactory replacement. It may prove impossible to combine the function of speed with that of stability in one vessel but the aquisition of a mooring raft will allow us to review the role of all the club working boats. SAFETY AFLOAT An increasing awareness of safety comes to all of us with experience and whilst it must always be the responsibility of individuals to avoid putting themselves into dangerous situations we can as a club do something to minimise the risk. The 1983 Sailing Instructions introduced a new rule encouraging dinghy sailors to wear adequate clothing for the Easter Series.

SAFETY AFLOAT Contd ah Our Cadets are taught safety afloat and have to demonstrate their ability to right a capsized dinghy but we have no formal training for novice adults. A natural tendency for beginners is to come down to Stansgate when it is quiet and make a fool of themselves in private. Whilst this is very understandable it is alos pretty dangerous in a tidal estuary. We should therefore encourage all beginners to contact their fleet captain who will arrange basic training as necessary. One of the easiest and safest ways to begin sailing is to join in at the tail end of a race, and follow the fleet round (some of us go on for years doing just this) Seriously though it does make it easy to decide which way to point the wretched boat and the rescue launch is always on hand if you to for a dip or want a tow back. We have an excellent team of regular rescue launch drivers now who are not complacent about their skills and subject themselves to bouts of further training. For our major events such as the Regatta and the long distance races we are indebted to the support given by the Cruiser Fleet in providing mother ships at the remote ends of the course. The need was brought home to us this year when we had to abandon a Hornet at Bench Head in the Rum, Tub and Bung race which further demonstrated the limitations of our Mariner in rough seas. THE RIVER Subtle changes take place in the Blackwater each year and the first sail of the year becomes a search for the new gravel banks. The more obvious things to avoid whilst sailing are the river marks and this year has seen No 2 (Lawling Creek) edging out into the main channel and sprouting a light. The North Doubles (No 7) also received a light, but our local river mark Goldhanger (No 1) had its light discontinued. Our "F" buoy marking the eastern end of the cruiser moorings is being replaced by a Fisheries Protection buoy which will be lit. The ground tackle from "F" buoy has been recovered and will be used to locate "D" buoy more accurately on the start line for next season. TROPHIES We are indebted to the donors for four new trophies this year. To Norman Kerridge for the "Jack Kerridge Trophy" which is awarded to the winner of our new Figure of Eight race in memory of Jack who loved a ride on the rescue launch, particularly when we went up river. To Ron Greygoose for the "Captain's Trophy" awarded to the winner of Solo Autumn points. The beautifully hand made model solo has a helm bearing a striking resemblence to its maker. To Richard Spillsbury for the "Spring Fever Cup" awarded to the winner of Mirror Spring Points, and finally to Mike Boreham for the "Autumn Reflections Cup" awarded to the winner of the Mirror Autumn Points. An interesting point came out this year as we prepared the trophies for prize giving, when we realised that the Pilot Cup has always been incorrectly referred to as Pilot's Cup and the Mugs Mug was first mispelt in 1968 and has remained so ever since. CONLCUSION The 1983 sailing year was not an unmitigated disaster, our Cadets and the Autumn Open Meetings saved us from that. However, I would ask you to reflect on the general fall off in sailing activity and let me have your considered and constructive views on whether this is a problem to be solved or do we accept it as a fact to be faced. Either way your comments can influence the construction of the 1984 sailing programme. Malcolm Stuart Sailing Secretary

EDITORIAL Isn't January boring after all the rigours of Christmas and the New Year? At least we've got the Barn Dance in the near future. John Salmon Solo Fleet Publicity Director SOLO AND WHAT I FOUND IN IT Not exactly in it you understand; more, the sailing properties thereof, It was ten years in a Mark IX Merlin Rocket and crew problems that led me in search of a single hander. Many a boat did I try, some with trapeze, some with sliding planks, but my attention repeatedly turned to a pretty 12 footer designed by Jack Holt with the idea that lightweights and heavyweights alike could compete on equal terms. The rig was so versatile that I decided to give it a chance, but witn reser- vations that it would hold my interest after such a machine as Merlin Rocket. So, off to purchase an old Solo I'd heard about living in long grass down at Fishers Green which, on trial, proved to be a poor example! So, the building of a new compo- site Solo was the order of the day, with a view to entering it in the Nationals at Southend. It was finished the evening before the meeting and was launched with due ceremony in fading light off the Harlow jetty, appropriately named 'Shiver'. So there was I, of Merlin Rocket fame, all set to make my debut and maybe my Name in this new chosen class. Lesson one: don't Sail it like a Merlin Rocket. There was I gamely powering this little fat boat straight through the waves and wondering why I was slower than most. it took me until the end of the week to realise that Solos are to be coaxed, sailed free, kept upright, and not to tack with the tiller extension up your sleeve! I know I have to be very careful here as this is a very touchy subject (no "double entendre" is intended here). Suppose, however, your crew turns to you at a crucial point in the race and says something like, "What on earth are you doing? That boat that's just overtaken us is not only 10 years old, but it's crewed by a 12 year old girl!" Whilst this may well be justified criticisn, I would say that this is not the time to come out with it. The atmosphere in the boat will now be strained and the mental attitude of the helmsman at least will not be one that enables him to get the best out of the boat. It would be better for the crew to have kept quiet here, waited until the boat had shot past another on a@ plane and then said something like, "That's great! We're really shifting now. Let's go for it!" _ Not, I hasten to add, that I would actually like any crew of mine to use these exact words. The atmosphere in the boat will now be harmonious and therefore conducive to better performance. This is all pretty obvious, you may think, but it's surprising how many people come almost to blows in the course of a race. The same ideas apply to the helms- man as well. A good helmsman should praise a crew for doing things correctly and only criticise constructively, and preferably after the race. This is obviously a subjective point, as some people may be able to sail fastest when they are shout- ing at each other all the time. Speaking for myself, I like to enjoy the sail as well as the race and rowing (as in having an argument) spoils both for me. Next month I shall list the points, in order of importance, that I think have helped me to sail faster over the past two years. I would point out here that I am not trying to claim that these ideas are my own or that they will work for everyone, but I am convinced that they have helped me. Ron Greygoose Fleet Captain SOLO —- A RECENT LOVE AFFAIR It was back at the tail end of 1979 when, having resolved to join M.S.C. because of the enjoyment gained from crewing an Enterprise with Geoff Josey, I looked around for a suitable class of dinghy to buy. I wanted to try my hand at helming @ racing dinghy but knew of no-one mad enough to risk sailing with me, so the choice was simple. The only single-handed fleet at the Club was Solo. Picking up a second-hand glass-fibre boat, I suppose I must have made a fairly lucky choice, for it subsequently proved fast and reliable. It seemed appropriate to name it Greenfield for, apart from the obvious connection with its dark green decking, the name also represented the street name in Dearborn, U.S.A. where we had stayed for the previous two years — the trip which provided me with the funds for boat buying, a luxury we certainly could not have afforded previously. Launching then, with my newly-acquired green machine, into the virtual unknown, I started to learn the necessary skills and judgement the hard way, which involved the involuntary gulping of large quantities of Blackwater and frequent tests of the efficiency of my life-jacket. I was not, however, without considerable help and advice from some of the more experienced Solo helms at the Club — notably, John Rutherford and Geoff Josey, to whom I remain indebted. It was only as I slowly and somewhat painfully began to climb the learning curve that an awareness of the virtues and potential of the Class which I had so haphaz- ardly selected gradually developed. Whilst fundamentally a young man's boat, demanding as it does a high level of athleticism, fine balance and physical endurance but offering in return high perf+ ormance, responsiveness and excitement, it also has the unioue quality among single- handers of having a very adaptable rig. This means that with careful choice of rig and sail, and tuning to match, it is possible for people of vastly differing weights, age and technique to be competitive at Club level. ‘lhis of course is exactly where classes such as Laser and Topper fail to measure up as practical club boats, and it is perhaps appropriate here to acknowledge the great debt which M.S.C. owes to Frank Savill for pioneering this splendid class at the Club. Frank has served the Club very well in many respects, but to my mind none more so than in his excellent choice of single-hander. A well-prepared wooden-decked Solo is a beautiful sight, both ashore and on the water, but for those who prefer the relatively low maintenance demends of glass- fibre boats they have the satisfaction of knowing thet both types are very closely matched for performance, and quite competitive boats of either type can be picked up for under £500. Small wonder then that the Solo class has for years been the best supported and most dynamic class at the Club. Anyone fed up with handicap fleet racing or crew problems could really do no better than take up the challenge offered by what mst surely be Jack Holt's greatest masterpiece. John Salmon SOLO, THE FLEET WHERE THE CAPTAIN BUYS THE BEER

In an continued .ecose

~~ 2 endeavour to reduce the problem the Council is recommending to all their licensees that they provide a minimum size of mooring buoy, as follows: For moorings which are adjacent to a navigation chennel, the buoy should be not less than sixteen inches in diameter; For moorings not adjacent to a navigation channel, the buoy should be not less than ten inches in diameter, Mooring buoys should be of sufficient size and buoyancy to ensure that at least half of the buoy shows above water at high tide. 420 HELPFUL HINTS This month, in the last of the series, I am going to jot down some of the things that I think have increased my boat speed over the past two seasons. I am sure that not everyone will agree with the ideas expressed here, but I remain convinced that they have helped me! Factor affecting speed Importance rating (out of 10) (1) Wind shifts 10 (2) Keeping boat level 8 (3) Tacking well (roll tacking) 6 (4) Mark rounding 4 (5) Tactics > (6) Boat tune 2 (1) Wind shifts - I have given this by far the most importance. It can be shown that when two boats are travelling at 4 knots and are both tacking for the windward mark, the boat that ignores a 5 wind shift will be over 45 feet down wind of the one that tacked on the shift after only one minute. It is therefore possible to lose more ground by ignoring windshifts than by any of the following methods. There are, however, many times, especially in our tidal waters, when it is far more beneficial to tack in order to keep out of the tide. (2) Keeping the boat level - Most people would agree, I think, that the best boat speed can be obtained by doing this. It is particularly important when going to windward, as this is when the full centreboard is needed and any heeling is effectively reducing the depth of the centreboard. It is there- fore surprising how many people allow their boat to sail heeled over at an angle. I think the main reason is that it feels more comfortable, in that the boat is less likely to capsize on top of you. (3) Roll tacking - Especially in light winds roll tacking can gain you a lot. Even if you can't do it very well, it causes the sails to make a lot of noise and can disconcert other competitors who aren't trying it. (4) Mark rounding = Now we are getting to tne bottom end of the list. There will probably only be about 10 marks on a given course, so it is only possible to lose a small amount of ground by poor rounding. One thing, however, that has been convincingly demonstrated to me is that you should always try to round a mark on the inside. If someone has an overlap on you and is calling for water, it can be beneficial, though not always possible, to deliberately slow up and round the mark behind him but close to the mark. This is especially true if there is more than one boat inside you. By doing this you will lose a lot less ground than if you allowed yourself to be pushed away from the mark by the other boats. (5) Tactics - Except in team racing, these should normally be restricted to keep- ing clear of the other boats and their dirty winds. Luffing matches only serve to slow down the boats involved. (6) Boat tune — Beyond basic setting up of mast rake, I don't really understand this subject! Pete Chrystie

ie SA oe 420 FLEET NEWS Many thanks to Rumpole of the Hornet Fleet for his comments last month on the new 420 trophies. Any doubts he may have unwittingly aroused concerning the seaworthiness of the fleet were dispersed on the occasion of the first organised sailing of the season (April 1st). The sun was shining and the wind was blowing - unfortunately at around Force 6 and the R.O. made a wise decision to cancel the planned racing. It was decided, however, to test out the new procedure of launching and recovering the rescue boat each weekend. As soon as the rescue boat was in the water, a bevy of frustrated Solo sailors generously launched their dinghies in order to give the rescue crew some practice. Two 420s were also launched and gave a convincing demonstration of high speed sailing. Anna and I only lasted about 15 minutes as my head had gone numb (yes - more numb than usual) but the Sayers didn't seem to notice the cold and planed back and forth for about half an hour. Back on shore there was plenty to do, picking up bits of Solos and their bleeding crews (a literal description - nothing personal, Malcolm) and, after some hot soup from the very efficient Galley, there was general agree- ment — we were all mad. So - the sailing season has started, and with a bang! Six boats were out on that first day - 4 Solos and 2 420s (not enough to race anyway). The less sturdy, morew highly tuned fleets will no doubt be out when the weather improves sufficiently but, if you own a 420, why not make use of its excellent high-wind-sailing Cape- bilities and extend your sailing season? See you at the Club. Pete Chrystie Fleet Captain ~ SOLO NEWS Four Solos (well, their mad helms, anyway) were ready for Spring Points 1 and 2 on Sunday, April ist. an 1 oes LOCAL KNOWLEDGE 7 When we sail to other waters we read the pilots and charts for the area conce med and very frequently see a recommenda tion along the lines "local knowledge should be sought before attempting to cross the bar" et cetera. Sometimes the need for local knowledge arises even closer to home. Unfortunately, we have experienced the damage of two Club boats during the March winds . The owners were unlucky = or were they? We recognise that our waters can be rough at any time of the year, and especially so in Winte r. The alternative to taking the boat out is to move it to a sheltered location - Heybridge Basin, Maldon, Lawling Creek or one of the marinas; they are all used by members as an alternative to laying-up at Stansgate. On occasions, owners have been unable to deal with @ boat themselves, so friends have helped in some way. It follows in full. COLWYN STONE TROPHY 1984 The 1984 visit to the Marconi Sailing Club on the Blackwater by Rochester sailors was again very successful. Despite a bad forecast 5 cruisers made the trip led by Jack Pateman, the Marconi Sailing Club President, continued .ceceoe

se, 2 The Rochester dinghy team was Richard Stone, Peter Belcher, Gordon Belcher (all in Lasers), with Maurice and Pam Chapman in an Enterprise and their son Mark in a Topper. The Marconi Sailing Club team was Frank Savill, Ron Greygoose and Malcolm Stuart in Solos and D. Webb and J. Walker in Enterprises. The wind was ideal for Lasers at the top end of force 3, gusting to force 4 and in a direction to give mainly reaching courses. In the first race the Lasers quickly pulled away, chased by the Solos. Richard Store led at the windward mark, but Peter Belcher overtook him down— wind and stayed ahead to win. The broad reaches gave some fine planing. At the second gybe mark Gordon Belcher capsized allowing Ron Greygoose to catch up and beat him on handicap. Maurice Chapman, despite a prestart capsize, sailed well to beat the two Marconi Sailing Club Enterprises, whilst Mark, though last on the water, sailed above his handicap to be fifth. For the second race the course was changed to give more beating. Despite this the Lasers again pulled away from the start. Again Richard Stone led at the windward mark but Peter Belcher's faster speed allowed him to overtake, despite hitting a mark, Peter gradually pulled away to win the race and the trophy for the third year in succession. Richard Stone was second end Gordon Belcher third. Maurice Chapman was close to the Lasers until the wind increas-— ed on the third lap and he finished fourth equal. Again Ron Greygoose was the highest placed Marconi Sailing Club boat at equal fourth, but the unusual wind direction puzzled the home team more than the visitors and they missed crucial wind shifts, The trophy was presented to Peter by Joan Stone. - 6 = SOLO NATIONALS: 29 JULY - 3 AUGUST 1984 This year the Solo Nationals were held at Brixham, South Devon, in a joint Championship with the Seafly class. A disappointing entry of 36 Solos was explained by the fact that a large UK contingent had travelled to the Netherlands two weeks earlier for the Worlds, and that Brixham was a long way from the Solo centres in London and the Mid- lands, especially in the peak of the holiday season, John Salmon and Roger Smith were the Marconi representatives. The practice race and the first two points races were held in light, changeable winds with the water in Torbay fairly choppy. The Wednesday saw a two hour delay before the start, which with the race and the journey out and back meant seven hours on the water. The race finished in a force 4 which made Pacing a little more exciting. Strangely, on Wednesday and Thursday the two Marconi boats finished within a boat's length of each other, which ‘seemed to make the journey to Brixham rather unnecessary. Friday's last race was much more exciting with a force 5 = 6 and some bigger Wavese Overall, however, the two Marconi boats were not in good finishing positions with John Salmon 21st overall and Roger Smith 24th. The overall winner was S. Cray (3406) from Hollowell SC with Craig Moffet second. Geoff Carveth, who had retained the World Championship in Holland, did not compete. The Solo A.G.M. was held at Brixham on 2nd August 1984 end this year there were no long arguments about masts, rudders, etc. The most eventful subject was a vote on the election of president, with the incumbent Gordon Walls being challenged by Craig Moffet who won the vote. The next most eventful subject, which for some reason caused much hilarity, was a proposal that where the Nationals are held amid interesting scenery the programme should include a "lay day”. The gentleman's lady friend endor- sed this proposal, I was pleased to see that there were quite a few young helms at the Nationals as well as the old faces, which is a good sign that the Solo is attracting young helsmen who find it en easier boat to handle competitively in heavy weather compared to the Laser. John Wade Fleet Captsin [redacted] HORNET WORLDS 41984 Four Marconi Hornets set "sailTM for foreigm parts on 3rd August. The "sailing" was done in a Townsend Thoresen ferry bound from Felixstowe to zeebrugge, and thence to Hoorn, Holland, where we would be joined by the fifth Marconi boat with Colin Harper. The Fleet were soon found esconced in the “Viking" bar and savouring their last taste of English beer. The sailors comprised Gvnahane Mead/ Mike Turner, Pat Black/Tony Cockerell, Murray Todd/Keith Boyles and Phil Gray/ Kate Nicholson. The supporters consisted of Sue Gray, Barbara Mead (her first mention in Navigans), Laura, Becky and Geoff, After landing at Zeebrugge, we flashed our newly acquired (and expensive) Small Ships. kegisters at unsuspecting and slichtly confused Customs Officials and then drove the 200 miles to Hoorn, The majority of the Fleet looked and felt the worse for vear cfter this first exhausting day and when, in the fail- ing light, we finally found our hotel we just collapsed into the nearest chair with a beer. The Fleet (minus Colin Harper) had taken over #1] but one room in a small hotel only ten minutes' walk from the bozt park. The proprietor, who spoke better English then Murray, was called Basil by his friends after his uncanny resemblance to a certain T.V. character. We were able throughout the week to change in the hotel end he didn't mind us walking in and out in wetsuits. This proved a boon, as the Hoorn Sailing Club facilities were a little stret-— ched,. «f= The first day was taken up with boat measurements, sight-seeing and a welcome by the Mayor in a local church where free wine and beer was served! Sail meas—- urement gave several crews near heart attacks when two sets of brand new Hood's sails failed and two new Hyde genoas failed to satisfy the Dutch measurer. The Hyde genoas were quickly passed when it was established that the English rules were applied at World Championships in cases of measurement discrepancies and since the Hyde sails conformed with English rules, they were 0.K. after all. The Hood sails, however, were too large whichever rules one applied and a fair amount of on-the-spot surgery was carried out before they were passed. The sailing was held over a triangular course some 2 = 3 miles offshore and the race instructions said we would race over 10 nautical miles. In fact, I can advise my readers that a Dutch nautical mile is probably twice the inter- nationally accepted distance. Generally, as one sailed up and down the start line to determine if there was any bias, one could not see the windward mark. The Race Officer did a fine job of setting an accurate start line for all six races and there was only one postponement for a course change and only two General Recalls all week. The longest time spent on the water was approximately five hours one day, with the shortest race (race 6) being about 14 hours when the course was shortened (probably due to worsening conditions, but possibly because the Smithers brothers were winning their first race!) The number of boats competing was 45, of which 22 were British, the remainder being Dutch. Our Dutch hosts were very pleased that so many of us had made the journey and spent the whole week enquiring as to our well-being, etc. I was surprised as to the gentlemanly way the boats raced, especially at the start line where it was always possible to find a spot with a hole to leeward. The racing conditions were superb right through the week, with wind strengths generally between force 3 and 5. The average water depth is only about 10 ft in.the area, so these winds produced a heavy chop which made beating difficult for the inexperienced crews. Racing through the chop with spinnaker up on a reaching leg proved to be the most exciting point with many spectacular cap- sizes to be had. With the exception of Grahame and Mike, all the Marconi boats capsized at various times during the week, but none so unluckily as Colin Harper, who capsized just before the finish line in one race when he was lying in fourth position. As the week advanced it became a test of endurance (both on end off the water), a test of the boat and its fittings (Colin's mast fell down during one race!) and a test for the support teams who were fed up with all the sailing, the children (bless their little cotton socks) and supplying food and drink after the sailing. I'm sorry to say that Sue did not get her promised trip to Amst- erdam, which is a good excuse for us to go back to Holland one day. However, it was a lovely sight to see Sue and Barbara (sscond mention in Wavigens) wait- ing patiently for their loved ones (Ed's. note: And Phil and Grahame) as the exhausted sailors came in from the troubled waters, The new World Champion is Peter Bennett from Shoreham SC and since the Chanp= ionships he has subsequertly won the Nationals, The Marconi boat positions were as follows: 12th "Ultimatum" Grahame Mead & Mike Turmer 15th "Renaissance" Colin Harper & crew 28th "Kyle" Murray Todd & Keith Boyles 32nd "Stimulation" Phil Gray & Kate Nicholson 38th "Ultimate" Pat Black & Tony Cockerell Phil Gray Fleet Captain

— : MARCONI SAILING CLUB SAILING SECRETARIES REPORT = 1984 I have set out this year's report chronologically picking up the successes, disasters and light relief as we progressed through 1984, JANUARY: The year started with a huge success for Marconi. We raised a total of £500 in sponsorship for the RNLI rowing race, the £350 raised by our official entry was the highest for any cne boat, although it was left to our unofficial entry rowed by two St. Trinians old girls to win the race. The first of six Cadet Winter Meetings run by Derek Hall started in January. The meetings held at M.A.S.C. between 6.00 and 7.00 pm on Saturday evenings were well attended and the benefit to our Cadet Fleet became obvious as the season progressed. FEBRUARY The 1984 Year Book came out with the promise of lots of new trophies:— ww Points Series Trophy Donated By 420 Spring Jumbly Trophy Pete Chrystie Mirror Spring Spring Fever Cup Richard Spillsbury Hornet Autumn Leaf Trophy Mike Turner Enterprise Autumn Autumn Blues Trophy Steve Evans Mirror Autumn Reflections Cup Mike Boreham 420 Autumn Seaweed Trophy John Weedon Only one failed to meet the Laying—Up Supper deadline but Mike Turner gave himself another year by winning Autumn Points and promised to turn over a new leaf next year. Steve Evans was seen to be handling the Autumn Blues Trophy with some trepidation. His wife revealed later that the glue was still wet. MARCH The main working party attempted to get Stansgate ready for another season in heavy rain. Aside from the hurly burly of the routine fun jobs Pete Chrystie aw and a small slave gang erected a totem pole to protect sailboards. The Sailing Sub-Committee came up with an excellent idea to offer the use of our gravel covered hard to Tillingham Fire Brigade for routine pump tests. The request got to them a little late for this year but the idea is worth a repeat. APRIL The first dinghy race of the season was scheduled for All Fools Day = 6 turned up. The wind matched this effort by blowing Force 6 with occasional sleet. Commonsense prevailed and racing was cancelled for the day so that we could concentrate our resources on a first trial of the Mariner launching and recovery procedure. The launch procedure worked perfectly in the adverse weather conditions and the 4 solos and 2 "420's" joined the Mariner in its new high visibility livery for a short thrash. MAY Spring Bank Holiday Monday was devoted to the somewhat novel pursuit of safety traininge Leaving the drowning activity till later in the season, when hopefully the river would have warmed up, we concentrated on perfecting the recovery of capsized dinghies and sailboards using the Mariner. After trying out everyone's fanntiniiod

as Se theories we concluded by making the following recommendations := ~ Capsized dinghies lying with sails on the water are most effectively righted by the rescue launch working towards the dinghy from the top of its mast. This was shown to allow better control and to minimise the risk of damage. - Practice towing showed that dinghies towed most successfully from a stern line, although care had to be taken not to put any snatch load on forestay fittings which are designed for mainly vertical loads. The tow line should be clipped or looped either side of the forestay to damp down yawing whilst any snatch loads are taken back to the mast or a thwart. - Sailboards should be de=rigged in the water-first bring the board over the side of the Mariner followed by the rigging after releasing the clew outhaul and collapsing the boom against the mast. - The safest method of beaching the Mariner was demonstrated using a buoy close inshore from which the Mariner was pulled or quanted ashore after raising the outboard. On the Regatta I must first remind you that it was the coldest and wettest Whitsun Bank Holiday on record. Not surprising therefore to find total entries down to 110 compared with 158 last year and 223 in 1982. We can draw some consolation from the atrocious weather, it gave sxcellent sailing conditions and, judging from comments made by competitors, must have been one of our most successful Regatta sailing programmes. I feel this has given us a healthy base on which to build a really good 1985 Regatta and a little publicity to those friends we have made at past Regatta’s will prove well worthwhile. It was appropriate that the first Wednesday evening race this year was sailed in Regatta week for the Mud Trophy. JUNE The end of Regatta camping week brought the Rochester visit and some decent sunny weather. Rochester took the team prize by a convincing 182 to 35 points margin whilst Peter Belcher from Rochester won the individual Colwyn Stone Trophy with two firsts in his Laser. The visitors concluded that an unusual(sic) wind direction had puzzled the home team more than: the visitors and that we had missed crucial wind shifts. The following day we entered four teams in the Maylandsea Bay Challenge Cup extracting our results for the Jack Kerridge Trophy. An excellent race this, round Osea and Northey Islands with a multitude of individual and team prizes at stake. We failed to reecapture the Boothby Cup this year. After a closely fought first leg at Stansgate we failed to get a team together to contest the second leg at Osea. A big disappointment in recent years has been the relunctance of some of our better helms to compete for the Club. We have the talent and ability to win many of these events but so often fail to rise to the challenge. Summer Points 4 gave rise to an interesting debate on race abandonment procedure and it demonstrated that the Race Officer must exercise some care when seeking to abandon a race under Rule 5.1. Certainly where the situation arises because of insufficient wind it is very difficult to abandon a race where a competitor demonstrates his ability to complete within the timescale. The safest course for Race Officers is to keep an eye on the weather conditions and if necessary shorten the course either at the race box line or from a committee boat at any rounding marke The Rum Tub and Bung went off without a hitch this year attracting 38 cruisers and /continued.

28 dinghies. Summer Points 5 scheduled for the afternoon was cancelled because of the late finish of R.T. & B. The trial inclusion this year of points racing on days allocated to traditional races failed on this and other occasions to attract more entries to the traditional races. JULY This month brought problems with the Marine Band radio at both the clubhouse end and on the Mariners “Seavoice"., A starting problem was identified on the Mariner engine but the true cause was not found until the engine was stripped down for its winter service at the end of the season. I am pleased to report that despite the extensive electrolytic corrosion the bill for winter service will be little different to last years, The best trained fleet in the club again persuaded Dave Hall to come along for a one day session. This year he concentrated on spinnaker gyberipokery.e The "420" and Enterprise fleets in a somewhat desperate attempt to maintain fleet racing nominated certain Sundays when they would make a special effort to ensure at least three boats made it to the start line. Unfortunately this had little effect on numbers but nevertheless seems to be a good commonsense idea. ed AUGUST This year's Jackpot was as enjoyable as ever and unmarred by past excesses. Nobody had to be poured back into their boat after lunch, none of the geriatrics lost their teeth and the ladies of Heybridge escaped any overwhelming displays of gallentry. The Pilot Cup was somewhat unusual with a Cruiser only entry. We had two Barnacle Points races this year and we seem to have arrived at the right formula of four races with results extracted from Mona's Cup, Rum Tub and Bung, Pilot Club and Marconi Cruiser Cup. On Pilot Cup day the dinghy fleet chose to wait for Summer Points 16 despite weather conditions which would have favoured most dinghies. I have been surprised how reluctant some of our better dinghy helms are to enter one-off races. Perhaps we could encourage more entries by simply pointing out how much easier it is to win a trophy for a traditional one-off race than the long haul involved in the Points Series. ed Robin Smith managed to gain some good publicity for the club by winning the Dart Nationals at Worthing. The Hornet Fleet avoided any adverse publicity over in Holland and with five boats they formed the second largest contingent after Brightlingsea S.C. at the World Championships. The premier fleet had two representatives at the Solo National Championship. Their finishing positions were explained by the fact that the Solo is now attracting young helms who find it an easy boat to handle competitively in heavy weather. The August Bank Holiday Series saw the resurgence of a real Cadet presence at Marconie For many years we have nurtured Cadet helms with adult crews but at long last the chickens are leaving the nest. Neil Salmon and Clair Savill won the series and another cadet pair, Damian and Lucy Boreham camefourth. Hopefully next year we can encourage more pairings and start to do battle with our neighbouring Cadet Fleets particularly Maylandsea Bay and Blackwater who both use Mirrors for Cadet racinGe The August Bank Holiday weekend gave us the opportunity to continue the safety training. Two of our more athletic rescue drivers spent an interesting afternoon /continuede

= 2 Pishing a very game Claire Urry out of the water by every conceivable method. Claire's life saving qualifications making her performance very real. For an unconscious casualty the optimum method evolved was to drop off the rescue crew who gave support in the water, cleared the casualties airway and gave the first vital inflations of the lungs. Meanwhile the driver brought the Mariner alongside with the ladder down on the port side, which is clear of the engine controls, then with the engine idling the crew climbs aboard to help the driver bounce the casualty over the side. We may only get an unconscious casualty once in ten years, but when it happens the rescue driver and crew of the day must be prepared to respond efficiently. SEPTEMBER The Marconi Cruiser Cup this year gave us some organisational problems with a Jeaem. start from Thirslet Spit and a long line finish at Stansgate on what turned out to be a very popular weekend for river traffic. Criticism of our ability to identify finishers reliably led to a 8.3.R.C. proposal to start and finish the race at Thirslet Spit. We have countered this by proposing a start at Osea Pier with a short line finish at Stansgate but inside a committee boat rather than 'D' buoy to avoid too much action inside the moorings. A last minute switch of dates by the Hornet Fleet took everybody by surprise but the organising Dart Fleet coped well with what turned out to be the best attended Hornet Open of the year with 29 entries. The Solo Open only attracted three visitors largely due to a conflict of dates which kept the Fishers Green contingent away. However a good turnout of nine Marconi boats and Force 6 winds kept up the interest particularly when beating down Goldhanger Creek at the bottom of an exceptionally low tide. Capsizing in a gale with only an inch of water to lubricate the hull is an experience only bettered by trying to get sailing again. OCTOBER The Dart/"420" Open Meeting was organised by the Hornet Fleet who were grey with Fatigue by the end of the weekend. Their task was made more difficult by not having the support of an 0.0.0. which led to the first problem with keys, then the committee boat turned out to have no obvious place to hoist flags. The rod that broke the back of these waspelike insects was the additional burden of organising Autumn Points 9 and 10. Despite the problems the visitors thoroughly enjoyed their racing particularly the Dart Fleets quick flash round Osea and Northey Islands which nearly ruined racing at the up=river clubs as everyone stopped to watch. Entries were 18 Darts (7 Marconi Boats) and 14 "420's" (4 from Marconi). The formula of a long first leg true beat created by a Committee Boat start followed by an interesting chase round the river buoys provides an attractive course for our visitors giving them some relief to the open water Olympic courses. Helm of the Year final was sailed in Lasers of which Pete Moseley had managed to scrape together four club boats including his own. The four races turned out to be an endurance test ending in a sudden death one lap run-off between Ron Greygoose and Pete Moseley who tied for first place. In the end the overall result hung on the crucial decision of when to tack for *A* Buoy on a fast ebb tide. Putting the club into mothballs at the end of the racing season we reviewed the use made of the club boats and whilst "Idle ViceTM had been used extensively and "Brazil" occasionally, no use had been made of the Cadet or the Graduate. It was decided therefore to dispose of these last two and consider acquiring a training sailboard. ° /continued.

NOVEMBER With dinghy racing at Stansgate over for another year and setting out to give a polished performance at the Laying—Up Supper I noticed that whilst Cruising Prizes are listed in the Year Book none have been awarded since 1975 and few members could recall what they were for. John Witter was able to turn up his note from September, 1965 Navigans which clearly identified them as intended for a members first cruise and not as some had thought a sort of runners-up prize in the Mamgu stakese One obvious contender, which should have been recognized last year, was Ann Bates! log for their first cruise up the East Coast. I was pleased to be able to rectify this omission on Ann's birthday at the Laying—Up Supper. Whilst keeping Ann's prize a surprise I did suggest to our Rear Commodore that since half our members owned cruisers, and the Laying—Up Supper was supported more or less equally by the Dinghy and Cruiser Fleets, we should give more awards for Cruising. Murray Bates was in the middle of finishing off some 65 hand made trophies at the time and I was perhaps lucky not to have ended up in the hot water bath with the screen prints. Nevertheless it is worth thinking about for next years; we may even see the Sea Wife's Prize back again. Despite its title and camnatations of creature comforts I understand it has more to do with climbing ew masts and remaking halliards in the teeth of a North Sea gale. The 6 trophies, 28 prizes and 8 spoons not collected at the Laying—Up Supper will be presented at a date to be arranged, but most likely the New Year Working Party at Stansgate! SAILING FUTURE Looking back over the year reminds us of all the things we intended to do and of lessons learnt. A further 16% reduction took place this year in dinghy points racing on top of last years 36% reduction. Whilst the average entry for Wednesday evening races remains around 15 the Points Series are only attracting an average of 10 boats per race compared with over 14 last year. It is interesting to compare this with attendance at Committee Meetings = the Main Committee meeting alone averages 16 and the Sailing Sub-Committee has on average more people sitting round a table talking about sailing than we see on the water the following weekend. yy Certain changes have already been instituted for next years sailing programme with the main objective of encouraging activity on the water. For 1985 the Summer Points series will be abandoned and Spring Points extended to the end of June. In July and August many Sundays will be occupied by traditional races but where there is a gap a half—handicap pursuit race will be run in the morning, along the lines of the popular Wednesday evening races, and in the afternoon there will be Handicap Races split into one, two or three handicap classes depending on the days weather conditions and numbers of entries. The Summer Points Club Trophies will be re-designated as the Clubs premier trophies for each dinghy class and will be awarded on the total racing programme of Spring Points plus Autumn Points plus any other relevant closed races. REFLECTIONS It was 1981 when Murray Bates took on the Sailing Secretaries job after making me promise to help with some of the donkey work. I have enjoyed our four years together looking after the Clubs sailing activities, but will always remember our half-term doubts when we sat down together and wondered what if anything we were achievinge I think the moment of gloom had been brought on by yet another hole in the Regatta marquee. I pulled Murray out of this abyss by pointing to some of the things that seemed /continuede

« Yu to be going right. Starting gently on a non-controversial issue he had to agree that we were getting the Year Book to press a little earlier each year and in sight of getting it printed in time for issuing with membership renewals. The Autumn. Points series was introduced successfully in 1982 and Wednesday evening sailors have welcomed the new pursuit race formula. Perhaps the most significant and long lasting improvement in the last few years has come from an increasing reliance on Fleet Captains to find the resources to cover major activities. What we are finding now is that fleets have accepted an on-going commitment to specific activities making the organisation from one year to the next so much easier, However, a group activity such as that provided by the fleets is not always appropriate to a specialist task. The sailing activity is equally dependant on the individuals who turn up quietly at the appropriate time and get on with what they have made their own job. Few of these individuals are on the Committee, or any sub-committee for that matter, so I should like to end by paying tribute to their help and by encouraging all club members to look around for some task, however small, that they can make their own. Perhaps this is just as well, as it looks as if the hall- owed pages are to be desecrated - I mean decimated = in order to save a few pounds. However, I digress (something that won't be allowed in future?) The 420 annual Fleet Meeting took place at my home on 5th December 1984, First item on the agenda was to elect a new Fleet Captain. Unfortunately, the person singled out to be cajoled into the position must have got wind of it and cried off coming to the meeting at the last moment. However, undeterred, we elected him anywsy and so the new Fleet Captain is Alan Woods. Alan's main worry sbout taking on the job was that he will not be around for a few months of 1985 and so it was agreed that Len Graves would join with Alan t© give the Fleet the considerable benefits of Joint Fleet Captaincy. A lively discussion then ensued on how to arrange the duties. It was felt that the best way was to send each fleet member a list of duties required and ask them to take on as many as necessary. This would minimise the amount of swapping reguired and therefore make the turn-out for duties more reliable. There was majority supp- ort for the new format of the Wednesday evening series. A weekend cruise was svgg= ested and it was agreed that some sort of cruising activity would be arranged for 1985. The possibilities of persuading cruisers to participate as support (e.g. to carry gear and provide a measure of safety) would be investigated. It was felt that a boat tuning/ race training day or days would be of use. The Dave Hall sessions were very successful but it was felt that it would be imposing on Dave's good will to ask him back for a 3rd year. Perhaps something could be org~ anised in conjunction with Maldon S.C. or maybe a "self-help" practice day could be organised. It was agreed to advertise the willingness of fleet members to take out any other Club members, on request, in order to encourage new members and those thinking of changing class to ¢p® for the 420. This offer to be repeated on a regular basis throughout the sailing season. There was criticism of the new rescue boat procedure. Not so much because it wes a nuisance to launch and recover but more because it so often caused delays to the start of racing. Also, it does not seem to have helped the engine. It vresunably has solved the problem of the double skin filling with water. The Laying-Up Supper was very pocrly attended this year - this presumably means that the present format is unpopular with the majority of Club members. The Fleet thought it woule be a good idea to hold the prize-giving at a more popular event, say the January Barn Dance. Most people would welcome a break of about 30 minutes at half-time and the prize-giving would fit nicely in here. Well, that sums up the 420 4.G.M. It only remains for me to thank the members of the Fleet for their support during my 2 year stint. I would also like to take this opportunity to thank all the Club members who have helped make our time with M.S.¢. such fun. Most of all, I would like to thank whoever it was who had the foresisht to persuade M.A.S.C. to buy the Stansgate site. Teo my mind, it is the best site on the River Blackwater.and with the facilities it offers, makes M.S.C. one of the best clubs in the country. 7a _—. COMMODORE'S NOTES It is with profound regret that I report the sad and sudden loss of our dear friend and colleague, Eric Payne. On Monday 4th February several members, including Eric, had assembled ready for the February Main Committee Meeting; Eric was talking, then peacefully passed away. It was a dreadful shock to us all. The M.S.C. members send sincere condolences to Mrs Payne and her family. The Committee Meeting was postponed to the following Monday (and has not yet been held at the time of writing). Continuing my aim to keep members informed of activities, since my last Jan- uary issue report we have continued to make much progress in readiness for the sailing season:- A.meeting was held at M.A.S.C. on Wednesday 23rd January during which Mr G, Wignall, M.A.S.C. Club Manager, and I discussed:- 1. The problem with the water supply at Stansgate —- M.A.S.C. have agreed to replace the old pipework and aim to complete the task before Easter; 2. -5- SAILING PROGRAMME 1985 As you will probably have noticed from your Year Book, there is no Summer Points Series arranged for this season. Over the past few years the entry for this Series has been low in comparison with those held in the Spring and Autumn, so a new format is being tried this year. The Spring Series has been extended into June and the Autumn Series into September. The Summer Points trophies are to be awarded on the basis of points extracted from the handicap races held on Sundays during the Summer months and those closed Club races which all helms are elig- ible to enter. For the purposes of points extraction only, there is no minimum limit on the number of boats competing from any one Fleet,.e.g. if only one Mirror enters and finishes a race in accordance with the Sailing instructions, first place points will be awarded in the Fleet Series. Retirement and disqual- ification points are derived from the whole series, as normal. To qualify as a Fleet Series, a minimum of three different helmsmen must have taken part in any of the valid races. I have to report two amendments to the Year Book. Steve Evans SAFETY ON THE WATER Just a few notes to remind any who may need it that our sport is not without hazard, particularly at this time of year when even on a warm, sunny day the water remains very cold. I would offer the following points for your consideration: ~ Dinghy sailors at this time ofyear must wear wet suits or equivalent; ~ Check every part of your boat thoroughly before the start of the season and replace any gear which is suspect; - Discipline yourself to re-check your boat with care from stem to stem each time before you use it; - Dinghy owners must pay particular attention to buoyancy, both personal and boat. Check it carefully yourself and get a qualified measurer to certify the boat, even if you do not intend to compete in Open Meetings; - Do not assume rescue facilities will be on hand to help you. They are usually somewhere else, so your salvation must always be in your own hands; - If inexperienced, or unfamiliar with our sailing environment, please ask advice from the 0.0.D., Fleet Captain or other experienced helms; = One of the most sinister aspects of hyperthermia is that rational thought becomes impossible. If you reach that stage, you are really in trouble; so, if you feel cold and tired - get ashore. There's always another day. Take care and have a great 1985 sailing season. wo EE es SAILING — SPRING 1985 (SO FAR) The season started this year with the Easter Series. The weather on the Sunday, rain and a Force 5 Southerly, was braved by 2 Solos and an Enter- prise who were unable to race due to the lack of rescue facilities. Undeterred, the three boats went for a “thrash" anyway, resulting in Roger Smith looking as though he had been five rounds with Frank Bruno! Monday's weather showed little improvement with the wind even fresher than the pre- ceding day. Two Solos, a Hornet (briefly) and a Dart entered the morning race but Ron Greygoose in his Solo proved to be the only survivor. Three Solos entered the afternoon race which was sailed in a wind of increased strength, resulting in a total "wipe-out" with no finishers. Spring Points 1 and 2 were cancelled due to bad weather. Enterprise, Solo and Handicap fleets sailed Spring Points 3 and 4 on a day which started with light airs, gradually increasing to a nice sailing breeze by the end of the day. The Solo "lads" were the only sailors to raise a fleet for races 5 and 6, but were joined by a Laser and a Fireball who went along for the ride. These races were Sailed once again in strong winds and Malcolm Stuart was seen plodding round sporting his specially modified reefing mainsail, which en- abled him to survive where others didn't. Solos were the dominant species sailing races 7 and 8 and were kept company once again by Enterprise and Handicap fleets. The afternoon race called heavily on the Rescue service with capsized boats spread out over the numer- ous gybe marks, Steve Evans in particular causing confusion by hiding one of these marks with the upturned hull of his Enterprise. Speaking from personal experience, the water is gradually warming up now and this should encourage more of you to join in the thrills and spills and beauty of sailing at Stansgate. See you there. Derek Webb Sailing Secretary HUNGRY ON WEDNESDAYS? That's caught your attention, hasn't it? The good news for all you hungry Wednesday night sailors (and supporters) is that a Galley service will start on Wednesday 5th June (that's Midweek Race No. 2) for a limited period of 3 weeks to judge demand, run by yours truly. In any event, there will not be a service on 26th June (Race No. 5) as I'm on holiday. This service will offer sandwiches, some cakes, sweets and hot drinks from 6.00 pem. to 7.00 p.m. and again from 8.30 p.m. to 9.30 p.m. I'll be closing while the race is on so that I can watch the fun and put my feet up! Anyone who is accustomed to using the Galley on Wednesdays should please be undeterred by my presence and carry on as usual. See you at the Regatta.

Mike Turner Cruiser Racing Representative SALLBOARD SAFETY With the advent of more sailboards at the Club and recent problems encount-— ered rescuing people from other clubs, the Main Committee would like to ask all sailboarders to operate their own safety code. The Club does supply rescue facilities in the form of the "Mariner" but this is usually tied up with the dinghy racing programme. Since it is not obvious to the Rescue Boat when a boardsailor might be in trouble and since their priority is to check on capsized dinghies (more conspicuous), it is important that boardsailors are aware of their own limitations in the range of tide and wind conditions. So, please, if you are a beginner, stay near the Clubhouse and keep up-tide with respect to the Clubhouse. If you are an expert (or an aspiring one), ask yourself whether you are not too tired to get back unaided.
