C'ford [redacted] SALLBCAT '86 The Club put on a stand at Sailboat '86 again this year. The exhibition at Crystal Palace attracted over 10,000 visitors and was opened by Prince Andrew, who toured round the show. It was a lot of fun to put up the stand, which was a credit to the Club and attracted plenty of interest and a number of enquiries about membership. We must wait and see if these result in any new members. Many thanks tO Dave Nixson and Steve IcCulloch (have I got it right yet, Steve?) for setting up and dismantling the stand, to Phil Gray for his help on Friday and to all the Club members who helped by manning the stand over the weekend. Roger Smith CRUISING IN COMPANY There is no Sailing Regatta at the Club this year and our Fleet Captain had hoped to organise a cruise to St. Katherine's Yacht Haven, London, to cover the Spring Bank Holiday weekend. Unfortunately, there are no berths available over that period, so this idea will have to be put off for the time being. Continued. iéé«ex

— However, there is no reason to abandon the idea and, if there is sufficient ‘ interest, the trip can be made later in the year. In the meantime, there could be some form of Cruiser Rally over the Spring Bank Holiday weekend, which can be continued into the following week for those members who have the available time. The suggestion is that Cruiser members and their crews meet at the Clubhouse at about 8.00 p.m. on Friday 23rd Ma , when a destination can be agreed. With at least three days available, this could be the River Swale, Medway or any of the Essex/Suffolk waterways. Subject, of course, to weather, the Walton Backwaters would make a good destination as there will be ample moor- ings available at the Titmarsh Marina or there is good free anchorage. The steward at the Walton and Frinton Sailing Club is prepared to make an evening meal for under £3.00 a head and these could be booked prior to leaving the Club. Once the decision as to destination has been made, details of the passage can be discussed for the benefit of members with limited experience and any mis-— givings hopefully resolved. One of the aims would be to encourege members new to cruising and draw on the vast experience of others within the Club. In practice, as we all know, boats would not be Sailing abreast or immediately behind or in front of one another, but there should always be a friendly vessel in sight throughout the passage. The actual cruise, rally or whatever we call it would commence on Saturday 2'th May, time depending on destination. I envisage that some members will have to be back for Monday evening, ready to start work the following day, whilst others may decide to extend the weekend. This can be talked through on the Fridey eve- ning and of course anyone who cannot make the evening meeting but would like to participate by arriving in time for the departure on the Saturday can telephone the Clubhouse for particulars during the evening, This form of activity is commonplace in many sailing clubs and it would be very nice if this cruise proves to be the first of many. There is such a large range of Cruisers at the Club and it would be nice to say that anyone would be welcome, but I do not think that this would be practical. I suggest for this particular weekend that the participating boats should be capable of maintaining at least 4 knots under power. If anyone would like to make any suggestions or raise any point in connection with the above, please contact me, either at the Club or at my home telephone number. “whilst it is not essential, I would at the same time apprecia te some indication of the response. Arthur Hodges Tel. C'ford [redacted] CRUISER NOCRINGS Last year, as in previous years, a nunber of moorings dragged and the presence of barnacles on the anchor flukes indicated that the anchors had landed on the bottom with the flukes uppermost. The weight of the ground chain holds the boat and it is only in strong conditions that the problem is apparent. I have spoken to members of the Chelmsford Diving Club and they are prepare d to visit the Club to check individual moorings. It will require at least two divers for safety and one would swim down the scope to follow the ground chain continued .eceec

mF ae to each of the two anchors. The points of the flukes would be correctly posi- tioned and bedded as far as possible. The mein thing is that the flukes would be the correct way. There are of course expenses and the charge would be £3.00 per complete mooring, irrespective of position. This is payable by the individual and I expect that the job will be done sometime towards the end of April. If you want your moor- ing checked, please let me know. I will then Supply the Diving Club with a numbered list of the moorings to be checked and receive back a list when the job is done. Arthur Hodges Tel. C'ford [redacted] CRUISER FLEET NEWS By the time you read this, the season will have started and, hopefully, the winter forgotten. Words of warning. Last season we had a case of one member using another member's mooring. His boat broke loose and caused damage to other craft. His Insurance Company took action against the owner of the mooring for all damage done. This could have been quite nasty but for the expertise of ano- ther member of the Club, who saved this from succeeding. Moral. If you pick up someone else's mooring, you are responsible for all eventualities, not the owner of the mooring. The Marine Police are introducing a scheme for reducing thefts et cetera from boats. It is called larine Watch and a copy will be attached to the back of this issue (Ed's note: I hope). Anyone interested should fill in the form and return it to me or the Marine Police. John Wade Fleet Captain [redacted] CRUISER RACING It seems as if, suddenly, the season is upon us again and, for those inter- ested in racing cruisers - judging from reading David Harper's comments in last month's Navigans about his new Pandora - it will be a competitive one. I would like to encourage all cruiser owners either fancying racing compet- ition on the odd occasion or as a regular thing, to join the B.J.R.C. this year. Their registration fee has risen in 1986 from £3.00 to £5.00 to cover increased printing and postage costs, but for this you get a Year Book which will include all details of the racing programme, plus details of each race result soon after the event. There are no extra entry fees and all the races are local, so therefore do not involve travelling problems. Six Marconi members registered with the B.J.R.C. last year and, if you are interested this year, I shall require the owner's name, address and telephone number, plus the boat name and class or make, together with your sail number and PY handicap if known. Do please send these details to me with your fee as soon COntINUGd sce

-8- as possible, or face me accosting you at the Club in the next few weeks! My address is 1 [redacted], Linton, Cambridge [redacted]. As well as the B.J.R.C. races, I am hoping we will be able to revive some of our Barnacle Points races, to give all arconi cruiser owners a chance of some racing on one or two Sundays during the season. Finally, for those who do intend to register with the B.J.R.C., please note that our Marconi Cruiser Cup this year will be held on Sunday 3rd August. Mike Turner SOLO NEWS By the time you read this the season will have started, with the premier fleet first on the water, I expect. Things look good for Solo sailing in 1986. We have some good new sailors joining the fleet; Phil Gray is selling his Hornet and will look for a Solo; Malcolm Gandy had bought John Murphy's boat to return to the sailing scene; Colin Willsmore is a new face who we are pleased to welcome; George White has bought Bob Anderson's old boat; and the one-third owner of the red and white boat is Mr Weston. We had a pleasant evening at Marie and Dennis Dear's house in February, which made a nice break despite the snowy weather. In January, Bob Anderson arranged with Dick Batt to give a winter talk, which he did with great enthusiasm. Recently, Malcolm Stuart organised a fleet party at the Club. This was a ‘great success, due to much hard work by Malcolm. The Solo helms cooked the meal and, as fer as I am aware, everybody is fit and well! The highlight of the evening was a Victorian melodrama featuring that dastardly fiend, Sir Mountifield Dickbatt! On the sailing scene, four Solos went to the first Open Meeting of the year at Chess Sailing Club. It was a very good turnout, but the Marconi results were not of the highest order. It must be said, however, that there were seven or eight helms present who hed been in the top ten in the Nationals in the past two years. Ron Greygoose was the top Marconi helm, with his new Batt sail looking good for the new season. Happy sailing. In October last year I came to the conclusion that, unless I did something soon about the paint flaking off my boat, then by next season there would be none left at all! So, one cold Cctober evening, I set to work in the garage with an electric paint stripper. It shouldn't take too long, I thought; after all, most of it is flaking off anyway. Some hope! later Several hours and with only a small indent made into the wood, I realised that I had under- taken a longer job than I had first anticipated. Why didn't I buy a G.R.P. Mirror? It was around Christmas when I finally had the hull filled, sanded and generally ready to paint. I decided that, as Spring was on its way, with bright flowers and sunshine, black was the colour to have. So TI returned to the garage with continued .....

= TO? me a new brush and a couple of cans of International's best black. Halfway through February and after four months of working in a freezing cold garage, (I think I've got frostbite!) I finally had it finished. Okay, so it has a couple of runs and it's a bit blotchy, but it's finished now and that's that! Having consulted the Mirror Year Book and fixed up a crew, I decided that it was time to hit the water and the Bough Beech Open would be the boat's proving ground. So, on March 23rd, I set off with Nigel and the dad to Kent. I'm beginning to think it wasn't such a good idea. After getting up at 6.15 a.m., we arrived only to find the gates locked and nobody about — the first start was an hour later than I had thought! Eventually someone showed up and let us in, only for us to find a howling gale sweeping across the reservoir. The three races turned out to be survival lessons and, in the first race, after a broad spinnaker reach, we came to a sticky end, upside down in a bit of a vi- cious squall. After two races spent freezing at the back of a quickly dimin- ishing fleet (20 boats in ist race, 9 in 2nd!), we had had enough and decided to retire for the day without any idea of whether the boat was going any better than last year - the peak of which was an amazing 4ist at the Nationals! But don't let me put you off visiting the local Opens - how could 1? Itisa lot of fun and does your sailing a lot of good to get amongst larger fleets aad and harder competition. I intend to visit a number of Open Meetings this year and hope that some other (keen and adventurous - there must be some!) Mirror sailors will join me. eo 4 a SAILING INSTRUCTIONS RULES Races will be sailed under the rules of the |.Y.R.U., R.Y.A., and class associations, except as provided for by these sailing instructions. The R.Y.A. prescription to |.Y.R.U. Rule 57 (leaving boat) shall not apply. The 720° turns penalty as provided in Rule 72.4, Alternative Penalties, and Appendix 3 of the yacht racing rules shall apply, instead of disqualification, for infringement of a rule of Part IV. COURSE INSTRUCTIONS Details of courses will be available at the club house at least one hour before the start of the race, but may be varied as above. STARTING LINE The starting line is the continuation of a line between the triangle on the racebox and the mete on the foreshore. When starting, boats must sail a course which passes between the mark D, and the mete, unless the letter ‘L’ is displayed after the course sign, when the boats must sail a course which passes between the mark No. 1 and the mark D. FINISHING LINE The finishing line is the line between the triangle on the racebox and the mark D. (There is no long line finish) PERSONAL BUOYANCY Personal Buoyancy shall be taken and must be worn by the helmsman and crew when the red flag ‘B’ is flown from the Club House, Cadets (under 18) must wear buoyancy at all times afloat. SIGNING ON Starters must sign on, at the Club house, on their Class Declaration form not earlier than 1 hour and not later than 15 minutes before each scheduled start. If you do not intend to start, please indicate this before the start. SIGNALS Flags flown from racebox masthead refer to the whole racing programme. Flags flown from racebox yardarm refer to individual races. All racing signals will normally be made from the racebox in accordance with |.Y.R.U. Rule 4 but Postponement (Answering pennant) Abandonment,- (flag N) and Buoyancy to be worn (flag B) signals flown from the Clubhouse also apply to racing and will not necessarily be duplicated at the racebox. When Flag N is displayed before the start of a race the race is postponed to a later date. WARNING SIGNALS and STARTING ORDER Starting Times will be displayed at the Clubhouse at least one hour before the start of the race. Flags to be used for each Class of dinghy will be displayed at the Clubhouse. For International and National Classes the Warning Signals will be as prescribed by the R.Y.A. RECALLS : Rule 8.2(b) will apply and no recall numbers will be displayed. If any part of a competing boat is over the starting line when the signal to start is made, another sound signal will be made and the class flag will be left flying at the dip, until the boats over the line have returned to the satisfaction of the Race Officer, or until such time as he sees fit. For a general recall the false start will be the 10 minute warning signal for the new start, unless other races are starting within 10 minutes, when the start of the last race will be the five minute preparatory signal for the new start. Rule 51.1(c) will apply after general recalls. 10. SHORTENED COURSE When the shortened course signal is displayed at the racebox. the race will end when the leading boat, continuing round the course, next crosses the finishing line. When displayed on the committee boat, the race will finish between the nearby mark and the committee boat. 11, TIME LIMITS Unless otherwise stated, if no boat finishes within three hours of the start, the race will be abandoned. Any boat not finishing within one hour of the winner, on corrected time shall not qualify as finishing. 12. SIGNING OFF All competitors must sign off on their Class Declaration form immediately after each race with a limit of half an hour of the . last boat finishing. Competitors retiring must declare this on the declaration form otherwise they will be disqualified. 13. PROTESTS Protests shall be handed to the Race Officer (or Reception) on the form prescribed by the R.Y.A., within half-an-hour of the last boat finishing, together with the protest fee of 50p., which is returnable unless the protest is judged to be frivolous The Race Officer (or Race Committee) will appoint three judges to hear and decide the protest as soon as possible. 14, HANDICAPS The handicaps used shall be those prescribed by the R.Y.A. unless otherwise agreed by the Blackwater Joint Racing Committee in which case details will be displayed at the Clubhouse. 15. POINTS For a points series of races, points will be awarded as follows; the lowest total score denoting the overall winner. First, 3/4: Second, 2: Third, 3: etc. Retired, one more point than the maximum number of entries for any race completed in the series. Disqualified or not ranking as a starter, 4 more points than retired. The number of races to count will be the nearest whole number above half the total number of races completed in the series. In the event of a tie, points from one more race will count. If the tie still results, when all races are taken into account, the place will be declared a tie. 16. SAIL NUMBERS Competitors will not be permitted to change sail numbers during the Meeting except under extenuating circumstances and then only by submitting a request in writing to the Race Officer for consideration. Uz. AMENDMENTS Any amendments to these sailing instructions will be displayed in the Clubhouse at the signing on form, at least one hour before the start of the race affected.

This year we are introducing Marine Watch which concerns boat owners looking after themselves. wm WMhat exactly is MARINE WATCH ? Well for a start let's make it quite clear - IT IS NOT A VIGILANTE GROUP The aims of a Marine Watch are:- 1. To reduce local opportunities for crime by deterring would-be thieves and vandals. 2. To establish a community spirit so that everyone can contribute in the protection of their property by mutual co-operation and communication. 3. To inform the police or the liaison persons of any suspicious activity. 4. To make everyone more aware of local crime problems and more security conscicus about their own boats. What's in it for me ? The successful operation of a Marine Watch Scheme would soon have obvious advantages: 1. Crimes such as vandalism and thefts of and from Boats should be reduced. 2. A better community spirit can be created. 3. Suspicious persons and incidents can be quickly reported to the police. 4, Crime Prevention advice can be quickly and efficiently circulated throughout our groups. 5. The use of a Police Property Marking Kit to Postcode all valuable property on your boats, and expert advice on how to use it. 6. Information about local criminal activity can be easily circulated to all members, so that everyone is aware of what exactly is going On. As you will know, the building programme was virtually on schedule and we expected to con- duct sea trials on Saturday i2th April. Since then, now four weeks ago at the time of writing, we have been plagued with petty excuses for non-completion. On Friday 2nd May, Murray Bates and Peter Clayton visited Deal - yet another abortive trip as the propeller was supplied with the wrong internal taper. On Saturday 10th May Peter and I arrived at Deal at 9.30 a.m. ready for the sea trials at 11.00 a.m. On entering Brian Corey's yard, the "Jack B" looked most impressive; the engine was running very quietly and with little vibra- tion. Almost unbelievable, I thought. Then the bad news - it would only idle and not rev. The morning was spent fault-finding and on the telephone to Geoff Josey, our Ford diesel engine expert. Despite all efforts, we event- ually gave up at 2.30 p.m. Geoff Josey will no doubt solve the problem. Sea trials will hopefully be midweek and delivery to Stansgate prior to the week— end of 17th May. On Saturday 10th May we held the New = Members' Evening, which was well attended. Now I know the meaning of being ‘hoist by his own petard' ; just as I thought nobody, but nobody, was interested in Personal PYNs, some clown decides to ask me when the results are going to be published. I suppose some might say I'm the bigger clown for suggesting it in the first place and I guess they're right. Things are not helped very much by the fact that my own Personal PYN looks distinctly sick -- as I said , hoist by his own petard (or is it 'on' his own petard - what is a petard anyway ?). After juggling with the Personal PYN 'rules' and rehashing the 'method', a result of sorts has been achieved. So, for what it's worth, the table below sets out, for all to see, the horrible truth about the Solo fleet. Why the Solo fleet you’ask ? Well, they seem to be the only fleet to sail regularly. Apart from that, I reckoned if they're hard enough to go ‘frost-bit.ing' then they're hard enough to suffer the ignominy of public exposure of their PYN. Now to the table - if we start out on the basis that virtually nobody sails to their PYN standard, then we're halfway to understanding the table. To make it easy, we assume that only one person (ie. the person who finishes 3rd on corrected time) actually sails up to the Class PYN standard. That obviously means that the two who finished in front of him/her must have sailed better than the standard whilst those behind clearly did not achieve such excellence.(it gets worse as we proceed). Let the doubters consider - if we all sailed to the class standard, we'd finish in a gigantic dead-heat. For any one race, each elapsed time was compared to the corrected time of the person who came third and this produces a unique PYN for that race for each competitor. This is added to the aggregate of previous unique PYNs calculated , divided by the number of races (+1) considered and a new personal PYN is the result. Where a helm has not taken part in, or completed, a race, it is assumed the unique PYN for that race is the same as his/her Personal PYN , and so the personal PYN doesn't change. This is fair enough since there is no evidence to show it has changed. £G. to date, Colin Willsmore hasn't completed a race

due to either not entering or due to retiring. Consequently, he retained the full class PYN of 122; this would obviously be a distinct disadvantage if the race results were calculated on the basis of the Personal PYN. The lesson is there to be seen - you must finish the races (ie be timed in) to get a more favourable personal PYN (unless you're the champion and you're then likely to find your PYN getting somewhat onerous as the season progresses). It is worth noting that a very good (or very bad) result has a more dramatic effect early in the season than it does later on in the year since those later in the year are masked by the aggregate PYNs of the past. A PYN which is rising with each subsequent race would suggest the person is sailing below (ie.worse) than the current personal PYN attributed to them. Conversely, a falling PYN indicates sailing better than the personal PYN. No prizes for guessing that a substantially unchanged PYN indicates you are sailing up to (your) standard compared to others in the list. Conclusion No conclusions . As with all handicapping systems, nobody is satisfied except the winner. One could argue the merits, or otherwise, of a particular handicap system for as long as it takes to find the QOD to put toilet paper in the ladies loo (I'm told it sometimes takes a very long time - or used ww to ). For those who think Gods smile on the virtuous, they can take comfort that they (the Gods) are falling about laughing as far as my personal PYN is concerned. The thing is, the personal PYN is not a measure of personal skill, only an indicator to past performance. Thus although Jack, Dennis and Mike did not finish a race, we continue to attribute the class PYN of 146 to them - because there is nothing to say it should be anything else.., Final comment. wy As an experiment, the Personal PYN had its interesting sidelights as I worked it out; however, should we use them for series racing ? Roger Smith Saffron Walden [redacted] THE RIVER BLACKWATER If you've ever felt you'd like to know more about the River where you sail, I can recommend reading 'The Salty Shore' by John Leather. He writes of places so familiar to us by name such as Mersea, Bradwell, Tollesbury etc. A couple of years ago while visiting St Peter's Church by the sea wall at Bradwell we found a charming cottage nearby and wondered who it had once belonged to. It turns out that it was once lived in by a Walter Linnett, a professional wildfowler, and the last surviving one on the Blackwater by 1947. John Leather has also written an excellent book, '"Barges', about the sailing barges of South East England. We are still privileged with the frequent sight of these gracing our river and this book should be able to tell you all you'd want to know. In the Chelmsford library they can be found under the section 'Essex Books'., Maureen Ball

M.S.C. Spring Cruise On Friday 23rd May at 8pm several Cruiser members met in the Clubhouse to discuss 'Cruising in Company' as suggested by Arthur Hodges in the April edition of Navigans. Following a few drinks and a lot of chat, it was decided that we would head for Titmarsh Marina the next day. The wind came up in the night and it was none too comfortable on the moorings. We still had the high winds Saturday morning so a council was called ashore at llam and the decision made to sail down-river under head-sails, I was glad to be off; although I have not suffered the miseries of sea-sickness I was beginning to feel decidedly queasy, and some other crews felt the same way. Eight Cruisers left Stansgate between 12.15 and 12,30 and enjoyed a comfortable sail up the Wallet. Pye End is just one of the buoys we have trouble finding, but our boat, Veruna II, was saved from sailing into Harwich by the crew of Kellys Eye, 4.30 found us all at Titmarsh with Viridia aground in the entrance, but not long after there was enough water for all boats to enter, We were soon safely berthed, as crews helped each other with fending off and tying up. Everyone had a good night's rest, and Sunday morning was spent relaxing, pottering about on our boats. Ron decided to put his inflatable on the coach roof of Tekin Two, and the crews of Kellys Eye and Veruna II were engaged in the same task. Pete and Kelly were somewhat surprised to find a swordfish in their inflatable that they had been towing. I can't say I saw the fish, but can vouch they had not had a drink at that point in time. Unfortunately, Snoopy had a sick little boy on board which was rather worrying, but I am pleased to say he soon recovered. At 4pm the crews of Viridia, Kellys Bye, Tekin Two, Two Jays and Veruna II walked into Walton to be met at 6.30pm by the crews of Snoopy, Sandpiper, Olaf and ; Ebony Rose for dinner in the Walton and Frinton Sailing Club, We can all thoroughly recommend the cuisine at under £3 a head. After dinner, discussion was the laying of plans to sail to the Deben the following morning. Two Jays and Sandpiper could not stay any longer, so would be heading for home on the Momay morning. We bid them good night and safe journey, and I understand both crews had enjoyed cruising in company. 10am Monday mormming our flotilla of six were motoring out of the Marina, making for the Deben and the dreaded bar!! lpm found us at Felixtowe Ferry with every- one telling us that was the calmest they had ever known the entrance to the Deben,. I was pleasantly surprised, or more to the point relieved, after the tales I had heard. Tekin Two came on the radio, Ron and Joyce were enjoying their sail, and would meet us later, That later turned out to be the next morning! All the other vessels went on to anchor at the Rocks, but when the tide went out Veruna II was sitting high and dry on the shingle, so out came the bucket and brush for a scrub- down, It was a lovely, warm,calm evening so Arthur and Irene from Viridia, along with Pete, Kelly, Malcolm, Helen, their two children plus Malcolm and I, strolled down to the Ramsholt Arms. We managed a couple? of drinks and it was so pleasant getting to know one another. Coming back in the dark was good fun, Pete was telling me a creapy story which made me cry with laughter, not fright, sorry Pete! Arriving back at the Rocks we found Viridia with all her cabin lights on and it was suggested to Arthur that motoring up and down the river for 2 or 3 hours would charge the batteries, but I'm not sure he found this amusing, Sorry Arthur! Malcolm and I had to stay awake until 1.30 am until Veruna II came afloat so we could move her into deeper water. It was a dreadful night, every boat had a fair amount of anchor chain out but the wind was so strong the boats were swinging around and no-one managed to get much sleep. At the first light of day Viridia and Snoopy upped anchors and went on to Waldringfield. Veruna II had dragged her anchor, and was almost in mid-channel. Kellys Eye had anchored on the opposite shore and had spent a comfortable night. Here was a lesson to be learnt, Pete had experienced anchoring at the Rocks, so a

=e knew what to expect.It had been such a calm evening we didn't listen to the voice of experience but , we will in future. Malcolm and Helen appeared on Olaf, they were heading back to Stansgate as they could stay no longer, but had told us the evening before how much they had enjoye d cruising in company and when would be the next event? We waved good—byp to Malcolm, Helen and their two little girls. At mid-day Kellys Eye and Veruna II left the Rocks to meet up with Tekin Two, Viridia and Snoopy at Waldringfield, Snoopy's crew were feeling tired, so leaving them on a mooring the rest of us made our way to Woodbridge, be ee, ee > Ea % he. ale. Ge Doha Visit A most successful return match which was won by M.S.C. Herewith copy of report that appeared in the 'Daily Gulf Times’ on August 23rd 1986. quote Marconi Sailing Club of Essex England won a recent racing competition for 420 and Laser class dinghies against Doha Sailing Association. The event was a return match as the Marconi Sailors had visited Doha in October 1985 when the visitors were defeated at West Bay. Marconi tactics were somewhat evident with a change of class in the single sailed dinghies from Laser to Solos. However DSA had ample chance to practise. With slack tide conditions for the first race, DSA were victorious in the 420 class but came second in the Solos. On the afternoon of the first day of the competition, strengthening wind and a rapidly rising tide created a new experience of the relatively "tide free" Gulf team, resulting in a defeat in both classes. Although two further races had been scheduled for the next day, the result of the first was in favour of Marconi who won the competition on aggregate points for the two classes. Sailing was concluded with a well organised but largely "rule free" fun race in which the DSA were winners. Prizes were presented by the club Commodores Mr. David Harper of Marconi and Sami Abu Shaikha of the DSA. Sami Abu Shaikha presented prizes to Marconi Sailing Club, provided by the Qatar Supreme Youth Welfare Council. A cup donated by TRAGS was also presented to David Harper. Sami Abu Shaikha then invited Marconi to return to Doha in 1987 for further team racing. Unquote I forgive the 'bias' of report and thank the Marconi team and all members associated with the event. I take this opportunity to personally thank Ron & Mary Greygoose who helped Pat andme with the planning and organisation and MalcolmStuart who did a first class job as race officer and for organising the fun race. We now have a superb cup to add to our trophies. I have requested that the sailing Sub Committee decide upon an event to be associated with the trophy. 7. John Weedon has highlighted some problems with regard to our dinghy racing acitivites. We are grateful for the comments and have organised action by our sailing sub committee. We now look forward to the Hornet/Dart open weekend and hopefully more Marconi sailing success. Hope to see you at the Club. David Harper Commodore

CRUISER NEWS It is quite a common sight to see cruisers anchored between Bradwell Power Station and the Baffle, and one of our new members decided to drop his hook there whilst he made a cup of tea, On leaving he found the anchor snagged and after a great deal’ of effort managed to get the anchor to the surface together with a very obvious Power Cable, He had no choice really but to pass a rope under the Cable whilst the anchor was released with a great sigh of relief, Yes! The Cable is live, I am told 415 volts, and there are notices on the land and on the Baffle, but thought I would mention the incident to prevent a recurrence, Cruiser Laying Up ‘I know it sounds early to think about laying up boats, but one boat is already out of the water and I expect others will soon follow, It is anticipated that extensive excavations will take place this Autumn and Winter when the new sewerage scheme starts and much of this will take place in the Cruiser Laying Up area. I mention this now as many members may not be able to park in their usual spot and some will even be outside the Cruiser Park, a There is a strong possibility that some places will be permanently lost,as the sewerage pipes may be near the surface and the ground in the vicinity will not stand the weight of a cruiser, If you do come out of the water before the plan is published then please do not jack up the trolley onto blocks — to permit movement of the unit if necessary. There is to be a drive to dispose of old trailers and boats with no record of membership which should help the space problem a little. Some members have purchased new boats during the season and the replaced boats are still in the park. If these boats are not removed by the end of the season please let me know early and I will endeavour to make some arrangements, Night Sailing I think most people who have sailed at night can recount some incident, and one gentleman from Brading Haven Yacht Club (I of W) reverted to verse, The following appeared in the Newsletter of the above club and I thought some of our members might appreciate it: When both lights you see ahead Port your helm and show your red, When to your starboard red appear ‘Tis your duty to keep clear But when upon your port is seen A steamer's starboard light of green, There ‘s not so much for you to do For green to port keeps clear of you, Green to green and red to red Perfect safety, go ahead, When in danger or in doubt Always keep a good look-out. When in danger with no room to turn, Ease her, Back her, GO ASTERN. —-000000-— Winter Meetings will be held in the Committee Rooms of the Main Club, Beehive Lane, Chelmsford, 7.30pm on the first Wednesday of each month, commencing WEDNESDAY 5th NOVEMBER 1986 Arthur Hodges Fleet Captain Chelmsford [redacted]

CADET WEEK Cadet Week and Summer Camp On behalf of the Camping Club Boating Group we would like to thank the Marconi Sailing Club for a super’ fortnight of camping and sailing. All the Boating Group members who camped at Stansgate thoroughly enjoyed themselves and sincerely hope to come again next year, Two members made a point of writing to thank the Club. I quote from one letter: "Thanks to the M.S.C. members, particularly the Committee members, who worked so hard and made the Boating Group so welcome," Graham & Chris Boustred, -——000000——= Cadet Week Activities Sunday First day, and a list of over 30 cadets was drawn up, followed by capsize drill on dry land. In the afternoon we did the capsize drill on water using ‘Idle Vice’ tied to the mooring raft, also practised rowing and paddling, Evening: Rounders. Monday Not much wind, sailed up by Osea and back again. Afternoon: sailed by Osea again, got bored, sailed back! Evening: Non-stop Cricket, it rained, Tuesday Cadets divided into Groups 1 and 2, Group 2 continued the week as follows: Barely any wind, sailed through moorings and back again. Afternoon: No wind at all, we practised tacking and gybing inshore with someone holding the boat. Tried to sail up by Osea, no progress, so came back, (Ed. - Yawn!) Evening: Volleyball. Wednesday A strong NW wind blew up which was wonderful after Tuesday's calm, Sailed a simple triangular course a few times, A few capsizes, Afternoon and Evening: Royal Wedding celebration games, high tea in the Lounge, and a disco, Water fight and disco enjoyed very much, Thursday Another good strong breeze meant that we were able to sail by Osea and go round a course, Afternoon: Sailed to Osea for lunch (all cadets), afterwards a race round Osea = some made it and some didn't! Friday A very strong SW wind which was against the tide making it choppy and rough. One boat turtled but righted and sailed on. Practised heave-to and man overboard. Afternoon: Races from the start line, Evening: Prize-giving after watching video of afternoon racing. All the cadets greatly appreciated the work put in for them by Derek Hall, Mike & Maggie Boreham and all the other people in the rescue boats, Thanks also to Chris & Graham Boustred for organising so many of the activities on land for Cadet Week, Jennifer Ball, Cadet. SAILING SECRETARY'S NOTES Because of pressure of work, new baby and stress of fatherhood, Phil Gray had to step down from the job of Sailing Secretary, and being in the wrong place at the wrong time as usual I have ‘volunteered’ to finish off the season. We will be putting together next year's sailing programme soon, so if you have any ideas for the coming season, please let your fleet captain or me know. It would be nice to try and fit in a day for racing and non-racing folk, such as aquateering, but I warn you if you suggest it - well you know the rest. There have been times when people have not turned up for Race Officer or Rescue Boat Duty. Please try to avoid this happening next season, it usually means someone has to miss out on their Sunday sailing. As far as the Rescue Boat goes it is not just for racers, we have all learned to sail somewhere and the Rescue Boat is to allow anyone sailing from the Club to do so with confidence. EDITORIAL With the reports and minutes from our recent AGM, this edition of Navigans is going to be rather bulky, but it should prove interesting as it provides all the background information on the running of the Club, much of which is not obvious when visiting the Site. As we have sometimes had problems in getting Navigans to members in time for them to participate in the events featured in Dates-for-—Your—Diary it has been decided to 'shuffle' the months along and this Navigans has been named for November/December. The next Navigans will be headed January’ and should reach members at the end of December, If the system works then members will receive their magazine at the beginning of the month of events advertised. It will now be particularly important to let me have the dates of forthcoming events well in advance, Deadlines for Navigans are usually the Wednesday following the first Monday of each month (when Committee meetings are held). So, for example, I will need to know about February's events at the beginning of January. Cruiser News The first Winter Meeting will have taken place by the time that this is published and the next Meeting is on 3rd December 1986, when Ron Meadows will be speaking on the repair and maintenance of Fibre Glass boats. All Club Members invited and the time is 7.30pm at the Marconi Social Club, Beehive Lane, Chelmsford. I will be taking orders shortly for discount paint products, but at the present time the suppliers have not come up with a firm offer. This should be resolved in time for the next (Ed. - 'January') issue of Navigans and I anticipate being able to reduce the retail price by about 33%. This will be subject to a minimum total order so I am asking for your participation, The offer will include paint, varnish, anti-fouling, gel-shield etc. More about this later, Most of our boats are now out of the water and as you well know it has been a tight } squeeze to fit everyone into the existing allocated space. * . * . 7 — The Committee has asked me about the apparently abandoned trollies and trailers that are parked at the back of the field on the right of the Club entrance —- the field used by the Dart Fleet. I was not in a position to answer as most of this metal tangle is unmarked. If any member owns and desires to retain any of these trailers or trollies, please mark them with the owner's or boat name and advise me accordingly. I will then arrange future storage. Otherwise it is intended to invite a scrap dealer down to the Club in January 1987 and dispose of the unwanted bits. Arthur Hodges, Cruiser Fleet Captain. Chelmsford [redacted]. —— eee Ee ES SS

'Travels of a Calor Gas Bottle' Dave Thomas. What a holiday!! Two weeks in the Scottish Highlands sounded OK and the people looked nice but, oh dear, the weather was awful.. I was strapped to the front of a caraven and looked forward to some scintillating scenery, but beyond Watford Gap the heavens opened and remained that way. By the time we returned to Maldon I was exhausted and beginning to show signs of rust. Time for a re-charge and a general face-lift. I refer to myself as Dora - well Dumpy Dora actually, as my shape as a gas container has long been referred to as a 'Dumpy' by all the people I have worked for. Somehow I have been diverted since my recent service and now find myself highly charged and in company of other friends at a Yacht Chandler's in Bradwell. There is an atmosphere of anticipation and excitement but I am somewhat apprehensive at the prospect of what will be my first sailing trip. Indeed the thought of so much water brings on some painful memories, By Saturday however I have been exchanged and almost lovingly installed aboard the yacht 'Marinero'. I am impressed. The boat hardly rocks at all excevt when the elderly couple stumble aboard late at night singing some hit from the 1930s, From the final clinking of the Geneva bottle it seems no time before they are up and untying ropes. The engine has erupted and we are moving off into what looks like very deep water to me. After about an hour the engine stopned and I was disappointed that the journey was over so soon — but no, there is activity on deck and contrary to some of the rumours I had heard in Bradwell, sails were being hoisted. Three days later having touched down briefly in Ramsgate and Brighton we were in Cherbourg and the boat began to sink!! Well, it seemed like it to me as a constant procession of Frenchmen called out for Marinero and deposited box after box of what they referred to as ‘ship's stores' onto the deck and into the cockpit. Now I can tell you there was nothing edible in the whole consignment and either we were destined for a voyage well beyond my capacity or an army of guests were coming for a long stay. I was not aware at this stage of the drink problem called "Becketts" which emanated apparently from a travelling companion named 'Northerner'. In due course all stores were stowed reverently away and we sailed to Guernsey and thence to Lezardrieuy in northern Brittany. The river approach was magnificent scenery of steep rocky’ hills on both sides and without exception all the natives gave a friendly wave or call. My services were not called upon too much during the next few days as the owners were enjoying the gastronomic delights of true French cuisine ashore, About a week later we sailed north again in brilliant sunshine upwards but thick fog sideways and I for one was pleased to arrive in Jersey. 2 Although by now > I was beginning to feel a little drained it was again a relaxing few days for me, Then we left for Cherbourg and I did not enjoy the conditions round the Cap de la Hague although I gather that 'those upstairs' judged it a good sail and celebrated in their normal manner. It was in Brighton that I had my first tummy rumble, that feeling of emptiness that signals the need for a re-charge. Before I could blink I was yanked roughly upwards and shaken and the adjudged to be fit for a bit longer, then dropped unceremoniously back in my box. contd...

There never is a convenient time for a gas bottle to run out acnarently. ‘ell, I won't be treated like that and I've learnt = trick or twe over the years, - That night the flag officers of alcoholics anonymous came over from 'Northener' and amidst the drinking there was Obviously some attempt to cook dinner. I know because 2 gas rings, the grill and the oven plays havoc with my insides and ordin- arily I would have quietly given in at this stage, Not this time though. I strained and sucked and held on until I could smell the pastry starting to rise and then I switched off. The singing eventually stopped and there was an awareness through the haze that all was not well in the Galley - then came the language, totally unrepeatatle, and from such nice ladies too, I chuckled then and I stiil do in my new paint, waiting at Dan Webb & Feezey for my next purchaser, Dumpy Dora. Ed. said: There have been several interesting sailing programmes on television during the past year, more than I can ever remember seeing in the past. At the time of prevaring this Navigans is an interesting series on the forthcoming battle for the America's Cup in Australia. It is on Channel 4, 6.30pm Saturdays, and called the Great Australian Boat Race, There is some exciting filming of boats racing, and amusing reports of the razzamatazz on shore. B.B.C. There being no further questions, the Meeting was closed at 15.10 hrs. —_—— ae eee —— _—— — — COMMODORE'S REPORT — AGM 2nd November 1986 A year ago I was able to report that the MSC membership had been significantly increased during the 1985 season - I now have to inform you that despite all of our efforts, we have experienced a 4.2% decline. However it is with much pleasure that I am able to inform you that the majority of the problems previously highlighted to you have been addressed and resolved. Before talking about the events of this season, I must remind you that there is a national decline in dinghy sailing activities: in fact, some well established clubs have had no alternative but to close their dinghy sections. I1 feel sure that our success is based on maintaining varied interests and promoting a friendly and helpful atmosphere throughout the Club. We have achieved a better sense of belonging into the membership and made huge strides to unite our dinghy and cruiser sections, Incidentally, following the last AGM we wrote to the MASC confirming the two AGM proposals —- Agenda Items 9.2 and 9.3 regarding: 1. Levy imposed upon MSC by MASC 2. The amendment to the rules to permit Associate Members to participate fully in the running of the Club, i.e. to become Flag Officers. Although no formal written answer was received, Gerry Wignall showed me copies of the MASC Committee Meeting minutes where discussion took place on this subject. The MASC ruling as interpreted by Gerry Wignall is that the Commodore, the Hon, Secretary and the Treasurer must be Ordinary members. This is now a subject to be steered and handled by your new Committee. From within our membership we again received requests for reduced subscription rates for retired members. This subject has been debated and agreed by your Main Committee and is tabled vefore you as a proposal today. You will also see proposals introduced to overcome certain other problems apropos Club operational management. The following comments relate to significant events in the 1986 season. I will avoid talking about the weather this of course, no doubt played a role with resvect to the reduction in our membership levels, CONT 6s ais

Sewerage I will not dwell on this topic as I have kept you informed through Navigans reports. We are pleased that at long last we have approval from the six authorities and that approval has been given by MASC, and work commences tomorrow, The project will be completed and working before the start of the 1987 season. The 1985 Laying-Up Supper at the County Hotel was a great success - all tickets being sold well before the event. Next followed the Christmas Working Party during which two of the scrubbing posts were replaced: a base was prepared for the new winch: part of the old sewerage herring—bone system was excavated; the Cruiser park was cleared and further Clubhouse decoration completed. We next addressed the problem of replacing the Sailing Support Boat. Although this was a tortuous exercise, we eventually took delivery and commissioned the boat in time for the more active part of our racing season, A competition was organised to name the new boat which was formally launched on Saturday 19th July 1986. Our next objective was to examine our position in order to maintain our membership level and establish our viability. We therefore debated ways of improving the appeal of the Stansgate site. A significant consideration was to those members and friends ‘left on the shore’, Initial suggestions were to build a verandah on the north wall of the Clubhouse and provide a 'play area’ for children. We also decided to consider catering and manning the bar on certain Friday, Saturday and early Sunday evenings. The play area was completed but the verandah project hit a snag when we were informed that due to the Thames Barrier Scheme it is planned to increase the height of the sea wall on the south bank of the River Blackwater by three feet. Our planning approval has been held up but the retiring Committee envisages that this is only a temporary hold and that approval and implementation of the project should be achieved in 1987, or 1988 at the latest. The Barn Dance held at the MASC on Saturday 25th January 1986 was another total sell-out and a very enjoyable event. Unfortunately we then had bad news with the sad and sudden loss of our dear friend and colleague, Jack Bigden ~ a former Commodore, A new telephone was installed at Stansgate and a '100 Club' introduced. My thanks to Alan Goss for organising the Club. I will leave it to Niel to report on the Club —- if he has the courage! Personally I feel that the '100 Club‘ has been the best scheme I have ever joined! The Solo Fleet party was held on Saturday 22nd May 1986 - a super event. Pat and I feel all sections should consider a party. Maybe Malcolm Stuart could take on yet another job and become Party Manager. We are sure you would all enjoy them. The winter series of lectures were all very well attended despite the weather. Murray and I offer our sincere thanks to all the organisers, The Fitting Out Party on 5th April 1986 was exceptional with most members joining in the spirit of the fancy dress, Another success down to Sheila Wade and her team. Let us hope that we find another energetic replacement to follow Sheila's excellent term of office, On 10th May we held the New Members' Evening. This must now surely become an annual event. This year we had a cabaret provided by a flock of sheep! The stage was the dinghy park and there was quite a remarkable performance by a number of animals on Malcolm Stuart's Solo. This was to the delight and amazement of our new members and Committee members alike — Malcolm was not so delighted!

Our extended bar and snack service commenced on Friday 30th May 1986, and on balance is considered by the retiring Committee to have been an overwhelming success. I feel sure that the membership will all join me in thanking June and Robert for the excellent and much appreciated service. Unfortunately, June and Robert will not be able to help us next year, so I appeal to you all for volunteers. Bank Holiday Weekend 25th - 26th May brought the Catamaran/Solo Open Meeting, an alternative to our normal Regatta, Fifteen Catamarans and nineteen Solos entered, the event being very well run, mainly by the Mirror Fleet. During the weekend we collected £50 for the Sport Aid Fund, The next Committee will have to decide upon the formula for next year. I feel that our active dinghy members will plan fora Regatta revival, probably in 1988. Mrs Connie Bigden formally launched the'"Jack B." - Doug Field won the prize for naming the boat. His suggestion was supported unanimously by the Main Committee. On 14th June the team from Rochester visited us - at least MSC won, if only by a narrow margin, It is unfortunate that Jack Pateman will not be able to attend our forthcoming Laying-Up Supper .... something about "he who laughs last..." remembering his comment to me when Rochester won the previous year, The Cadet Week followed by the Camping Week, 18th - 26th July was again very popular this season - my particular thanks to Derek Hall, our Cadet Skipper, for all of his efforts, energy and enthusiasm, On 19th July of that week we had the Barbecue —- an excellent evening, a record attendance and thoroughly enjoyed by all concerned, Let us hope that the verandah project is completed without too much delay as this should also reduce the burden of setting up the Barbecue bar. On Friday 25th July 1986, the Doha team arrived and, as I have recently reported fully in the September issue of Navigans, I will only remind everyone here that MARCONI WON and that we have been invited back to Doha next year for another return match. Our future Projects are: 1. Road resurfacing. 2. Repairs to the Hard. 3. Implementation of the verandah project. 4. Improvements to the catering facilities. 5. Re-examination of all aspects of site security. To complete my report, I must inform you that Murray Bates has declined the nomi- nation of Commodore. I confess that I was deeply disappointed and concerned when ke informed me of his decision only a few weeks ago. Murray and I and the Executive Committee had formed a very good working relationship and at last were realising the rewards of our efforts. We felt that most of our problems were over and that the way ahead had been paved for a good future of the MSC and a sensible term of office for Murray. I respect Murray's reasons for not continuing and am delighted that he has agreed to accept nomination for Vice-President. At least we can now rely upon his continuing. interest albeit not as active as in the past, Peter Clayton had previously agreed with me to complete this year's term of office and then retire from the Executive Team, As usual, Feter has very kindly helped us out by agreeing to stand as Vice-Commodore for one year, with George Robinson acting as his assistant. George is very capable and has been a most active member of Committee. I hope to see him as Vice-—Commodore in the not too distant future, Our main problem was to find a new Commodore. Murray, Peter, Pat Black, Neil and I are indebted to Robbie Sims for agreeing to accept nomination. Robbie is a well established member of the Club am was Vice-—Commodore in 1962 when the Club was at Heybridge. Also he was instrumental in the procurement of our present site. We have had to introduce a rule change to allow Robbie to become Commodore - this is included in your AGM notice. CONTC...0.0:0:6

10 I take this opportunity also to thank Malcolm Stuart who has agreed to accept nomination as Rear—Commodore, A final note is to thank everyone for supporting me during my two years as your Commodore, My thanks are extended to the MASC, particularly Tony Mayhew and Gerry Wignall, who unfortunately are not present today. ---- And a very special "Thank You" to Pat (my wife) for her tireless support, encouragement and understanding. This was overspent by £1500.00 mainly on the opportunity to purchase the farm equipment from Osea, the necessity to put Roll over cages on the tractors and the Scrubbing posts platform. In addition we failed to budget for the trailer for the JACK B. Generally I believe that we contiue to have a healthy situation and that the Reserve will increase during next year. Looking forward to next year, the M.A.S.C wrote to us in April and asked us to budget for a contribution of £5250.00 compared with £5000.00 this year. The Committee accepted this figure. However the basis of the contribution is still the subject of negotiation to determine the ground rules for the years after next. During next year there are a number of projects which may be able to proceed if the budget allows. These may include the provision of a CB radio system with a semi portable unit, the construction of the veranda, etc.. In addition both the Road and Hard are in need of repair, however the expenditure on these last two items is part of the discussion on the contribution to the M.A.S.C.. The ONE HUNDRED CLUB at present has a membership of 17 and needs at least 25 to break even. It will therefore be necessary to subsidise the prizes from the general club funds unless there is a sudden increase in membership.

Mirror Mania Winter is upon us and I must put away the wet suits, roll up the sails and think about Christmas, which may well be over by the time this is in print! w The Mirror Fleet grew during 1986 and the Autumn Points races were well supported, due partly to the enthusiasm of some of the Cadets, following the very successful camping weeks. The Yorston family have now joined us to be a three-boat family. They found the same problem that we had: all the family wanted to sail but brother and sister not keen to sail together!! Next season should see Debbie with Helen Bates as crew and Jon with Jenny Ball as crew, in Mirrors of course, I must mention Peter Collis, who has sailed regularly this year on a Sunday as well as a Wednesday evening and won both the Summer and Autumn Points single-handed. He puts us all to shame, seeming to find just the right line to sail as it were, and without a spinnaker! Dave Omyons and Graham Baker joined the fleet this year and sailed most of the races, also single-handed most of the time. Once again the ‘regulars’ were out: the Battle family (Mike is Fleet Captain), Neil Salmon with Nigel Leeder crewing (they won the Spring Points), Jack and Diane Rusbridge and the Borehams, Neil Pembleton sailed some races single-handed as did Dennis Dear, still without a ‘premier’ fleet boat. Peter Brown helmed his Mirror, and the other Cadets who either helmed or crewed a Mirror this year were: Grant Strong, Rory Strong, Stuart Golding, and David Ball. If I've missed anyone out in this article please let me know and you can have a special metnion next time! ww I hope that next season everyone will get going early, let's see if we can make the lst Spring Points race. We, or rather Mike and Damian, have taken all the varnish off "Bumble" and hope to have it ready on time next year! Damian will be sailing with Katherine Rutherford as crew in 1987 which leads me on to an advertisement from our familys Experienced Lightweight Mirror Crew - available all 1987 season, 13 years old, has sailed 420 and willing to try any Boat. Plenty of experience with bad-tempered Helms and can take any amount of shouting at. Mirror Available, Phone: Lucy Boreham, [redacted] Mike and I hope to sail our 420 even more next year but the Mirror is still my first love! Happy New Year, see you at the Barn Dance, Maggie Boreham, (Self-appointed Mirror Press Officer/Scribe! )

Solo News The Fleet AGM was held on 14th November with 11 members attending. Roger Smith resigned his fleet captaincy because of his new appointment as Sailing Secretary of the Club. During Roger's term of office the fleet activity has increased as has the membership and he deserves most of the credit for this happy state of affairs. His energy, enthusiasm and constant good humour has been an example to all, and deserves our sincere thanks. I was elected as the new Fleet Captain and have resigned from the Main Committee as a result. This meant that a new Committee member was needed to represent Associate Membership and the dinghy sailing activity. John Rutherford has agreed to do this so Solo interests will be well represented on the Main Committee. Associate Members should channel their concerns through hin. A few of the other key points from the AGM are as follows: It was agreed to count finishing order in local open meetings towards our 1987 Summer and Autumn points series (Results Secretary please note). We have done this for several years now in order to actively encourage our Fleet to support these meetings as this tends to stimulate the growth of the class in this area. I believe this adds variety and enjoyment to the sailing season whatever your standard of performance. I will publish meeting dates as soon as they are confirmed and recommend you note them and give it a try. In 1986 the meetings concerned .were: Halfway Y.C. and Fishers Green but in 1987 it is possible that: Dabchicks, Up River and Berwl Valley may be added. A vote was cast on the desirability of staging a Regatta on Spring Bank Holiday 1988, Result: 10 in favour, 1 abstention. It was recommended to modify the proposed 1987 sailing programme as follows: a) take the last 2 races from Spring Points and add them to the Summer Series. bd) extend Autumn points by adding 1 additional week to end of season, Our Open Meeting entry fees are excessive compared with other clubs. They should be no more than &4 for a 2day event in 1987 with no camping levy for participants, Solo Fish & Chip Supper is postponed from December to January 16th 1987, Please let Mary Greygoose (tel. [redacted] know as soon as possible if you wish to attend, so that tables can be booked. Barbecues after Sunday sailing should be increased in 1987. We will aim for the 2nd Sunday of each month. Boat measurement ~- Bob Anderson has written to Jim Gates of NSCA to arrange for his training as a Solo measurer, 1987 Solo Fleet duties include a Dart/Hornet Open on 5th-6th September which will require all hands. Please make an early note of this date and keep it clear. Happy Christmas to all Solo sailors and if you have not bought yours yet, remember this is a very good time of year tc buy, so get your Yachts & Yachting and get — busy. John Salmon, Solo Fleet Captain, Tel. Billericay [redacted].

Bar/Galley 1987 One of the aims of the current committee is to improve the facilities at the club generally and to create more of a Club atmosphere. In order to do this we need to make more use of the Clubhouse, Last season we made a start by providing an extended bar service and meals facility. Members may be interested to know that the increased bar profit achieved has gone a long way towards keeping us solvent this year. The excellent service provided by Robert and June last season has taught us a lot of lessons, not least the fact that we need to provide ‘professional’ catering equipment if we intend to provide an efficient service. It appears to be the general concensus of opinion among members that the bar/galley service be continued and perhaps even extended if there is sufficient demand. However before we can do this and invest in the necessary equipment we need someone, (preferably @ couple) who would be prepared to operate it. oTM I would like to ask ALL MEMBERS to consider whether or not they know of someone (not necessarily current club members) who may be interested in doing this. In particular members living in the Stone, Steeple Southminster areas may know of people looking for a part-time interest. A retired couple would seem eminently suited for the position, so don't forget to ask relatives and friends. It is too early to give specific requirements and dates but we would anticipate running the service from approx thé end of May to the end of August. Anybody even vaguely interested in taking on the task or who can think of someone we might approach should contact me at the earliest opportunity. 8. A WINTER'S TALE (continuing the tale of Dumpy Dora). Dumpy Dora was glad to be spending the winter in the chandler's- it was very cold with thick snow made crunchy by a daily coating of ice and a biting wind that stirred the gas bottle from her hibernation each time the chandler's door opened, as it had just then. A customer was asking for gas and the chandler obligingly lifted Dora from his stock rudely awakening her from her dormant state. The customer carried Dora out into the cold air and into his car, In the car was a pile of clothes and blankets, but as the man drove away he started to talk to the pile, ‘New, you know the plan, you will work on the outside of the boat, while I concen- trate on the cabin interior.’ The pile answered in a strange language but the man seemed te understand: "No, my dear, you can't doinside the cabin, you're net experienced, and no you have not got frost bite, yeu haven't get out of the car yet.’ After a short journey the car stepped and the man got out saying: "Right I°11 get the cover eff the beat and this gas bottle hitched up, then every so eften we can have a hot drink.' Dumpy Dora blinked to see a woman appear from the pile wrapped up like an eskime w and sniffing in a most unbecoming manner. The man set te work cheerfully while the woman sniffed leuder and staggered frem car to boat with armfuls ef Tools. "We want all this old paint and varnish off, here's a new Skarston scraper for you and I'll get cracking inside.’ With that the man disappeared into the cabin with the gas bottle, calling out: "Don't put any nicks in the wood, my leve.' The woman eyed the scruffy little boat Palefully then, wrestling with a ladder in the wind, eventually managed to bash it onto the boat, climbed up and started to scrape and sniff. So the winter wore en, all::week Dora and the little boat lay warm beneath the heavy cover, but come the weekends, the ceuple arrived to rub and scrape, ‘They are wearing me out,' Dora told the boat. ‘Every hour ‘er out there knocking to come in for a hot drink and mean about her cold and chillblains. Did you hear it this week?' ("How's your cold?* asked the man. "Gene to my chest,‘ she said w 'That's why it's best you work outside, the fresh air will de your lungs good. Are your chillblains any better?’ he enquired, ‘I've made medical history with them,’ was the doleful answer, ‘The doocter said he's never seen them in places where I've got them," ‘All that rubbing and scraping sheuld help your circulation,’ the man told her.) ’ "He's a decent chap,’ Dora told the boat another time. ‘Do you know, this week he bought her a new blade fer her scraper and a tin. of Nitromors, and she never even smiled,’ As spring approached the smell of paint and varnish enveloped the little boat and Dora hoped the better weather would cheer the woman up, but,as yet another cup of tea was being made, her hopes were dashed when she heard the reply to the man’s conversational question: ‘Did you have a good week at work, dear?’ "No, the manager called me into his office and said that punk-rock may be in style for the younger generation, but he expected a woman of my age to have a little "taste". I explained my hair was red and blue from anti-fouling, but all he said was "I suggest you change your hairdresser."' contd....

9 ‘Well, I told you to wear something on your head,’ said the man. Then more kindly: ‘Here, borrow my balaclava, it was issued to me in my RAF days, it should help while you paint between the keels.’ The weather improved and the little boat took on a new look with coats of paint and warnish. At long last launching day arrived and the boat slipped gratefully into her natural home. "Summer's here, and we're afloat. Surely that woman will smile now,’ mused Dora to herself, feeling a bit empty and sleepy with the rocking motion, ‘I"ve never sailed before, will I be sick?" she heard the woman ask. ‘No, of course not,’ said the man. ‘We'll take it nice and easy. Tonight we will have a few drinks in the pub, and tomorrow,a run to Bradwell. Weather forecast is good, you'll enjoy it - I know you will.’ So the little boat was left rocking gently on her mooring but as the sun went down the tide went out leaving her aground on soft mud. Much later the plop, plop, of oars announced the couple's return and Dora woke to the sound of the man's voice: ‘We're aground, Hop out, my love, and give me a hand to pull up the dinghy.' * "Oooh! ‘What's the matter?" "My leg has sunk.’ "Put your other leg out, even up the weight.’ * ‘Aaagh! "Now what?! ‘That's sunk as well.’ The gas bottle heard the note of annoyance creep into the man's voice: ‘Why aren't you wearing wellies?' Giggle - 'I am.' "Right, let go of the dinghy, get your legs out of the mud and be quiet. Other people are asleep on their boats.’ Giggle - giggle, came the reply tothe astonishment of Dora and the boat. "Are you drunk?’ whispered the man angrily. ‘NO, DON'T SIT DOWN!’ Too late - Dora heard a splosh then the giggle turned to laughter. "You look so angry,’ howled the woman, "You're not coming on board in that state,’ thundered the man. ‘Get your clothes off. ‘What, now? Someone might see me.' gasped the woman. ‘I don't care,’ replied the man, and it was clear he was not amused. ‘Stand still while I throw sea water over you.’ The lady's language-during the sea water bath was unprintable, and again while she struggled on board dripping and shivering, we leave to your imagination, ‘I'm putting the oven on to warm myself up,’ called out the wet woman. "Oh no, I'm nearly empty,’ gasped Dora as all the taps were turned on. ‘This will be the end of me.* A few minutes later it was: ‘I'm drained,’ sighed Dora, So it was the next day a little boat sailed into Bradwell and Dumpy Dora was left without ceremony, to be replenished and await her fate. Margaret Yeoman.

2. MARCONI SAILING CLUB TROPHIES, 1987 During this season we will be sailing for our Fleet points series and a number of traditional races. A brief description of the trophies awarded for these races is given below but the best way to find out what they are all about is to join in. See you on the water, Malcolm Stuart Rear Commodore Chelmsford [redacted] CLUB POINTS SERIES RACES Meteor Trophy Presented by Meteor Sails and now awarded for Solo Summer Points. Spring Fever Cup Presented by Richard Spillsbury for Mirror Spring Points. One Up Cup Presented by Eleanor Witter a keen Solo sailor for Solo Spring Points President's Cup Presented by our late president, Sir Eric Eastwood, originally for Fleetwind Class now allocated to Mirror Class Summer Series. Edwards Cup Trophy presented by Mr Edwards of Eddystone Radio on his retirement, awarded to winner of Dinghy Handicap Summer Points. — Captain's Trophy Presented by Ron Greygoose Solo Fleet Captain 1982 for Solo Autumn Points. A hand-made model of a Solo complete with helm topped out by the distinctive red crash helmet favoured by Ron. Reflections Cup Presented by Mike Boreham, Mirror Fleet Captain, for Mirror Autumn Points, to encourage competitive sailing in the Mirror Fleet. Costain Cup Presented by Sir Richard Costain, builder of MASC Clubhouse. Awarded to winner of Helm of the Year dinghy handicap series. Mug's Mug Presented by Peter and Sally Harris. Awarded to the Crew who brings his helm home first on the most occasions during the season. Named after Peter's Fleetwind 'Muggs' Barnacle Trophy Presented by Dennis Byatt for points series for any sailing boat normally kept on a mooring. Ladies' Cup Presented by 'Queenie' Hallam originally awarded for one annual race.” Payne Cup Presented by Eric Payne (Vice President and past Commodore) for winner of Cadet points series. LOSED RACES (MSC Members only) Pilot Cup Presented by Cecil Stebbens, former River Bailiff when club was at Heybridge. Awarded for a long distance all-in Cruiser and Dinghy Handicap race. Now sailed to mouth of estuary or Benchhead buoy and back. Mona's Cup Presented by Miss Mona Clark, proprietor of the 'Jolly Sailor' during our time at heybridge. This event is an all-in Cruiser and Dinghy Handicap race and is sailed to Heybridge and back. Mud Trophy Presented by Eric Cottam, Commodore of the Club in its early days. Report from Gur On The Spot Correspondent In conditions far beyond those normally endured by other members of the Club, (S.1s), the Cat. fleet dipped their paws on the first Sunday of the New Year. Force 6 - 7 winds over a strong tide, whipped up to a steep chop, which together with horizontal rain provided the ideal sailing weather. The race course was set from the slipway, up-river to Osea Pier (no extra points for sailing through the gap in the pier!), down to Fisheries mark and back to the slip. Three boats turned out for the event, two Darts sailed by Mike and Tom Duckmanton, Andy Rimmer and Anthony Prior, and the Stampede with Trevor Milton, John Nickalls and Morris Brill. The Duckmantons got away first but half way up the beat, Tom was involved ina dramatic incident, As conditions deteriorated Tom decided 30 knots was a bit fast for Mike's Dart. He bravely sacrificed his personal comfort by breaking his trapeze wire and plunged into high seas to provide a sea anchor in an attempt to help his helm control the boat. He clung, white knuckles straining to the jib sheet for a full two minutes, The boat slowed down and his helm, not wishing to lose such a valiant crew to hypothermia, insisted Tom came back on board the boat, Meanwhile the other two boats were sailing hard behind them, Andy Rimmer, well known for his autocratic streak, had wrested his crew from his sick bed for one of the most demanding events of the season. Anthony was later heard asking if water-proof paper-hankies were available, Trevor turned out a strong team on the Stampede, using the weight gained over Christmas to best effect, After the first half he made a quick pitstop for technical adjustments and a replacement crew as Sarah Brill became the first lady on the water in 1987. The race result left little to question —- Mike and Tom had to retire as, despite Tom's valiant efforts in slowing the boat, he was in breach of Dart Class Rule No. 7(a) which states that the person using the trapeze shall have at least one foot in contact with the boat. Andy Rimmer was disqualified under RYA . Rule on fair sailing for dragging his crew out of bed whilst suffering from flu, a sore throat and a cough. This left Trevor and his crews to take line honours with the Stampede, So with sacrificial sons, the risen dead and adjustable crews, the Fleet is ready for 1987 to be - The Year Of The Cat, ——_ He 4 HH HH He He BE THE FIRST —~ SAIL A CAT * # # # HH HH H %

Adventures Of A Gas Bottle It was late in the season when George and myself, carrying enough supplies for | a fortnight's sailing holiday, got on board 'Sagtob', George's Warsash One Designy We purchased two bottles of gas, one of which was brightly painted. Once on board we stowed the maps, food and drink. We connected the painted gas bottle to the cooker, lashing the other one in a locker, The easterly wind was fresh and, as we had arrived at Bradwell Marina early, we left almost immediately. The sun was brilliant and we made a good fast passage to Ostend, needing to make only two tacks. The next day's offshore trip to Flushing was an easy one and prior to entering the Walcheren canal we stayed overnight in the small yacht harbour and purchased duty free drink. George liked gin. Every day of the holiday started with a breakfast of boiled eggs and toast and the highlight of the day was ‘opening time’ at twelve noon. Drinks but little food! No wonder we were hungry come the evenings, Our journey through the canals was therefore enriched by good restaurant food. We ate well in Vere, where we had moored, nestled in the fisherman's harbour right in Wy the centre of the town. Kortgene marina in the Versemeer also had a good restaurant as well as showers, Willemstad will be remembered for its Victorian hotel and marvellous a la carte. We had sunny weather as we sailed (and motored) through the canals and had only two minor mishaps. After coming through the enormous lock gates into the Maas we kept inshore to avoid the many large ships and barges. At a bend in the river we went aground on a submerged slipway. Luckily we were quickly pulled off by a motorboat. The other fright was an engine stoppage coming up the river to Rotterdam. The Warsash OD had a Vire engine and, as is usual, the plug oiled up at the most incon- venient time. Until we reached the Yacht Club in Rotterdam I sat ready with a fresh plug in my hand in case of further breakdown, as the river was as busy as Piccadilly Circus. We had an expensive meal in a small exclusive restaurant before I flew back to England — penniless! George's wife was joining him for the second week. A week later I had a telephone call from George. He had returned to Burnham slightly slightly early and was doing some painting and varnishing inside the boat but would I join him for a weekend sail. So on the Friday afternoon I joined him aboard ww 'Sagtob’ to clear the holiday gear. We changed gas bottles and, before going ashore for a few minutes, George lit a small gas heater to help dry the paint, We had nearly reached the slipway in the Club launch when there was an explosion and we could see that ‘'Sagtob' was ablaze and sinking. There must have been a small leak of gas from the new cylinder, We were lucky that no lives were lost. Broken- hearted we cleared away and went home after leaving the empty gas bottle at the- Burnham chandlery. George bought an identical boat with the insurance money, and gave it the same name, I wish this story were fictional, but unfortunately it is not. George has never had gas on board since that time and neither have I, Geoffrey Bond

COMMODORE'S NOTES Your Navigans has been bereft of these notes for several issues now. This was a deliberate ploy on my part because I felt that until I had given myself a chance to work myself into my unexpected role I would be guilty of being a trifle presump- tuous if I launched forth my opinions on some subject or other. Oh, very well then, perhaps I can also plead guilty to being a little lazy also — but only a very little. Since the A.G.M. we have had two full Committee Meetings and three Executive Meetings at which I have been very much the new boy learning the business and I now feel I am beginning to glimpse the shape of our coming seasons. Coming in fresh as I do to the running of the Club I can appreciate that we have some quite difficult situations with which to deal - all, of course, revolving around money. It is the usual dilemma, we want to expand and improve our facilities but we want to do it without over-—burdening our costs. As some of you will know we now have a new sewage system which should make life much sweeter in future seasons. We are hoping that the veranda scheme will also stil] be possible despite the raising of the height of the sea wall necessitated by the advent of the Thames Barrier. There will, however, be a delay and negotiations/investiga- tions continue, The security system at the Club is ageing and we are actively seeking to replace it. Hopefully, at the the fitting out WORKING PARTY we will be providing only those who attend with means of future entry. Please do not think that we are TM doing it just to encourage you to attend —- because we ARH! These parties can be fun and fulfilling, for those actively participating are putting part of themselves into the Club. Something very close to my heart, for reasons which many of you will appreciate, is the Marconi Regatta, and I was particularly saddened when it had to be cancelled last year. Because of time and other reasons we are not able to have one again this year. I feel very strongly that we owe it tc ourselves and to the rest of the Blackwater as the occupiers of the most prestigious site on the river to hold a Regatta — BUT it can only bappen if there is sufficient positive response from you for such an event. Hence it was at a recent Executive Meeting that we decided to recommend, in principle only, a Regatta for 1988 (but only after very lengthy discussion) to the Main Committee. To turn principle into fact, 1988 will require commitment from many more of our members. Therefore, whatever your views, please write and tell me your feelings. No response means no Regatta for that will be your will. Robbie Sims, Commodore, RESCUE BOAT DRIVERS REQUIRED Any member interested, please contact Doug Brown on Chelmsford [redacted] after 7pm. Boat—handling and sailing dinghy experience would be an advantage, but those interested must be prepared to go out with the regular Drivers to famaliarise themselves with the four boats at our disposal, We operate a Rota, and usually are required to drive only one Sunday each month. Doug Brown, Coxswain.
