The clubhouse facilities are excellent and include: Two lounge bars. Hot meals. Showers. Children are welcome and can make use of a pool table and record player. Dogs are not allowed in the Clubhouse. Although the creek dries out, Benfleet can accommodate a number of boats both bilge keel and single keel, Having looked at the tides and social commitments of both M.S.C. and Benfleet Y.C. we arrived at twodtes which were most favourable. These were: 6th June and 18th July I have decided on the 6th June, since this will enable us to fall back to the 18th July if the weather is unsuitable. So that I can give Benfleet Y.C. some idea of the number of vessels to expect, I would appreciate it if those members interested in making this visit would let me know as soon as possible, I suggest we meet at the Clubhouse on Friday evening, 5th June at 8pm for a general discussion, and a 10am departure on the 6th is recommended. If you are attending the Committee Meeting on 4th March and you advise, I will bring the order along. Cruiser Funds On taking over the Captaincy of the Cruiser Fleet, I inherited on your behalf a modest amount of money which I have managed to increase. I had the opportunity to purchase a second-hand bottle jack which is somewhat lighter than the one we have and I will leave it for your use on a shelf at the back of the end garage. Please make sure the jack is returned after use and if at any time it is not working properly let me know, The next thing that we need which can probably be purchased out of Cruiser Funds, is a small compressor for inflating trolley wheels. This should be electrically contd. sas

6. powered, reasonably substantial but at the same time light enough to be handled by one person, If any of our members knows where there is such an item at a reasonable price then I am sure we can raise the money. It would save a great deal of effort and avoid all those problems that flat tyres bring when recovering boats. The third item I am currently hoping to obtain is a substantial set of sheer legs complete with block and tackle. The present systems used by some members to remove and erect masts fall far short of the ideal and some are positively dangerous. Most people agree that the sheer leg system is the most effective, but the equipment will have to be light, strong and capable of dealing with the largest boat in the club. I know there is one set in the club that meets these requirements, but this kind of equipment is so infrequently used that one set with common ownership would meet all our needs without relying on goodwill and asking to borrow. If you have any comments or can offer any assistance with this project, please let me know. To start things off, I have found a mature man, based in Chelmsford who is prepared to weld, repair, fabricate or in fact do anything in stainless steel, No job too small ani his rates are unbelievably cheap. Te DUMPY DORA HOMEWARD VOYAGE The morning of the third day was as calm and windless as the past two days during which we had motor sailed the entire distance from Poole to Dover, Naturally such conditions are not acceptable to any yachtsman, let alone one schooled in the tradi- tions of the East Coast, where the wind blows with exuberance and periods of calm are considered monstrous, offensive and even unholy. This persistent lack of wind and the prospect of yet another full day of motor sailing was, not surprisingly, regarded by the crew with distaste which manifested itself in slow, sullen and dispirited activity as the boat was prepared for sea, When the tide served we slipped through the Western entrance and set a course for the Downs. It was dawn. Movement through the water was reluctant, deliberate and sluggish, Now and again the helmsman would glance in at the cabin clock, not with anxiety, but merely to please himself with the thought that each minute gone by made it nearer the time when this ordeal would come to an end. So it was,in an atmosphere of gloom and despondency which hovered over the boat like a sea fog, we came, some two hours later, to Ramsgate. In Ramsgate we refuelled, collected vital stores and within the hour had once more put to sea. But now there was a change for during that hour the accursed calm had ended. At first we stared stupefied, unable to comprehend the scene which now confronted us. Then quite softly someone said, "It's wind," and someone else, as if this observation needed confirmation shouted, "It's wind, it's wind, a westerly wind!" A passion of intense physical activity now afflicted the crew so that before we had reached the Quern buoy, which marks the deep water channel to Ramsgate, the big genoa was up and sheeted in, the engine was off and we were SAILING! At the Quern buoy, where there was more sea room, we headed up into the wind and jubilantly raised the full mainsail. We bore away on to a broad reach,and with the boat moving at near Ats maximum speed, headed toward the Longnose and N.E. Spit buoys in the Thames estuary. The hiss of disturbed water as the wake streamed astern, the exciting sensuous rhythm as the boat plunged forward into a sunlight sea, heeling to the wind, combined to produce an assured complacent air of deep satisfaction which rapidly erased all memory of the tortuous movement of the past two days. The Westerly wind posed a problem because a course following any of the principal channels of the Thames estuary would have involved sailing to windward adding many extra miles. To avoid this a course was plotted which would bring the wind fair, but in so doing involve a passage across the notorious sands that encumber these waters. It was a bold plan for no one except Fisherman,who are accepted to be foolish, crossed the sands. It was a plan which depended upon exact timing and to have any chance of success our first objective, the North Edinburgh channel, needed to be entered just as the flood tide commenced, Sailing is an activity which is both repulsive and attractive. Repulsive because it is dangerous, mostly frustrating, wet, cold and uncomfortable. It is attractive because it brings adventure and exciting rewards at any moment, and because there are moments which elevate the spirit to peaks of supreme ecstasy. As we sailed in a silvery sea, under cloudless skies with a fair and constant wind we experienced one of these peaks. Very soon the Longnose and the N.E. Spit were astern and just ahead,at the time we wanted, was the Tongue Sand Tower and the Edinburgh channel. The first part of this channel is quite short and in less than forty minutes we were heading out into shoal water towards the Knock John. A dramatic change of depth from 40m to 2.5m was recorded just beyond the buoys marking the northern edge of this channel. The surface of the water which had all the characteristics of shoal water running off a sand bar caused some anxious moments, but the depth was adequate for our moderate draught. The Knock John was the first of the drying sands, reported to be .6m in 1973, but no sand showed now. About two cables to seaward of this drying area a shallow rill with

8. a minimum depth of 1.2m was shown. We estimated that as the tides were half springs, and the flood tide had been making for an hour, there would be sufficient water for us to pass safely. We stood on towards the sands. The colour of the water changed from deep blue to sandy yellow which streaked out East to West along the length of the sands. Ahead, only a hundred metres away, we could see the Barrow Deep with its usual traffic of commercial craft plying to and from London. Slowly the depth decreased until it was almost 1.2m, the draught of the boat. It remained at this figure fully five minutes as we skimmed across the bank, then quite suddenly we:'were in deep water again. When we looked back a plume of disturbed sand could be seen drifting across our wake. The keel had ‘smelt the bottom’ as the bargemen would say. Hazards of sailing in shallow water were now temporarily replaced by the problems of navigation in restricted waters. At least three ships were close enough to require a constant check on their progress towards us. A tanker and a container ship were approaching from the starboard and a Swedish timber boat from the port side. We took bearings every few minutes, with the hand bearing compass, on their respective bridge decks and in seamanlike fashion passed safely between them. The last of the ships had barely crossed our stern before once more we were confronting the shallow waters at the edge of the channel. Before us now were the East and West Barrow Sands. We cleared the West Barrow easily but we touched on the East Barrow close beside the Barrow Beacon. Undaunted, in the Swin now, we maintained our course toward the Maplins and found the edge of these sands halfway between the N.&. Maplin and S.W. Middle, We now faced the most critical part of the voyage and once more depth was the principal - concern, Those calculations, so carefully checked and recheched and upon which the decision to cross the sands had been made, were about to be tested. We were fast approaching the Ridge,a great hump of sand raised by the ebb and flow of the Crouch as it scours its course between.the Foulness Sands and the Buxey. Depths here are unreliable because with every gale the sands change, so with trepidation, tinged with no small amount of panic, we drew closer to this final barrier. Failure to cross would entail a long detour, also if we grounded the taunts and smirks of other yachts— men would be intolerable. The belief this sand bar could be crossed was encouraged by a certain familiarity,that is, I was acquainted with these waters as I had sailed in the Crouch for many seasons and often sailed past the Ridge, but I had not tried to cross it before. As we drew near I could see,two cables distant on the port side, the surface of the water dancing in Pyramidical confusion suggesting a concealed underwater obstruction. To starboard the sea was green, the surface untroubled and smooth like a pond. I chose this way Ww and freeing the headsail to slow the boat,steered purposefully towards it, The Gods were benign for there was no sudden shock, no bump or brating sound as sand and shingle ground beneath the keel. Instead we found a fathom, two whole metres, and swept across the fearsome barrier into the Crouch. I offerad silentprayers to those Gods whose whims and fancies determine the success (or otherwise) of our more desperate schemes, With deep sighs of relief we sailed on congratulating ourselves on our audacity. Without further anxiety we reached the Blackwater and somewhere near the Nass beacon made our first tack in forty miles. As we passed Bradwell there was barely thirty minutes of favourable tide remaining, but the wind held and we beat up river to pick up our mooring just twelve hours after we had left Dover, Then,as if satisfisd all was well, the wind fell away and a tranquil evening peace suffused both boat and crew, Never had here been such a day, and as we swung to our mooring we drank a toast to all the Gods who command the elements upon which our sailing is dependent. "And me — Dumpy Dora — how do I fit into all this? I was taken aboard at Ramsgate and stowed in the cockpit locker where I shared all these anxieties and excitements of the crew. During the following winter the owner sold the boat and me with it. The new owner, I have to say, is less adventurous - or should it be foolhardy?" Bill Chrystie

i MARCONI SAILING CLUB CODE OF PRACTICE FOR LAUNCHING AND RECOVERY OF CRUISERS Large Boats — Boats above 27ft. length will not be allowed on the hard when dinghy events are in progress. At other times they should be handled with great care due to their weight. Tractor — Only to be operated by authorised drivers. Winches -- When dinghy events are in progress the winches must be under the charge of an authorised operator. Only the East half of the hard may be used, leaving the West half for dinghies. The O.0.D. will be informed and suitable notices must be displayed for the information of dinghy sailors. At other times the following code should be observed: When winding up the slope always use the ratchet. Winching down the slope should be done by use of the brake with the handle removed. Avoid sharp bends in winch cables-shackles must be used for attachment to trolleys. DO NOT shackle winch wire back on itself. It is the responsibility of the boat owner to ensure that the operation is done safely. This includes providing a sufficiently strong team of helpers. Leave winches tidy, return shackles, strops, etc. to garage after use, rewind cable tidily riding turns can damage the cable. Report any damage or wear of any equipment to an authorised tractor driver. REMEMBERit is your responsibility to check for safety any equipment in use, if in doubt DO NOT USE. If the tractor is used to pull boats up or lower them down the slope, the boat owner must provide a rope or cable of suitable strength and sufficient length that the tractor may remain level and always clear of loose shingle. Boat Trolleys — If left submerged should be adequately marked to avoid damage to other boats. Handicap Fleet News The February Fleet Meeting at the Hurdlemakers Arms was very well supported with plenty of members both old and new turning out on a dark and damp night to ease the locals out of their corner of the pub. TREATMENT OF HYPOTHERMIA - Reprint from Navigans, June 1981 Just a few minutes in the Blackwater doesn't do some people much good, so imagine what half-an-hour would do to a sailor (not properly protected) after Capsizing - the rescue boat could be unaware of your trouble because he is helping another sailor elsewhere on the river. If you are called to a hypothermic casualty, this is what you are likely to find: The Patient Will Be: Blue with the cold. FPWwWNrF Stiff with the cold. Immobilised with the cold. Unconscious or semi-conscious with the cold. Possibly able to nod his head weakly in the affirmative to the question 'Can you understand what I am saying to you?" He is likely to be irrational. His respirations will be shallow, AN U slow and irregular, His pulse will be weak, slow and difficult to feel. His rectal temperature is likely to be below 31 “6. 8 His blood pressure, if you could record it, would be very low. 9 Since he is exposed to the cold and long baat the stage of shivering his deep core temperature is likely to be below 31 °c. I am not suggesting that you should stick a thermometer up his anus to find out! In any event, unless you take immediate action his temperature will accelerate downwards to death by heart failure, What You Should Do: 1 Treat him very gently. Rough handling may precipitate heart failure in a dangerously cold person. 2 Get him into the warm, out of the cold and away from the wind. 3 Keep him horizontal. His heart is weak and his blood pressure is low. Blood supply to the brain must be maintained at all costs to avoid irreversible brain damage. 4 If local conditions permit, get him to the nearest shelter and stop his heat loss. Remove his wet clothes — dry him — put on warm clothes - wrap him up in warm blankets with a‘warm human being beside him. 5 Do not waste time giving him hot drinks unless you are sure he can swallow. If he cannot swallow you may drown him, Unless he is getting warm and beginning to shiver do not give him alcohol. Alcohol dilates surface blood vessels and increases heat loss. 6 Trained mountain rescue teams carry special breathing apparatus capable of admini- stering heated, oxygen enriched, air. 7 Take him to the nearest available HOT BATH. 8 The water should be at A2~4ae. Test it by putting in your elbow, if your elbow will accept it - so will the patient. 9 Lower the vatient gently in. If sufficient help is available attempt to keep his upper and lower limbs out of the water. It is his trunk that needs reheating. The limbs have a larger surface area in relation to their mass than does the trunk. If immersed it is possible to reduce markedly an already low blood pressure by inducing vasodilatation over the skin of the limbs and, to make matters worse, excite the return to the heart of a pool of very cold blood in the extremities. This could prove to be the last straw that broke the camel's back and arrest cardiac function by lowering still further Deep Core temperature, 10 Do not forget to top the bath up with hot water to maintain the temperature at 42-44 "6, ll The first sign of positive recovery to look for is the onset of shivering. At that moment the patient will start dynamically to re-heat his own body. Continue to re-heat him passively with the bath treatment. His bodily functions will begin to nant

return, When you are sure he can swallow in spite of severe shivering, this is the time to give him hot grog. Alcohol is good fuel and quickly absorbed from the stomach, L2 You have now saved someone's life. Hopefully by this stage the patient is in hospital or medical help has arrived. Hand over, for the patient is not out of the wood yet. Lots of complications could occur - for instance a common one is pneumonia, Your patient is going to need expert medical care and devoted nursing. The practical aspects of survival training will now be considered under the following headings in decreasing order of importance: 1) Protection 2) Location 3) Water 4) Food. Contributor Unknown! SAILORS! IF YOU CAN AFFORD TO BUY A DINGHY OF ANY KIND — YOU CAN AFFORD TO BUY A WET-SUIT DUMPY DORA Dumpy Dora was fed up since her last trip at sea. She had been returned to the greatw dumping depot where all gas bottles are eventually sent when they are beginning to show wear and tear. Here they were either thrown on the scrap heap or smartened up to live another day. Dora was right at the back of the shelf looking forlorn. Her paint was chipped and she looked dejected. She was worried. From her position on the shelf she could see a large pile of gas bottles destined to be melted down, They were crying and groaning. A man was sorting out the shelves and throwing bottles on the heap with a crash, Nearer and nearer he came putting some bottles in a neat row on the floor and others on the ever growing scrap heap. Dora felt sick, all the sea air had got to her paint - it was peeling and she felt so drab, She could see her reflection in an old piece of broken mirror standing on the shelf. She looked awful and a tear rolled down her face, Suddenly a large brown hand came down on top of her and heaved her up in the air. Two large grey eyes stared at her. She trembled and tried to smile puffing out her chest and fluttering her eyelashes. The old man gazed at her. "You look a sorry old thing,' he said. Oh dear, she thought. ‘Still there might be life in you yet. Your body's not too bad.' Dora swelled a little, 'A might rusty though.' She felt sick again. ‘I guess with a new coat of paint you'll do, there are no holes in you.' Withy a big sigh of relief she found herself in a neat line of bottles waiting to be renovated. She was left like this for two days. It was cold and draughty on the floor and what was worse she would occasionally get kicked by people passing. I hope they don't have a dog here, she thought. She didn't fancy a hot shower, After two days she was heaved up and taken into the paint shop. Dumpy Dora felt quite embarrassed as wire brushes were vigorously rubbed up and down her until she was completely bare of blue paint. Then she was lightly rubbed over with sand paper, this tickled and she laughed. Then a man with a mask over his face sprayed her with a light grey flat paint. Dora was left for four hours to dry. She felt better with her underwear on and waited excitedly for her final coat of paint. When the paint sprayer came again she closed her eyes and mouth and sat very still while she was sprayed a nice blue. When she was dry her inside was refilled with gas and she was put back on the shelf, at the front this time. She felt wonderful, she swelled with pride and smiled at everyone who came near her, She knew it would not be long before someone bought her and she would be off on her travels again. She might even meet a nice Dumpy Daniel, after all those little Gaz bottles must come from somewhere. She smiled - suddenly the future looked very rosy, Julie Bloomfield. ‘Juliet '

Last year, as many of you know, I arranged a number of organised cruising trips which were termed ‘Cruising in Comvany'. ‘Organised! gives an impression of discipline but anyone who participated can tell you that the only organisation was the decision on destination and the time table. Even this was a joint decision taken after a meeting in the bar and everyone had been heard. There were once two schools of thought as to a destination and this was finally decided on a show of hands, Some of the people who took part had never been out of the river with their boats before and I am sure that we all benefited in some way as well as having a very nice time. I have been asked to organise something similar for the coming season so the first outing will be on Saturday 23rd May 1987. This is the Spring Bank Holiday Weekend when there will be a large open dinghy sailing meeting at the Club and it would be very convenient for the majority of the Cruisers to be elsewhere, If anyone wants to come along, we meet in the ww Club House on the Friday evening 22nd May 1987, sleep on the boats, and leave about High Water on the Saturday morning. As previously mentioned the decision as to destination will be democratic but we have been invited to the Walton & Frinton Sailing Club on the Saturday evening. The Steward will arrange a meal and there are good mooring facilities at the Titmarsh Marina. The Sunday can be a lay day or some may choose to return, whilst others may travel on to the Rivers Orwell or Deben as we did last year. Nothing has been finalised as yet and it will not be until the day, but for many boats this will probably be the first voyage of the season and a coastal trip will or should identify those little things we overlooked when fitting out. There will always be a friendly boat in sight and if anyone is thinking of coming along but feels a little apprehensive then speak to me or to someone who was involved last year. Te DUMPY DORA Christina's Tale The snow swirled around as Dora dozed in her snug locker on board ‘Moontide’. Although comfortable and well insulated from the elements, she was irritable and bored and wished that the winter would end so that she could be afloat once more, Then suddenly she was wide awake, disturbed by the regular crunching sound of . approaching footsteps. A great fear spread through her liquid and left a lump in her valve, for she knew that the locker door was broken and she was therefore easy prey for a robber, She turned for help to Clive, her key, hanging on his usual clip, but he slept on, snoring contentedly, unaware of the drama. The crunching stopped outside and was followed by the banging of a ladder against the hull and the sound of boots climbing the rungs. Something dropped into the cockpit and the boots returned down the ladder and crunched their way back into the gloom. Dora waited a few minutes and then nervously opened her locker to see what had been delivered in such a disturbing way. Dora's fluid gurgled with glee as she saw the envelope with a Greek stamp and recog- nised the strange hand of Christina Calabottapopoulos, her pen friend. Her sudden cry woke Clive and with his help the envelope was soon opened. Dora started to read and as she did so, the cockpit seemed to become sunny and the sound of swirling snow was replaced by the gentle lapping of warm sea against the hull. "Dear Dora, I just had to write and tell you what a terrible season I have had serving on a charter boat this year. There I was, minding my own business on a shelf in George the chandler's in Nidri, Lefkas, which is an island in the Ionian sea, when Captain Birdseye comes in with a very sorry looking bottle. Her body was all dented, the paintwork chippved, and she was covered in various dead creatures: the smell was unbearable, This was a premonition of my fate. I was exchanged for this poor wretch and rudely swung through the streets of the town on the way to the quay. New 'Alkadi' is a trim Aloa 27 and I was pleased to be installed in the vast port locker, especially as I was the sole occupant - luxury indeed! Birdseye stomped off muttering that he intended to "get yamassed at Nicks" and I settled down to a quist snooze in the warm sun, Suddenly all hell broke loose. The boat lurched and Alkadi reverberated to the stomping feet and shrill voices of Birdseye, Boozy Suzy, Krystos and Julie, my companions for two terrible weeks, To my dismay, the locker was thrown open and I was showered with a bucket, warps, boat hook, flippers snorkles, deck shoes, frisbee, fishing lines and a vicious octopus worrier. The next half hour was chaotic, as supplies were stowed aboard. Anything which could not be placed in the cabin lockers was heaved in on top of me, particularly Retsina bottles and containers of draught Metaxa. Eventually the engine, called Donka for some strange reason, was started and we eased our way astern, helped by Birdseye hauling in a line which led down deep into the clear water. Suddenly Birdseye fell back into the cockpit, followed by sodden rope and chain and the liberated kedge anchor, a performance to be repeated many times during the next two weeks. Then, horror of horrors, the anchor, chain and warp were thrown in on top of me, closely followed by the fenders - oh misery. There follows a precis of my two weeks as often described by Birdseye: 'The shakedown cruise to Paleros on the mainland passed without incident, except that Suzy's first rule of sailing was established, i.e. the angle of heel allowed is directly proportional to the amount of RetSina consumed, GONG, «4

Dumpy Dora contd, 8, Paleros will be remembered for the destruction testing of Ouzo and the enterprising Greek taverna owner who flushed his toilet with this spirit because of a water shortage. The voyage from Paleros via Kalamos to Astakos was noteworthy, as a sudden squall off Mitakos blew a hole in the mainsail and put Suzy's first fule to the test - she slept the rest of the way. Astakos is not one of the flotilla calls and is a bustling, lively ferry port. After much searching, the worst tailor in the world was soon found and he agreed to haul out his ancient machine into the main street and repair the sail. We couldn't bear to watch the appalling artisan at work: we thought he had a limp until we learnt that he was wearing one of his own suits, so we explored the town, A dingy bar was soon discovered which we christened "The Last of The Summer Retsina", The wine was served in copper jugs from vast barrels packed floor to ceiling. All four of us managed to become seriously yamassed for 50p. Many adventures were to follow in places with names straight from the pages of Homer: Sami, Fiskardo, Assos and Argostoli on Cephalonia, Frikes, Kioni and Port Vathi on Ithaca. Ah,the joys of bare boat charter! ed The time swept past and soon we were making a late evening run up the Meganissi channel, past Christina Onassis's island of Skorpios towards the lights of Nidri and the welcoming party at Nicks.' Christina continued - They may have had a good time, but my life was a misery, having all sorts of debris hurled into my locker. And as for that kedge anchor, no manners at all. Anyway in true bottle tradition, I gave my all and helped produce many delightful meals and I now await my fate in George's chandlery for next year: I pray for a gin palace to be my next berth and I hope you never have to serve Birdseye and his appalling friends. Hope you are well, Christina" Dora read the letter over and over again and each time she became more embarrassed, She was thankful that her locker was only large enough to accommodate Clive, herself and a few cans of beer during the season and that the kedge anchor on ‘Moontide’ was stowed in the starboard locker. However, how could she face Birdseye when he fondled her tap at the beginning of the season, knowing that he had upset her penfriend in Greece? Birdseye, *Noontide'

COMMODORE'S NOTTMS Midsummer is almost upon us and your Commodore still has not managed to move his boat from the back garden. Heigh-ho for the camping fortnight by which time, hopefully, I can look forward to being waterbound, along with a really strong suprort from our Members at large. I consider events such as this as crucial to the development of the Sailing Club by its Members, because most of us have to rush down to Stansgate to do something specific with little opportunity to stand and stare. ‘YVith a week or a fortnight, however, we can take time to appreciate and understand our zood fortune at having a Club with togetherness which will help to keep us the best CLUB in the area, So make the effort and join us. As most of you will know by now the new security system is almost fully implemented - in fact when you read this it should be! - and you will all be adept at wielding your bit of magic plastic, It has taken longer than we imagined but I am sure we will come to be grateful’ for it in the future. Despite my previous pleas some members persist in allowing their pets to roam unrestrained, This is anti-social. We have already had a youngster bitten and badly frightened this year. Please remember that the most docile of pets can unwittingly startle someone and thus initiate an unfortunate train of events. Roaming farm dogs are almost beyond our control but yours need not be. The one does not excuse the other either way. The Spring Bank Holiday Open went very well - despite the Saturday rain and I would like to express my grateful thanks for the enormous commitment to it made by Malcolm Stuart, Mike Battle and Mike Boreham & family to ensuring the weekend’s success. It augers well for next year. I was particularly heartened by very strong M.S.C. entry to the event. Keep it up. As for the Galley - The Jessops did us proud — thanks from all of us who savoured their sustenance -— More Please! See you at Camp. Robbie Sims Commodore _—— ee —-—— I called on Irene Hodges to gather in Lifeboat Boxes she had kindly taken to make collections for the R,N.L.I. and learnt for the first time that Arthur had been in hospital recently. He is home now and recovering well, but on medical advice, is to give up actively sailing, which means Viridia will be for sale. Malcolm Stuart, Rear Commodore, Chelmsford [redacted] CLUB DINGHY, ‘IDLE VICB' The Club's Challenger dinghy ‘Idle Vice' has now been fitted out for the season and has been allocated a space in the Handicap Fleet dinghy area. As she was leaking badly last season, the opportunity has been taken to give hull and rigging an overhaul, As well as the obvious work, such as revarnishing, a lot of effort has been put into resealing hull fittings, providing new aluminium keel bands and filling holes and damaged areas. Some running rigging has been replaced and a sailbag donated so that all Idle Vice's gear can be kept together and stored in one of the garages when not in use, To make this work (and the expense to the Club) worthwhile, I hope that maximum use will be made of the boat. Item 5 on Page 13 of the Year Book refers to use of Club Dinghies, Idle Vice is simple to rig but like all boats has a few 'quirks'. When the boat is ‘parked' the gaff is stored in the boat, projecting into the forward buoyance tank. Remember to replace the forward hatch cover before sailing and also check that the aft tank cover is in situ. To slot the gaff onto the mast, loosen the gooseneck fitting and remove the boom, slide the plastic 'slug' into the track and replace the boom (pushing it fairly high up the track). Hoist the sail until the gaff fitting is close up to the mast, secure the main halliard, pull the gooseneck fitting down the track to tension the luff, then tighten the gooseneck locking nut. I hope that considerably less work will be required on Idle Vice next year and she should be available for sailing earlier in the season. The assistance of users is requested to help keep her in good trim by observing a few simple rules. PLEASE: Do not allow the hull or rudder to be scraped or bumped on the hard or beach, Ensure that the boat is placed centrally on the trolley so that weight is taken on the chine and bilge keels (a look underneath will make it clear what I mean, ) Do not cut or alter the rigging in any way. If you have trouble rigging the boat, ask an experienced club member, When you have finished sailing, wash the boat and gear, return the boat to the dinghy park, tie down to stakes provided and cover up. Put sails and loose gear in sail bag and return to garage.(Consult 0.0.D. if in doubt) COMU + cece C

10 MIRROR FLEET NEWS Here is my first News as ‘official scribe' to the Mirror Fleet. Readers may remember I have been 'self-appointed'scribe' in the past but now it is OFFICIAL ! What have I done to deserve this ? It must be punishment for my non-attendance at the Mirror Fleet AGM (unfortunately, I really did have a prior engagement). The sailing season has started and although no Mirrors sailed in the first few Spring points races, three did race in the Easter Series - all with Cadet helms and crew. However, if there was a prize for the first Mirror on the water then it would go to Debbie Yorston and Helen Bates who had a short sail the weekend before Easter. Easter Sunday was cold and windy - such a contrast from the previous Friday and Saturday, but the Sunday morning race was sailed in a good breeze and the three Mirrors (Debbie & Helen, Jon Yorston & Jenny Ball and Damian & Lucy Boreham) all completed the course and were eager to try again after lunch despite the worsening conditions. I think they were very brave because Mike and I retired immediately- after the start cf the afternoon race whilst sailing our other boat (can't mention the class in this news letter). Personally I was TERRIFIED and Mike was none tookeen to carry on ;_ still, we were glad we did retire because all the boats left in the race capsized around ‘E' mark except for Malcolm Stuart in his Solo and Damian & Lucy in the Mirror. Unfortunately Jon and Jenny capsized only yards from the finish line and earned the accolade of being the unluckiest cadets. Malcolm Stuart was the winner with Ron Greygoose (Solo) finishing second despite a capsize, Damian & Lucy 3rd and Carén Stuart 4th (420) also after a capsize. Only these finished out of 18 starters - not unlike some Grand Nationals! ww The next weekend, the same 3 Mirrors raced in Spring Points 7 & 8 in very quiet conditions with slight crew changes. Katy Rutherford crewed for Damian whilst Lucy crewed for Jon. Despite bad starts (Dad moaned inwardly and outwardly) Damian & Katy won both races. They were the only Mirror with a spinnaker and it probably made quite a difference - they will have to watch out when Jon and Debbie each get a spinnaker for their boats. Spring Points 11,12,13 and 14 have also been sailed, with Peter Collis arriving in time to win Spring Points14 single-handed just a few seconds in front of Damian (this time with yours truly as his crew - too heavy says D.). If 13 is unlucky for some, then Spring Points 13 was aptly numbered. Three Mirrors started in a strong breeze but, close to 'E' mark, Damian's boom broke near Osea island and he had to be towed back to the club. In the meantime Jon and Debbie continued on to have a close race but both missed out 'A' mark and so were both disqualified. Its good to see the cadets racing so early in the season - it augurs well for the rest of the year. However, don't think that Mirrors are just for the cadets; it's an ideal boat for a parent and offspring Combination and lots of fun to race - even more so in a crowd. So come on you adults who signed your form saying you intend to race , let's see you come and join us. The only reason Mike and I are sailing our 420 (oops ! our ‘other boat') is that our dear offspring have thrown us off the Mirrors. See you on (or in) the water. 1l PYN-man returneth - repent ye sailors before 'tis too late. Those sinners/sailors (delete as you feel appropriate) who can remember back as far as March and June, 1986, might recall the articles on the Portsmouth Yardstick Numbers (PYN) which appeared in Navigans. Although written with a certain amount of, hopefully, obvious light-heartedness it was still the intention to test the reaction to the idea of the Personal PYN. In all, I received four responses to the articles; one indirectly from Eleanor Witter who seemed to have been enthusiastic (unfortunately Eleanor no longer sailed at MSC), a second from Maggie (who hinted I ought to do something useful - like slaughter the weeds in the garden), another from an MSC member who wasn't, however, included in the list (he thought it a good idea) whilst the last response was torn from a rather reluctant sailor who was included in the PYN list and who seemed to suggest the whole thing should be dropped - preferably on my head (not really that bad - just author's licence). The point is, no positive response was received from anyone involved so the whole thing was dropped . I was therefore somewhat surprized (and rather pleased) when one of our leading Solo sailors asked what had happened to the personal PYN, said he personally found it interesting and would be pleased to see it revived. Thus flushed with renewed enthusiasm, I have revived PYN-man. My idea is to post on the notice boards a list of race-by-race ‘Performance’ PYNs, together with a "Personal' PYN calculated for every 4 races you complete. With luck, by the time you read this article, the notices will be on the board and I might also be able to publish some ‘unofficial' race results based upon the Personal PYNs. Don't worry, the 'official' results (and prizes) will still be calculated using the standard class PYN. Performance PYN - this is calculated for each competitor in each race by taking the Average Corrected Time (ACT) of the top two-thirds of the placed yachts in the race, then multiplying the ACT by 1.05. Let's call this the New ACT (NACT). We now take the NACT figure and eliminate (from the calculation) those yachts in the top two-thirds whose Corrected Time is greater than the NACT. The Corrected Times of those yachts stil] left are now averaged to produce the Standard Corrected Time (S_ ) and it is this S which is divided into the Elapsed Time for each yacht in turn to produce the 'Performance' PYN for each yacht placed in the race . All this supposes that the Race Officer has remembered to time in all boats (SOSOTTI !). It also supposes that I have read the instructions correctly. Personal PYN - after the first four Performance PYNs obtained for any particular helm, the personal PYN is obtained by taking the average of the four Performance PYNs and then using this (new) Personal PYN for édlcutating the helm's Corrected times for his/her next four races ; we then repeat the calculation of yet another new personal PYN and soon. Will it work ? - I haven't the foggiest notion; all I can say is that if you understand the above then you're a good deal cleverer than me - andI wrote it ! Chelmsford [redacted] CASUAL SAILING I recently witnessed a disturbing but not unusual incident when two dinghies were launched in a Force 5 wind with a strong ebb tide. Neither dinghy was properly rigged and three of the four sailors were inadequately dressed for the weather conditions. Being midweek, no OOD was present to give advice and it was fortunate that both boats eventually got back to the hard without harm, one full of water and the other dragged in from Ramsey Marsh bay. If you are inexperienced, please admit it and seek help and advice before you venture out. Do remember that you need adequate clothing for sailing even in summer and particularly in a summer like this. It is a fine line between staggering back. tlue with cold and not getting back at all. To enjoy sailing you need a well—found boat and you need to be properly kitted out. The last thing we want is to lose members through disillusionment - or worse, This year's Cadet Week saw an increasing number of adults joining in and learning how to sail properly. For next year we will consider setting up in parallel with Cadet Week a special course for those adults who would like to learn how to sail but are not necessarily interested in going through the full RYA training scheme, Valcolm Stuart, Rear Commodore. SOLO TEAM RACE —- Saturday ist August Which could be retitled ‘Nine brave fools get blown into oblivion Team racing takes place between teams of three boats where the winner is decided on the TOTAL score of all three boats. The scoring is the standard 3/4 pts for ist , 2 pts for 2nd , 3 pts for 3rd, etc with 7 pts for retired and 10 pts for disqualified boats. The basic principle of team racing is to prevent members of the opposing team overtaking any of your team members, or to enable a member of your team to overtake a member of the opposing team, without losing a place yourself. By a wonderful piece of luck the Solo team race took place on the first really windy sailing-day of the summer. Starting with a modest force four the wind gusted up to a steady five by the mid-afternoon. Out of mine enthusiastic entrants three team captains were picked ; Roger Smith, Dave Nixon and myself. The other two members of each team were placed by the team captains picking their names from a hat. This gave teams comprising ; Roger Smith Dave Nixon Stephen Rutherford Dave Payne Colin Willsmore Steve Keeble Bob Anderson Malcolm Stuart Dennis Dear The COURSE for all three races was : E.st , Noi.st , F.st , Finish with D.st First Race - Dave/Colin/Malcolm against Stephen/Steve/Dennis A very scattered start left Dennis and Dave with a good lead ahead of the rest of us. With the wind blowing against the tide the beat proved slow and bumpy, producing little opportunity for team tactics . The following reach was little better, where boat-speed and control (or lack of it!) were most important. No it was the gybe mark which everyone completed without incident. The following run was a good test of tactics and I got myself in a_ diabolical position, stuck on the outside of Malcolm with Colin approaching fast from behind. At F Colin slipped round the mark right behind Malcolm and overtook me before I reached the line. Up ahead Dave had already managed to beat Dennis’ for first place. Second Race - Roger/Dave/Bob against Dave/Colin/Malcolm This race began with a very keen start that left three boats ahead of the line at the gun; Dave Payne, Colin and Bob. Although Colin turned back toward the line he was still a good twenty feet away from it when he decided to rejoin the race. It didn’t take long for the two teams to split into three fiercely competing pairs . Once on the reach the solos screemed across the river, all keeping surprisingly close. Because of a slight change in wind direction it was now

possible to gybe anywhere between 1 and F. Gybeing however, proved easier said than done, with the lumpy seas and gusty winds. The resulting capsizes where as spectacular as they were frequent. Due to either his enormous talent or good luck Malcolm avoided capsizing, but wasn’t quite fast enough to beat Roger to the line. Once everyone had returned to the hard, it was agreed to take a long lunch. Third Race - Stephen/Steve/Dennis against Roger/Dave/Bob By this time the wind was blowing at a constant force-five. After missing our first start due to lack of upright boats we managed a second, reasonable start. With the tide coming in, the beat was hard-going but fast with Steve Keeble going particularly well. Once on the reach Steve was just ahead of me, with Dennis and Roger both well ahead. Once out of the cover of Osea Island the boats really howled along. At No.1, I thought it best to tack around, allowing Dave and Bob to catch up with me. On the run to F Dave capsized and I nosedived, leaving us both in the middle of the river with a boats full of water. Steve managed to gybe at the emark, then almost sailed over Bob‘s boat as it capsized in front of him. The result of all this was Steve getting a third, Bob a fourth and myself (after plenty of messing about) a fifth. Dave capsized again at F and had to be towed back to the hard. Conclusion Judging from the response of those taking part, the day was a success despite the weather. It also seems that when approached in an unhurried manner’ team racing is a lot simpler and less ruthless than most people expect. Another point to be noted is that to be a success any team competition needs a whole day allocated to it. MIRROR NEWS This is being written at tie end of the Cadet week which was a great success despite poor weather most days. It was gre-t to see all the dinghies on the water particularly the red of the Mirror sails which were outstanding for their number as well as their-colour,. Let's hope all those dinghies will continue to sail during the rest of the season, both in the ordinary Points Series as well as the Cadet Series. On the Wednesday of Cadet Week, 16 cadets sailed up the river (in 8 flirrors) to the Blackwater Sailing Club to take part in their Cadet Week siednesday afternoon race. I'm not sure how meny Mirrors were racing but there must have been around 20 of them and it looked like a flirror Open meeting. Add the toppers, Lasers, Fireballs, etc that the Slackwacter cadets were also sailing and it was quite a fleet which set out on the race in almost windless conditions. A somewhat extenced start sequence found ‘our mob' too far up the line and in slack water whilst 'the locals' stayed at ' other end and took advantage of a stronger favourable tide anc what little wind was availe able. However, not too long after the start, with the leaders on a run back from the windward mark, a thunder storm struck us, bringing with it a very fierce squall and very heavy rain. For those of us in the work=boat we could neither see the boats nor make any headway against the onslaught for several minutes but eventually we were able to go in search of ‘casualties’, Many of the dinghies capsized but we're proud to say that all of the Marconi: boats stayed uprighte Jenny Ball sought the shelter of the causeway to Northey Island and we found her bright and cheerful, ticying the sails away before she and crew Ilelanie Keeble went off to be entertained to tea by some sea cadets camping on Northey . It seemed a shame to break up the party so we left them there whilst we went in search of other boats needing assistance, As already mentioned, all our boats stayed upright and sailed back under their own control to the Slackwater $5.C, the race having been abandoned, you when consider that on the previous Honday, few of our cadets had any real experien ce of sailing in normal conditions, let alone racing in bed conditions, then it is a tribute to Derek Hall's teaching of seamanship that they all handled the situation with no apparent difficulty. No doubt others will offer their thanks to the Blackwater SC for the very warm and generous welcome thay gave to our members; it would be nice to keep the link thus established »etween the two clubs, perhaps by organising a ‘Mirror Match' next year. Anyway, thank you Blackwater Sailing Club - we enjoyed our visit 2nd were very impressed by your hospitality. Four out of six Summer Points races have been seiled, with Peter Collis winning three and Dammian Boreham one, Summer Points 6 provided the closest finishes for some one of time, Peter and Damian Swopped between them all the way Youn the lead d, each Naving their moments ‘disaster! but Peter even of triumph and tually crossed the finish just inches shead of Damian to be creciited with a win by just 1 second, Two new names to add to the list of ‘Mirror Racers's; they are Noy Wood and Greg Hall. Greg is one of our younger cadets and has taken part in his First Mirror Series race, Other new members to the Mirror Fleet (even if not yet actually Pacing with us) are fiartin and Slison Edwards and the Family with 'Red Vavies Uwarf', Graham Baker and Dave Onyons (new members year) have also made a racing start last this season. All this augurs the Autumn Points well for series so I hope to see a big fleet sailing in all Taces, those Maggie Soreham Mirror Fllet Scribe [redacted]49 Let me know your news; it helps to keep 'the column! alive,

10 A Touch of Class - anda bit of soft soap. It's a bit difficult to write about the Handicap Fleet racing to date because, truth to tell, there have been precious few of us actually taking part in the racing programme. The Spring Points Series saw a total of 7 different helms and crews taking part in 9 races - but not more than 3 boats in any one race. I'm afraid we appear to be the only fleet not 'thriving' although we have plenty of handicap boats sitting in the dinghy park. Neverthéless, we've enjoyed our sailing and we can always try to catch the Solo Fleet up if we happen to be sailing the same course. Nick Edmonds and Sue McNamara won the Spring Points Series without too much opposition (with the noticable exception of Jean and Jack Hardy in their 420) . It was nice-to see Jean and Jack with us again even if they did rather white-wash us with the excellence of their sailing;. how about a few tips ? Some of the races were quite close; Nick beat me by 10 seconds in one race and I beat him by 12 seconds in another (but only because Nick was caught out by a change of start time). Willy Pitcairn suffered agony and frustration at not having a spinnaker for his Express dinghy, but I saw him flying a brand new spinny in the dinghy park the other day so he obviously means business. By the time you read this he and Joyce Allan might have got the Express trained to the new sail and be emulating the Flying Scotsman. Mike Hellewell is also waiting for a nice strong wind so that he can try out his new trapeze wire and harness; at least Irene will be trying it out whilst Mike sits at the back 'just a-steering”. At the time of writing (typing), 6 Summer Points races have been completed, TM with 11 boats in Summer 5 (mainly because the Solo Class did not have a race). Steve Gallant & Brad Flisher joined us with their Marauder as did D.Hitt and J.Davis (sorry, but I don't know your first names yet) with their Enterprise. Hopefully they will al] join us for the Summer and Autumn Points Series. Finally, it was nice to see Howard Knott take part in the first of the Summer Wine (sorry - Summer races). There's nothing drunken about Howard's sailing as he proved last year by sailing his Gull to.the equivalent of 138 instead of the class standard of 142. With his son, Stephen, as crew he will undoubtedly be in contention for the Summer and Autumn Points Series. From a personal point of view I'm in a bit of a dilemma as I reckon I'm too young to retire to the Solo Fleet, too stiff to move around in a Mirror, and too soft to try a Cat. Hopefully someone else will join me in the Handicap Fleet for some friendly, and not too serious, racing (someone else, that is, apart from Nick, Sue, Jean, Jack, Willy, Joyce, Mike, Irene, Caron, Andy, Steve, Brad, 'D' and 'J', Howard . and Stephen, with Maggie and me bringing up the rear). sielersteisies and on to the Cadet Series. With 6 boats entered for Cadet Race 1, a good start to the 1987 Cadet Series, especially for Lucy Boreham who gained a close win over brother Damian. A good sail, too, for Debbie Yorston who came third and was catching the leaders up all the time after a slow start. Richard Battle also had a slow start having run aground at the gun (so I'm told Richard) but he sailed well to pull back up to 4th place. Jon Yorston came in 5th and Douglas Hall followed him, in this his first race I believe. That made a total of 6 Mirrors in the race . With 20 or more cadets at last year's Cadet Week and attending the Winter lectures, there must be more than 6 cadet helms in the club. The cadet Series is a handicap series so you can sail any boat which*has a handicap number attributed to it. . . . . The change in type face tells you that this is being continued at a later date =— approxe 4 weeks later in fact, David Allan joined in Cadets 2 &3 with his Tornado and gained 5th and 2nd place. Two wins for Damian Boreham still le‘ives the door open for another cadet to take the Payne Cup. Cadet 4 was cancelled due to conditions and that leaves Cadet 5,6 & 7 to be comeleted,. As Maggie has already pointed out in her Mirror News, 8 sets of cadets raced at the Blackwater Sailing Club so there is no reason why they shouldn't all race at the fi-rconi Club. Mike Boreham Results Secretary

CADET AND CAMPING FORTNIGHT JULY 24th to AUGUST 9th CAMPING CLUB BOATING GROUP This was the 4th year that the Camping Club Boating Group was invited to camp with the MSC at Stansgate. All those members of the CCBG who attended thoroughly enjoyed the camp, and would like me to thank the Camittee and Members of the MSC for their hospitality and helpfulness. Some names were suggested for particular thanks, but I feel that to mention those would be unfair to all the others who also contributed to making this such an enjoyable holiday. The Camping Club Boating Group is a special interest group of The Camping and Caravanning Club (formerly The Camping Club of Great Britain and Ireland), and it is of particular credit to the MSC that several members of the CCBG have attended all 4 invitation camps, and same come fram as far afield as Leicestershire and Lancashire. Nineteen CCBG units attended this year, with eleven camping for the full 2 weeks, and we hope that next year we can match these numbers to the mutual benefits of both the MSC and the CCBG Graham Boustred CADET WEEK 1987 I would like to thank all those who attended and, whether press-ganged or otherwise, helped to run the event. I feel that there was so much willing help given that it would be wrong to single out any individual names. It is intended to organise a similar week next year, but it is apparent that the Cadet Skipper will require even more assistance on the water with the ever-increasing number of Cadets. Could I ask you now to consider how you could help, perhaps? Again, many thanks to all concerned and I hope we will see you next year. N.T. COMMODORE 'S NOTES Here we are in September; the season is nearly over and the period of mellow fruitfulness is upon us. Was anyone quick enough to catch our summer? Let us away with frivolity and think only of such jollifications as 'working parties' and ‘laying up’ and next summer. The first of the new season's working parties has already taken place and I offer our congratulations and thanks to the environs party for their splendid efforts in the Cruiser Park which is now free of all extraneous lumps of iron and material and is quite ready for its quota of winter custamers. I am assured that every boat has been allocated a place and we require owners to use those spots only. If there are any difficulties, please refer to Arthur Hodges who will be happy to resolve them for you. We have had one or two unfortunate incidents this year which make it necessary for me to bring to your attention our rules and bye-laws of which every member is expected to be aware. These regulations are the result of thirty-five years worth of experience and have evolved from this accumulated wealth. They are there to allow us all to live in harmony and SAFETY with one another. In this connection I must remind members that they must have insurance for themselves and any guests using their equipment. In an effort to to emphasise this need, members will be asked to identify their insurance Company and policy number at subscription time. One further safety point I must make is to tell you that children must NEVER be allowed to ride on the tractors. A child was doing so recently, fell off and was nearly run over - such an event must never happen. Another lot of unsung heroes of whom I must make mention are the crews who man our rescue facilities. They do a splendid job involving very long days and all that I would ask is that those who go sailing just as a long day is caming to a close should do so with due regard to their own safety and not stray so far as to require the further services of our hard-pressed rescue crews. Finally, on a happier note, I am sure you would like me to offer our thanks and appreciation to the Jessops for their imaginative menus of nutritious grub on offer to us these past few weeks. Thank you, we needed that. Robbie Sims, 13th September 1987

Tales from Stansgate (1) THE TAIL OF TERRY LINN There was once a field mouse named Terry Linn who lived in the farmer's field near to the Big River. Also by this river was a sailing club named after the famous inventor Guglielmo Marconi. Terry Linn would often sit and watch the sailors having a wonderful time sailing in, and falling out of, their boats and he resolved to build one for himself. He searched for materials fran which to build his boat, and had no trouble at all finding same scrap wood. Being a rodent with big strong teeth he soon gnawed a perfect little Mirror Dinghy camplete with a little mast, gaff and boon. He found same discarded whipping for sheets, halliards and painter, but he could not find any suitable material from which to make his sails, until one day in July, same Camping Club Boating Group members set up canp in the field next to that in which he lived. One of these campers, after a particularly wet day sailing, left his Mirror Dinghy sail spread out to dry on the ground in his caravan awning. In the middle of the night Terry Linn crept in and carefully nibbled out a piece just the right size to make a sail for his little boat. So now if you look carefully when the MSC Mirror fleet is out racing you will often see, right at the back, Terry Linn in his little boat - Sail No. Mouse 1 - and if Terry's friends can find enough sails left where they can borrow same pieces, then maybe next year Marconi's will have a Mouse Class fleet. THE END TERRY LINN

NOTES FROM THE SOLO A.G.M. - 27th AUGUST 1987 1. The AGM for the Solo Class Association was held during the World Champ- ionships at Mumbles Yacht Club. 2. The subscription is to go up to £10 next year with a view to holding it for two years after that. 3. The National Championships will be held at Whitstable next year, presum- ably on the long weekend formula. 4. The Meeting was chaired by Nick Yeomans in a brisk, constructive way. He was eventually elected President as Paul Hemsley resigned. 5. Most of the meeting was taken up by discussion of proposed rule changes, notified to members in advance. These had been proposed to update the rules to reflect modern construction practices and remove ambiguities. 6. No-one wanted the Solo to become a class where the ability to buy the most expensive equipment was the key to success. 7. The official situation is that where the AGM gave approval in principle to the rule changes, the Class Association will now get RYA lawyers to draft the changes in legalese before applying to the RYA for formal ratification of the changes. The basic information is as set out in the pack sent to members, I shall Comment on amendments, etc. 8. Transom flaps may be side hinged. - Instead of measuring mast weight plus C of G, the tip weight will now be specified. (Like Enterprises, apparently). - Internal (T-piece) fittings for shrouds were ruled out. It was felt they could be dangerous in a boat like the Solo with a slack rig. - It was stressed that shrouds must be removable; Jim Gates said that he would rule out shrouds connected directly to the hounds. - Wooden side tanks would be allowed on composite boats, they would have three buoyancy compartments like a wooden boat. - Centreboards and rudders may be glass sheathed in future. Most dis- cussion on this point - many people thought it could lead to very expensive construction, but it was thought this could be overcame by a minimum weight limit. 9. Bill Loy and Michael Barnes were elected on to the Cammittee. There was one space left unfilled. Nick Yeanans thought this could be filled by someone to represent the Eastern Area. " AUTUMN BANK HOLIDAY HANDICAP SERIES 1987 To be honest, at the time of typing this article, I do not actually know for certain who has won the Autumn Bank Holiday Handicap Series; it's a job for the Sailing SubCammittee to adjudicate upon. Hopefully, by the time I reach the bottom of the page, the Sailing Sub will have decided in their wisdom what is to be done, and then I'll be able to fill in the gaps I left on the page. Just think, if I hadn't mentioned it, you'd never have known of the drama I've experienced in preparing this report. Race 1 was ‘sailed’ in little or no wind; an occasional puff helped those fort- unate enough to be in the right position at the right time but 13 out of 18 didn't manage to finish, mainly due to lack of wind. Several of us spent a very frustrating 15 20 minutes only a few feet from the finish but the adverse tide thwarted our . efforts. Dave Nixson, however, persisted with his characteristic single- mindedness, as did Colin Willsmore, and they both finished same 15 - 20 minutes after the winner, Ron Greygoose. When you consider that Ron was only about 50 yards ahead of them, you can understand the situation. Race 2 did at least have same wind, even if not a lot. The course was good in that it gave a true beat fram Goldhanger to Breezy and this provided an interest- ing choice of route. As usual, I chose the wrong one and lost out badly, as did Peter Collis and Damian Boreham in the Mirrors. Mike Taylor, however, chose the right course and won the race; the point of this tale is that both Petery and Damian had a good lead over Mike at the time they chose the wrong way So, who knows, the Mirrors might have had 1, 2 and 3 in this race had they been as wise as Mike. ‘Ah! if only....' ought to be emblazoned in bottle tops over the club bar, for such are the tales of woe to be heard every week in the changing room and what would be the 19th hole if we were a Golf Club. Race 3 saw not only a much better wind, but also the first appearance of the catamarans. Trevor Milton won it in his Stampede, Joan Hardie was second in her 420 and Dave Nixson sailed a canny race to just beat fellowSoloist Malcolm - Gandy by 31 seconds on elapsed time. Again, the beat from 'E' mark to 'D' mark provided a choice of route- and again I chose the wrong one; it's getting to be a habit with me. Race 4 was sailed in the best wind yet and the catamarans won easily over the monohulls, filling the first three places with Mike Duckmanton providing his son, Tom, with another win towards his 'Mug's Mug‘ tally. A rush to pack up tents and caravans saw little time for frivolity, ending a weekend's sailing which saw varying fortunes as well as extremes of wind strength, a multitude of hard luck stories as well as a whole host of ‘'might-have-beens'; by the time you read this it will have all faded into the Club's history. ow’ The Results pts pts 1. CRUISER MEMBERS Firstly, apologies for not expending very much time with the Fleet this year, but as most know, I had an illness early in the Season. I was advised to stop sailing for same time and as a result made a calculated decision to sell Viridia. Initially I thought I could carry on as Fleet Captain but found it very difficult without a floating base and particularly when "Cruising in Company" needs the organiser to go along. I am therefore relinquishing the position as fram the A.G.M. To date a successor has not bee found, although Malcolm Yeoman has kindly agreed to arrange the Winter Meeting programme. He has also offered to organise the Discount Paint Order, and you will be hearing from him about the details. The Laying-Up plan for this Winter is desplayed on the Club Notice Board and this should be 99% correct. Slight inaccuracy has arisen through two boats remaining at the Club after initially giving notice of leaving, but if any member has a problem please give me a telephone call. That takes care of everything except the trip to the Boat Show in January - so I am asking for a volunteer to make the necessary arrangements. COMMODORE'S REPORT - A.G.M. 8th November 1987 When I came to write this report for you I was at first under the impression that in many ways the year has been a non-Year. Principally I think this has been the result of the non-summer of wet and not particularly warn weather we have ‘enjoyed' culminating in a hurricane the likes of which we have not had in the past century, or two, or three! Some serious losses have resulted from the hurricane to some members while others have had lucky escapes. I should like to express our sympathy to those who have suffered losses and offer felicitations to those who were lucky. There, but for the Grace of God, go any of us. I do not propose in my report to deal with a load of statistics of our events as I am assuming that these will be the basis of the secretarial reports which follow mine. My task as I see it is to deal with policy and to try to make myself sensitive to the wishes of the membership as a whole. In this connection T have found it to be an extremely difficult year since I found myself precipitated into M.S.C. politics after a break of 24 years. So I have had a lot of catching up, learning and re-organising of my thoughts to do before being in a position to offer the lead you could expect from my predecessors. ww My first impression of the Club was that it was well run by a core of able, well motivated, active members operating a well-established routine, developed over many years. This impression I have discovered to be well-founded. You do have such a core of enthusiasts to whom we owe a great debt of gratitude for their work and dedication and without whom we would not have survived so long. Thank you from us all. I refer, of course, to all those members of committees, sub- committees, project groups etc., both official and unofficial who have for so long dedicated their lives (not too strong a term) to our better enjoyment of our chosen sport/pastime, call it what you will. What is worrying though, to me aS a new boy is the impression that we need far more active involvement from our younger members. SO come on you younger ambitious ones, help us to identify you and so harness your energies and ideas to the greater good! I should like now to turn to our ongoing sore which we are still truing to resolve and that is the question of our contribution to the MASC for the facilities which we enjoy here. We have so far signally failed ever to achieve a sensible dialogue with the General Committee of the MASC with whose philosophy and approach in this matter we disagree profoundly. To this end we have invoked the aid of the Trustees to see if they can offer some acceptable arbitration. Your committee does notTM object to making a contribution, or even its magnitude,Wthe MASC for our facilities which we think is only fair - but only to the manner in which the MASC wants to assess this hurden and with which we disagree fundamentally as being wrong. There is a resolution for you to consider later which, with your support, may help us to precipitate a solution to our difficulty. A solution to this difficulty is fundamental to our future development since we are coming to size and activity level when our tradition of self-help may no longer be possihle or even relevant. This will give rise to a great deal of serious thinking on how to go forward as additional substantial funding may be necessary and if we cannot have an acceptable, fair and predictable arrangement with our parent how can we expect to plan ahead? Your committee is nothing if not optimistic though, and I am very pleased to announce that 1988 will see us once again holding a Regatta at the end of May. This result is due in no small way to the dedication and imagination of Malcolm Stuart who has driven this project forward overcoming all the difficulties to produce a package which will make it work in practice. So I hope we can now unite 100% behind him to help the project exceed our expectations. As a spin-off we will be trying

oS) certain re-organisation of the garage areas and from this experience we hope to learn and then promulgate a 5-Year Plan of development where it will be possible to correlate funding and spend in a way which will do most good. It is terribly easy to blue a lot of money on eating out at the best restaurants when, perhaps by planned restraint, we should be planning to buy the restaurant. Another aspect of our Club which your Committee has recognised as a growth area is that relating to Winter Storage of boats which I can only see increasing both for Cruisers and Dinghies. This means improved storage facilities will be a must if we are not all to sink into a quagmire. This will need funding, and we have taken the initial step of proposing differential storage fees for Cruisers based on length - for want of a better yard stick! We hope you can support this important measure because the Cruiser fleet is growing in size and influence and, by definition needs additional facilities like hard standings, power, space etc. which we will try to provide as fast as funds will allow. One area which has become a bit of a minefield is our Rules where certain changes, particularly over the past few years have not (perhaps?) been properly ratified by the MASC. This is my fault because I did not really appreciate the extent of the situation early enough. (Sorry, Malcolm, you did kick hard enough - but I was too thick!) However, I have now had discussion with Gerry Wignall, and Pat is preparing a new corrected full set of rules which we will then submit to the General Committee of the MASC formally. I do not expect more than one or two changes will be necessary. Implicit in a lot I have been saying is the underlying need to increase our membership substantially and I would like to take this opportunity to promote the idea in each of your minds the resolve to say out loud on January Ist 1988 "This year I will find and introduce a new member to the Club." To succeed in this resolve would, at a stroke, dissolve many of our financial and funding worries and we could then do most of what we need to without having tag raise any additional funds. Before I conclude I am pleased to announce that Eastern Electricity has undertaken to divert our power lines underground (somebody must have worked hard on them) and because one of the new stays comes on our ground they will be paying us rent of £1.19 p.a. for the privilege. In conclusion I would like to say what an honour and a privilege I have regarded being your Commodore this past year. We are the best Sailing Club around and we can all take pride in being members and for my part - I thank you. -~ SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT A.G.M The main events over the year were as follows: si Thanks to the assistance of Mike Battle we have been able to return to the "book' type of Year Book; I hope this is satisfactory to members. 2% John Nickalls organised a stand at the SAILBOAT 87 Exhibition at Crystal Palace again this year. To someone living 75 miles away fron Stansgate, this kind of immediate action is especially welcome. I hope that the two volunteers who helped carry the mast and spars with trailing halyards and shrouds across what seemed like a hundred yards of Blackwater mud and_ then over the sea wall didn't suffer any pemnanent damage to their clothing fron that same mud. SOLO NEWS § @ne important decision from the Solo Fleet AG‘ which I amnitted to mention last month was that positions in selected Eastern Area open meetings would not in 1988 count toward points for the relevant MSC series. This is a deviation from our fleet practice in recent seasons. Would the Results Secretary kindly take note. In case anyone missed the information in last month's Navigans I will repeat here the details of arrangements for the Solo Fleet Supper: Date: Friday 15th January 1988 Time: 8.15pm Cost of meal: Approx £7.50 (depending on what you order from quite a broad- choiced menu.) Location: Cross Keys pub - Roxwell Leaving Chelmsford, travelling west on the A414 toward Hertford, the pub is on your left. Since a private roam has been booked for theis event, I really would like to know who is going to attend - the more the merrier, so please give me a call if you are intending to go. There have been some enquiries from Club Members interested in sailing Solo next season, for obvious reasons. I would welcame hearing fram any others who are similarly inclined, as I am planning to provide opportunities to sail the boat early next season, under racing or non-racing conditions as preferred. In this respect I would also like to compile a list of Solo owners who would be prepared to let others sail their boat on c .asions when they are tied up with Fleet Duties, OOD Duties, etc. Would any such willing souls please let me know. For most of us the season is now over, although one or two brave men can even now be seen of a Sunday up the darkest crevices of Mayland Creek challenging the elements and carrying the banner of the MSC. I am anticipating a report fram this field of conflict in the February edition. Looking back over the year should give us all a great deal of satisfaction since we have seen significant increases both numerically and in campetitive standard of our fleet without, I feel, losing any of the good sportsmanship and camaraderie which is an essential part of our enjoyment of sailing. Everyone who has participated in the fleet's activities, at whatever level, should take same pride and satisfaction in that achievement. It has certainly made the Fleet Captain's job an easy and a pleasurable one - thank you. I'm sure the Solo Fleet would like to join me in wishing all Club Members a very Happy Christmas*. Hope to see you all on the 28th December working party. ‘ites John Salmon, [redacted] *On behalf of the other Members Ed. returms your good wishes! COMMODORE 'S NOTES Christmas has come and gone and here we are at the start of a bright new Leap Year and may I wish you all a very Happy and Prosperous Year. In many respects the Sailing Club is facing a year in which I foresee not a few pitfalls and difficulties which we will have to address and overcome. As I said at the AGM your Committee would like to take time to discuss and draw up a plan which looks at the development of the Sailing Club on a longer term basis so that we have a chance to arrange priorities and finance in a controlled manner including having discussions and obtaining the full backing of all the Members. The way forward, however, is being frustrated right from the outset because we do not have enough volunteers to fill the vacancies on the Main Committee, particularly from Marconi employee Members. Being a member of the Main Committee need not take up much of your time, only as much as you want to give. Your views, however, in that forum are vital to the future of sailing as we know it. If you are interested then phone me NOW at [redacted] Ext 437, or at home on [redacted] - or contact any Committee Member. Your Club Needs YOU. We have had our post-Christmas Working Party on what was a mild and pleasant day which, speaking for myself, helped to blow away many a cobweb. It was well attended, much valuable work was accomplished and it gives me much pleasure to thank everyone who came for their efforts, which are much appreciated. I have always been very proud of our Club and one ofthe principal factors which has sustained that view over the years has been the spirit of independence demonstrated by the degree of self-help shown by the Membership. We are a self-help Club and we get things done because WE do them. I recognise that as the Club activities expand the work-load becomes more onerous and a time will come when we will need to consider some full-time assistance. With the departure of Claude into well-earned retirement, perhaps now is the time. Do you have any views? If so, please talk to me or any Committee Member urgently. THE ANNUAL RNLI ROWING RACE MALDON LITTLE SHIP CLUB (Sunday 3rd January 1988) Never leave a meeting even for the most urgent reasons, because those that remain have a nasty habit of volunteering you for something. It happened to me at the Sailing Sub-Committee Meeting when I returned from a short walk down the MASC corridor to find that I had volunteered to join the M.S.C. crew in the Annual Rowing Race to be held on January 3rd. As I have a cruiser, (they said) I must be good at rowing. (Have they never heard of outboard motors?) The final crew line-up was Malcolm Stuart (team leader), Roger Smith, Ian Lindsay and yours truly. Malcolm decreed that we needed a practice, so the date was set for Sunday 20th December. So rapidly did our fame spread that my sister and brother-in-law flew in from Virginia, U.S.A. to witness the practice session. (They did stay for Christmas as well, but I am sure the initial attraction was the rowing race practice.) Ian could not make the practice session (he must have known a thing or two!) so David Ball substituted as helmsman. The Fisherman was launched and we managed to row it up to No.2 Buoy against the ebb tide and a fresh westerly breeze. I enjoyed the trip back resting on the oars. All this time brother-in-laww (like a true American) was clicking away with his camera ("Hey, you guys are crazy!") The practice session showed that fine tuning of the Fisherman was required. Some new '‘'go-faster' rowlocks were required, a pair of oars had to be shortened and new grips fashioned (technical stuff). Christmas was spent gathering sponsorship and manufacturing the obligatory Viking helmet. Sunday January 3rd dawned after a very wet and windy night. "Tt's a waste of time driving to Maldon this morning, it's too windy, they'll surely postpone the event," I told myself, turning over for my second sleep. However a sense of duty overcame my inertia and complete with family (for moral, and possibly later, physical support) I arrived at Hythe Quay roughly on time. The rest of the crew were already there sporting a variety of Viking helmets. The Fisherman was equipped with mast and M.S.C. Flag, lowered by crane into the water and secured on the pontoon ready for the start. The race plan was to down a drink at Maldon Little Ship Club, run to the boats and row to Maldon Yacht Club, run to the clubhouse, down another drink andTM@ collect a balloon. Then it was a run back to the boat and the long row up to the Fullbridge for another drink and balloon. Here we had a problem as the pub was upstream of the bridge and our boat had a mast..... The final leg was back to the M.L.S.C. and a run into the clubhouse to sign-off. (No-one said anything about this running). There was a good turn-out of boats and crews for the event, many in fancy dress and a lot of fun was had by all. The West Mersea Lifeboat and Dick Townshend in his Mobile Coastguard Vehicle and quite a few spectators turned up to provide a bit of extra support. We achieved 3rd place in some class or other and over £100 of sponsorship. Many thanks to all of you who donated to this worthy cause. RAY BALL, Usually Bosun.
