LIS ST HELIER TO BON THOUGHTS AND FACTS RECORDED ALONG THE WAY ON "OCEAN CHAL ENGER" SATURDAY 2nd MAY 1987 Martin and I flew fran Heathrow on the 18.25 T.A.P. flight to Lisbon. The food was good and the drinks were free, and as I had never visited the capital of Portugal, I was looking forward to the trip. The boat, a Trident Challenger 35' long-keel sloop, had left Palma Mallorca two weeks previously amd had last been heard fran in Gibraltar. We were met at the airportby a tired looking skipper and crew. Spirits revived after a good seafood meal and a visit to a cafe in gardens right in the centre of Lisbon. The four of us sat drinking beer and watched the world go by, still in au shirt sleeves until 2.30an. This was a real transformation having left England enjoying a rainy Saturday in one of the coldest springs I can remember. We took a taxi aout to the marina, and rowed aut to the boat. We were moored next to a Swan which was bristling with winches. SUNDAY 3rd MAY This was a make and mend day. We worked @m the engine and prepared for sea in the morming. Weather was glorious amd sunny. In the afternom we walked a way alamg the banks of the River Tagus. My camera seized up at the top of an eight storey sum dial monument. We then caught a 1930's vintage tran (all cast irm and wood) to the city centre where we took in the sights of Lisbon - the architecture and the senoritas. There being no food shops open anywhere, we boarded a trolley bus back to the boat for aftermmom tea in the cockpit beneath the awning. A taxi was ordered in the evening for another hit at the seafood, which is plentiful and good everywhere in Lisbon. We still had to water and provision for the first leg of 150 miles north to Porto. MONDAY 4th MAY We shopped at the Co-Op first thing - fresh food for three days. Bought stamps but could not find postcards. Breakfasted and filled up with water. It was 10.30am when we slipped our berth and moved out into the river. We set our mmber two jib and were som doing 6 - 7 knots with the wind behind us. The sun was scorching hot. Rubbing my factor 5 suntan oil in, we were fighting for the best positions in the cockpit - look out Atlantic, here we cane! As we passed Estoril in the flat calm river I could see a line of white alag the shore beneath the cliffs ahead. Cauld they be breakers? They were! Lunch-time and we tumed northwards and the wind was now on the nose, and we encountered the Atlantic for the first time. The engine was tumed qm and we were doing 5 kncts in a la@g swell of 20 feet top to bottan. As me who had never been physically seasick before, I scoffed my lunch of tinned salman with asparagus and salad, feeling slightly uneasy. At 14.30 I caild not navigate any more, and had a total paralysis in putting my head down into the locker to get my Oilskins and seaboots aut. The wind and the seas head risen and so was my lunch abaut to. Once oilskinned and harnessed up, I practised the mariner's ancient call to "Hughiee!!! The swell had growm in size to samething I had never encountered before. We sailed up and up and up the side of each swell, and then down and down. They were very lag and we collectively estimated then to be 30 - 40 feet fran top to bottan. All I cauld do was steer the boat with the spray coming over the bow, over the boat, over the sprayhood and then over me. I was still heaving my heart out regularly, but eating the odd Ryvita. The night wore @ and I finally went below at 0400, wet, tired and still very ill. Martin had also been sick since teatime and many plastic bags had came up and over the side fran my berth where he lay prostrate. My relief at 0400 was very perky with a cheery "Good Moming!" - I won't repeat my reply! TUESDAY 5th MAY 0800 I was fast asleep in the pilot berth when I was awakenend as the engine was shut off with claxis of smoke. The engine water inlet seacock had broken off and overheated the engine. The top of a mastic tube cured the problen. We sailed for fair hours to cool off the engine. The winds were still strong and the seas still raugh. 1000 There was a lad crash as our radar reflector crashed down aon deck and then over the side. The rivets a the crosstrees had pulled aut. We had eight attempts to get alagside it and it took all four of us to get it a= board. TI think we were all thinking how difficult it would be if it was me

of us, but no-one said anything. I was cold, wet and sick, and my gear below had got wet. Oh what had I let myself in for? 2100 Nearing Oporto, the evening meal was served up and I tried my first meal for a day and a half. Cannellani an Ryvita. The seas were flattening out and I felt a lot better. 2300 Secured in Oporto after having a devil of a job finding the entrance. We were now pumping the bilge every half an hour. 167 miles logged so far. I didn't think much of the first leg! WEDNESDAY 6th MAY The moming was spent finding the leak and curing it. We also had to change the altemator which was putting too much charge into the batteries and boiling them up. The boat was also in quite a mess after the heavy weather. Brunch and went shopping. Tasted a super crab salad in a local restaurant. We were so tired after brmch a sleep was called for. Late aftemom, provisims were bought in the port area where the ladies kept smiling at us? The Oporto Yacht Club visitors' books made fascinating reading of all the worldwide ocean voyagers who had called there. In the evening we caught a bus to take us the 14 kilanetres into town. We were directed to a tourist restaurant by a policeman, but we decided not to eat after qe beer. They wanted 350 escudos for the beer and 1800 escudas cover charge. It was a total rip-off and after a near punch-up we left and paid for beer Only. I sent postcards fram a hotel and had a meal @ good old Barclaycard because I had spent all my escudos. We pooled aur last momey and had to mun for the last bus at 2330. My, what jet setters! Pp slept the sleep of the dead again that night. THURSDAY 7th MAY To sea again. 175 miles for the next leg. I silently hoped it was not going to be like the last me. 0600 We slipped, hoping to get the local easterly winds which blow in the momings q@nly. Weather was superb. Six hours of great sailing, but by mid-day the winds had becane northerly again. Engine mm, we fought for the best in the cockpit. The sum was great. I was determined to get a sun tan before we got too far north. The day passed slowiy by as we sailed a couple of miles offshore in 50 metres of water, watching the mamtains through binoculars and keeping station with a Spanish yacht further inshore. PM We were suddenly surrounded by dolphins playing all aromd us. They were fantastic. They took it in turms to get right under our bows and keep station there. We were travelling at 5 - 6 knots while another dozen or so ducked and dived and rolled a their backs - a truly magnificent sight. Late aftermoa a large cruise liner was seen ahead caning out of Vice. We later faind it was the ‘Canberra’. The night passed by under a blaze of stars, and we could see many lights of the large fishing fleets all alang the coast, which we managed not to get involved with. There were also many friendly lighthouses, same of which were 150 metres up the side of the cliffs and mountains. The Admiralty pilots disapprove of then being so high, because any mist or fog and they are obscured above the mist which is not uncammam an this coast.

CRUISER NEWS For the March Cruiser Meeting I have arranged a talk and video film covering an event of a slightly different flavour. The subject is '‘'The Three Peaks Yacht Race' and the speaker will be Duncan Phillips. As an introduction to this event I have included Duncan's comments providing some background to the race: "The Barmouth to Fort Willian Three Peaks Yacht Race was the brainchild of the fanous explorer and venturer, Major H.W. Tilman. At the time, 1977, he was living in Barmauith in West Wales, and two local doctors conceived the actual details of the Race. The Race has been canpeted each year since then and has grown in number of entrants and is now a fiercely contested sailing and munning race. An outline of the race is: Yachts of any size or type may canpete with no handicapping. Crews to number 5 in all, with any 2 to mum and climb each mountain. The overall sailing distance is about 400 miles, amd running about 74 miles, with maintain ascents totalling 11,176 feet. Boats have to sail fran Barmouth to Caemarfo - mxunners ascend Snowiao, 3,560 feet and distance of 24 miles, retuming to boat totally unassisted. Fran Caemarfon to Ravenglass q@ Cumbria Coast by any route; mmners scale Scafell Pike, 3,210 feet and 32 miles, — Then to Fort Willian (Corpach) by Mull of Kintyre to climb Ben Nevis, 4,406 feet and 18 miles. The Race finishing when runners returm to boat. Total number of boats restricted to 35 because of berthing problens in the harbours. Boats must canply with D.O.T. and Yacht Racing Standards for Category 3 Offshore Races. Runners' equipment must contain minimum for mountain survival. The race is run in June - usually the nearest Saturday to mid-summer with a convenient late aftemom high tide. I have personally canpeted sane 6 years now, skippering a boat for 5 of these and taking part in the running. We have had various results fran finishing 10th to not finishing at all. The important point is that anyone can enter. The purpose of the Race is to prove endurance; capability of finishing at whatever place is a tremendous achievement for those taking part." 5 The second of three instalments of Cadet Skipper Derek Hall's account of his sailing trip last year from Lisbon to St Helier.... FRIDAY 8th MAY 0400 My watch began. We had been dodging the inshore fishing fleets all night and we had now rounded Cape Finisterre (I had always wondered where it was) with our diesel mmning lo. At Cape Villano lighthaise we altered course eastwards. We were now round the tip of northem Spain and entering the Bay of Biscay. A decisiam had been made to pull in samewhere for diesel although nme of our charts had any details of approach. We had large scale charts of only the places we were to visit. Our present charts covered Gibraltar to the Bay of Biscay, sane 500 miles. After a day's nm at 54 knots average, we moved Only several inches @m the charts! Not like navigating on Thames estuary charts. On our approach to the most beautiful bay in which the town of Comme is situated we were directed across the bay to the village of Laxe where a fuel pump had been seen aon the end of the jetty by a passing Moody. 1030 No qe could be famd to sell us diesel, until, with a lot of sign language, we ascertained that it was tokens only for the local fishing fleet. The sun was very hot by now after being at sea. I had drawn the short straw and, amned with a five gallm can, I climbed aboard the fish collectio lorry “mon a ane way trip inland. The driver spoke no English and me no Spanish. He was taking me sane 16 kilanetres to a service station at Cabanas. I had my piece of paper with the name of the village where I started from firmly in my pocket. It seamed to me as if he were taking me to Madrid. My head was spinning fran lack of sleep and no food, but the scenery was beartiful and lush. I was dropped off at a garage where I bought 25 litres of gas oil at a cost of 1300 pesetas. I then started thumbing a lift, much to the amsanent of the garage staff. Thirty minutes later the lady in the garage fixed me up with a lift with a lady and child in a Renault 5, again I had a language barrier, but, with lots of smiles, off we went. I was dropped off 3 kilanetres fram Laxe and the boat, and started walking the last two miles carrying the five gallos of diesel. There were no cars around as it was lunch time. The soinds and smell of the camtryside in summer were breathtaking, the vegetation was green amd lush and the scenery was beautiful. At last I got a lift from a Spaniard who spoke English. He got me back to the boat and my breakfast at 12.30. The others had been shopping and had sampled the local hostelry. I had been up since 0345 and was now sanewhat Green crackered. 1300 To sea again. launch was fresh grilled sardines, with the grill pan tied into the cooker as we met the Atlantic swell again. Delicious! - followed by fresh strawberries and yoghurt. I slept the aftermmoanaway happily. I was third in line to shower at teatime as we approached La Carma. TIwas all soaped and lathered up when the water ran out —- oh bother! om1930 Secured at a pontoo for the first time this trip, we then went ashore and re-showered and telephmed wane. La Carona was a very lively place as we ate a hearty evening meal ashore. Everyone was aut pranenading or sitting in the many cafes. The atmosphere was very friendly. SATURDAY 9th MAY After a good night's sleep we spent all moming working an "Ocean Challenger", cleaning, repairing, checking, refuelling and watering. We all went into tow for brunch of Paella and beers followed by a walk aromd town. The shops were closed in the aftemoa, But they were impressive and expensive for Spain. We faimd a supermarket open and spent £45 on food, and then lumped the six-bags-full back to the boat. Talked to three people who had just arrived fram Falmouth in a Westerly Corsair. They'd had a force 9 wind up the backside all across Biscay, it didn't sod too good. We met many other voyagers, sane going north like us, but most going south. We had a good yam with all of them, swapping experiences. Yau do meet interesting people who cruise - three of them had arrived just behind us in a traditimal thirty footer called "Mrs Muir" en route for Southampton. She was crewed by two guys fran Liverpool, and skippered by a chap fran Chester. It was their first delivery job. Saturday evening was spent in the Company of "Mrs Muir's" crew. We had a most disjointed meal with large helpings of wine followed by a taur of the town ending in the waterfront cafes with local brandy and cigars. The is sanething special about the Liverpudlian humour. SUNDAY 10th MAY Today's The Day! 7099 Awoke after a sound night's sleep. A thunder stom was in progress and nobody wanted to get up.

1000 Preparations in progress, but it was still raining heavily. 1100 Slipped La Carma after eating our first meal all sitting rod the salom table. The rain had stopped and we were all full of hope as well as breakfast. We headed north with a bit of west across the Bay of Biscay. 1300 Two hairs out and what little wind there was, was an the nose. The sea was calm,only 300 miles to go before we get to land again. I slept the aftemom away - the calm weather was a real treat. 1800 It was my watch now. The sea was still flat, but the day had became more and more overcast. It looked as if there was a lot of rain about. No more lying an deck sunbathing. Everyone now in hats, jumpers and oilskins. We were now 42 miles aut and the wind was just picking up fram - guess where - northerly! We were in radio camtact with "Mrs Muir" who had left several hours after us. They were steering 018 degrees true, more directly across the bay than we were. We intended altering to a north- easterly course the next day, when we were expecting to pick up a NW 3 ~ 4 wind. Not a thing in sight as I looked forward to my dinner of corned beef hash. 2200 All alme mTMm Deck. No.1 genoa still was up, but with the engine still ticking over. Darkness fell with overcast cold clear weather. Wind was still mm the nose. Y 2400 Off watch, I wedged myself into the forecabin and slept peacefully. MONDAY llth MAY 0400 Not much shipping around, although we had encountered a giant floating crane lit up like a Christmas tree. I understand we were slow at altering course, our helmsnan of the hour was mesmerised, thought it was a block of flats! Whilst aon my own I looked at the chart and saw that we were in a position where we had 5,000 metres of water beneath us. That's over 3 miles deep! Not at all the Thames estuary. 0500 Three ships had cane up and gone down my starboard side but the fourth came slowly @m. Would you believe it, I had to go about and pass under her stem, all this sea and I had to do that! It was now bitterly cold and four of us were sharing two pairs of gloves. 0615 Spoke to a Russian Cmuise Liner, the "Leonard Bresnichoff" who was very helpful and gave us aur latitude and lagitude, as our Satellite navigator had lag since given up the ghost. Our dead reckming was about 3 miles out, which wasn't bad after a run of 102 miles. 0700 I dropped the genoa and headed 037°, more into the bay. Everyone was rested after we had introduced a new watch-keeping systen. The day was fine but overcast, wind still N.E. I was fed up with the sam of the engine. I cooked breakfast - fresh orange juice, boiled eggs with french bread and coffee. TM A whale was seen in the distance as 50 - 100 dolphins descended an us well spread out. They were a truly fantastic sight. Lumched q@m lasagne, good old Marks & Sparks their food is very good. We were getting silly with the boat's standing jokes, the skipper hid the foot away whilst Martin and I were always hungry. Don, the other crew member, was permanently asleep when not an watch. 1600 - 1800 My watch again. The wind had finally arrived, we were tranping alang at 7 knots. 2000 We now had five rolls in the mainsail amd a full genoa, and were doing eight knots. We all sat and discussed the sky and claxd fommatim and thumbed our weather books, all agreeing it to be a wam front caning through. Final instaJment in next Navigans.

CODE OF PRACTICE FOR LAUNCHING AND RECOVERY OF CRUISERS The O.0.D to be informed and suitable notices must be displayed for the information of dinghy sailors. Large Boats Boats above 27ft. length will not be allowed on the hard when dinghy events are in progress. At other times they should be handled with great care due to their weight. Tractors Only to be used by authorised drivers. Winches When dinghy events are in progress, the winches must be under the charge of an authorised operator. Only the East half of the hard may be used, leaving the West half for dinghies. At ALL times the following code should be observed: e When winding up the slope always use the ratchet. Winching down the slope should be done by use of the brake with the winch handle(s) removed. e Avoid sharp bends in the winch cables. e DONOT shackle the winch wire back onto itself. USE THE CHAIN PROVIDED. e tis the responsibility of the BOAT OWNER to ensure that the operation is done safely. This includes providing an adequate trailer and a sufficiently strong team of helpers. e Leave winches tidy, return shackles, strops etc. to the garage after use, rewind cable tidily as riding turns can damage the cable. e Report any damage or wear of any equipment to an authorised tractor driver. e REMEMBER, it is your responsibility to check for the safety of any equipment in use, if in doubt - DO NOT USE! e _ If the tractor is used to pull boats up or lower them down the slope, the WIRE STROP MUST BE USED to allow the tractor to remain on the level and always clear of loose shingle. Boat Trolleys _ If left submerged should be adequately marked to avoid damage to other boats. MOORINGS INFORMATION 1988 The system we adopted in 1986, which is outlined again below for reference, was largely successful. We again did not receive any criticism from the River Bailiff for being too far out in the fairway. C row was marginally too far inshore but this will be rectified this year. One boat went adrift in 1987 due to a scope failure, so check your mooring tackle in plenty of time. Replace anything which is worn or suspect, IF IN DOUBT - RENEW. New gear is a small price to pay for peace of mind or against the real cost of damage to your own or other boats. Make sure your mooring buoy is of adequate size to support the additional weight of scope and bridle. During 1987, dinghies have been damaged by striking submerged trailers whilst approaching the hard. Trailers must not be left submerged. It is the responsibility of the owner to ensure the trailer is recovered immediately the boat is launched. Dave Thomas undertook a survey at the end of 1985 which confirmed that C row has a fairly constant depth but that A and B rows get significantly deeper towards Stone. So to allow for this please note the changes to recommended bridle lengths etc. Below is a sketch using B1 and B2 as an example. CRUISER DOES & DON’TS Over the last twenty years the Cruiser Fleet has developed from one of just a handfull of 18’ to 20’ cruisers to the present 120 plus fleet of boats up to 45’ in length. During this time a code of practice, based on practical experience, has been evolved, some parts of which are now Club Bye-Laws others are custom and practice. The purpose of this booklet is to acquaint new members, and remind existing members on how the Club operates with respect to cruisers, what equipment is available to you and how to get access to it. Moorings The Club leases the moorings area from Maldon District Council. The moorings are laid in six rows, three are deep water (rows A, B &C) and three drying (rows D, E &F). Rows A, B and C are laid in the spring and lifted in the autumn each year to ensure that they can be properly inspected and maintained. This is done in teams over a number of weekends, the dates of which are published in Navigans and in these notes which accompany the Year Book. Members will also be notified by their Team Leaders, see page 2, and they or their representative MUST be present on these occasions. Mooring buoys must be of an adequate size to be afloat at all states of the tide and be marked with the mooring number. Mooring strops, if made of rope, should be protected against chaffe by polythene tubing. Anchors in A, B and C rows should preferably be of the CQR or Danforth type, but if Fisherman types are used then provision must be made for lowering themin the correct plane. Chain sizes and lengths are given on page 3. It should be noted that 9/4 inch chainis the maximum size that can be laid at the Club. Shackles should be wired, and shackles and swivels should be of the largest practical size as they are THE WEAK LINK in any mooring. Tenders All tenders should have some form of identification on them. Tenders must NOT be parked on the sea wall (Anglia Water Authority Rule), or on the foreshore by the White Hut (Obstruction of a Right of Way). During the winter, tenders are to be stored with the cruiser, only one rigid tender per member. Cruiser Park It is the resposibility of each member to keep their allocated area tidy-PLEASE put any rubbishin the bins provided. DO NOT park your car in the cruiser park if you are going out sailing, it may obstruct the movement of boats or tractor. If you need electric power, thisis availablein the park from the standpoints and you must use the correct 15amp waterproof plug - LEWDEN Part No PD 160/3. DO NOT ATTEMPT TO USE THE OLD DOMESTIC ROUND PIN TYPE. High The high pressure hose is available via the 0.0.D at weekends and by prior arrangement Pressure with the Cruiser Fleet Captain during the week. Please read the operating instructions Hose carefully and always ensure that there is oil in the reservoir. Scrubbing At present there is no booking system to use the posts, this may have to be reviewed in Posts the light of the current Anti-Fauling legislation. Drinking water is available at the posts, the stop cock being situated by the green Bio-Pack. Jack There is a 15 tonne toe jack in garage No. 5. Key available from the O.0.D or any tractor driver. Trailers It is the responsibility of each member to ensure that the trailer used for launching and recovery of his boat is suitable, not only for the boat but also for the conditions at the Club. e Axles must be big enough to take the weight of the cruiser. e Uprights must be strong enough to cope with the effects of the tide. Pea sticks and string will not do! e Wheels must be suitable for the hard and the field. Small solid wheels will not do! e Good steering is needed. With the increasing number of boats laying up at the Club it is important that trailers have reasonable steering as space is becoming limited. IF IN DOUBT - ASK! Page 6

z The third and last instalment of Cadet Skipper Derek Hall's log from his sailing trip last year from Lisbon to St Helier. TUESDAY 12th MAY Midnight + 5 minutes, my watch again. It had taken me 20 mimutes to get aut of my sleeping bag, dress into full oilskins and hamess up. We were being throw about samnething awful. I decided the genoa must came down. We put the working jib up, not an easy job in the dark with the seas building up, and every third wave caning on board. We all now knew we were in for a a blow! 0630 Called up on deck again, I had not been able to sleep. We landed the mainsail, the seas were getting bigger by the hour. We were doing 6 knots under the working jib only, the wind was up to a NW 7, they had said it would be a NW 3 - 4, oh hell! The seas were getting bigger but were much shorter between waves, very uncanfortable. 1030 Skipper managed to do beans an toast, followed by yogturt and biscuits with hot coffee. 1130 It was now up to a full Force 8 and the boat is being flung aramd everywhere. "Sea Scout", a large bilk carrier, altered course for us, but didn't answer our VHF call. Our positign was now very approximate. "Mrs Muir" had caught us up, we met up in the middle of Biscay and were now three miles astem after a photo call. My writing in my notes at this point is almost illegible due to the rough seas. Biscay was really getting its revenge now. Very cold and wet an deck: now and we were two to a watch, both an deck. We are hand steering as our Autohelm 3000 cannot cope. wy WEDNESDAY 13th MAY There is nothing worse than getting out of a wazm sleeping bag, putting a@m danp clothes and wet oilskins to face a contimous Force 7 and 20-foot waves with sameone throwing cold water at you for four hours at a stretch. Night watches were now very cold. The other three were now all sharing my gloves. Mostly we went over the beam waves which were now huge, although every now and then the dam things broke as we reached the top and and were sent crashing down, which shook every filling in my head. Sametimes when we were at the bottan, the force of the wind blew the crest off and dow anto us. It is great fun trying to fix our position as we are now approaching Ushant. We sighted land after breakfast. I had never seen so many evil rocks and as many lighthouses in one area. Ushant is certainly a treacherous place. After a lot of time and effort we finally identified the correct approach to Brest (no roan for mistakes here). 1430 We entered the Part of Camaret in France, very glai to be there too. Our. log had recorded 388 miles. I stayed awake during the aftemoon to have an early evening meal at a local hotel with our friends off "Mrs Muir". For 95 francs I started with half a dozen oysters which were scrumptious - although I had trouble opening my throat to let them slide down - followed by Cordm Blew chicken with cheese, coffee and brandy. This was followed by one of the best night's sleep I had ever had. THURSDAY 14th MAY Up at 0800 ready for the off again as we were @ a tight schedule. The weather was awful, blowing a hooli, with poor visibility. We poked our nose out and ran down-channel to fing, the entrance to the Dufore channel, "Mrs Muir" had decided to stay put. 1130 We were back again having had the only dissent of the trip over the decision on whether to continue or returm. My decision was to retum, which was what we did. The rain was caning dom in sheets and the visibility very low as we were cleared by the Port Authorities and the Custans after we had secured alongside and had dropped off to sleep. The day was spent reading and sleeping and exploring the village of Camaret which was picturesque and still very sleepy even in mid-May. Our evening meal was cooked an board followed by drinks ashore. FRIDAY 15th MAY 0800 We were ready to try again, our forecast was Northerly 4 - 5, visibility good. 1000 Slipped Camaret after paying mooring fees and a further visit fram a Coastguard boat. We were followed out by "Mrs Muir" and a Swedish boat who was heading for Brightm en rate to Gothenburg. The narrow channel Dufore is not so bad in good visibility. 1400 After tacking for two hours we were into the English Channel. Wind was still @m the nose after thirty miles logged, only one hundred and ten to go to St Helier. 1500 Amazing, we had freed off the wind and were sailing well.

2000 Off watch and was not @ again until 0200 to 0400. Still creaming along at 7 knots off the Brittany coast, really fantastic sailing and we were knocking off the miles with a strong tide with us. Oh no, it was lasagne again for dimer. Taight was to be our last night at sea and we were allowed an extra tot after the weather forecast and evening news. The forecast was good and we were just beginning to pick up lighthouses. It was more demanding again allowing for tides and strong anes at that. SATURDAY 16th MAY 0145 Up to relieve the skipper. It was very cold. To think I was due hame that day, it seamed impossible I could make it. We were still sailing well, logging 6 knots, but we were now against a foul tide. 0400 A gocd watch with brilliant sailing @ a very cold but clear night, although I had been unable to get a good fix q@m the small scale chart. Had to get my sleep now to be fit for Jersey later in the day. 0830 I was up again. The engine had been started at 0545 when the wind died. We were approaching Jersey which looked good in the clear visibility. We entered through the Middle Passage, passing a type 42 Destroyer anchored in the bay. 1100 Secured in the marina at St Helier, just scraping over the ledge. I was looking forward to a good ~~ shower, several pints of Jersey's cheap beer, a slap-up lunch followed by an aftemoon's kip and Saturday evening an the town. As it tumed aut I got the shower and lunch time pints, ate lunch in the Wimpy bar as everything had closed after air drinks. I went shopping in the afternoon for gifts and caught the evening flight back to Southend. There were no flights left Sunday or even Monday to either Southend, Stansted, Gatwick or Heathrow. In two weeks we logged 885 miles spending six nights at sea. An enjoyable experience although hard work at times keeping up a tight schedule. Cruising is my thing, I would go again tanorrow if I cauld. Don't rely too much an electrmics thaugh, our Sat. Nav. never worked; our VHF gave trouble, and our Autohelm gave up an the last two days. Well done everyone who played a part in the preparation or manning of the stand, particularly Mike Battle for the really excellent printed material he was able to provide for us this year. Let's hope we are rewarded with some active new membership as a result. Thanks again, John Salmon. WORKING PARTY REMINDER (20th March) Work to be done includes: ditch clearing, flagpole, race box, club boats. Also cleaning of lounge windows, replacing of curtains, washing bar glasses & shelves, and Galley crockery & cupboards. Ed. GALLEY Though we still have no Galley Supervisor, I'm sure there will be members who would like to step in for the odd Sunday. There will be a list of dates on the Galley notice board allowing those interested to book a space. Tea, coffee, sugar, sauces, salt and cling film will be stocked in readiness, but rolls, bread, fillings, cakes and milk will need to be brought along on the day, and unused fool taken home. Sadly for our ‘workers', our microwave was stolen from the Galley towards the ena of last season, so I recommend bringing along one of the soft margarines - unless you enjoy playing with plates of liquid butter under the grill. Ed. SOLO NEWS The party at Diane and John Rutherford's house was a great success enjoyed by all who attended. Many thanks to our hosts for their hospitality. One of the main attractions seemed to be John's new exercise bench which provided an opportunity for all those athletic Solo helms to demonstrate how fit they were not! Most of the news on the '‘go-faster' front seems to be about buying new sails, with ‘Performance Sails' appearing to be the flavour of the year - we shall see. I hear that Bob Anderson has bought John Walker's boat, so now has two. Does ww? Plan to swim in between? CAVITATION & VENTILATION are camoanly confused with rubber bush damage but it is entirely different and costs consideraby less to rectify. Cavitation could be the result of poor propeller design, wrong blade area, or pitch for the application for which the propeller is being used. Usually the result of cavitation can be seen by metal "eaten" or “bumed" off the propeller surface or gearcase. These "bumed" areas are the result of vapour bubbles which have been formed by the water's inability to flow over or around poorly developed areas, such as damaged propeller blades, which impede the natural water flow. These bubbles attach themselves to a surface af higher pressure, such as the propeller blaje face, and cause mimite but high pressure impacts which erode the surface where they collapse. Ventilation is the effect of extemal air or exhaust gases being made available to the propellers. The propeller blades, during their operation, have a pressure- and a suction side. When air is induced into the propeller's working area, the suction, or back side, of the blade will accept any migrant air, thus causing loss of thrust, increase in motor rpm and poor performance. Causes of Cavitation and Ventilation are: Too high a transan setting Severe tuum when in use Wrong motor angle Damaged and out-of-balance propellers Fauled boat bottan or lower unit aa Loss of converging ring fran a thru-tub exhzist propeller In general, incorrect boat ‘set up' Although it is not possible to repair cavitation bums it is possible to reduce cavitation and therefore reduce the production of cavitation bums. This is dme by cupping the propeller. upping is a slight tum on the trailing edge of the propeller. This reduces cavitatim, increases acceleration and reduces vibration. Cupping is also the equivalent of increasing the pitch of the propeller by me inch and this Should therefore be taken into camsideration when thinking of cupping a propeller. Cavitatim can also be reduced by having the propeller blade thinned down as this reduces the high pressure build up. ELECTROLYSIS eeeeehhy is a propeller beyond repair when it has electrolysis? Because the metal structure of the propeller becanmes so weak with fatigue that it would be dangeraus to use it an a boat because considerable damage cauild be caused to the vessel, namely by a whole blaie being “thrown off". It is also impossible to weld anto a propeller when it has electrolysis because the zinc, which would nomally be present in the metal of the propeller, is dram out and this zinc is needed to weld. w ---.eHow is electrolysis caused? Water, even fresh water, can act like acid in a battery. Two dissimilar metals immersed in water may fam an active "battery" actually generating a small current and eating avay ane of the metals. This is called galvanic corrosion which is a wasting process that can go on all the time the craft is afloat and can attack all metal canponents immersed in water, especially the propeller. Propellers painted with anti-fouling paint, especially anti-fouling which is high in copper content, may react with the metal of the propeller and cause electrolysis, render the propeller inguseless. Bronze Propellers should not be covered in any wey. This is because an oxide layer builds up naturally over the top of the metal which renders the propeller slightly corrosim resistant. If there is no oxygen getting to the propeller metal, then no oxide layer can be built up and thus no “self protective skin" is present.

«+e.eH is electrolysis ow stopped? To stop electrolysis all you need to do is fit an anode. Many boat builders fit Cathodic Protection (anades) as standard on new craft. It may be canpletely absent, or need renewing on older craft. There are many different types of anode available. There are anodes which attach to the hull of yaur craft, directly anto the rudder or skeg etc., or to the propeller shafts themselves, and also hanging anodes. eeeeeWhat do Steel Developments Ltd recammend conceming electrolysis? We strongly recamend that anodes be fitted to all craft. Installation of anodes to GRP and wood boats is simple and straightforward and can be undertaken by any owner or boatyard when the craft is hauled out. The anodes must, however, be correctly fitted to the boat or it will not protect the propeller ani stem gear, etc. Every time the craft is hauled aut, the anode should be checked and, if corroded, then replaced. The propeller should also be overhauled ready for the next season ahead. PROPELLER CARE AND SERVICING Why have your propeller Serviced and Repaired? Roughness, Cavitation, Corrosion and surface damage to @ propeller reduces its efficiency and hence raises fuel consumption. Steel Developments have canpiled a list of useful hints about propeller care and maintenance: Propellers are made usually of either Bronze, Aluminium or Stainless Steel but it is vital that all are fTMnaintained properly. A propeller not Only pushes the boat alamg but regulates engine rpm of which the rpm is directly related to horsepower and the propeller pitch is related to mpm. An example of this would be if your engine should have an rpm af 2500 but you can qmly get 2300, your propeller has too coarse a pitch. This ca bealtered by having the pitch reduced by 1" which will give you the needed 200 rmm tobring the engine to its full revs and efficiency and so reduce fuel costs. On your propeller there will be the propeller's measurements. If these are, for example, 10 x 12 then this means the first mmber (in this case 10) is the diameter, which is determined by doubling the distance between the blade tip and centre of the hub. The second mmber (which is 12 in our example) refers to the pitch. Pitch is the blaje angle, and the 12" pitch indicates that in each propeller revolutia the boat theoretically would advance 12" - but due to slip loss the actual advance is sanewhat less. Using a damaged propeller will not only reduce the boat performance but can cause costly engine damage. To obtain the best possible performance fran your vessel you should have your propeller serviced at least Once a year - and every time you damage it - by an expert. frying a "do-it-yourself" repair cauld well cost you more in the lmg mn. alte following hints should be followed in order to achieve the best possible performance fran your vessel: lt. ADWAYS CARRY A SPARE PROPELLER TO USE IN EMERGENCIES. 2s Propellers and stem gear must NEVER be coated with anti-fauling or metal-based paints, to avoid Problens of severe corrosion. 3. A suitable propeller puller should always be used when removing an inboard propeller. 4. NEVER run a vessel for lag periods with a damaged propeller as you may cause same severe damage to your engine and stem gear. 5. Make sure you have an anode fitted to your vessel so yau reduce the risk of your propeller and stem gear fran electrolysis. CRUISER RACING Now that we are working up to a new season, it is time to give som serious thought to what type of sailing will allow us to obtain the most from our yachts and from our time available. Often, due to pressures of work and family comnitments, we find we are forced to plan our sailing and we are not always able to go as far, or for as long as we would like. Racing on the Blackwater is an excellent way of having an enjoyable day out and of using your yacht to its full potential whilst developing your sailing skills. The B.J.R.C. (Blackwater Joint Racing Cammittee) run a series of ten races through the season from May to September, aimed at the family cruising man and woman as well as at those who are cammitted racing helms. Races are timed to go out to sea on the ebb tide and return on the flood, having sailed around a series of navigation marks in the Blackwater and Colne estuaries. Entry for the B.J.R.C. race series costs £5 regardless of whether you enter one or all ten races. This nominal charge also includes all the information necessary, such as the basic rules and race courses. You must, of course, comply with a few safety rules. Races are run using the P.Y. handicap system. Yachts without a recognised handicap would be rated by the B.J.R.C., and therefore no yacht is excluded. In addition to this, there is also our Marconi Barnacle Points. This year there will be two races held on the weekend of 23 - 24 July. With more than 100 cruisers in the Club, I am hoping for a good response. Don't forget, racing is a good discipline. It checks your ability and sorts out those weak points, boat and personal, as well as being good fun. As the Cruiser Racing Captain, I am interested to learn how many people would like to join us racing this year. Therefore I would be very grateful if all Cruiser owners would camplete the form below and retum it to any sailing sub- committee member. I will be only too pleased to answer any questions you may have, so please do not hesitate to contact me any time. BOSUN'S LOCKER Much work has been done on Jack B during the winter. The less obvious items are that the propeller has been repaired and rebalanced and new sacrificial anodes fitted. Not very exciting, but necessary. Fron the safety point of view the most important job has been to change all the windows (which were only ordinary window glass) for safety glass. Thanks are due to Doug Brown and to the lads at Highway Windscreens at Witham, for providing the new glass, cut to size, Free of Charge. A marine, parallel sweeping, windscreen wiper has been fitted and works well keeping the centre window clear of rain and spray. (Rumours that cockpit heating and GT car seats are to be fitted for the crew are unfounded). Malcolm Stuart arranged for a cockpit cover and that, together with a lick of aint and varnish had Jack B looking very smart at launch time. (Pity about the ddy wellies, mine included, which have clambered over the boat since then). The club name has been put on the side of the boat, but unfortunately the stick-o lettering is not proving equal to the scuffing received - further thought required on this. Thanks are due to Geoff Josey for servicing Jack B's machinery as well as the Club's outboards and to Dennis Dear for becoming Club Radio Officer. On the subject of Jack B's Radio the VHF set on the Jack B has a ‘dimmer' control which can be operated to campletely cut out the control panel illumination, giving the impression that the radio is not working. Of course you radio buffs would know about that, but it took me same time to rumble it - so be warned. The offending control is marked 'dim' and is located with the squelch control - clever eh? A final note of thanks to all those who have assisted me over the winter/spring with sandpaper, brushes etc. etc., in particular Malcolm Stuart and Gordon Golding who both spent a very physical afternoon reglazing the cuddy, (the Instant Windscreen _Replacement firms have nothing to fear from us). Finally a plea to all users of Club Boats: Please report any defects or missing gear to me or the OOD so that repairs/ replacements can be arranged. Ray Ball, Bosun. Chelmsford [redacted]

MIRRORS SET SAIL FOR ANOTHER YEAR An excellent turn-out to the Mirror AGM on 18th March, started a season of renewed vigour and enthusiasm. Well, that is the theory. All we have to do is to put it into actual sail power. Following the threatening letters, all Fleet Duties are covered for the year and duly posted on the board at the club for all to see! Don't forget, if you cannot undertake a duty, then please arrange to swap with sameone else. Our duty roster is samewhat depleted this year by the keenness of many of our fleet to help out with the Jack B drivers' duties. Dave Onyons has done a great job in building up a strong fleet to cope with one of the primary tasks in the Club. Whilst all in attendance at the AGM look forward to the spectacle of the East oast Piers race (7th August), we, too, expressed concern over the organisation = the weekend, in particular to the camping and boat park facilities. It would seem that it could be quite cosy. All in all, however, this first East Coast Piers Race should be exciting to watch and help again to put the club fimly on the map. The view of the fleet with regard to Galley duties was one of thanks to all the volunteers who provide food and drinks. In general most of the fleet are DIY merchants, however we thought there was merit in the Cammittee advertising locally again for outside caterers. The Regatta is now well and truly on its way. The Mirror fleet will be there, not I predict in entirety however, but those that will be taking part look forward to a good weekend's sport. By then we may have new junior fleet members: Martin and Alison Edwards, we hope all goes well! My thanks to Maggie Boreham for her words of inspiration each month in Navigans. I am sure this dissertation does little for thought-provoking ideas for the future, but it is about time I did my bit. -~ trust that Club Members will note that this year all our regular sailing cadets are booked to do duties as assistant race officers. Following on from the sterling work of our Cadet Fleet captain Derek Hall and his team, we have decided to continue the cadets' learning into actual duties in the Club. My thanks in advance to the Cadets. Congratulations to Damian, Lucy and Nigel for their joint efforts in coming 4th out of the entries in the Easter Series. To date I have counted four Mirrors on site at the Club. Where are the rest?. Mike Battle Mirror Fleet Captain Tel. Chelmsford [redacted]

ENTRIES Key positions have been fixed for running the Regatta and I hope as many members as possible will enter the event. Malcolm Stuart, Rear Commodore SAILING IN ROUGH WEATHER In the spring and autumn at Stansgate we frequently experience strong winds and. when these blow against the tide we can get very choppy and confused water, particularly between Stansgate Point and Osea Pier. In such circumstances the Race Officer, the OOD and all members who have turned up to race will be faced with a decision. Firstly, irrespective of what the Race Officer decides, members remain responsible for their personal safety and should not sail if they judge the conditions to be well beyond their present level of competence. The Race Officer will, in reaching his decision, assume that members have considered the weather conditions and have reached the decision that they can survive them when they sign on. fhe Race Officer's job is therefore not that of deciding what is suitable for the least experienced and worst equipped member, but only that of deciding whether or not it is safe to start a race for the more experienced members. We must recognise here that the only way of getting experience in sailing in rough conditions is. to get out and do it and we are only going to improve our skills by pushing ourselves a little. The Race Officer has therefore to make the difficult judgement on how far to let those who sign on for a race push themselves. In circumstances such as this the Race Officer will consult with the duty Coxswain, the Fleet Captains and the oOoD. Any course set for racing must take account of the ability of the rescue facilities available on the day to recover crews who may get into trouble. He may therefore restrict sailing to the shorter courses, and faster boats like the Catamarans will have to put up with having their wings clipped. The ultimate authority for all matters relating to the conduct and welfare of club members is the OOD, however in practice he will normally only exercise this authority in response to a request from the Race Officer for guidance, and would in any case take any decision affecting racing after consultation with the Race Officer. fo summarise what is a cautious justification of racing in conditions that prompt thoughts of more comfortable hobbies: 1. Competitors must decide themselves whether or not they are competent to go out in rough weather. 2. The Race Officer must consult the duty Coxswain, Fleet Captains and OOD and set a suitable course or postpone until such time as a suitable course can be set. CONTE isk

4. Sailing in Rough Weather - continued 3% If these two points have been properly addressed then racing will only be abandoned in the most extreme weather conditions or in the absence rescue cover. Malcolm Stuart, Rear Commodore BOSUN'S LOCKER I would like to add my personal thanks to Murray and Peter for replacing Jack B's prop. shaft bearing, and re-aligning the engine. To replace the bearing (a 5" bronze cylinder with rubber lining), without removing the engine and shaft was a tricky operation requiring considerable thought. As well as spending a couple of evenings planning the job, Peter and Murray gave up a day's leave to do the work, I confess to having had doubts that the job could be done, and certainly did not expect that Jack B would be ready for the Bank Holiday weekend. (I even went as far as phoning a local marine engineering firm for a quote - THEY did not want the job). When an item of club equipment is found damaged one weekend, but is ‘miraculously' repaired and back in service a week later, it must seem to many members that the club has a ‘fairy godmother' with a magic wand. I hope the above notes will dispel such thoughts. The Club's ‘fairy godmothers' are usually, guys in boiler suits wielding, not wands, but tool kits (or on the admin. side, lounge suits and pens)..... That was the enjoyable part of my article, now for a gripe! The failure of the shaft bearing was a ‘mixed blessing' because upon hauling Jack B out for that repair it was found that the boat had suffered some damage to the hull. Damage to the port bow had removed some of the glass fibre covering the edge of the foredeck, exposing an area of unprotected and splintered plywood. Chipping of the gel-coat on the corner of the transom had laid bare small areas of glass-fibre, None of the damage was in itself serious and a few hours' work and a fiver's worth of materials put things right. BUT despite requests in Navigans I was not actually informed about the damage. If Jack B had not been brought ashore and repaired, rain and spray would have soaked into the damaged areas possibly causing delamination, etc., etc., Please, if you damage a Club boat, or notice a fault in it or in its gear, please let me know as soon as possible. I know it's embarrassing confessing to making a mess of things and I will probably growl and mumble in my beard, (I enjoy a good moan before getting on with the job), but at least I will be able to put in hand the necessary ‘stitch in time'. ‘nuff said. End of gripe. Ray Ball, Bosun Chelmsford [redacted] SAILBOARD RACK ACCESS Please keep the area between the sailboard rack and the otside stairs clear of hardware. At present it resembles a scrap merchant's backyard: rusting barbecue grills, mooring lumber, signals mast, a lamp post (I kid you not - a lamp post!). MIRROR FLEET NEWS. . The sailing season started on March 27th - but racing was abandoned for the morning because of strong winds. However, on April 10th, Spring Points 3 and 4 were raced with five (I think) Mirrors turning out; is this a record for the Mirror fleet so early in the season ? A longish course was set,for the morning race which was sailed in a good breeze. Alec Pembleton and Damian Boreham were single-handed {with Damian managing to capsize twice) but Steve Keeble, crewed by daughter Melanie, were well in the lead and looked all set for a good win. Unfortunately, the leading boats in the Catamaran Fleet discovered that the Goldhanger ('C') mark was missing and so all races were abandoned. Also taking part in the Mirror race was new member Alec Goodwright, with Georgina as crew. A warm welcom to Alec and Georgina who soon discovered the delights of mud walking by capsizing in the shallow waters just aroumd the corner of the Stansgate Point. No harm was done and Georgina didn't appear to be bothered at all in this (her first) race. Lucy Boreham with Jenny Ball as crew maintained an upright stance throughout to make up the quintette of Mirror Maniacs. The afternoon race was won by Janet Keeble (single handed) to end a day which very definitely belonged to the Keeble family with Steve and Melanie finishing 3rd, just behind Alec Pembleton's 2nd place. Spring Points 5 and 6 were sailed in very strong winds and and-adverse’tides, Again a good turnout with 6 and 5 entries respectively. This time, Damian had his crew, ‘Katy Rutherford, with him and they won both races . Janet’ Keeble was 2nd, Lucy 3rd and Jack and Diane Rusbridge 4th in race 5, whilst Lucy ftnished 2nd fn race 6 and the others suffered disasters of various sorts and all retired. Spring 7 and 8 were held on Sunday, 24th April, which was bright and windy - and cold. Just how wy cold that wind really was showed after the races with everyone complaining of numb hands, blue feet, pinched faces and wondering if a sunny, but sheltered, spot in the garden picking up weeds would have been a more sensible plan for the day. However, pleasures are relative; how wonderful those hot showers were -- you have your choice and takes your pick. It just proves how essential a wet or dry suit is for dinghy sailing at this time of year. Race 7 was postponed until 12.15 because the Jack B was out of action (prop shaft bearing’ gone - or something), and then a short course using 'F' mark was set. Only two Mirrors took part with Damian and Katy finishing lst with Lucy and Jenny in’2nd>pesition. This was repeated in Race 8 with Lucy reckoning she-was a little closer to her:brother this time - but not a lot. For both races, the wind was quite brisk, around 3-4. A good start to the season and hopefully more of you Mirror Mariners (makes a change from Maniacs) will join in the fun and games of racing with Steve, Janet, Melanie, Alec,P, Alec G , Georgina, Jack and Diane, Lucy and Jenny, Damian and Katy in what is, undoubtedly, a marvelous place to sail. Maggie Boreham Mirror Fleet Scribe ww Stop Press} Our Fleet Captain, Mike Battle, with Richard as crew, won his first Mirror Race!! It was Race 2 of a series of 4 over the Weekend May tst/8nd.

e¢ HANDICAP FLEET NEWS Now that we are well into the Spring Points series I would like to congratulate those folks who have got their boats out of hibernation to brave the cold water and join in some interesting and exciting racing. One of the benefits of sailing at this time of the year is not having to weave in and out through the cruisers when sailing between A and F marks! If you, like me, have a boat with sagging shrouds that does not seem to want to point up to wind and is always getting overtaken by Idle Vice, then come to Stansgate on the afternoon of Saturday llth June where those experts on the 420, Jack and Joan Hardy, have agreed to show us how to tune up a 420. They will be bringing and demonstrating the few special pieces of equipment required to make your boat go faster. Everyone is welcome, as a lot of the points on boat tuning will be applicable to other classes and perhaps we'll have a chance to try out the improvements afterwards. We have also an offer from Dave Hall of Hyde Sails to give us some instruction on 420 sailing. I will try to arrange this for some time in July/August. Watch Navigans for a date. Again everyone will be welcome, so come and try out a 420 if you have not got one already. When Did You Last Capsize? If you are out of practice or are new to sailing you should be able to get your boat back upright as a capsize can happen to anyone, even experts, (as our Solo sailors can vouch for). If you would like to practice capsize drill safely then get in touch with me and I will organise an afternoon with safety boats and experts on hand, where we can capsize to our heart's content. See you on the water, Mike Hellewell, Handicap Fleet Captain PHOTOGRAPHY COMPETITION Lots of new photographs will be required for display at next year's Sailboat Exhibition, as the current ones have been seen by most of the dinghy sailors in the country. So in order to encourage you to get your cameras out and to get snapping, this summer we intend to hold an informal photographic competition. There will be prizes (though not too extravagant) for both cadet and adult age~ groups. Photographers whose photos are selected for display will get enlargements of their photos and the distinction of their photo being admired by the world. The scope of the photos has been left very wide to cover all aspects of the Sailing Club activities, eg Racing, Cruising, Camping, Social activities, Artistic, etc. - even Glamour (if there is a boat somewhere in the picture). Photos and enquiries should be directed to myself or Malcolm Stuart, The closing date will be announced in the near future. So get clicking, Mike Hellewell, Handicap Fleet Captain.

Further to David Beane's Marathon Run and donation to Burnham-on-Crouch Lifeboat Station, you may be interested in the following: BURNHAM-ON-CROUCH Lifeboat Station is busy raising funds for a replacement Lifeboat- House forits 16' D Class Inshore Lifeboat. The site and launching ramp is generously supplied by the Royal Corinthian Yacht Club. The new Boathouse will be of brick and large enough for the boat and its launching tractor (with some spare space in case the boat is changed for a larger one in the future), and will include a crew-room and shower. 6 < Jolly Boating Weather or The Spring Bank Holiday Cruise The Cruiser Fleet's first Cruise-in-Canpany of the season was a visit to Brightlingsea over the Spring Bank Holiday Weekend. The organiser/flotilla leajer for this event was Malcolm Yeaman in VARUNA II. TARA's crew consisted of myself as skipper/cook, Cadet David Ball as First Mate/Washer-Upper and Cadet Stuart Golding as everything else. Having a small boat amd a yamg crew I intended to be quite choosy about the weather so, like a respmsible yachtsnan, I visited the Landm Weather Centre qm the Friday before the cruise and paid £1.50 for a 5-day weather forecast. The forecast was for predaninantly sautherly winds until Bank Holiday Monday, when the wind was to strengthen fran the South-west. Malcolm had called a pre-cruise meeting for 10.30 am the Saturday moming bit unfortumately our car chose to have a flat tyre so aur arrival at the club was sanewhat delayed. However we arrived in time to load the boat, make a quick phone call to the Colne Yacht Club order dinner and to depart for Brightlingsea in bright sunshine at about lpm. The sautherly wind ('Super, a reach all the way to the Colne') lasted as far as Bradwell when it went easterly and freshened - right qm the nose! Waves getting bigger - to go on or WM into West Mersea or Bradwell was the question. Decided to put in a reef and plug @TM (axe again I blessed the day I fitted slab reefing). We som settled dom to the motim and devoted ourselves to a bit of navigatim. Name of this 'Down to the end of the Blackwater and tum left for us! To be hanest, ane bit of sea looks much the same as another to me so we used charts and campass to find the cardinal mark marking the 'Molliette' wreck an Mersea flats and were then able to bear away for Brightlingsea. By 5pm we were safely tied up almgside another yacht in Brightlingsea. Another 10 or so Marconi boa’ were already there. At 8pm we all gathered for dinner in the Colne Yacht Club and as usual the Col® laid an an excellent meal. Qn Saturday night the wind freshened and the rain cane down. The boat inside of us wanted to move aut at 8am qm Sunday so it was a reluctant sortie to move aut at 8an into wind and rain to let him art. The rest of Sunday was spent in Brightlingsea eating and taking the occasional walk ashore. The weather forecasts were unfavourable for days ahead and I was beginning to think of leaving the boat at Brightlingsea until the next weekend. Watching a small yacht being towed in by the Lifeboat at Sunday lunchtime did nothing to inspire me to leave the shelter of Brightlingsea creek. By Sunday evening the crew of the good ship TARA were getting a bit 'cheesed off'. The midnight shipping forecast was for more of the same (strong South-westerlies) on Monday so I resolved to have a lie-in m Monday moming. I awoke on Monday moming at 7an to find the friendly face of Niel Pembleta@m peering through the hatch. It appeared that there was to be an easing of the wind for a few hours, did I fancy heading back to the Club? The initial reactio (fron a wam sleeping bag) was No! However a sense of nautical responsibility prevailed and rapid arrangements were made to leave - no time for breakfast. We. broke the good news to the boat an the autside of us and they let us out. The wind was sautherly which meant plugging against the wind and tide down the Colne but a reach up the Blackwater - not a bad bargain. J An hour was spent motoring down the Colne against* the wind and rain, and as som as we cauld set a course for the Blackwater, the mainsail was set, double reefed, and about half the jib unrolled. A very brisk, if bumpy, sail was enjoyed until Bradwell was reached, when the wind dropped! Was this the lull before the storm? Engine an for a quick dash back to Stansgate, and still it rained! The mooring was reached about llam when a hearty breakfast was enjoyed before tidying up. The cooker heated the cabin and allowed my lag-suffering crew to thaw out. Thanks are due to Malcolm Yeaman for organising the cruise and the evening meal at the Colne Yacht Club. This was a well-supported Club event which was only marred by the weather. Let's hope for better weather next time. Ray Ball, TARA Cruiser Fleet has now appointed its new Fleet Captain, Mike Smith of 'Rubicon of Osea' Tel. Brentwood [redacted].

It swims in surface layers of the sea feeding mostly a yang fish and crustacean larvae. It has long beak-like jaws and the head is me-fifth of its whole body length. It is famd in the sarthem and westem coasts of Britain in early summer when it moves into shallower wamer water to breed, laying eggs with long sticky threads which tangle in seaweed and flotsan. 10 Rescue Boat Competition -— Saturday 28th May 1988 This year saw the introduction of what we hope will become an important annual event giving some recognition to the valuable service provided by our rescue boat coxswains and crews. We were fortunate to get a very professional judging panel led by Dick Townsend (Bradwell Coastgard), two representatives from the Essex River Police and David and Ione Saunders from st Johns. David went out on the water to monitor closely how the casualty was treated. The brave casualties James Brill, Emma Henderson and Debbie Yorston jumped in from the scrubbing post two or three times each and stood up well to the manhandling. Its not often you see a drowning person smile. The seven teams demonstrated a variety of different techniques for recovering the casualty but the most impressive by far was Trevor Milton in his catamaran whose very smooth pick up brought a spontaneous round of applause from the spectators. This years entries and the first three placings awarded by the judges were:-— Malcolm Grant MSC Jack B Dave Onyons MSC Jack B Brentwood Sea Cadets Baddow Star Trevor Milton MSC Stampede 1st John Chandler MYC Jacomar 3rd Barry Parker MSC Jack B Bill Fletcher SSC Zodiac 3 2nd Next year I anticipate a much bigger entry from local clubs and our Regatta visitors from Fishers Green are going to bring their rescue boat with them, so what has started as a local event for BJRC clubs could blossom into a Regional Competition. Malcolm Stuart A MATURE INTRODUCTION TO DINGHY SAILING Over the years an increasing number of adults have asked to join in Cadet week so that they can learn to sail dinghies. This year during the week 31st July to 7th August we propose to organise special sessions for those adults who would like to learn to sail but cannot stand up to the punishing pace of Cadet tuition. The adult training sessions will be fitted in with cadet sessions in such a way that parents can get their offspring sorted out and meals organised. This will probabl involve a short get together over coffee in the morning whilst the cadets are out on the water and an afternoon session in dinghies. If you are interested in learning to sail during cadet week, or would just like to have a go in a dinghy, please let me know and I will lay on the appropriate facilities. Malcolm Stuart Chelmsford [redacted]

id REGATTA '88 I could get wildly enthusiastic about the way everyone got involved in making REGATTA '88 one of the friendliest and most enjoyable Regattas on record. However, as my old school reports used to say "this boy could do better if only he would apply himself", so lets look forward to an even better REGATTA '89. Mike Battle gave our predicted entry of 100 boats in the Essex Chronicle May 27th — he was one boat out, we only achieved 99. Our publicity officer more than made up for this error in getting 24 column inches of write-up on the Regatta into the Essex Chronicle on June 3rd, and 17 column inches in Yachts and Yachting. Frank Saville and Mike Hellewell played computer games on the hard over the weekend in the dry half of Charles Anderson's caravan, and came up with race results in record time. No problems with power failure thanks to the new cable provided by Malcolm Grant. Mike Battle's new token system also worked well, and avoided the problems of interpreting soggy signing on sheets. The reception girls Pat Harper, Mary Greygoose and Pat Stuart never had such an easy time - they were even seen sunbathing on the Saturday. Mike Turner took on the daunting task of following Robbie Sims as race officer acquiring Robbie's old team of Joan, Malcolm and Alastair Sims in the process. - Mike, Frank and Robbie coped very diplomatically with the GP14 and Enterprise Fleets who sailed the wrong course for Race 4 after a general recall and were (or. at least some of them) understandably upset. The Clubhouse extension, after passing the EEV destruction test, stood up well to the gales on Sunday, and the new outside bar worked well thanks to Dave Payne who got us the plastic material, Pete Clayton who welded the tubes, Murray Bates who acquiried the fixings, and Eddy Yorston who gave us a new set of neon lights. The erection team were Mike Clark, Norman Taylor, assisted by Colin Willsmore who load tested the framework, and Maurice Brill who put it together again. The extension cost the club less than the hire charge for a marquee and its cost was more than covered by. Regatta profits. With care it should last five seasons. We will use it mainly for Regatta, Barbecue, Cadet Week and Open Meetings but the downstairs bar in No 2 Garage can be used any weekend when it is too hot to stagger upstairs. The garage bars worked well thanks to Dave Payne's expert advice. What a lot of effort we have wasted in the past through not keeping it simple. Andrian Wright was plunged into the job of head daytime barman and grabbed hold of anyone who wasn't moving quickly enough to reward them with the dreaded yellow sweat shirt. Any ideas for next years colour? Organised by the capable hand of John Salmon and led by John and Eleanor Witter, Jean Flook and young Toby Saunders spotted together under John's windshield. Ideas wanted for an easily erected structure at the race box giving a good view in all weather conditions.

Bob also had a good sideline in straightening masts after Sundays racing. We found in erecting the extension that the bricks have all been layed upside down. I only hope the end of the clubhouse where masts are straightened is truly square. Thanks to all our rescue crews over the weekend. Roger Camp in his boat "Capricorn", the Brentwood Sea Cadets in Baddow Star and our regular coxswains Dave Onyons, Graham Baker, Keith Gurney, Malcolm Grant, Derek Howroyd, Barry Parker, Andy Rimmer, Bob Leader, Steve Gallant and their assistants who manned Jack B and anything else they could lay their hands on. We also quickly lost our Sunday and Monday rescue co-ordinators, Charles Anderson being called out by HM Coastguard and Norman Kerridge having to rush back to work to salvage a sinking £%m tender. Robbie Sims and Steve Keeble stepped in to cover. St John's this year showed us how first aid should be covered. The Cruiser garage was transformed into a field hospital with Ion# Saunders waiting to pounce at the first sight of blood whilst David Saunders was out looking for more work on the Jack B. MIRROR REGATTA REPORT Where were you all ? The turnout of Mirrors was either apathy or charity - apathy because you weren't interested or charity because you all thought it was about time your fleet captain had a chance to win something. A meagre five Mirrors entered the Regatta, four club boats and one visitor. Liz Ballard and son Adam from Maylandsea Bay joined Janet and Melanie Keeble, Jack and Diane Rusbridge, Elizabeth and Anne Goodwright and yours truly, who with a choice of three crew decided to opt for the heavyweight version, Janet, due to the prevailing strong southerly wind on Sunday. Capsizing was the order of the day on Sunday with both the Keebles and the Ballards taking a dip. Again this was a charitable jesture I'm sure, to give Janet and me a good chance in both races 1 and 2. The Monday however was not the day for the more portly crews and helms. Having said that, the first wins must have gone straight to my head because on the first mark at A buoy, I decided it was best to sail back through the cruiser lanes rather than head out towards No.1. Both Janet Keeble and Liz Ballard stormed away and on the long haul from C to B they tussled against one another to gain tactical advantage with Liz just coming out on top. With 2 wins and a third place for Battleship we decided to sit out the final race, which started in the lightest of breezes. Mike Turner (RO) put in an extra mark off Osea Island for the Mirrors. The conditions were a westerly wind (such that there was) and an outgoing tide. Having conquered the Stansgate spit, the Mirrors had to sail almost to Osea pier to take A mark and E mark to starboard. Liz Ballard came out the winner in this the final race but with Janet Keeble second, her fourth in the series, Liz Ballard was beaten into 3rd place overall. So the Battles marked up their first major win and collected first prize - a bottle of Gin! Not that we are ungrateful to win anything, and that it is the competing that counts not the winning, but I do think bottles of booze for winners of the "premier" event in the club's calendar is a bit OTT, especially for a fleet primarily made up of cadets. I've scoured every page of "Clubs and Classes" in the last three editions of Yachts and Yachting and in not one article or photograph have I seen winners presented with alcohol. Perhaps the Sailing Sub-Committee believe that it should be consumed and Che CompletelieDed 3 sealed again with a message saying "' I won “¢ Saltlor this at Marconi's Regatta" and then Lee thrown into the Blackwater as a promotional campaign. eres Eye (Foe Tort I jest, but I do think that we could do ) <— SPRAY DEFLECTOR better, next time? WELL DONE AND CONGRATULATIONS Talking of next time, I must put out a grate big CONGRATULATIONS to Malcolm Stuart. Regardless of individual views on whether we should or should not hold a Regatta, nothing can detract from the enormous effort Malcolm put into the event. (If all BR employees had his vigour to achieve results I'm sure I wouldn't swear and curse twice a day eA

SAILBOARD NEWS Summer Points Racing: This has now started and it's fun, so where are you all?! So far, of the 20 registered Boardsailors, only 6 have actually competed to date. Our earliest starting time is 11.50am on a Sunday and there are 10 races in total (see Yearbook for dates). There is no need to enter them all to do well. If there is sufficient interest, there should be no problem in participating in the Autum Points as well. Procedure is very simple: entries need to SIGN ON and identify their sail (not the board) by any visible marks or colours (so far this has proved sufficient, but if the numbers increase I will see about acquiring some stick-on numbers). On finishing or retiring, SIGN OFF. The race start is preceded by a 10-minute warning gun when our class flag is raised - a yellow and blue vertically halved flag. Lots more information in the Yearbook - read it! NOTE: I have been infommed that it is etiquette to keep out of the way of other classes starting before us - races usually start at 5 minute intervals. So far a certain Darcy Roberts is doing rather well with 2 wins out of 2 and Ian Savage, after an initial demonstration of his board's unique reverse gear, has now picked up al, 2 and 3. Rescue Boat Facility: I have been advised that the only really suitable boat for even moderately rough conditions is the Jack B. To handle any boat in any conditions requires a certain amount of seamanship and has to be learnt. Anyone who wishes to do so can learn to use the Jack B and would then be able to operate it when they felt appropriate Those sailboarders who are interested in doing this should contact either me or Dave Onyons, the’ Coxswain, directly. If there are a few interested people then I will arrange some group training sessions. Experience on the Jack B can be obtained most Sundays and Wednesday evenings - just ask the helmsman of the day - he will probably be willing to take an extra crew. It is the long term aim of the MSC to acquire a semi-rigid inflatable for rescue work ich would be much more suitable for sailboarders, but unfortunately this will not kr pen yet! Buoyancy Aids: I have agreed with the Club Canmmodore to make it clear that when the red flag is flying, all sailors are advised to wear personal buoyancy, and furthermore those participating in Club races will not qualify unless they do so. NOTE: Personal buoyancy does not include nappy- or waist-type harnesses which, whilst they might keep your most important parts above water, will not stop you drowning. Boat and Mast Racks: The area around these has now been cleared of lumber - many thanks to Pete Clayton. Both racks are now nearly full so if anyone desires a place then let me know and I will see about constructing another. Adrian Wright, Sailboard Fleet Captain.

KRKEKKKRKEKKKKKKKKKKEK CADET SERIES Helms and crew had to face a fair old wind on Saturday, 2nd July, for Cadets Races 1 and 2, and sailing conditions were both exciting and testing. In Race 1, Richard Battle capsized (twice I believe) but David Ball (crewed by Janet Keeble) sailed into a good 2nd position behind Lucy Boreham (1st) and Debbie Yorston (3rd but catching up fast as they approached the finish). In the afternoon, the number of entries increased to 6 when ‘the morning mob' were joined by Greg Hall (sailing PATCH) and Damian Boreham (released from duties at his local Gateway Supermarket). David Ball got a superb start, trapping Damian to leeward and spilling dirty wind onto Lucy astern. With the course of 'Jack B' mooring, D, F, and 'E* (somewhere near B) David held the lead to E with Damian 2nd and Lucy third; unfortunately, tricks of the tide got both David and Damian into trouble and, much to her surprise, Lucy found herself in the lead which she held to the finish 14 laps later. On the way, Greg hall's mast fell down and Damian provided a spectacular spinnaker capsize with screaming accompaniment from his crew, Maggie Boreham. Richard Battle finished but retired (hit mark) and again Debbie Yorston was catching up fast in 2nd place, Damian was 3rd and david Ball 4th. Debbie's crew for both races was Melanie Keeble.

so CATAMARAN NEWS The more observant amongst you will notice that this is the first Catamaran newsletter this year, entirely due to the fact that the scribe's duties have been delegated by the Fleet Captain. This allows him more time to indulge his propensities for amour, female wrestling and amateur radio, not necessarily in that order. The Cat Fleet is undergoing a healthy resurgence in numbers. A recent count showed a total of thirty boats, not counting those which the writer has never seen on the water. of these thirty, nineteen are regularly sailed. By far the largest class is, of course, the Dart 18, of which there are currently seventeen. Has anyone noticed the phenomenon amongst our Dart 18 sail numbers? We have 2626, 3131 and 4747. The Dart 20 (Stampede) section of the fleet has recently doubled its numbers, no less. That is to say that we now have two instead of one. | Whilst on the subject of mumbers, it must be noted that whilst we have this large fleet . the boat park, rarely do we get many boats on the water at race time. So come along, helms, you will never discover your true talents until you pit them against others. It gives us great pleasure to welcome the newcomers to the Fleet, namely, Clive from Leigh Sailing Club, Keith an ex-Windsurfer, Graham Baker and Steeve Keeble. Before someone else says it, I am well aware that there are newcomers that I have missed. Some I do not know about, some I am aware of but do not know names and origins. So my apologies to those. Please come and give me the facts and you'll get a mention next time. Graham Baker and Steve Keeble are the more notable newcomers for the fact that they are recruited from other classes within the club, Graham graduating from Mirror to Dart, and Steve from Solo to Hurricane. (The wind of change?) Now the Hurricane has_ the reputation of being very sophisticated, amongst other things. So ‘hi tech' is it, that we hear it will be christened "Fly By Wire" (but only in very small letters.) The word is that once the in-mast water ballast system system is sorted it will be something to watch. Go for it Steve and Dave. Qn the racing front the summer points season is upon us, although there do not seem to many races taking place or people taking part. Nothing changes does it, and Trevor Milton seems to win them all (well, almost all.) Within the Dart class the normally all-conquering Duckmanton boat has developed a tendency to couple with racing marks. The age-old remedy of a well directed bucket of water hardly seems appropriate here. At the time of writing the Piers Race is almost upon us and by the time you read _ this, will be over - God and meteorology willing. Barrie Palmer will then be free to answer queries on next year's race. There will be one more order of commemorative sweatshirts, and orders, complete with ten pounds cash should be passed to the writer. The writer would also be grateful for any items of interest to the Fleet, e.g. news, requests for information, rumours, lies and scurrilous gossip; you know the kind of thing. As an example where are the photographs of Regatta Days promised by Andy Rimmer? Your roof-top reporter, Peter Flook (Dart 4747)
