ADULT TRAINING 1.- 5 AUGUST 1988 As an alternative to the arduous routine of the full Cadet Week course we offered this year a rather laid-back course for adults which attracted a total of 17 with the four men well outnumbered by the fairer sex. We spent a very pleasant five days drinking coffee, socialising and, when the mood took us, learning how to handle sailing dinghies. The course fell into a pattern of morning chats over coffee, with sailing in the afternoon: MONDAY Tiller Waggling, or how to make the boat go where you want it to go. TUESDAY Capsize Drill, or how to get back in the boat when it decides to go its Own way. Sailing practise round the buoys. WEDNESDAY Resucitation Practice with St John Ambulance. Man Overboard Practice, but only with plastic bottles because we had done the getting wet bit on Tuesday. THURSDAY Basic Seamanship - getting the dinghy away from the shore and back again without hitting anything on the way. FRIDAY Cruise Day - not a lot of wind so we sailed to the nearest ice-cream shop. Many thanks to the instructors Mike and Maggie Boreham, Janet Keeble, Caron Stuart and Bob Anderson, and to Niel Pembleton and Peter Coote who let us use their boats for the week to supplement those that course members and instructors managed to hide from the cadets. 8. SOLO NEWS I have hardly visited the Club in the two months since my last notes so have very little home news to report. However one event I did manage was the Solo Team Racing Day on 25th July. This was once again very well supported with eleven Solo helms present plus, in the afternoon, Steve McCulloch guesting to make up 4 teams of 3 boats. Each team raced the other 3 in turn and the result, determined on a league table basis, gave victory to Roger Smith, Steve Rutherford and Janet Keeble. Special thanks are due to Ray Ball who coxed the rescue boat for us all day, and to _ the Battle family who did more or less everything else including the race management, thus ensuring a very successful day. Latest and very welcome addition to our Club Fleet is Peter Collis who has procured Steve Keeble's boat. There has been quite a bit of activity away from base involving fleet members. Firstly back in June Dave Nixson and I attended a sail pumpers convention at Chew Valley Lake near Bristol. In mostly light and tricky winds we battled gamely but not very successfully to get some undisturbed wind in a fleet of 75 (Inland Nationals). I finished 36th overall with Dave 56th (write out 50 times - I must practise my pumping!) Three weeks later were the ‘real' Nationals at Harwich, which this year received the best Marconi turn-out ever of 6 boats, although the total entry was a disappointing one of only 50. Malcolm Gandy did well to reflect his usual club form in his first Nationals, the rest of us also ran. Ken Falcon won the event (again), and Marconi's results were as follows: Malcolm Gandy 23rd Dave Nixson 29th John Salmon 32nd Janet Keeble 41st Dave Payne 42nd Roger Smith 43rd Special mention deserved for Janet who battled gamely through some fairly heavy conditions despite some gear failure and for Dave Payne who put in a lot of overtime in the dinghy park as chief boat fixer. Even as you read this your Fleet representatives will be once more locked in combat,this time at the Worlds at Uitdam, Holland. Three important upcoming dates for your diaries are: 27th - 28th August: UpRiver YC Solo Open - a re-arranged Eastern Area Travellers Event. 10th - I1lth September: Marconi Cat & Mirror Open Meeting. The Solo Fleet are responsible for running this event so it is essential that we have a good turn-out for both days. Would fleet members please advise me as soon as possible as to their availability as I would like to assign specific tasks in advance. 17th - 18th September: Marconi Solo Open, which is also an Eastern Area Event. John Salmon, Billericay [redacted]

CADET SERIES 1988 il. Races 3 & 4 - the weatherman certainly had it in for the Cadets when he ( presumably a ‘he' ?) followed up the fairly stiff winds of Races 1 and 2 with even stronger winds of Force4-5 plus for Race 3. The Race Officer set a prudent course of Jack 'B' mooring buoy, F_,E ,OD_ (three times around), thus keeping the boats within a confined area within the lee of the Clubhouse and sea wall. Even then, the waves and winds proved difficult to contend with and, of the four starters, only one managed to finish the race. Richard Battle (Mirror), Nigel Leeder (Laser) and Lucy Boreham (Mirror) all retired but Damian Boreham (Mirror) completed the course which was shortened to one lap. With winds very soon Force 6 gusting, the Race Officer abandoned Race 4 without setting a course, not least because the Jack 'B' was, by now, busy assisting with the rescues at the Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championship at Stone. In fact, the Jack 'B' spent the rest of the afternoon on this task and it is understood that at one time in the afternoon some 12 dinghies were capsized, whilst Yachts and Yachting reported Force 7 winds and 8 broken masts. Races 5 & 6 - these races were held on 6 August at the end of the camping fortnight and, in contrast to the previous four races, the Race Officer had a hard job to find any wind at all. Race 5 was schedulled for 11.30 but was successively postponed to 13.00, 14.30, 15.00 and finally started at 16.00. in pretty light wind conditions. This race was won by Lucy Boreham (Mirror) with David Ball (S/H Mirror) 2nd and Ian Fletcher (420) 3rd; Stuart Golding (S/H Mirror) sailed well to finish 4th as did Michael Fletcher (Topper) 5th, Melanie Keeble (Mirror) 6th and Greg Hall (Mirror) 7th. In race 6, Stuart Golding (S/H Mirror) did even better scoring a good first win after having quite a tussle with David Ball (also S/H Mirror) which, since they were the same handicap boat, produced some close quarter racing which was interesting to watch from the Jack 'B'. However, Ian Fletcher (420) also sailed well to take 2nd place and push David into 3rd place on corrected time. Race 7 = was held on Sunday 7th August and, like all major sporting events, attracted a great deal of attention from spectators and media press, as well as having a full supporting programme in the form of the East Coast Piers Race (catamarans) and the Rum,Tub and Bung race for BJRC clubs. To be honest the ‘supporting races’ actually took precedence and Cadet race 7 had to be started at 14.00 as a quarter handicap pursuit race starting from the hard. Having scored a 3rd and 2nd in the previous two races, Ian Fletcher went yet another place better by scoring a very clear and convincing win in the 420 in quite windy conditions. Stuart Golding (Mirror) finished 2nd and Michael Fletcher (Topper) finished 3rd. The Ladies Cup - 1988 % For the second year running.the Ladies Cup was contested as a series of 3 races on a single day (ie. Sunday, 31 July) and some 14 lady helms signed on for the first race. The classes of boatS taking part were Stampede catamaran (1), Dart Catamaran (2), 420 dinghy (3), Wayfarer (1), Solo (1), Mirror (5) and Embassy (1). Our thanks to ihe Race Officer, Rescue Boat Driver and their assistants. Race 1 - a somewhat short race (KF1l) of about 14 miles taking approximately 20 minutes to complete. The 'sausage' Course meant that the race was sailed pretty well in the lee of the sea wall with a dead run to Breezy and a beat in the reverse direction. This course was a severe handicap to the catamarans and they finished well down the list, two retiring and the remaining Dart finishing 10th out of 11 finishers. However, the course and short duration did have the advantage that all boats sailed in similar conditions of wind and tide and this resulted in a close finish with only 101 seconds on corrected time covering the first 8 places. Those helms who took the inshore course up to Breezy (in order to cheat the incoming tide) found they had to gybe to reach the mark - a manoeuvre which appeared to worry their menfolk ashore more than it did the lady helms. However, the men needn't have worried - most of the ladies competing have helmed before but (as usual) give up the driving seat to the men for the 'serious' racing. Janet Keeble (Solo) kept very close inshore up to Breezy and won the race by 7 seconds from Lucy Boreham (Mirror) who, in turn, finished 11 seconds ahead of her mother Maggie Boreham (Mirror). Debbie Yorston (Mirror) must have thought she had got 3rd place ahead of Maggie because, as they both raced neck-and-neck for the finish line on a dead run, Debbie's bow was actually ahead of Maggie's bow - but Maggie was flying her spinnaker and presumably it was the spinnaker which reached the finish line first. If you'véqw read Eric Twiname's book on the sailing rules, he illustrates a similar situation in his definition of ‘finishing’. Race 2 - the problem with a single lap race is that you don't get a chance to correct the mistakes you made on the first (and only) lap. Thus, Race 2 with its course of KT2 was welcome news - not only for the two laps but also for being able to get away from the lee of the sea wall and sail some reaches. Certainly Rosie Duckmanton (Dart) found this course more attractive to sail and she came lst, 31 seconds ahead of Maggie Boreham (Mirror). Lucy Boreham finished 3rd (23 seconds behind Maggie) and Debbie Yorston sailed consistently to again finish 4th (12 seconds adrift of Lucy). Then followed the two Janets - Janet Battle (Mirror) in 5th place and Janet Keeble (Solo) in 6th place. Race 3 - this time the course was further extended to 3 laps (KT3) and Rosie Duckmanton again came Ist - this time by a rather bigger margin of 2 mins 20 secs ahead of Caron Stuart (420) and Charlotte Burck (Wayfarer) Caron and Charlotte always look as though they enjoy their sailing and both improved considerably on their previous results. An interesting (and significant) deadheat for 4th place between Irene Hellewell (420) and Janet Keeble (Solo) meant that they shared the combined points for 4th and 5th places, each having 45 points to their credit. The much slower Mirrors and Embassy found the extended course of 3 laps too much as they battled with the increasingly adverse ebb tide on the last lap. None managed to finish the course, the best being Lucy and Maggie who managed to struggle round No.1 but couldn't get round 'A' mark; none of the others managed to get around No.1 and all retired. Overall result - Rosie Duckmanton (Dart) was a very convincing winner with two lsts to count and the 10th position from the lst race as her discard. Lucy Boreham and Maggie Boreham both scored a 2nd, 3rd and Retired and so tied for second place overall, just 1/4 point ahead of Janet Keeble. Had Jdnet managed to beat Irene Hellewell for that 4th place then she would have come second by 1/4 point ; as it was, that extra + point made all the difference. It is not often that a dead-heat in the lower ranking places plays a real part in the overall result but, on this occassion, it made a difference. For those interested, TYRU Rule 11 applies. Full results listed elsewhere in this issue of Navigans. Sue Fletcher (Embassy) was probably the youngest and most inexperienced sailor taking part but, nevertheless, had a good sail and came ahead of her mother, Val Fletcher, who was sailing the family 420. Irene Hellewel] usually serves at the sharp end but, having swopped places with husband Mike Hellewell, no doubt enjoyed the experience and was pleased with her =4th with Janet Keeble. Pat Stuart (Mirror) had Adrian White as crew and one wonders if Adrian was tempted to stand on the gunwale, grab the boom and try to crew the boat 'sailboarder-wise'. Family Note - did this year's entry establish some sort of record ? Have you noticed the three sets of mother and daughter helms ? In order of mother/daughter, they were Val/Susan Fletcher, Pat/Caron Stuart and Maggie/Lucy Boreham . How about trying tobreak that record next year ? Report by Lillie of L ‘ ed Littfe Anite Parne*

COMMODORE'S NOTES It is some considerable time since I put thought to paper and produced a few more notes. My only excuse is that I never seem to be able to synchronise my times with your Editor's deadlines! I am making the effort now, however, and I hope you will think it worthwhile - although, perhaps, you may not like some of the views expressed. We have had a varied season so far wherein I can safely say that the lasting feature has been rain! That apart we have nevertheless had some very good times which, as far as I am concerned, were: New Members' Night, Regatta, Rochester Visit, Camping Fortnight & Barbecue, and the Fun Day. Sailing has been good (though personally you don't give your Commodore much opportunity to indulge!) and I had a very invigorating trip up to Walton Pier with John Hooper while we sampled the potential route of the inaugural Piers Race, which subsequently took place under nearly ideal conditions. If we can iron out just a few logistical problems we will have the makings of a very successful, I hope annual, event for the future. At this time of year we are very concerned with the arrangements for the running of the Club next year and are very anxious to find people prepared to contribute their time and effort towards helping their fellow members for one or more years on the various management tasks/committees - to make the same sacrifice that members before them have made and which has enabled them to do 'their thing'. This we are finding more and more difficult a task - particularly to find Ordinary Members. We must have Ordinary Members to fill certain posts to comply with the rules - but that aside , if it was not for the enthusiasm and sacrifice of our Associate Members, our Club would be in a very poor state and I wish to express my personal and the Club's gratitude for their efforts - and long may they continue. Committee work in its broadest sense is something which, frankly, anyone who puts their mind to it can contribute. So never say "I can't do it" because I don't believe you - you just need to decide that you would like to try, and I do not care if you are a new member this year or go back to the Fleetwind days. So please search your consciences and contact me or any Committee member with your offer of help or of the help of anyone too shy to put themselves forward. This is urgent - we must have names, particularly of Ordinary Members before the end of September. The Committee will be putting forward a change of rules at this year's AGM wherein the Main Committee will consist of persons elected to fill certain posts and will act in detail through Sub-Committees whilst representing their interest on the Main Committee. It was felt that this was worth trying rather than having a 'general' Committee Member and then at the first meeting of the new Committee, trying to dole out the various tasks. Do not worry if sameone is already doing a job you would not mind trying - a replacement designate is a very valuable commodity, so please, please, please, make contact. The Sailing Club has finally concluded a contribution deal with the MASC which gives us financial visibility up to 1992, so now what we want are ideas on how you_ want your Club to progress - a 5-Year Plan. Some ideas, like a full-time steward, will necessitate funding changes, perhaps partially offset by increased utilisation of our existing assets, e.g. more members, more activities/functions, longer season, etc. More working volunteers will, however, inevitably help to maintain existing or reduce increased costs. CATAMARAN NEWS The event looming largest in the memory during last morth must, of course, be the Piers Race. The event will, no doubt, be well chronicled by other correspondents but we have some comments of our own. It is reported that those left behind were somewhat disappointed at the end, when, joyously greeting the returning sailors, they were met with deflated, perhaps disinterested, attitudes. It should be remembered here that the spectators saw two peaks of frenzied activity and in between nothing was happening. The sailors themselves had been on the water for around eight hours, and when returning to dry land the sensation of getting a sore backside off the hard deck led to relief rather than elation. So we apologise for not seeming to appreciate your support. For my own part the lasting impressions of the race are how long it seemed to take from Clacton to Walton on the way out. There are wide spaces of open water out there. With other boats only visible on the horizon it was hard to suppress feelings of fragility and insecurity, particularly as the last rescue boat seen was at Bradwell. This was not helped when, at the turning mark, the sea-fret descended and a Visibility was severely reduced. For all that, it was a great day and all seemed to have enjoyed it, courtesy of the weather. I won't attempt to re - thank all those helpers who have already received their thanks. MIRROR FLEET NEWS. I am afraid I've been very lazy about writing for Navigans this year - somehow the time flies by and, before you know it, another navigans dead-line has passed by. As you read this, the Summer Points Series will probably have been completed and we can look forward to the Autumn Points Series before finally putting the boats to bed in mid-October. Congratulations to Mike and Janet Battle on winning the Mirror Class in the Regatta - it was quite windy at times so I am told. I wouldn't really know because I must confess that we were on a canal boat holiday with another family and, I must say, it was one of the nicest, most restful and most peaceful holidays I have ever spent. Congratulations to Damian and Katie for winning the Spring Points Series; hard luck to Lucy and Jenny for coming 2nd but getting no prizes - the Mirror Class was the only one which didn't manage an average of 4 entries for the series and so lst place prize only was awarded. The camping fortnight (inclusive of Cadet Week) was, aS usual, very enjoyable and equally most successfu 1. This was the 7th (or was it the 8th) Cadet 'Week' we've attended and all have been well-worth the effort This year 'the effort' not only covered teaching sailing to the very young, but also the somewhat older members who, in their spare time, carry out the duties of being parents to the Cadets. Although the lst week was a bit windy at times, the weatherman was kind to us for the following Cadet Week with its programme of sailing instruction. The wind was just enough to sail pleasantly, the sun hot enough to give us a tan and the number of people enough to keep things lively. Even our ‘traditional' thunder- storm (yes - we usually have one at night) was a very muted affair and hardly anyone noticed the rather weak lightning and the low-level growl of thunder which followed it. . More significantly for cadet Week was the large number of Mirrors which took to the water - there must have been 12 -15 sailing .. At one time, as I looked towards Osea Pier, there seemed to be so many Mirrors sailing there thatI thought Maylandsea Bay must have been holding an open meeting but not at all - it was our members having a fine time sailing on the mighty river Blackwater. The point is, if you can get your boat on the water every day for the ‘once a year’ week of sailing tuition, it seems apity not to consolidate what you've learned by taking part in the Sunday racing programme. So don't pack your Mirror away until next year's Cadet Week - keep it sailing and join in the Sunday racing. The club's Mirror 'open' event is to be held on 10/11 September. This is an event that definetely needs your active participation and it's worth having a go. We usually only get a few visitors from local clubs so you are not going to find too many Mirrors buzzing around. In fact, most will be the same people you sailed with during cadet Week. DON'T FORGET - OQUR MIRROR OPEN NEEDS YOU 10/11 SEPTEMBER Happy sailing _ Maggie Boreham (Honorary Scribe to the Mirror Fleet) Note: The above article was intended for September Navigans, but it just missed the bus!

16. Mona's Cup 1988 e=. This year's Mona's Cup was rather sparsely populated with entries, only 6 boats taking part compared to 16 in 1987 and 26 in 1986. The Mona's Cup is an ‘all-in' race (ie. cruiser and dinghy) and, for this reason, the 'long line start' is used. The 'long line start’ is indicated by the letter 'L' after the course code letters and means that you must start between '‘'D' mark and No.1 but in line with the triangle on the race box and the mete pole . Those with long memories might recall that in the 1986 race some 21 out of the 26 entries were disqualified because they started between the mete and 'D' mark; this year only one boat made this mistake. : Of the 6 starters, 4 were catamarans and 2 were Mirrors, thus the entries represented the very opposite ends of the ‘speed spectrum'. In fact, it was reminiscent of the Hare and the Tortoise fable and could well have been a re-enactment since Mirrors often do quite well in this race. The wind was Force 4/5 (forecast rising to 6), the watex was rough and there were plenty of ‘white horse' to be seen off Osea. Mike Battle andDerekHolroyd (Mirror) found their weight both an advantage (keeping the boat flat) and disadvantage (slower speed, no spinnaker) whilst similarly Damian Boreham and Jenny Ball (Mirror) found themselves having difficulty in keeping the boat upright and consequently they shipped water up to the gunwales (without capsizing) and had to 'sail' into the shelter of the smoother water by Osea Pier in order to bail out. Their lightweight advantage was boat speed - plus spinnaker. The catamarans had a fine old time and they didn't take too long to get up to Heybridge and back. The finish leg was to round Breezy to starboard and finish into the wind between 'D' mark and the mete. Graham Baker showed distinct signs of not being able to find Breezy and, in the race box, we were taking bets on whether he would (a) sail to Stone (b) round Breezy to port or (c) capsize. However, he did none of these things and finished correctly having, as always, thoroughly enjoyed his sail (this time crewed by Dave Onyons). Rob Stahl was the unfortunate cat disqualified for incorrecTM start and it seemed a shame to have to deprive him of a finishing 'hoot' having sailed all the way up the river and back again. However, he was 'timed in' and would have finished third. Steve Keeble Shows every sign of mastering the techniques of sailing his Hurricane every time he goes out and he certainly looked as though he was enjoying himself, as was his crew Dave Payne. Trevor Milton found the going very much to his liking and won the race; if he can tell me the name of his crew then he/she will get a 'credit' in the Mug's Mug League Table. CADETS - BRADWELL FIELD STUDIES & SAILING CENTRE My daughter Jenny and Lucy (Boreham) went to the Bradwell Sailing Centre for a week in August with the aim of achieving their RYA National Dinghy Certificate Level 5 to top up on their qualifications earned with Derek Hall's excellent tuition of our Cadets over recent years. They succeeded in gaining their Level 5 certificate, and enjoyed their week so much that they intend going back again next year if possible. Ir case there are other Members who might be interested in their Cadets trying this course I have typed out below all the relevant information on what the Centre offers, taken from its own literature. Jenry's one week residential course cost £60 which we considered very reasonable for 6 full days at the Centre - from llam Monday till 2pm the following Sunday (though Jenny and Lucy did leave at 10am to hurry back to the Club to take part in a vital Cadet Race! The Centre is situated beside the Creek at Bradwell Waterside on the River Blackwater. There is a main residential and administrative building, boat yards, workshops and a laboratory for field studies. The Centre can house 40 studerts plus six accompanying staff. Accommodation is in centrally heated rooms with full toilet, shower and drying facilities. There is also a lounge, dining/lecture room, ard a recreation room with table tennis and juke box. The meals are cooked by permanent catering staff but the students are required to assist ir other domestic duties. All equipment, including protective clothing for the various specialised activities, is provided by the Centre. (Ed's note: You'd need to take along your own wet suit if you usually wear one for dinghy sailing, they are provided by the Centre for those doing the Boardsailing Course orly.) SAILING Instructior is given in Toppers, Yachting World Day Boats, Oysters, Wayfarers, 505's and Bradwell 22's. Teams of experienced helmsmen and instructors enable complete novices to receive expert tuition. A safety boat is always in attendance. The Centre also has a 26' auxiliary sloop, in which all off-shore sailing, coastal and foreign cruising is done. Basic equipment for courses in seamanship, navigation and meteorology, covering the theory of the RYA/NSSA Proficiency and Coaching Scheme is also offered. The Centre is recognised as a Royal Yachting Association/National Schools Sailing Association Examination Centre. CANOEING instruction is given in a variety of single-seater kayaks. Expeditions by canoe can be arranged on request. CAMPING: Sailing and canoeing camping expeditions are also arranged, using modern lightweight camping equipment and craft suitable for sleeping aboard. All the necessary equipment is supplied. BOARD SAILING. The Centre is equipped with a variety of boards, also with junior and intermediate rigs for the beginner. ELIGIBILITY AND SAFETY REGULATIONS Courses at the Centre are open to all aged 13 and above. tudents who are candidates for a sailing or canoeing course must be able to swim 50 metres in light clothing. All persons using the Centre must abide by the Education Committee's safety regulations and accept the guidance of the Warden and his staff during the course. Contd.cee

CATAMARAN NEWS Event of the morth this time goes to the Catamaran Open held on the weekerd of lOth/llth September. An overall entry of 23 Cats. looks encouraging urtil it is realised that 14 of them are Club entries. Our Cat men must be complimented on this turnout whilst bemoaning the lack of visitors in any numbers. The weather was not kind to us over this weekend, bursts of reasonable wind strengt always quickly abating to nothing at all for long periods. This weather of course did nothing at all to assist the administration of the event which was being run by our Solo colleagues and the courses can only be described as interesting. Thank you, Solos, for a job well done in difficult circumstances. Results as follows: First: Stampede 63 Trevor Milton Second: Dart 4469 D. Lloyd (Stokes Bay) Third: Tornado 290 John Nickalls An interesting innovation was the donation of a new trophy for Marconi Sailors participating in this event by Steve and Janet Keeble, entitled the "Old Codger's" Shield. Its concept is brilliant, Steve, quite the best thing you've done this year. Modesty prevents me from publishing the names of the first winners but carn I just add that if anyone knows of a 72-year-old trapeze artist, please put them ir touch with me. THE MARCONI CATAMARAN OPEN MEETING - 10/11 SEPTEMBER (through the eye of the hurricane) (This is not meant to be an unbiased view of the evert, as from on the water it is impossible to see all of the action throughout the fleet.) Saturday dawned bright with a force 2 wind blowing from the West. Owing to confusion over first race start times the meeting was reduced from 4 races to 3, but to keep the troops happy Ron Greygoose, our intrepid Race Officer, set a practice race up to No.8 Buoy. The race got under way after postponed start, and Janet (my better half who was crewing in place of Dave) and I had an excellent view of the rest of the Fleet streaming from us towards the first mark. By the time we got to No.2 we were in the lead and pulling away from the Fleet. The run back from No.8 to No.1 was fairly uneventful except that the wind was gradually fading. A quick reach to C and back “brought us into contact with Paul Metcalfe who was just rounding No.1 on his way to C. We reached across to round A only to find that the wind had died completely and we were forced to slowly tack up the shore by the Club. As we reached the middle of the Hard, a voice cried out 'race abandoned!' and there on the Club flagpole was a limp ‘abandon' flag. At least we didn't have far to go to get ashore. Paul Metcalfe crept ashore about 15 minutes later ard most other boats drifted in on the falling tide. After a leisurely lunch we dragged ourselves onto the water for the second race. Again the wind was very fickle and we made one of our yet to be forgotten lousy starts. John Nickalls_ shot straight into the lead. He started to cross the river towards the Club but the wind died and he tacked to the Osea_ shore. We were following a similar course but the wind held up and we made it across. We were accompanied by two Darts and the three of us spent the next ten minutes trying to get around the corner. The Fleet was now divided into two halves. One on the Osea shore and one in the bay. The wind made the race a lottery as it varied from force nil to force 2 and boats ten yards apart could experience the extremes. We swapped places with our little group, losing out by our slow tacking. A Dart led the way round No.2 eTMclosely followed by John Nickalls and Caroline. Two more Darts followed and then us, closely followed by another Dart. As we drifted with no wind towards No.1 we watched Trevor Milton and Tom _ sail serenely up and round No. 2 with their own personal breeze. They must have gained 600 yards on the leading boats and then continued on towards the leading group containing John and the first 3 Darts. The rest of us? We still had no wind, just tide. Rounding No.1 and heading for C the leading group were in line astern. The wind was very localised with both Trevor and I managing to lift hulls at some point whilst others were just coasting slowly towards the mark. The shallow water forced me _ to bear away as the rudders were grunching on the bottom. This forced me to put in a tack at C and the yellow hulled Stampede shot past on his own personal gust. From C to B was again a procession and then followed the usual short tacking duel to the Club finish line. Although we overhauled the yellow Stampede, it was a race in which the Darts took the honours. CONT. «<<

10. Cat Open contd. Sunday was a lot better with the wind blowing 3 gusting 5. After a much delayed start, the Fleet headed to No.2. This was our most disastrous start, with me actually falling off the boat! John and Trevor made their usual good start with Rob and Matthew not too far behind. We had Graham Baker and Dave Onyons for company as we set off to catch the rest. By the time we got to No.2 we had passed everybody except John, Trevor and the leading 2 Darts. Mike Duckmanton and Rosie were trying to make life difficult by trying to catch us on a port/starboard meeting. At No.8 just John and Trevor were ahead. JI do wish Johr would get a more colourful sail as it is almost impossible to pick him out from a distance, and a distance is about the closest we ever got! Downwind to No.1 we chose a different route from Trevor. We were behind him and had nothing to lose. It paid off as we were first to Osea pier, where we promptly found @ hole in the wind. John and Caroline were well on their way to the E mark and the end of the first lap as we crossed them when tacking between No.1 and C. "They will Finish after one lap," we thought. We had been racing about 90 minutes and the Sparks were a long way back. But no! There was John and Caroline goirg around again! By now the river was filled with boats and as we headed for No.2 we thought we could see the Committee Boat. But alas no. As we came up towards No.2 we found ourselves slightly to windward of an echelon of cruisers. We were all on starboard and in front were 2 Windsurfers crossing on port. "Starboard!" we cried as one. "Starboard!" again. No reaction from the Windsurfers. "Starboard!" we cried. - "You don't own the river!" came the reply. They were very lucky, as a Hurricane is 8ft wide and they must have been $8ft 6ins apart. The cruisers were all trying to take evasive action as well, but we were clear so we left them to have an accident with some other unfortunate boat owner. The rest of the race was uneventful, except that as we passed Osea pier on the way back, there were Sparks still heading for No.2. Janet and I were pleased to finish ahead of Trevor although he beat us on handicap (28 seconds in 3 hours). Race 4 was a short affair and after our usual bad start we did not see the leaders at all. We spent the first part of the race trying to get through Peter Flook's dirty wind and the second part catching and passing Tim Dieu de Bellefontaine and _ the yellow hulled Stampede. Although we crossed the line ahead, they murdered us on handicap. JI understand that Trevor beat John across the line by 1 second, which gave Trevor and Tom the meeting overall. John and Caroline finished 3rd overall with Janet and me 5th. Typical, they only had prizes for the first 4! The highlight of the presentation was the award of the 'Old Codger' trophy to Peter Flook. It couldn't have happened to an older (and nicer) man! Thanks must go to the Solo fleet for running the event and to the people who manned the Galley and Bar, and we look forward to returning the compliment with a couple of 3-hour races in a force 5 wind. Steeve Keeble (fly by wire) P.S. I understand that those little wooden wash tubs with the red flannels on a broom pole were also racing. Did anybody see them?

MARCONI SAILING CLUB - 1988 A.G.M. Commodore's Report Fellow members - friends - another year has gone by since I last gave you my report. Little did I know then what a traumatic year it was going to turn out to be both personally and Clubwise. Over the past year we have had quite an eventful time which started with the retirment of Claude Emerson to some well earned rest in the middle of England. This resulted in two abortive attempts to recruit a single replacement, with us finally finding two people to share the job viz: Dave and Darren, with all its attendant difficulties in effective control and we are back to one again now! For some time past now, members have been increasingly suggesting that the load of work, or rather chores, falling on their shoulders was becoming unacceptable and as a result we asked the MASC to investigate the possibility of being able to offer a full-time steward accomodation. As a result, planning permission for a house was sought - rejected - and is now on appeal. Whether, if the appeal is successful, the house is ever built will depend entirely on us the members because the cost will not be insignificant. The only help against this will be increased membership and -~if you remember, this was one of my messages to you last year - each of you recruit one member and our financial worries sink into the background. As Pat will no doubt be telling you, the recruitment drive was beginning to show some success, but we do need more. Over the years I have always been adamant and vehement that our Club was successful because the members belonged and they belonged by being involved and were involved by supporting the essence and spirit of self help. This support must continue and we will remain successful - BUT I think the time has now come, because of our size, when we must seriously consider removing the burden of chores from our members by having a full time steward. If you agree then give your new Commodore your support by recruiting one more, at least, new member each by Easter. Remember though, I said CHORES - not Working Parties - you are and will continue to be essertial work units for these belonging activities! We have made a start in trying to drain the Cruiser Park - but it obviously still needs some more work done on it - but at the end of the day I think we will have to spend a great deal of money and have it done properly. um There were for me three highlights this year. First we had a Regatta which, with Malcolm's energetic input should continue to improve over the years especially if we build on the new conditions and procedures we introduced this year. Second, I actually managed to spend the whole of the camping fortnight at Stansgate which I found very instructive and enjoyable despite never having a minute to myself. z think a lot more members should consider attending this camp. Third we had an inaugural Piers Race which, thanks to the clemency of the weather, allowed us to see and learn our mistakes without getting into a serious sailing incident. Long may it continue and become the prestigious East Coast Race it deserves to be. You will note from the papers already issued to you that your Committee has managed, I think for the first time in several years, to announce Committee nominations for all positions. This is excellent and it is essential that everyone will offer their services from time to time without being specifically asked. In particular your committee must have visibility of ordinary members who will be prepared to ‘do their bit' So do not be bashful, drop broad hints to Officers and Committee about what you may like to do. You will note that your President, Jack Pateman, is relinquishing his post and that we have been very lucky in securing the services of Martin Jay for this position. Our grateful thanks to Mr Pateman for all he has done for us in the past and a rousing welcome to Mr Jay for taking on the mantle. One note I had hoped I should not have had to announce to you. We have still failed

4. to reach a final agreement with the General Committee of he M.A.S.C. for the use of the assets. On two occasions in the past 9 months we thought we had an agreement only to find the General Committee would not ratify the plan. We were trying right up to Friday evening to come to some compromise. In this respect Gerry Wignall has worked very hard to arrive at a settlement and we have found him helpful and constructive. It is now obvious we must have some representation on the General Committee, and to this end, John Weedon offered himself for co-option during the summer, but now faces an election this coming week. WE MUST ENSURE JOHN IS ELECTED so please every ordinary member of the Club make the effort to go to the M.A.S.C. to vote. Voting is all week, so do take your MASC membership card, and take the few minutes it needs. You will have up to seven votes to cast, but you need only cast one for John. We are on the last legs of the negotiated compromise and I think that if we had not been up against an election next week we may well have had a settlement for a five-year term with an extension of two years if a new five-year term had not been agreed by the end of the fifth year. But in case of difficulty Niel and I intend to brief Mr Jay in the next week or so. What we can say is that the total figure is known to within a few hundred and this should enable us to formulate reasonably accurate budgets. I have kept you all long enough but I cannot conclude without paying unstinting tribute to the other Officers, Committee and Members for the wholehearted support I have enjoyed over the past two years as your Commodore. And finally, if I may turn to the personal trauma I alluded to at the beginning of this report. It is not unique to me - there are many others here today who have suffered; are now suffering; and unfortunately still others who don't know it, like me last year, yet to suffer. I mean of course the indignity of redundancy or redeploy ment. I mention this not to raise any oohs and aahs but to try and show you all the strength and support our Club - or which should more appropriately be called our Community - can afford to its members. The true empathy which emanates from its corporate being and which can be so effective in combating depression is priceless -guard it well -it is what makes our Club GREAT. Continue to show my successor and all his successors the same support you have shown me and you will - No, we will - have a still greater Club. I hope my family will be able to remain members for many years to come and if we can escape from Lincoln, the Sims' tent will be with you for Regatta and Camping fortnight. Robbie Sims, Retiring Commodore, A.G.M. 1988 Sailing Secretary's Report to A.G.M. ed The year started with the RNLI rowing race at Maldon, then Sailboat '88 which has attracted several good members to the Club. Events The Club has run two major events this year, both of which have been a success. I refer to the Regatta, re-introduced as a favourite local event after a break of 2 years, due to hard work and perseverance of Malcolm Stuart. Secondly the Cat fleet invented the East Coast Piers Race and that looks like being another regular. Cruisin As a dinghy sailor, one does not get too much feel for what is going on in the Cruiser world but I get the impression that this year has not seen so many ‘going foreign'. Am I wrong? Let us see your log in Navigans and win the Mamgu Trophy - also open to dinghy sailors. Cruiser Fleet have been very supportive of the dinghy open meetings by providing Committee Boats, back-up rescue services etc. Disappointing - the Barnacle Points was not run this year. Dinghy Sailing Another increase in the number of entries to Club events - a lot of that due to the Cat Fleet who also provide a significant input to the Club

De activities generally. Solos continue to have highest average entry despite attempts by Cats to decimate the Fleet if a good number of boats get on the water. Good to see Handicap up this year. Sailboards have started racing with a Summer and Autumn points series and they are another group who contribute to the running of the Club. Open Meetings Solo, Cat, 420 and Mirror well supported, others not. It does cost the Club money to run these events so we must work hard to get 12+ entry or not hold them. Team Racing In a word abysmal - we lost the Boothby Cup (again), the Rochester visit and made no impression on the MBYC Challenge Cup. Must do better next year. Representation Cat fleet and Solos, plus 420 of the Cunningham's have been travelling. Robin Smith puts MSC's name in Yachts & Yachting regularly. Malcolm Gandy was a creditable 23rd in Nationals at Harwich. Overall it must be considered a successful year with more boats on the water, more big events and more enjoyment of Sailing. Finally having done the job for 2% years I shall miss it - both good and bad. SOLO NEWS At the end of another successful sailing season I would like, on behalf of the Solo Fleet, to express my appreciation to Dave Onyons and the other Rescue Boat Drivers for the excellent support provided for the racing this season. Our thanks also go to those members of other Fleets who supported our racing programme with Race Officer and other duties. The Fleet AGM took place at MASC on October 12th and I will summarise a few of the key decisions taken here: 1. The Fleet would support the Eastern Region's attempt to field a team for the Inter- Region Championship at Littleton S.C. on 6th November, even though this clashed with the Club AGM. For this and other reasons the Fleet felt that it would be more appropriate to hold the AGM at MASC midweek. 2. The provisional 1989 sailing programme was found to be generally acceptable although it was felt that pursuit-type racing on a Sunday should be kept to a minimum. 3. More Sunday evening barvecues would be organised in 1989 - Ron Greygoose to arrange. 4. John Salmon agreed to continue as Fleet Captain for a third and final year. Dave Nixson agreed to continue as Vice-Captain. ew 5. The September 1989 Solo Open meeting should be a single day event (on a Sunday) with three races in a day. In order to achieve the tight timing of such a programme it was felt that the meeting should be for one Fleet only. 6. John Salmon (Fleet Captain) and Malcolm Gandy (Spring Points Series Winner) were charged with deciding who should receive the Frank Savill Trophy which is awarded each year to the Fleet Member showing most improvement. The 1988 winner is Janet Keeble. 7. The January Solo Supper should be repeated, preferably at the Cross Keys again - Pat Stuart agreed to investigate. 8. A provisional date of April 8th was fixed for a repeat of the Solo Fleet Dinner Party at Stansgate but this event will only be held if someone volunteers to organise it. Any Fleet member who would like to take this on should let me know. The final Eastern Area Open Meeting of the season took place at Fishers Green on 2nd October with the usual minimal breeze. The event was won comfortably by Joly, Reece from Broadwater SC. Seven MSC helms competed, gaining finishing positions of: 2nd John Salmon, 3rd Ron Greygoose, 5th Malcolm Gandy, 6th Dave Nixson, 8th Roger Smith, 10th Janet Keeble, 14th Colin Willsmore. This left Alan Burrell of Half Way YC as Eastern Area Champion with MSC helms filling the next five places in the order: Malcolm Gandy, John Salmon, Ron Greygoose, Dave Nixson, Roger Smith. Pembleton, Chelmsford [redacted] or Clubhouse Secretary, C. Davies, Chelmsford [redacted], if you have a problem. MIRROR NEWS The Mirror Fleet AGM was held at MASC on Friday 11th November. 1. Mike Battle agreed to continue as Fleet Captain for one more year only, with Debbie e~Yorston as assistant, Debbie to take over as Fleet Captain at the end of the year. 2. To encourage a larger turnout for Mirror Racing, it was suggested that a Mirror Teach-in would be held in the summer - less confident sailors to be put in with experienced ones to help them improve their skills and learn about racing. Also it was proposed that advanced sailors could be shown tuning of their boats for best performance. 3. Mike Battle said he would like to put up a Prize for the lst ‘Beginner Cadet' over the line in the Mirror Open to encourage Cadets to enter the race who have not done so in the past as they felt they had no chance of winning the race. It was also suggested that the Mirror Open should be a series of 3 races on one day, instead of over a whole weekend. 4. It was decided that the Cadet Races should no longer be held on Saturdays because this can be less convenient and makes the Cadet Series seem not as important as that of other Classes - which of course is not true! It is intended that on each of two Sundays there would be 3 Cadet races, with the rest of the Series fitted in as normal. On these two Sundays it was proposed that Pursuit Races would be held for the other meTMFleets. It was also hoped that a Mirror Fleet Barbecue be held after sailing on these two Sundays and that the Mirror fleet might hold one or two other social activities. 5. The Fun Day during Camping Fortnight was a success and it was hoped it would be an annual event. The Club's Regatta had also been a great success though Mirror involvement was disappointing and it was hoped that more would take part in the future. Finally, it was generally accepted that 1988 had been quite a good year, but next year we are going to boost our numbers and get more of those sixty-or-more Mirrors sitting in the park out on the water! LOWESTOFT COLLEGE - SURVIVAL COURSE FOR SMALL BOAT USERS This is a ome day basic Sea Survival course designed for the small boat user. Instruction is divided into two main Parts: a) Theory and demonstration of raft and equipment in classroom, Survival problems and solutions! - by Practical wet drills with liferaft and jackets. The course is based on the inflatable liferaft, but it also covers aspects where a liferaft may not be available. The actions required at any particular stage during an incident are dealt with so that threats to life are minimised. Courses are normally held at Lowestoft College where there are purpose facilities, including a heated training tank and a wide selection of survival equipment. The course starts at 0900 hrs and finishes at 1700 hrs with a lunch break of about an hour. A lounge area is available for use at coffee and lunch breaks, and coffee machines are on site. HELMSMAN OF THE YEAR FINAL saturday 8th October saw the top Helmsmen from the four major fleets in the Club assemble at Stansgate for the ‘High Noon' of the season to decide the Marconi Sailing Club Helmsman of the Year 1988. Damian Boreham represented the Mirror Fleet, Mike Boreham was to have represented the Handicap Fleet but pulled out to be subst ituted by Mark Savill, Malcolm Gandy was the Solo Fleet representative and John Nickalls from the Catamarans. The contestants are the helms who achieve the most consistent performance throughout the seasor: up to the end of September. Again this year the Sailing Sub-committee agreed to sail the Final in Lasers, arranged that each helm has a sail in each boat. Boats were provided by Mark Savill, Mark Strong, Derek Webb and Derek Holroyd. Zz would like to thank the owners on behalf of the Club and the Contestants for making the ever:t possible. October 8th saw a Force 4-5 Westerly making life difficult. All except Malcolm Gandy had ar involuntary swim to freshen themselves up and John Nickalls enjoyed it so much he kept going back for more. Either that or he was looking for the other hull! Malcolm and Mark had a close race with Mark getting line honours and Damian battling mtoa gallant 3rd. At this point, much to the disgust of the Race Officer, the combatants decided that gardening was much more fun on such a day and downed tools to come back another day. Needless to say Murphy's Law applied and as soon as the boats were put away the wind dropped to a benign 3. So episode 2 of this mind-warping susperse thriller was staged on 22nd October wher the weather was Southerly 1-2 at most. Thanks to Graham Baker, Colin Willsmore and Debbie Yorston for rescue and race-box duties. John Nickalls jetted in from the States to participate but obviously had difficulty in adjusting to the time zone. Race 2 was easily won by Damiar and we all thought that his skill combined with the lighter weather would make it his day. All apart from Mark Savill who won Race 3, which was a particularly well contested race. 5. BRADWELL SAILING CENTRE Lucu (Boreham) and I spent a week at Bradwell Sailing Centre where we were trained and tested for our Level 5 (this now replaces Seamanship 2). However, we got a fun holiday out of it as well which you can see in the following write-up of our week there. MONDAY We arrived at the School about 10.45am having had some trouble finding the entrance. Lucy had arrived already and had managed to get hold of a room for just two. All the other dormitories in the girl's section were for four people and these were mainly taken up by the Basildon Swimming Club who were there on their week off from training At about 11.30 we all met in the TV room where the warden told us about the school and the rules about meals and the fact that the girls' rooms were out of bounds to the boys and vice versa! In the afternoon we all went out for a sail with the instructors in Wayfarers and Oysters. There was a strong breeze at first and we all sailed to Stone where the wind conveniently dropped totally, leaving us all to drift (or row) back with the tide. seTUESDAY Breakfast was at 8.15 and so by 9.30 we were all down at the boat-yard across the road to get our gear. Lucy and I were put in a Dayboat and left to get on with rigging a boat we'd never even heard of before, let alone sailed in. All the dinghies there are moored up on the water making rigging quite difficult as you have restricted space. Luckily, two boys who were also doing their Level 5 were on the next Dayboat and they had sailed in it the day before. This meant they would be able to tell us what to do if we could not work it out. However we did not have too much trouble and the only questions asked came from the bovs wanting to know how come we had ended up on the best Dayboat and why had they got stuck in the one that was the worst? There was barely any wind so we rowed out of the creek and drifted along with about four other boats. (Most of the Swimming Club had gone in the Toppers, canoes and sail boards.) We drifted about a bit and then had lunch after which a sea breeze came up and we sailed all the way out to sea just past Bench Head and back agair: in about a Force 4. WEDNESDAY Today was when Lucy and I really took our Test. We went through everything; sailing without a rudder (not as hard as it sounds), sailing without a centreboard, @sailing a triangular course, man-overboard drill, hove-to and sailing backwards. We managed everything except sailing backwards which we just could not master. What made it harder was that the sail has to be pushed out against the wind and as the wind had increased from a steady Force 4 to a strong 5 it became almost impossible to hold the sail out against the force of the wind. However we completed the other tasks without difficulty and with much more success than the two boys in the other Dayboat! All the people involved in the Level 5 testing had lunch (the others in the Toppers had eaten ages ago!) and we set off again to practise coming alongside and sailing a tight circle around the rescue boat. Both Lucy and I were now very cold and tired having fought the elements all day, and the boys were too. We were all sent ashore to swap round (Lucy and I were supposed to be showing the boys how to sail without a rudder, however the wind was too strong) and we just sailed all the way out towards sea, turned round and came back again. As we were nearing the entrance to the creek I heard several voices calling my name and I saw our very own Jack B motoring past with my family aboard and a couple of my brother's friends as well! I though they had come all the way just to see me but I was wrong, they had come to fetch 'A' mark after it had wandered downriver and been towed for safe keeping into Bradwell Marina. We moored up and went ashore very tired after a long day. CONTG :0::«:«

-..- Bradwell continued... THURSDAY The boys had been told, much to their relief, that they were not good enough, so now it was just Lucy and I doing the Level 5. We had spent all the previous evening poring over a chart of the river, phoning up Lucy's parents for the weather forecast and tides, and asking the advice of one of the instructors, working out where we would go for a day's cruise. We had worked it all out as a part of the Level 5 and set out, with one of the adults from the swimming group as ballast, in a Wayfarer expecting to have to actually go on the cruise, but we did not have to in the end which was a relief! During the morning we finally mastered sailing backwards as it was only a Force 3 breeze. By this time Lucy and I were sick of dinghy sailing, we both wanted to go in the Toppers as everyone else was really enjoying themselves so we were pleased when we were told that we could go in the Toppers in the afternoon. During lunch there waS a massive shaving-foam fight where everybody, including the instructors, got totally covered! After we had washed ourselves off in the water (which incidentally is not warm at all, despite the rumours!) we sailed about in the Toppers. The wind had steadily increased and was now a Force 4 - 5. This and the fact that there were not enough Toppers to go round meant that there were two people to each Topper. Everyone was capsizingall.round but Lucy and I stayed upright without much difficulty. That is until my helm (i.e. Lucy) slammed the tiller across too hard when tacking and we went straight into irons. I am not sure quite what happenec yy (probably something my helm did) but the next thing I knew was that I was floundering in the freezing water while my helm had struggled over the top in an attempt at a dry capsize. However, while standing in triumph on the daggerboard it bent under her weight and she slipped off and fell into the water which saved me the job of pushing her in! By now we were thoroughly enjoying ourselves and were not too happy when everyone was told to come in because it was too windy. Reluctantly everyone packed up the Toppers which were towed back and we all walked back along the sea wali, back to a nice Silower. FRIDAY We woke up to what seemed a howling gale on Friday morning. The forecast was for a strong Force 6-7 and there was a gale warning until Sunday evening. On days like this the Bradwell 22s are used and so all of us rowed out and rigged these massive dinghies. As the name tells you they are 22' long and are built at the School's boat yard across the road from the school itself. They have the foredeck of a Wayfarer, a huge steel centreplate and four sails (two jibs, a mainsail and a mizzen), and are very sturdy and strong. Lucy and I ended up doing most of the rigging as the Instructor decided thar if we were good enough for Level 5 then we should do all the work. We motored OUw - each Bradwell 22 has am outboard engine for emergencies - and then began the struggle down towards Osea. In all my time on the river I do not think I have seen anything like it. The waves were enormous, there was spray everywhere and the wind was howling fiercely. The wind was so strong that even the Bradwell 22's were heeling (gasp!) and the Instructor heartened us by saying that one had even capsized before (double gasp! ) Apparently it took three people oan the centreplate as well as two on the skeg to stop it from turning turtle!!! Our destination was to be Osea Island, and although we enjoyed it at first, by the time we had been thrown about, continually soaked to the skin by the spray and been out in the freezing wind for ten minutes, we were all ready to go back. However, the powers-that-be in the nice warm cabin of the safety boat, with their cups of coffee, had other ideas! Tacking was an awkward affair. The centreboard case is just below waist height so getting over it was extremely difficult, and trying to control a flapping jib that was determined to catch itself on the other jib, the mast fittings and everything CON EG + 35.6

..-Bradwell continued... ee else, was almost impossible. In the end we worked out a system of two people either side of the centreboard case (one for each jib), and when we went about we just unwound the jib sheet from its bollard and handed it to the person on the other side. It got so windy that in the end all three boats took down their mainsails, (another job for Lucy and me) and just relied on the other three sails. When we got as far as Stone we beached, because our safety boat had spotted someone in trouble. Just off Osea we could see a dinghy on its side (hardly surprising) and our safety boat spent a good half an hour before they had even got the boat upright, and it took a long time then to tow it back. These two totally mad people had set out from Stone in this wind, which personally I thought rather stupid because if we had not been there, no-one would have been there to help them out and they could have ended up a lot worse than just spending a long while in the freezing water. Nobody could face turning out again, even for the short part of the trip just across to Osea as we had all slowly frozen up just sitting there cold and wet waiting for the safety boat to bring our lunches across. After lunch we back on a broad sailed reach. By now the sun had come out and because the wind was us, we all felt behind a lot warmer and everyone fell asleep, including the Instructor, apart from the four of us who were watching the jibs and the poor boy who got lumbered with helming. I do not think that I have ever enjoyed a hot shower as much as I did that day and wmI hope I do not get as cold as that ever again! SATURDAY As everyone had been so cold on Friday and the weather was still rough it was decided that we take the motor boats and go across to West Mersea. The ex-Liverpool class Lifeboat had broken down (sob!) so we all piled into three motor boats - one similar to Jack B but smaller; one similar to the work boat but bigger; and another that was a cross between the two. However the boat similar to Jack B broke down outside the Power Station which meant that those on board crammed into the other two boats which were already well loaded. We went up the river to West Mersea and were just working out where to moor up along the slipway when we ran aground on it. Local teenagers had struck up a good trade ferrying people from the shore to their Cruisers in huge tubs with engines and one had just zipped before us into our selected space and as we turned around we grounded on the slipway. It did not help when another lad came by in his boat and said "Don't hang around here or you'll go aground!" We all scrambled out and waded ashore to have lunch and spent part of the afternoon looking around before we motored back to the Sailing School. The broken-down boat had been repaired in time to come and collect us. On the last evening it is the tradition to march off to some woods nearby and have a Barbecue, but because it had been raining, the food had been pre-cooked and we took it into the recreation room to have our feast there. We all played silly games like passing waterbombs along a line from under chins etc. and needless to say it turned into a waterbomb and shaving foam fight that involved everybody - this of course took place outdoors so we did not make a mess! After we had washed and changed into dry clothes, most of us went to the TV room and watched TV until bedtime. SUNDAY Lucy and I left early to get back to MSC in time for racing. The others were due to be collected at 2pm so they went sailing again in the Bradwell 22s for the morning, so even on the last morning you get a sail. We thoroughly enjoyed out stay there, and you can just go for a week's sailing, without having to do a certificate. If you want to know anything else at all about the week, just come and ask me or Lucy. Jenny Ball

8. R.N.L.I. ROWING RACE We were lucky on 26th December with mild and dry conditions with some sunshine. Malcolm/Roger/Ray/Ian, dressed as clowns, completed the course and earned Ist prize for fancy dress. It was a full hour of rowing and he finished the course tired and with a couple of blisters, but obviously pleased. 5. RESCUE DRIVERS Roll up! Roll up!.... Once again the sailing season is upon us and it is time to think about planning and resourcing the Club's Rescue Services which, thankfully, have so far enabled our activities on the water to continue in relative safety and with the reassurance that assistance is near to hand. Whether one is venturing out for a tentative first try or is a hardened competitor, the knowledge that the Club is providing these services is a much welcomed aid to one's confidence. Last year the response to my ‘recruitment campaign' was first class, and has enabled me to establish a solid nucleus of experienced Rescue Boat Drivers. To enable us to provide an even better service this year, it will be necessary to recruit additional volunteers and organise further training sessions. Aside from providing a wider service - perhaps by having two boats out at a time - with sufficient manpower we will also be able to lessen the burden on the _ stalwarts who have provided the service to date. At present there are four boats which are used for rescue purposes and training: Jack B Baddow Star The Workboat The Fisherman Primarily we use Jack B, with Baddow Star as back-up. It is the Club's intention to complement the above with a fast inflatable in the near future. The communications are by CB and VHF, and although there is an increasing array of equipment, the maintenance is taken care of for us. All we have to do is drive the boats - although obviously there is a training programme to enable would-be drivers to attain the required level of competence. Further to this I intend to arrange some training in the correct use of the Communications Equipment and some First Aid sessions with the help of the St John Ambulance Brigade. It is envisaged these will be held both at the MASC and at Stansgate (more news on this in a later edition of Navigans.) We will also be sending some representatives to the Bradwell Field Studies Centre for specific training in handling rescue craft - although places are very limited. In a lighter vein, there will be the Annual Inter-club Rescue Boat Competition which last year served as an excellent opener to the Regatta. If anyone is interested in entering a team please let me know. Finally, if you haven't already, you will soon be receiving a copy of the Sailing Schedule. This once again promises to be an eventful mix of Opens, Regatta, Team Races and, of course, the East Coast Piers Race, not forgetting all the normal Points events. As a small Club the organisation of these events necessitates a great deal of work by a small number of people. Let's get things moving - IF YOU CAN HELP by driving or crewing a rescue boat, please contact me now! , Dave Onyons, Coxswain, Tel. JURY RIG FROM ST PETER PORT Some of you know that Geoff Vines was unfortunate enough to lose the mast from Seabrume last Summer. He was entering the Big Russel between Sark and Herm and the wind was SW 5 when a lower port-hand shroud parted at the deck causing the mast to buckle at the cross trees and fall to starboard. The mast was recovered and Seabrume limped into St Peter Port under engine. Most of us would have put the boat into a yard at that stage and left it for the insurance company to sort out. There followed a period of several days of much telephoning and letter-writing when the extent of the damamge needed to be surveyed and negotiations with the insurance company started. By this time Mike Vines had joined his father and the decision was taken to set a jury rig and sail the boat back to the mainland. The boat would be much more accessible in Portsmouth than it would be in St Peter Port. The remains of the mast were cut in two and the upper portion rigged with cordage salvaged from the original rig and other bits and pieces which were on board. The genoa was rigged so that the foot was set to the improvised forestay and the peak led aft to the jib track with a sheet to the winch. The rig was evidently sound because Geoff and Mike arrived safely at Portsmouth having sailed across the Channel in 5's and 6's. Now Geoff Vines is a member of the RNSA and a fellow member had observed his activities in St Peter Port. It turned out that he left at about the same time as Mike and Geoff and was also headed for Portsmouth. The result of this coincidence was that Geoff's efforts and successful voyage back to Portsmouth had been monitored and Geoff was subsequently nominated for a seamanship award of the RNSA which was duly presented at a ceremony in January. I feel sure that the Club would wish to congratulate Geoff on his well deserved award. Incidentally the trophy, now in pride of place on Geoff's mantelpiece, is known as the Sex Pot. I have been repeatedly assured that it really is an award for seamanship. Seabrume is currently being repaired and fitted with a new mast and it looks very much as though Geoff will be in the water well before the rest of us for the 1989 Season. Dave Steward >< >>> 2. COMMODORE'S NOTES m*oe. Last year Jack Pateman retired and the Club invited Martin Jay to became our President. For those who do not know Martin, he started sailing at the age of two with his grandfather in dinghies. In the 60's he owned various dinghies leading to a wooden Folkboat and an Iroquois Catamaran in the 70's. Since that time he has sailed extensively in the UK, France, Spain and the Mediterranean. Currently he sails "other people's" boats. He started work with BP before joining GEC and becaming Managing Director of EEV and MOVs. In the mid-eighties he was Managing Director of Lewnar Winches who supplied equipment to almost all of the last America's Cup boats. He recently rejoined GEC as Managing Director of GEC Electronic Devices. On behalf of the Club, I would like to welcame both him and his wife and hope that we will see them at the Sailing Club during the season. The winter programme of refurbishment of the Club continues apace. The Gents Changing Room and the Lounge have been repainted and I am assured that the Ladies and Entrance Lobby will be complete before the Working Party. CAT CHAT THE PINOCCHIO TROPHY For those of you who didn't know, it was my 40th birthday in early January. As befitting such an august occasion I was treated to a surprise birthday party, cunningly arranged between my devious wife and that 'snake in the grass' Dave Payne. The Party, of which I had not the slightest inkling, was full of surprises, least of all being a package hand-franked 'Grafham Sailing Club'. On opening the package I found two small shields, one for me and one for Dave, engraved 'Pinnochio Trophy, ist, 1.1.89" So what is the Pinocchio Trophy? Our story starts the previous week on Monday of the New Year. Along with Robin and Lisa; John and Caroline; Trevor and Christine; Tam and Mike Duckmanton; we dragged ourselves to Grafham to campete in the Grafham Grand Prix. Meanwhile Janet went to my mother's for the day. Dave and I were back hame by early afternoon and about 6pm Janet rang me to find aout am how we had done. "We were up-wind of everybody right from the start. Trevor and Christine got close but were just behind; Paul Smith (a friend who sails a Hurricane) was about ten yards behindssas” When Janet had finished talking to me, she rang Dave to sort out the surprise party. She also asked him about Grafham and he told her the same things as I had. Fram all of this Janet believed that we had won the Grand Prix, but was surprised to see that we had left the boat at Grafham. After intensive interrogation the following day, I finally admitted the truth. “There was no wind and racing was abandoned without the boat ever going in the water." But every word we had said was true. We were furthest to windward of all the boats waiting to launch; Trevor and Chris were next to us, but our bows were slightly ahead: Pawl Smith was parked behind us, etc.... I didn't think any more about it until we received the trophies. The significance of the ‘Pinocchio Trophy' was that Dave and I told the most _m velievable pack of porky pies Janet had ever heard, and that she was campletely taken in by our consistent stories. The ‘Pinocchio Trophy' was her revenge. It has pride of place on the shelf amongst all of her genuine trophies. Steeve Keeble, Fly-by-Wire. Preparation over, dawned the long-awaited day To see our Steve afloat, and safely on his way. A man whose name was Hobie shouted same advice "If your mast fills up with water, send for us in a trice." The sail progressed quite smoothly when alas, alack and zap The campass, map and sextant fell from poor Stevie's lap As if this was not enough for any man to face, A Tornado had been forecast, Stampede-ing at a pace. "Oh, Dave. Oh, Dave, Where are you? Wish you were here with me. There's Shearwater everywhere, just me the boat and sea." No Spark of inspiration, No 'A' Class thoughts were there, Nacred into the bargain, Steve started to despair. Just then a gust filled the sail right to overflowing. He Catapulted in the air, oh where , oh where's he going? He Darted here, he Darted there, but to no avail, He lost all his provisions, 'cept for same olde tyme ale. They found poor Steven later upon a desert isle, Alone, shipwrecked and legless, but still he had a smile. The moral of this story, if to sailing you aspire, Don't take your 'cat' to sea alone, takes two to FLY BY WIRE. Christine Milton, Cat Fleet

en SAILING IN SAFETY _ About this time last year Malcolm Stuart wrote an article for Navigans on Sailing in Rough Weather. The article is reproduced here as advice to new members and a reminder to existing ones. Malcolm's notes are mainly directed towards racing, but much of the advice is relevant to non-racers as well. Adrian Wright also offers Similar advice to Salboarders (see Page 8). Do remember at all times that, although the sun may be keeping things warm ashore at this time of year, the water is still very cold, and this could put life in danger for the sailor who is in the water too long. If you are inexperienced, do let saneone ashore (e.g. a friend or the OOD) know that you are going out. The moral is: Get out there and enjoy your sailing but do make sure that you and your boat are properly kitted out and that the conditions are suitable for your own level of experience. SAILING IN ROUGH WEATHER In the spring and autumn at Stansgate we frequently experience strong winds and when these blow against the tide we can get very choppy and confused water, particularly between Stansgate Point and Osea Pier: In such circumstances the Race Officer, the OOD and all members who have turned up to race will be faced with a decision. Firstly, irrespective of what the Race Officer decides, members remain responsible for their personal safety and should not sail if they judge the conditions to be well beyond their present level of competence. The Race Officer will, in reaching his decision, assume that members have considered the weather conditions and have reached the decision that they can survive them when they sign on. The Race Officer's job is therefore not that of deciding what is suitable for the least experienced and worst equipped member, but only that of deciding whether or not it is safe to start a race for the more experienced members. We must recognise here that the only way of getting experience of sailing in rough conditions is to get out and do it and we are only going to improve our skills by pushing ourselves a little. The Race Officer has therefore to make the difficult judgement on how far to let those who sign on for a race push themselves. In circumstances such as this the Race Officer will consult with the duty Coxswain, the Fleet Captains and the OOD. Any course set for racing must take account of the ability of the rescue facilities available on the day to recover crews who may get into trouble. He may therefore restrict sailing to the shorter courses, and faster boats like the Catamarans will have to put up with having their wings clipped. — The ultimate authority for all matters relating to the conduct and welfare of Club Members is the OOD, however in practice he will normally only exercise this authority in response to a request fram the Race Officer for guidance, and would in any case take any decision affecting racing after consultation with the Race Officer. To summarise what is a cautious justification of racing in conditions that pramnpt thoughts of more canfortable hobbies: 1. Competitors must decide themselves whether or not they are campetent to go out in rough weather. 2. The Race Officer must consult the duty Coxswain, Fleet Captains and OOD and set a suitable course or postpone until such time as a suitable course can be set. 3s If these two points have been properly addressed, then racing will only be abandoned in the most extreme conditions, or in the absence of rescue cover.

GATE LOCK Though the Gate Lock broke down completely on 7th May (design fault), it is hoped it will be repaired by the time you read this. When it is back in action the following accumulation of knowledge might be useful to help prevent difficulty in operating the lock: 1. Make sure the gate is firmly shut hame before you begin, and avoid pulling, pushing or leaning on the gate in any way while you are operating the lock. 2. Insert key fully -= and remove it in one continuous motion, (ensure that the key cames to a stop against the reader frame before removing it). 3. Listen for the distinctive sound of a 'click' from the lock mechanism, which will tell you the lock has operated, allowing you to open the gate. (This is more useful sametimes than looking for the green light which can be difficult to see in strong sunlight.) 4. If the lock fails to operate at the first attempt, wait a short time before inserting the key again. (The instructions with the keys say: Do not insert the key into the reader if the red light is on - which is probably saying the same thing.) Ed.
