Any camplaints/suggestions to: Adrian Wright, Sailboard Fleet Captain [redacted] (home) or Chelmsford 73331 Ex 3653 (work). SOME PEOPLE HAVE ALL THE FUN A rather unusual title that! It was prompted by Malcolm Stuart's rather serious article in the last Navigans about safety and the responsibilities of the inidvidual, the Race Officer and the OOD. What Malcolm said was absolutely spot on, but don't let the serious side of officialdam spoil the fun you can have if you are Race Officer. The Race Officer has the ideal opportunity to get his own back on all of his rivals, both within the Fleet or in other Fleets. What is a good course for one Fleet can be a B...... awful course for somebody else. So - if you are Race Officer, what must you consider when setting the courses: The relative speed of the Fleets. Obdviously the Cat Fleet proceeds around the course at approximately twice the speed of the Mirror Fleet, (difference in PY numbers indicates this), but that is not always the case. If there is an average wind and a strong tide, then the speed differential between the fast and slow boats will increase. e.g. If the tide is 3 knots and the Mirrors can only do 5 knots then their speed will vary between 8 and 2 knots, depending whether they are sailing with or against the tide. (In fact the boat speed will vary also with the tack of the boat, but for the purpose of this explanation we have taken a fixed speed). If a Cat can do 10 knots then its speed will vary between 7 and 13 knots depending on the angle to the tide. The ratio is now not 2:1 between the Fieets. contd....

6. This example highlights that a course with legs into the tide favours the Cat Fleet (ratio 3.5:1), but that a course with lots of down-tide legs favours the slower boat (ratio 1.625:1). Unfortunately life is not this simple, as courses are a combination of up, down and across tide legs, and boats vary their speed with the legs of the course. So that it is at best an indication that strong tides favour fast boats. However, light winds favour slow boats. If a fast boat is stationary for any length of time then it has to make up that time on the slower boats by the ratio of their Py numbers. However, if the Race Officer shortens the course, the fast boat will find it almost impossible to make up the time. e.g.- If the Fleet is windless for twenty minutes at the start of the race, and the race is shortened to one hour, then the Cats need to make up that 20 minutes (times the difference in PY) plus the difference in PY for the forty minutes sailed. This means that a Hurricane would need to beat aMirror by approximately 55 minutes in 40 minutes of sailing! Time ticks faster for fast boats when there is no wind. But then again, a dying wind favours the fast boats and a strengthening wind favours the slow boats, for obvious reasons. Having disposed of the impact of the wind and tide, let us consider the sea _ state. Flat water favours the boat with the least wetted area, as there is less friction with the water. This is why it is important to lift the sterm going upwind, and to plane with the bows clear going downwind. If you look at the record-breaking Windsurfers, they are designed to have minimal wetted area when planing downwind. I have heard quotes of as little as 200 sq am being in contact at any one time. That is about 2/3 of the sole of your foot! As the waves become steeper and the wave tops closer, then the longer boats are favoured, as they do not dip into the troughts as much. If the distance between the waves is 12 feet, then a Mirror will fall into every trough, but an 18-foot Cat will generally ride across the peaks. The hull shape also is impacted (just the word) by the waves. A pointed bow will cut through the waves, whereas a flat bow will slam and slow the boat down. A flared bow will lift the boat over the waves, whereas a sharp bow will tend to nosedive into the face of the wave. The final part of the equation is' the characteristics of the boats themselves. Monohulls can tack more quickly than Cats, so a course that requires a lot of tacking favours a monohull. Trapeze boats are favoured by long legs in strong winds as the crew expends less effort in keeping the boat upright. High aspect ratio sails are favoured in light winds, but can be difficult to manage in strong winds. Fully battened sails are favoured in light winds as they hold their shape better. Spinnakers are favoured in light winds as they provide extra drive. So where does this bring the fun into being Race Officer? Well, it depends on your dd point of view. If you hate the Cat Fleet you set a course with lots of tacking. ibs you hate the Mirrors the course has legs into the tide or the waves, etc. However if you want to set good courses, then the Cats want long legs in good winds and the tide can generally be ignored. The Mirrors want legs where the tide assists them to the next mark and where they are out of the waves. The Solos want similar courses to the Mirrors but with less emphasis on avoiding all of the tide; while with the Handicap Fleet you payS your money..... The Windsurfers prefer to avoid downwind legs in steep waves. Setting courses can really be fun, especially in Club racing where the Fleets can be given courses suitable to them individually. It only becomes difficult in a Handicap race where the boats are mixed. One other thing, same helms/crews have poor memories, sO you can always send them around odd-shaped courses to further confuse them. Sailing the same old courses, week in week out, becomes very boringl I love it when my turn for Race Officer comes around. I like to see the Fleets work, so the courses are always unusual. I look forward to seeing what courses you set. Steeve Keeble, Cat Fleet

NEW RACING RULES Every four years the International Yacht Racing Union revises the Racing Rules. The last changes in 1985 were mainly to clarify the existing rules, this year however the changes will affect every sailor. These new rules came into effect on lst May this year. A brief description of the rule changes that effect yachts at this club is’ given below. The new RYA rule book (YR1/89) should be consulted for a more detailed and definitive description of the rules. Rule 4.1 The individual recall signal is now the display of the 'X' flag instead of lowering the class flag to the dip. Rule 5.4(c) The Race Cammittee may now abandon or cancel a race when it considers that to continue would be unfair, even if this has come about due to a change in the weather conditions. Rule 25 This rule, which defines the sizes of class insignia and sail numbers, has been changed but will only apply to sails made after lst January 1989. Rule 26 Advertising and Sponsorships: This rule has been rewritten. A further description of this rule and how it will affect this Club will be given in a future edition of Navigans. Rule 32 Avoiding Collisions: The change to this rule has put a new obligation on the Protest Committee when serious damage has occurred. The Protest Cammittee MUST now penalise the right-of-way yacht if it finds that the right-of-way yacht had the opportunity but failed to make a reasonable attempt to avoid the collision. Rule 42.3(c) This rule which was about luffing another boat the wrong side of a mark has been deleted. For a boat to be allowed to luff another boat the wrong side of a mark, the leeward boat must have luffing rights and the leading boat must not be about to round the mark. Rule 43.2 When two yachts are approaching an obstruction close-hauled on starboard tack, and the yacht to leeward or ahead needs room to tack and hails the other yacht for roan to tack; if the other yacht shouts "you tack” and the yacht requiring water tacks - under the old rules the hailed yacht (on starboard tack) had to 'keep clear' - now she simply has to give room for the hailing yacht (on port tack) 'to tack and clear (the starboard tack yacht.)' Rules 45, 52 and 51.2 A yacht is now required NOT to touch a mark, this was not actually specified before. If a yacht does however touch a mark, the standard exoneration procedure has changed from re-rounding to doing a 720° turn. The offending yacht is required to sail well clear of other yachts to do the 720 as soon as possible after hitting the mark. Rule 54 The ‘pumping and rocking rule has been reworded and a definition of sailing added. Ooching (sudden movement of the body forward or aft) is now always prohibited. When roll tacking or gybing the mast must now not move away from the vertical more than Conta s.<4<

Racing Rules (continued) once. A Protest Cammittee may now disqualify a yacht for infringing rule 54 without a hearing, although if one is requested by the yacht, one must be given. Rule 68.4(b) Protest flags. If after a collision oe of the yachts involved displays a protest flag but does not subsequently lodge a protest, a third yacht having witnessed the collision may lodge a protest even though she herself did not display a flag. Appendix 3 The 720 rule has been rewritten such that a yacht that infringes a rule in the preparatory period must take the penalty as soon as possible after the infringement, instead of waiting for the starting signal. 10. April showers and May Day blues - a view in the Mirror The sailing season is well underway now with most of the Spring Points Series already sailed as I write this article. It was lovely to see 6 (yes '6') Mirrors sailing a few weeks ago and I hope to see this number of boats out again very soon. I would like to welcome the Mander family to the fleet and also the other new.members whose names I haven't discovered yet. Don't forget that we need people to do the Mirror Fleet duties; we're looking for volunteers and if you don't volunteer than we'll have to ring you up and persuade you to volunteer (in the nicest possible way of course). Here are the dates we need to fill:- Wednesday 14 June Sunday 13 August Wednesday 12 July Sunday 3 September Wednesday 2 August The duties are those of Race Officer (its very easy to be Race Officer in our club because we do not have too many boats to deal with) and Rescue Boat Crew (a rather pleasant job to do in the sunny days of June, July and August cruising along in the Jack B). Please make a positive move to offer your services by ringing up Damian or myself on Billericay (0277) [redacted]; please don't asssume that someone else will do it. There are three Mirrors still parked by the large hedge on the west side (ie. side nearest ‘way! Maldon) of the site; these boats need to be moved into the dinghy park so that the grass can be cut ready for the various camping days.SO PLEASE would the owners move their boats into the dinghy park URGENTLY. On the racing side, the nice weather of the Easter Series was followed by winds of Force 4-5 for Spring Points 1 and 2, making the water very choppy. The weather and wind has been sometimes hard, sometimes light since then and we've had some interesting racés. Jenny Ball (my usual crew) borrowed my boat LARS TINN to sail a couple of single-handed races whilst I borrowed Damian's boat BUMBLE. James Brill has joined us on the water as has Jenny's brother David Ball; also with us has peen Ben Hoiroyd and Paul Mander. The good weather is with us now so come and join us and make the most of the sunshine. your Mirror Scribe Lucy Boreham kkk KKKKKKK On the record - but off the wire ! ed During the May Day Bank Holiday Handicap Series, Richard Willmot ‘slipped his leash' on the trapeze of Graham Baker's Dart and plopped into the water. Rumour has it that Graham sailed on all unknowing and engaged in lonely conversation with himself that is the hallmark of those who choose to sail solo. Having finally realised he had lost the 'helmsman's best friend', Graham returned to pick up his errant crew and, all now safely gathered in, continued the race and no doubt wondered whether ‘the rules' would have allowed him to finish without the company of his companion-in-arms. I can certainly ‘feel' for Richard since, many years ago, I did the self-same things whilst crewing in Suva harbour. The problem was that I fell off just a few yards short of the finishing line; I still held the rather Tong length of jib sheet and was dragged over the line mindful of the fact that, very occassionally, (small) sharks were to be seen in the harbour. I must admit I got back in fairly sharpish. The above reminiscence was sparked off by a snippet in The Times which reports that the Royal Naval Sailing Association (organisers of the Whitbread Round the World race) has apparantly decreed that any boat finishing without having picked up, ‘dead or alive', a crew member who has been swept overboard will be disqualified. Time was when such a boat wold have been generally expected to respectfully retire but obviously times have changed. However, the mind boggles at such a situation; does a disqualified yacht appeal against the Race committee ? what comes first, the coroner's inquest or the race committee meeting ? Could a helm, having lost his crew ‘dead or alive’ in an inland reservoir race, wait for an uncomfortable race committee to disqualify him (unlikely to be a ‘her' I’think) if he chooses not to retire ? o*—¢-e “= It is with deep regret that the Club has learned of the recent deaths of Roger Smith's wife Wendy and of Eric Royle. On behalf of all the Club, I would like to offer our sympathy and condolences to Roger and his daughter Caroline; and to Eric's wife Wendy, his son Julian, daughter Sally, and to all their families and friends. Their warmth and friendship will be greatly missed within the Club. COMMODORE 'S NOTES Regatta. What can I say? The sun shone; the weather was dry and warm; there was a magnificent amount of help and support fram within the Club; we didn't even seem to have a last minute panic to find Spotters. Even the sailing was reasonable - although I can probably hear those who wished for more wind on the Monday - but because of the fantastic degree of co-operation we still managed two Races that day. The additional race arranged very quickly by the Cat Fleet provided both amusement and same very much needed light relief during the frustrating wait for wind. In view of the vast amount of help received, I would like to take this opportunity to thank everyone who helped in any form to make it such a success. I would also like to thank Malcolm Stuart on everyone's behalf for taking on the not inconsiderable co-ordination role and for overseeing all the individual effort. The only blot on the horizon was the Water Supply. After struggling for many years at events like these to dispose of the Waste (before installing the new sewage disposal system), we now see that the Supply is insufficient. I would like to thank you all for co-operating with the crash action that had to be taken and can oly apologise for the necessity to supply only cold showers. However, this did reduce the consumption sufficiently to keep both the toilets and Galley supplied with water, and I promise that by the start of the next Season we will have a much improved Water Supply, and in the meantime every attempt will be made to reduce the problem for the camping weeks and the East Coast Piers Race. Next we have the Rochester Visit and Sea Vets Windsurfing events, both on 24th June, followed by the Camping Fortnight from Friday 21st July - Sunday 6th August. We also have the MIDSUMMER PARTY on SATURDAY 29TH JULY, another attraction arranged by the Social Cammittee which promises to be an enjoyable event. Finally, I would like to express my thanks again to all who helped at the Regatta. N.T. Pembleton, Commodore

MAYDAY AT MAPLIN 7. The mens were bad fram the start. The bank holiday cruise was for at least a week to posh places - and I'd forgotten my shaver. As is well known, it is almost impossible to get bits of rope like moorings, painters, etc. hooked up around a saildrive with folding prop; and we managed to avoid this, but a deep spade rudder and shallow skeg can be lethal for mooring buoys which are too buoyant to depress to free. It was freezing cold in swimtrunks battling with the buoy and the elements, and in the end it was a knife job. We motored down to a mooring in Bradwell Creek which seemed preferable to bouncing about on the Club moorings, so at least the first night was OK. Next moming we rejoined the fleet near the Bench Head Buoy for the beat to the Spitway. Once through the Spitway it was a more-or-less dead run in the direction of the Medway and Thames, but the wind reduction hoped for when everything was going the same way was not very obvious. I had chosen my largest Genoa (a lightweight cloth) for the season and omce on the headfoil this was not likely to be changed as the joins in the foil luff groove were no longer perfectly aligned. In order to protect the nearly new lightweight cloth I decided to use the main only and make a series of donwind tacks after controlled gybes. The conditions were such that it could easily be described, after a few Grinks at any Club bar, as a Yachtsman's Gale but realistically it was only a good Force 5. My crew on this occasion was the better half, who now sails only against medical advice due to an assortment of mechanical problems. This meant I could not leave the tiller in such conditions and no way would I trust the Autohelm. My previous practical experiences have included strong wind and an uncontrolled gybe and, yes, it does bring the mast and supplementary gear down to deck level. Apart from the occasional change of tack when the echo sounder suggested it, the only other excitement was the antics of the Even being towed astern. The three main modes of behaviour were: steadily filling up with water and acting as a good sea anchor if only the painter glue joint holds; upside down; and airbome, attempting a fly-past. Nevertheless there was no apprehension and the use of harnesses or the washboard to shut up shop was never considered. Anyway, at this rate, it would soon be peaceful again. The conditions were modest compared to a never-to-be-forgotten incident, surfing in on enormous breaking waves some years ago in Holland, when precise rudder control and hence my ability to take the seas just slightly on the quarter (Cape Horn style, never dead square,) left me with 100% confidence in the underwater details of my boat. At the Maplin Bell Cardinal I aybed for a port tack about due south. The echo sounder, mostly on 10' flashed 8' a couple of times, but the alarm set for 7' (twice our draft) was not sounding. The waves were looking nasty and we were rising and falling more than the 2' indicated by the echo sounder. Then it happened. About three horrendous crashes. Nothing else occurred to me other than that we were aground on sand as hard as concrete and no boat would take that for more than a minute or two in such waves. The fact that I spotted the remains of the rudder aster and the crashes had ceased should have told me we were still travelling forward, but I'd lifted the engine hatch and saw water coming in from the direction of the transom. The Prospect has many attributes, that's why I chose her. Among them are the inner mouldings in the hull and topsides; super for insulation, but it does mean that it Contd.s:.<s«

MAYDAY contd... takes a lot more than lifting the berth cushions to see the inside of the hull and confirm the presence of keels - or otherwise. Frantic activity inside while upside down, attempting to evaluate the problem, also caused seasickness and I subsequently abandoned the task to despatch what must have been an unusual Mayday format. My brain had just about managed to work out that if we were breaking up and about to sink, the rest of the fleet could not approach us in such seas, and taking to _ the Even would have been difficult for me and impossible for Joyce. With hindsight I'd probably do the same things again, as to delay until it was too late could have been an even greater mistake. . The crisis lasted about 10 seconds, but I managed to pad it out for a couple of minutes. Derek Hall of 'Staggers', with a calmer appraisal suspended the ‘'Mayday' action until the need was confinmned and since we were still afloat and not aground, he managed to carry out a difficult tow to Thames Haven Yacht Club, where I could dry Out and assess the damage and temporary repairs necessary. Many thanks once again to Derek and also to Peter Bloanfield for standing by. The plywood, saws, drills, clamps, Isopon paste etc. were ordered from home, pranptly~ delivered and after a night-shift duty spent sitting and lying in the mud, _ ‘'Tekin Two' returned to base the following Monday. A new rudder is required; the hull/transan join requires a complete new section; the port bilge keel needs rebedding and tightening up; but it could have been a lot worse. The sounder was used for a survey of the area on the returm trip, without result. I have not learnt anything from the incident I didn't know before and I am still uncertain about the possibility of a large log in the water, or same similar obstruction. In a sudden crisis, time is vital for major decisions, 10 seconds or even a couple of minutes are inadequate unless you have all the facts. I have been once before adrift without any form of control or propulsion. The elements were the worst ever recorded in the area, anno domini was not a factor in September 1951, and I had 9 full days (and, worse still, nights) to consider the only variable, for all the use it was. This long-ago incident does throw up same analogies for the small boat scene, so ITM pass them on for what they are worth: 1. Once out of control, ships and boats are beam-on to the seas and that's the worst attitude. 2. Roll angles of over 90° (over 45°heel) can occur and can never be got used to. 3. Revise your Physics. The future depends on the relative positions of the ship's (and its cargo) centre of gravity and its centre of buoyancy, which is called the Metacentre.* 4. Always have a large reserve of fuel on board for long trips, in bad weather it is possible to use it all up with no progress over the land. 5. The last 10-15% of fuel in a low tank is generally unuseable, sediment and sludge on the bottam become disturbed and that's your lot. contd. eee

MAYDAY contd... 6. Never rely on outside help in extreme conditions, sametimes even aeroplanes can take days finding you. 7. Oil on troubled waters, sea anchors, even lifeboats (if they are still in the davits) are useless, they are only for story books. A small boat sailor may try a sea anchor fram the bow if he's not too paralyzed to move. See, I've experienced all that and I still don't know what happened! Here's to the next time, Father Neptune. Ron Phillips, Tekin Two. Ed's Note - I believe there is an automatic membership of an Association for people who have used a parachute to save their lives. I wonder if an equivalent group for those who have ever been rescued as a result of a Mayday call would be very popular. Perhaps’ the numbers qualifying would be too great. Or would those eligible very much prefer to keep their heads down and not take part in an annual get-together when hair-raising yarns could be swapped! * The following from the Oxford Campanion to Ships and the Sea: Metacentre. The point of intersection of a vertical line, in relation to the ship's structure, drawn through the centre of gravity of a ship when she is lying upright and a vertical line drawn through the centre of buoyancy when the ship is heeled. To make certain that a ship is stable so that a righting moment comes into play when she is heeled, the metacentre must be above the centre of gravity. 100 CLUB DRAW Dave Harper won the £50 prize and Malcolm Yeamnan won the £5 prize in the June Draw.

George Robinson, Vice Commodore CATAMARAN NEWS Regatta weekend has come and gone as I write. Whilst being blessed with glorious sunshine, there wasn't a lot of wind, so that racing did not claim too much of our energies. Nevertheless everyone seemed to enjoy themselves. In spite of the fact that there seemed to be more people about than ever before, Catamaran entries were disappointing, only five Darts participating, none of them visitors. The Hurricanes were here in force because it was the venue of one of their travelling events. Nice to see Marconi getting in on the act. However, in view of the lack of consideration and rudeness exhibited by same members of the Hurricane party, I personally wouldn't worry if I never saw them again. On a more pleasant note, may I extend a warm welcome to new members of the Fleet, namely, Chris and Bruce with Dart 3993, Steve and Nigel with the Prindle 18.2 and Colin Kidner with the Spark. We all look forward to your frequent participation in Sunday racing. Two of our boats will be travelling abroad soon to take part in the round Texel race. Steve Keeble & Dave Payne, and Trevor Milton & Rob Stahl. We wish them luck and look forward to reading a blow-by-blow account in a future edition of Navigans. In spite of the large numbers of Cats in the park, very few venture out to race. I know that I'm always on about it, and to be fair, it has improved a bit. But it could be much better. With a little improvement we could have, for instance, class racing for Darts alone without all that messing with handicap numbers. So if you know of another Catamaran owner who likes to race, bring him along. And all you new members, don't be nervous about joining in, it's the quickest way to polish your act. Your Catamaran Correspondent Peter Flook

SAILBOARD NEWS 1. Seavets Event, 24th June This proved very successful with 34 competitors taking part, and ages ranged from 35 to 78! Four races were sailed and a great deal learnt by all concerned about the organisation of such an event. Over £200 was raised for the charity 'Research Into Ageing’. Ian Crumpen must be praised for obtaining so much pre-publicity, and together with his father, Joe, for operating 'Kingfisher' as a Rescue Boat-cum-TV platform - many thanks to both of them. Nigel James' help was invaluable in organising the food; producing superb recording forms; registering entrants; and running the Race Box. (Any camplaints about the start of the 3rd race to me - I'm not very sure about all those flags - very confusing! ) Guy Chevenix-Trench, the sponsor, provided Les who worked hard all day, as well as prizes and a trophy to be campeted for on an annual basis. My thanks also to Bob Leeder, Graham Baker, Malcolm Stuart, Jean Flook, Lee Tridini and Barry Marke, all ¢ whan helped make the day go very well. (Anyone I've amitted - kick me when you se@ me). 2. Board Identification The Seavets event did make apparent to me the reason for the increasing number of complaints we have been getting about identifying Sailboard race competitors. There seems to be one effective solution - sails must be clearly marked with a number on both sides. Please can those who race, or intend to do so, set about this as soon as possible. For the purpose of internal Club racing it doesn't matter what letters/numbers are used - the only rule is that no two can be the same! I will compile a list of existing Sailboarders and numbers and place a copy on the Club notice board opposite th signing-on counter. Please let me know of any additions. If you wish to get an official RYA 'K' number, you will need to pay £12 per annum for membership of the RYA, and this will also provide 50% off 'Boards' magazine and free third party insurance. Phone the RYA (0703 629962) to obtain a registration form. 3. Class Flag ow Racing sailors should note that the Sailboard class flag has changed to 'O'. The reason is that the previous 'K' was too similar to the Catamaran class flag. '‘'O' is a diagonally halved, red above yellow, flag (and also signifies 'man overboard' - not entirely inappropriate! ) Adrian Wright

Se CATAMARAN NEWS Recollections of the last weeks seem to be a haze of hot sunshine and sparkling waters. Can you remember a time when you had to take so much care to protect against the sun? I assume that it was this good weather which swelled our fleet to such proportions. Competitors have been numerous and the racing close. Is it the sun that has brought about this alarming tendency on the part of young Richard to frequently detach himself from the rest of the equipment at the most inopportune times? Nice to see Paul Metcalfe back in harness again after his enforced lay-off. He is already back amongst the front runners, I would add. Cammiserations to our much beloved colleague Dave Payne who suffered a painful injury to his ribs whilst launching 'Fly by Wire' in heavy surf in Holland. We miss your Gulcet tones, Dave, came back soon. It is reported that our ex-Dart ace Robin Gmith is at it again amongst the Hurricanes. His second place at Texel, followed by winning the European Hurricane Championship is no mean feat when one considers the relatively short time he has been sailing this new boat. I am sure you would all wish me to tender our Congratulations wto Robin and his crew, Lisa Gatton. (Ed's note: see next article for the full story of these great successes.) Also among the Hurricanes, Rob and Matthew got a mention in Yachts and Yachting for their good performance on their first outing in their new boat at our regatta. Well done, Rob and Matthew. By the time you read this there will be a sample for your inspection of this year's Piers Race Sweatshirt, price to be announced later. So hurry along with your orders, remember, all proceeds to Charity. Your Catamaran Correspondent, Peter Flook @CAT FLEET NEWS - ROUND TEXEL AND ALL THAT Whoops! Saneone in the Hurricane Fleet really stood on Peter Flook's toes by the sound of it. A pity to see a petty personal disagreement brought to Navigans though. A third Marconi Cat went to Texel and in spite of being forgotten in the "“well-wishes" list, it was Hurricane 101 'Flying Colours' that put Marconi SC high in the honours list. Robin Smith and Lisa Gatton crossed the line 5th behind the 'Specials'; were first production boat to finish and when the prizegiving was finally held at 12 noon on Sunday, were placed second overall from 950 starters. Texel is the first Friesian Island off the North coast of Holland, is only 3 miles from Den Helder on the mainland at its southernmost point, and is served by a gqocd, if mot expensive, ferry service. The event started same 12 years ago when 5 boats challenged each other to a race around the Island o Catamarans. From there it quickly escalated. In 1980 there were 410 Cats in two starts. Now the format is for one mass” start. 1988 saw 870, and this year a massive 950, to race the 100 kilometres - 60 miles - around the Island. The biggest Cat Race in the world without doubt.

6. Round Texel contd... The island is long and thin, surrounded by shallow water and shifting sand banks. The western shore is straight, runs approximately North-South, and has long, sandy beaches pounded by the North Sea surf. At the top of the Island is a lighthouse at the entrance to the sound between Texel and the next Island, Vlieland. Here the water is very shallow but with a very strong current. As the shore curves around the back of the Island, the course follows a line of withies eastward same 15 miles to the 'VC' buoy, where the Cats turn southward to close the shore again about one-third down. The water is too shallow to navigate inside the line of withies. From here to the bottom of the Island the shoreline is very much like the edge of the Blackwater, marshy, but like everywhere else in Holland, backed by a sloping dyke or sea wall. The course then goes back up the westerm shoreline to the finish about half-way along at Strand 17. The organisation is superb. On arrival at the beach road, competitors are marshalled on to a hardstanding area where trail©&TMS are unhitched from the cars and inmediately picked up by oe of a fleet of 20 tractors, to be towed along the beach where each class has its own area. When you are ready to leave the beach you simply queue a few minutes at the marshalling point for a tractor and direct it to your trailer. The start line is between two huge trawlers and is over a mile long. At the ten, five and start signals a helicopter flies along the line with white, blue and red smoke respectively to complement the signals from the Cammitttee boat. There are no general recalls. With strategically placed video cameras at both ends, and in the air, they get your number. The weather was glorious with a breeze of around 12 to 15 knots from the north-east, which meant that everybody started om the same tack of the close fetch up to the lighthouse. This drastically reduced collisions campared with last year's event, but the start was delayed for 1 hour because the wind was holding the tide out around the top of the Island, across the shallow sands between Texel and Vlieland. Most of the Hurricanes and faster boats started at the outer end of the line, which had a slightly favourable bias. From here these crews were able to twin trapeze immediately. showing amongst the early leaders was Rob White and Jeremy Newnan while 100 yards to weather, Robin Smith & Lisa Gatton tailed the Dutch team of the Hoekstra brothers. Slightly further ahead the Hurricane Turbo with wing mast and new extra-long racks sailed by Reg White and Steve Olle was doing battle with the giant Roberts 27s. ew Towards the lighthouse a number of singlehanded 'A' classes, Hurricanes and Tornadoes, that had started further inshore, found a band of stronger wind just off the surf line, and these boats led around the light to start the beat across the top of the Island. Robert White and Robin Gnith steadily worked their way through the pack, and in fact passed the Roberts 27s when they ran aground near the 'VC' buoy. Robin & Lisa were the first Hurricane round the mark on to the long downwind leg behind the Island, in 5th place behind 3 'A's, a French Formulae 20 and a Tornado. Down the back of the Island Robin & Lisa overtook two of the 'A's, the Formulae 20 and the Tornado, but were in turn passed by the faster 'Specials', the Roberts 27s and the Hurricane Turbo, when they hoisted their huge spinnakers. At the bottom of the Island Robin & Lisa started the twin trapeze beam reach back to the finish same mile behind the leading 'A'; and with helicopters clattering overhead and chase boats to leeward, ‘Flying Colours' was pushed to the limit as the gap was reduced. But at the line the 'A' Class was still 50 yards ahead. A few moments earlier, Reg White &

Round Texel contd... 7. Steve Olle had crossed in 2nd place after their spinnaker had exploded while just leading a Roberts 27 to the line for line honours. Sane 2 hours later, between 4.30 and 5.00 pm, same 500 boats crossed the 100-yard-long finish line. Even with video cameras running at both ends, the Race Cammittee had a major headache and at 11.30pm announced that the prizegiving was delayed until 12 noon on Sunday. The results were worth waiting for. Robin & Lisa were 2nd overall, just over 4 minutes behind the A Class on corrected time. Third place was a Nacra S.S. There were 4 Hurricanes in the top 11 boats, the next British boat being Robert White & Jeremy Newnan. Other Marconi Positions: Trevor Milton & Rob Stahl Dart 20 i23ra Paul Ellis Dart 15 204th Steeve Keeble & Dave Payne Hurricane 238th —_— HURRICANE EUROPEANS OUD NARDEN - HOLLAND 17 - 18 JUNE Just one week after the Round Texel Race, Robin Smith & Lisa Gatton beat the best in Europe to win the Hurricane Europeans, and _ became Marconi Sailing Club's first European Champions of 1989 with 'Flying Colours' Racing took place on the 'Gooimeer', 10 miles east of Amsterdam, and to the south of the new town of Arlmere. The huge waterway, once part of the Zuider Zee, is renowned for its unpredictable windshifts and is also very shallow with the occasional drifting reed bed. The Dutch Hoeksbra brothers were out for revenge after being beaten the previous weekend by Robin & Lisa in the Round Texel, but the Marconi duo sailed a very consistent series, with one first place, two seconds, a third and a fourth position, to accumulate 11.7 points to the Hoeksbra's 17.0 points in second position. Third place was Robert White & Huub Lambrieks. Steve Keeble & Dave Payne did not disgrace ethemselves with a 28th in their first European Championship, especially when Dave ceturned hane to find out he had me _ broken rib and two cracked, caused when the boat hit him while launching through the surf at Texel. (We thought the Grolsch at 28p a bottle might have samething to do with it....) Robin Smith, ‘Flying Colours' CONGRATULATIONS... 2.00% belatedly to Yvonne and John Weatherley on the birth of their first grandchild, Matthew, born on 8th April 1989. I'm sure it won't be too long before Matthew has his first sail in 'Viridia'.

The Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championship. (Through the Eye of the Hurricane) This event is held annually at Stone Sailing Club and consists of a number of different races. On day one, there is the Stone Dinghy Challenge, which is effectively a practice race for the following series, followed by the first race of the championship proper. Day 2 has the rest of the championship and is followed by the "Cock o' the River" race. This last race is a pursuit event between all of the class winners in the championship event. Many years ago, the two premier sailing events on the Blackwater were the Marconi Regatta and the Blackwater and Colne championship. However, in recent years the Stone event has seen a falling off of entries, although a revival is taking place. It was disappointing to see so few entries from Marconi, although I do not believe that we had any entrants at all in recent years. This year, the Marconi fleet provided entrants in the Cat Menagerie andw the Laser fleets. Mark Savill was our sole entrant in the Laser fleet and despite some excellent and consistent sailing was unlucky to place only third. Mark scored two second places and a fortn out of the three races but was beaten by a first, second and DNS by the winner, and a first, third and fifth by the eventual second overall. That is close racing by any standards, and I am sure that we will see Mark amongst the pots ( and not just beer and toilet) in the very near future. Well done Mark! The Cat fleet was represented by Fleet Captain, John Nickalls accompanied by the ever blushing Caroline (It's not often that a good looking young lady gropes my thigh under the table!); Current European Hurricane Champions Robin Smith and Lisa Gatton, myself (wearing the loudest trousers in the competition) crewed most ably by Mike "Crocodile' Duckmanton and on the Sunday Trevor Milton crewed by Chris and Paul Ellis. Trevor was taking the opportunity to test drive the demo Hurricane. } — Race one on the Saturday afternoon got off to a bad start, as John had broken the goose neck on the Tornado and everybody (thanks Darcy) was trying to help get him on the water in time. The effort did not succeed, but did mean that Mike and I missed all of the signals and were about 50 yards behind the line when the gun went. It was only because we saw Robin screaming in, that we were even facing the right way. Needless to say Robin and Lisa screamed into the lead, followed by a couple of Unicorns and about 4 Shearwaters. It was a reach to the first mark and Mike and I had passed all except the leading Unicorn, who we passed at the second mark. It was then a chase after Robin and Lisa. We maintained our distance on them to the next mark, after which we had a long reach up to the Baffle. At this point John and Caroline joined us and we both chased Robin and Lisa. John stayed down to leeward and claimed after the race that he was under powered, whilst Mike and I tried to pitchpole on several occasions. Unfortunately, we had knocked

Blackwater & Colne contd... the port rudder back and every time I tried to bear away, the rudder just acted like a brake, sending up a spectacular plume of spray. Meanwhile Robin and Lisa had reached the paffle and fallen into a hole in the wind. Both John and I had been gaining on Robin, but when he reached the Baffle the distance was dramatically reduced. However, despite our best efforts, we both fell into the same hole! The wind was going through all points of the compass, but Robin snook round and was off on the reach back to Stone. John rounded second and raced off, and after two involuntary gybes Mike and I began the chase. There is no way you can catch Robin and Lisa when they have got a 100 yard lead, so Robin took line honours, John crossed second and we were third. Meanwhile the leading Unicorn seemed to sail straight around the Baffle without stopping. Robin won the race, the Unicorn was second by 7 seconds and we were third. Race 2 was on Sunday morning. Robin got to the line a little early and consequently had to dip back. John Nickalls and I made perfect starts and John led by about 10 yards at the first mark. Around the second mark we went, with Robin and Lisa breathing down our necks. You just can't keep that man back, and he sailed over us on the reach. John kept him at bay, and the two of them fought tooth and nail (or is it forestay and tiller) around the course. Mike and I held our position about 100 yards back until about halfway around the second lap, when two ‘dead in the water tacks' lost us about 400 yards. We had just passed Mark Savill when we did the first bad tack and he proceeded to sail effortlessly passed as we floundered about. He had requested a tow as we overtook him; we could have done with one when he went passed. John managed to hold Robin off to the finish, but Stone were sailing the Tornado off of a lower handicap than the Hurricane, so Robin took the race on handicap. Trevor Milton had taken the Demo Hurricane (Robert Whites Boat!) out to race, but was forced to retire at the first mark when the tiller , extension broke. He's a strong lad that Trevor! A liberal application of brute strength and lashings of adhesive tape meant that Trevor, accompanied by Christine, were out for the second race. The one advantage of a fast boat is that you are back with plenty of time for lunch. When the second race times were reached, a large portion of the monohull crews were still in the galley queue, so a postponement was signalled. Unfortunately, 3 out of the 4 Marconi cats were already on the water, so for 30 minutes we practised heaving to. John Nickalls claims he is faster than me even when he is hove to! Mike and I made a dream start to the third race. Well, anyway, I woke up when I hit the water after bouncing off of the mainsail! Robin and John rushed off into the lead again, whilst Trevor rushed ashore to pick up Paul Ellis in place of Christine. (Sailing is now getting like football, with substitutes on the touch line). Mike and I pulled the Hurricane up and proceeded to chase Trevor around the course.

10. Blackwater & Colne contd... Robin won again, with John close behind. A Unicorn finished third, with Trevorfourth and Mike and I fifth. The Shearwaters were no longer racing in the same fleet as us, as they now had enough boats to have a class of their own. Overall, with three wins, nobody could touch Robin, but John and Caroline finished second and proved that Robin isn't unbeatable. A Unicorn from Stone finished third with Mike and I forth. Next year we intend to make it a clean sweep for Marconi. The final race was for the "Cock o' the River", but Robin did not realise that he was eligible, so he was back at our club when racing commenced. The race was won by a Shearwater. I am sure that Robin could have collected that trophy as well. Well done to Robin and Lisa, and John and Caroline. Maybe next year a few more Cat sailors will make the effort to 'beat up the Blackwater’. Steve Keeble, 'Fly-by-Wire ed

*ode< COMMODORE'S NOTES I cannot remember the last time that the Club enjoyed such warm and dry weather for the Camping Fortnight, we almost made it through the evening of the Mid Summer Party as well. Although I was not able to be present for the Camping Weeks, I understand that a very enjoyable time was had by all. My grateful thanks to all who helped make a success of the event. Similarly to those who helped at the Midsummer Party which was a tremendous success, especially the band, many thanks Pete, and others. It will soon be the Annual General Meeting and amongst other items will be the election of Club Officers for next year. Following the rule changes last year, the list of Officers who are elected at the Annual General Meeting are: Carmodore Secretary Vice Commodore Sailing Secretary Rear Commodore Social Secretary Treasurer Clubhouse Secretary In addition to the above there are a large number of other positions to be filled, some of which are elected by the individual fleets. A full list of all positions will appear in a later Navigans, along with the request for nominations. However, can I appeal to everyone to start to think now whether they can help to fill any of the posts. The next major event for the Club is the EAST COAST PIERS RACE over the August Bank Holiday. The sight of all those 'Cats' last year was really impressive and I hope that the weather is kind and that this year's event will be even better. N.T. Pembleton, Canmodore MARCONI ENTRIES AT’ DART 20 NATIONALS Two Marconi Dart 20s took part in the 4th Dart 20 Nationals which were held at Seasalter YC, Kent, on the weekend of 8th-9th July. The first race was sailed in light fluky airs at 3.30, Saturday afternoon and was won by Peter Ewing & Amanda Harman of the Laser Centre. CAMPING WEEKS One interesting spectacle that hasn't been at our camps before was the presence of a dolphin amongst the moorings. He had already been seen in the river earlier in the season and during our fortnight spent time up at Stone and also visited our owm moorings on most days. If we were at the right place at the right time (perhaps about an hour or two before low water) we might see him leap right out of the water a « times, and fall back with a huge splash. I've been informed that he (or they - for there may have been two of them) was probably feeding on fish who graze am_ the weed growth on mooring chains and boat bottams. Perhaps the warmer water attracted him or it may be a more desirable spin-off from the grossly overpriced and totally ineffective new environment-friendly anti-fouling the yachtsman is now legally obliged to use! There was lots of interest playing 'spot the dolphin’ by people both afloat and ashore. He usually kept a respectful distance from boats but if you kept stationary and patient afloat you could get quite a good view of him. Peter's cartoon arose fron the frequent discussions among us on whether we were seeing a porpoise or a dolphin - I'm sticking to dolphin! Our fortnight's weather was warm and dry except for the middle Sunday which was rather grim. For the rest of the time, though it varied occasionally from too much to too little wind for enjoyable sailing, those of us mm site had enough variation to allow everyone to have same of the sort of sailing they liked. Calm hours allowed everyone to safely swim, paddle and generally play around in the water. contd....

CADET WEEK Cadet Week followed the patter established over the last few years with dry land instruction, capsize drill in a dinghy attached to the moorings barge, a trip to Maylandsea for lunch, a trip to Osea for lunch, and a First Aid lesson for sane younger Cadets. On Tuesday there were two separate Raft Races organised, one for younger Cadets and ome for the older oes. Each of two teams were given 2 long pieces of rope, 3 barrels, 4 planks, and the task of assembling a raft and propelling it out to the moorings barge and back. The whole task kept them busy for some hours. The last day, Friday, was rather short of wind but there was no rest for the Cadets who had a busy programme of organised games on the water all day. All their activities during the week were videoed by Maureen Bigden and Janet Battle, and there was just time for the results to be shown on the Friday evening after the Presentation of Prizes. The Presentation was made more interesting by the use of a 'Sin Bin' - any Cadet who had supposedly ‘stepped out of line' during the week had his nose held over a barrel containing seaweed liberally dosed with, I believe, pickled onion vinegar. The audience decided how long the poor victim suffered by electing how long the count should last - anything up to a (sametimes very slow!) count to 20. And by the end of the evening there was a new saying - if anything at all to do with sailing ever goes wrong it's now always “Ben's Fault" (Holroyd, that is). Thanks are due to Ione & family and her friend who came along with their First Aid skills and the St John Ambulance Caravan for Cadet Week. Ione was much less busy ee last year, but there were one or two custamers, and it was peace of mind for us CONG 660%

CADET SERIES, 1989 The winner of the 1989 Cadet Series is:- LEE HARRISON (DART 18) Many congratulations to Lee Harrison (Dart 18) on winning the 1989 Cadet Series in what turned out to be a ‘nail biting' finish and all hinging on the last race. This is what a race series should be like and the 1989 Cadet Series must rank as one of the best for some years. Cadet Races 1,2 and 3 were raced on Sunday, 2 July, in Force 4-5 with at least 5 entries in each race. Lee Harrison won all three races very handily and, truth to tell, the Cadet Series looked to be well and truly ‘wrapped up' for 1989. Apart from Lee, the other entries were Jon Yorston (Dart 15), Jenny Ball, David Ball, Lucy Boreham and Damian Boreham (all Mirrors). Cadet races 4,5 and 6 were scheduled for Sunday, 23 July. For race 4, the wind was somewhat lacking in strength, very patchy and very variable around the course, so much so that only Damian Boreham (Mirror) and Michael Fletcher (Topper) managed to round Breezy mark to complete a shortened course. Unfortunately, Michael inadvertently infringed a rule at the start and was disqualified. There were only three starters for Race 5 which was sailed in slightly windier conditions but was still pretty light and made it difficult to make way against the tide. This race was won by Lucy Boreham (420) with Lee Harrison (Dart 18) second. This time it was the turn of Damian Boreham (Mirror) to be frustrated by lack of wind at 'A' mark and he eventually retired. The Race Officer decided to postpone Race 6 until 30 July (when Cadet Race 7 was scheduled, together with the Jackpot for the club's senior citizens). The gods deceeed that Sunday 30 Ju'y brought with it a wind of Force 7 - occasionally observed to touch Force 8. Problems with the Jack B delayed the start of the Jackpot and eventually the Race Officer postponed the Jackpot to a later date and the Cadet Races 6 & 7 to Saturday, 5th August. Despite Lee's three previous wins,the Cadet Series was now still far from over ; Lee could be beaten by Damian if he (Damian) won both races 6 and 7 and Lee finished no higher than 4th in each race. Thus Cadet races 6 and 7 promised to be very interesting. Cadet 6 was raced in Force 3-4 and was won by Damian (Mirror) with Lucy Boreham (420) 2nd, Ian Fletcher (420) 3rd and Lee (Dart 18) finishing 4th. Clare Davies (Mirror) and Sian Caruth (Mirror) both retired whilst David Stewart (Topper) unfortunately missed out a mark and was disqualified. So, the scene was set for a nail biting finish with all depending upon the last race. Cadet Race 7 was sailed in Force 4 and, although Damian again won the race, Lee won the series by finishing 2nd with Lucy 3rd, Ian 4th, David Stewart 5th and Kirsty Jolly 6th. The Final result - since both Lee ana Damian had 4 1 ' points . each, the series . was decided . on countback; Lee's vital 2nd place in race 7 overtook Damian's 3rd place in race 2 and so Lee emerged the overall winner. The 1989 Cadet Series came to a marvellously exciting end , having been sailed in a wide variety of condition of course, tide and wind, thus providing a good test of all round sailing skill and knowledge. Lee dealt with the varying conditions with great competence and thoroughlydeserved his win but he had to fight hard for it. Lucy Boreham (helm) and Jenny Ball (crew) discovered they liked sailing the 420 and came 3rd overall; alas, no prize because the Average Entry fell just short of the magic number of '6' required for the award of 3rd prize. With 4 races to count, only Lee, Damian and Lucy competed all 7 races. David Ball and Jon Yorston each competed 3 races, Jenny Ball 2 races as helm (but she also crewed for Lucy) with Ian Fletcher and David Stewart also competedin 2 races. Stuart Golding, Richard Battle, Michael Fletcher, Kirstie Jolly, Clare Davies and Sian Caruth all sailed one race, some of them taking part in their first race ever. A total of 14 helms took part in the Cadet Series which is not a bad total compared to some previous years. However, in view of the large number of cadets taking part in the Cadet Week training programme it would be nice to see more cadets taking part in 1990. lst Lee Harrison (Dart 18) ala pts 8th David Stewart (Topper) 37 pts 2nd Damian Boreham (Mirror) 4 34 o 9th Kirsten Jolly (Mirror) |: ee 3rd Lucy Boreham (Mirror/420) 8°°4 " =10th Richard Battle (Mirror) Ap 4th David Ball (Mirror) 25 i =10th Sian Caruth (Heron) 42 " Sth Jan Fletcher (420) 29 . =10th Clare Davies (Mirror) 42 " 6th Jenny Ball (Mirror) 30 " =10th Michael Fletcher (Topper) | i 7th Jon Yorston (Dart 15) 32 " =10th Stuart Golding (Mirror) 42."

COMMODORE'S NOTES It is extremely unfortunate that the fine weather of the summer broke on the August Bank Holiday weekend when we ran the second major event of our calendar - the East Coast Piers Race. While Malcolm Stuart, John Nickalls and the rest of the organisers tusselled with the problem of the course to set, I was at Walton listening to the wind howling in the rigging and I whole heartedly support their decision to _ shorten the course despite the pressure of the event and the natural desire to sail the course. The events of the actual race demonstrated the correctness of their decision. On behalf of the Club I would like to thank all who helped for making a success of the event despite the conditions. We still have the Autumm Series to be sailed, the Solo and Mirror Open on Sunday 17th September and the Helmsman of the Year Final om Saturday 7th October. All of these should provide good sailing and I am sure that the Helmsman Final will provide interest for any spectators who are there. These events are followed by the Working Party on Sunday 5th November when the Club TM is dismantled for the Winter and prepared for the winter maintenance activity. Following the pattern of last year, the Main Cammittee will be contacting each Fleet Captain to arrange for them to carry out a specific task and the Fleet Captains will be looking for your support. By using this method last year, a great deal was achieved. The Laying Up Supper is on Saturday 11th November. Because of the increasing number of people attending, we are holding it at the Heybridge Moat House at Ingatestone this year. Peter Bloanfield has succeeded in booking the same popular band as we have had at the last two events. Please book your tickets early to avoid disappointment, either via your Fleet Captain or the normal ticket sellers (see below). Finally, to round off the year we have the 'Last Fling' race on Sunday 19th November followed by the Annual General Meeting and Prize Giving. N.T. SOLO NEWS -_ The recent National and World Championships at Plymouth again enjoyed excellent sailing breezes and sunshine - what a miraculous summer this has been! It was a really first-class event in all respects and thoroughly enjoyed by the six Marconi participants. At the end of the six-race series, in a fleet of 97, our overall results were: Malcolm Gandy 21 Dave Nixson 33 Roger Qnith 49 John Salmon af Colin Willsmore 73 Janet Keeble 77 Both Malcolm and Janet finished in exactly the same positions as they achieved in the Inlands - how's that for consistency. Additionally, Janet polished off the 4 other Lady competitors to become Ladies World Champion!!! A just reward for her terrific determination and the steady improvement she has achieved since joining our Fleet. I think this makes her Marconi's only current World Champion and certainly the first our Solo Fleet has seen, so Congratulations, Janet. _~Malcolm Gandy also won the latest Eastern Area Open at the Wilsonian Club mm_ the Medway, though all the other positions were still in doubt when I left, due to protests and lamentable deficiencies in race management. The next round is at Stansgate on September 17th so let's hope for a good turm-out and a decent sailing breeze. During the Cat Open weekend at August Bank Holiday I was very grateful for the wholehearted support for our Fleet Duties. Almost the entire Solo Fleet turmed out and made a contribution at same time over the 3 days, and if at times we appeared overmanned for the job, I'm sure you appreciate that with the size of camnpetitor fleet which was anticipated it was essential to have sufficient people ao site to adequately cover the safety aspects. My sincere thanks to everyone who contributed. The Eastern Area travellers season finishes as usual at Fishers Green on October lst. This is always a well-run event at a very friendly club and not far to travel. It would be very nice to have a few more Marconi entries from same of the fleet who do not often travel - so how about it? John Salmon, [redacted]

COASTGUARD COMPLIMENT Having survived the rigours of Marconi's East Coast Piers Race, I was aroused fran reasonably deep slumber to answer the telephone. In a matter seconds I was of briefed with the details of an incident at the Club by the Duty Officer of Thames Coastguard at Walton. I was requested to rendezvous with the Bradwell Marine Rescue Unit (MRU) at the Sailing Club. Mersea Inshore Lifeboat had been launched and an ambulance had been requested to stand by from Burmham-on-Crouch. As I pulled into Stansgate Road, I was aware of the blue lights of the MRU fast approaching and we both arrived at MSC together, approximately 6 minutes after the initial cail, quickly followed by the ambulance. Having identified the yacht involved, which was on its mooring, the casualty was a 44-year-old male who had been loading stores fram the boat to the dinghy alongside, had inadvertently slipped, upturned the dinghy and ended up in the water. The amily other person on board the yacht, the Master, quickly threw the main sheet to the casualty who tied himself securely under the arms to it. The Master had made several attempts to raise the casualty by using the boamn, but because of the physica’ exhaustion of the casualty, was unable to get him on board. A call was made tw Thames Coastguards who raised the initial alarm and hence our attendance at the Sailing Club. The Lifeboat arrived same 8 minutes after us and put the casualty ashore, where he received inmediate medical assistance. My reason for writing this note is that it may serve as a lesson for all - the casualty was fortunately all right although hospitalised for the night, but in the space of a very short time he became close to hypothermic on a flat calm night while the yacht was at anchor. It had been impossible to get him aboard and it was aly through the skill and presence of mind of the Master, who attempted in every way to recover the casualty, acted in text-book fashion to ensure that he was safe and secured to the yacht and called for assistance, all of which, had he not done so, could have ended in a very sad evening. I trust he is not embarrassed by my mentioning his name, but credit must go to the Master, Mr Derek Hall, for his commendable action in saving the life of his crew. Charles Anderson _

10. EAST COAST PIERS RACE (or "Thank Goodness we didn’t go to Clacton......") With a forecast of "Force 6/7 occasionally 8" one has to look on the bright side; a wind direction of NNE, whilst not bright, was at least less gloomy, so we took the plunge by setting the full course. The buoys were already in place, the spotters had set off for the four gates, and Roger Smith Ml ah to tell the competitors that they were to sail down to the mouth of the river, up the coast to Clacton and Walton, and then back to Marconi’s. Perhaps the competitors had suspected what we were going to ask them to do and found an excuse to be elsewhere, or perhaps their families had simply demanded their presence at some other Bank Holiday activity - either way, there weren’t as many faces at the Briefing as we’d have liked, and the reasons for this are still a subject for some conjecture. The preparations had been based around accomodating 150 boats, trailers, cars and tents - the site looked quite empty as a near-gale rattled through the dinghy park. As the fleet gathered for the Briefing the so far unaccomodating weather did us a favour. A particularly strong squall threw itself at the clubhouse, the water turned streaky-grey, and the race committee's hearts fell. A quick rethink, the course was shortened, and the Commodore in Titchmarsh Marina became ten years younger in a trice. Even with the strong wind course in use only 38 of the entrants were adventurous (foolish?) enough to venture out to the start, but the race set off a few minutes late from Osea Pier, with the boats fetching up toward No.1 before beating up Goldhanger Creek. This first beat saw the first real evidence of the wine cena as Reg White’s Hurricane Special’s mast broke in two- it wasn’t to be the White family’s weekend. The reach from Goldhanger to Mill Beach threw off most of the ‘fast’ rescue boats, and they rejoined the leaders as the fleet emerged having passed behind Northey Island. By this time Rob White had assumed the lead in his standard Hurricane - Will Sunnucks, also sailing a Hurricane, was lying second, and we'd let our Tornado drop back to third place. Past the club in 31 minutes and on toward Bradwell the cats with less sail area were able to pick up valuable time against the more powerful boats struggling to stay upright on the tight reach. The wind increased as the leaders passed through Bradwell Gate, and the spotters watched as half a dozen boats capsized in quick succession. With a multitude of rescue boats having volunteered their services for the day all the casualties were quickly attended, although a number of boats suffered minor damage and several retired. The beat across the river to the Nass Beacon gave a brief respite from the stinging impact of high-speed salt water and a chance to re-establish communication with the crew - even if this was limited to the expression of mutual interest in keeping the mast out of the water. Bearing away at the Nass was exciting, and the downhill ride back to the Club gave the water a chance to numb the other side of the face. Downwind, the cats lost their tendency to lift one hull clear of the water in a gentle attempt to deposit slow-witted sailors in the water; instead they adopted a more effective bow-down attitude. Every gust pushed the lee bow further under the waves, threatening to trip the boats (now travelling at over 20 knots) forward into the spectacular, but most disconcerting, “pitchpole". On our boat, Caroline took the helm, leaving me with both hands free to haul on the mainsheet, and with four eyes glued to the port bow we careered upriver. Rob White was leading as we passed the Club, and Will Sunnucks was still ahead of us, but the second White mishap of the weekend happened as Rob rounded No 2 mark in the belief that it was a large inflatable near No 4. The Race Officer didn’t approve of this - indeed | understand a mild panic set in as Will Sunnucks followed Rob on the wrong course and visions of the entire fleet failing to complete the race arose in the organisers’ minds. Luckily (mainly for us !) we psa the mistake, rounded the correct mark, and screamed back to the finish line. Although Paul Smith very nearly passed through our lee as we pinched up to the windward end of the line (anticipating a second lap), a scream from Caroline sent us reaching down to a two length lead over the line. Was the event a success? Well | certainly think so. All those who sailed enjoyed the race: several thought that we ought to have had another lap, but we were very pleased that we hadn’t! The organisation seemed to go well - several visitors observed that we had clearly planned for a lot more entrants, and that we’d have been able to cope without any real difficulties with over a hundred boats. Whether to hold any future Piers Race on the Bank Holiday weekend must be a critical question, and we've learnt alot to apply in the future. However, several aspects were particularly satisfying - not the least that we had 24 rescue boats of assorted types covering the course.

Sincere thanks are due to all those who helped out at the weekend: to the cat fleet members who helped with the setting-up and taking down; to the other Club members who put in a lot of time and effort to provide rescue cover, to marshall the competitors, to staff reception, and to make the event run smoothly in a hundred and one other ways; to the Solo fleet (and in particular Roger Smith and his team on the Piers Race day and to John Salmon for providing the additional races); to all the Club members who weren't directly involved yet tolerated the inconvenience that the race inevitably involved; to all our sponsors for removing the financial burden and allowing us to make a generous donation to the RNLI and Sailing for the Bisabled: and to all those members of the other clubs who willingly gave their time and services to bring us all safely back to shore. My own special thanks must go to Malcolm Stuart, who (as always) was tireless in his efforts for the event, to Charles Anderson who put all his local knowledge and organisational skills into making sure we achieved such an effective rescue cover (and what a seductive radio voice he has!), and to Mike Duckmanton whose calming influence rescued me from many a panic! And what of next year? Well, we have a good foundation on which to build. We’ve built up a broad range of contacts, and we've seen many (but I’m sure not all) of the pitfalls. The final decision remains to be made, but personally | hope 1990 will see the best Piers Race yet. It’s unlikely to be faster (we everagee 16 knots), but a warm sunny day, flat water, and an on-board store of cold beer would let me orgive that! Part of this requirement is that at least one distress flare should be carried, and the most popular choice has been the ’miniflare’ pack made by Pains-Wessex. This pack contains a launcher and 8 shells, each of which rises to a height of 80 m and burns for 6 seconds. The pack can be carried conveniently in a pocket. Pains-Wessex made a number of these packs available for sale in support of charity for the Piers Race, and we have a number remaining in stock. They have come direct from the manufacturer and thus have a long shelf life, and we are selling them at a price of £15... the standard chandler’s price is £20. Although the Piers Race is a long distance race over quite exposed water, many of the Cat fleet have chosen to carry these flares whenever they're sailing a distance from the Club. During the Piers Race it was educational to hear that an upturned catamaran not far from the Bradwell gate became totally invisible to watchers on the shore... and we've experienced a number of instances lately when sailors have become separated from their boats. These flares are equally useful to cruiser sailors; whilst they are not suitable for use offshore, they have the distinct advantage of being able to be slipped into a jacket pocket and thus offer direct personal protection. Should you be carrying some? . Only £15 a set, all proceeds to RNLI and Sailing for the Disabled. Available from the Club bar.

There were also other activities that went on in the two weeks, including a boat and camping Jumble (hopefully ” next year this will attract more items Yes we diol get through a lot of for sale); coffee and tea get- tent ; i togethers; and a Raffle for the RNLI pegs this EL iw (we raised £23). Amongst the winners were Maureen Ball, Leonie Golding and Marie Greenhalgh. . 4 Two dinghy picnic cruises were held. The first when 19 boats went downriver to Thirslet Spit, where we lunched and played boules on the shingle which is only exposed 2 hours before and after low water. Because of the rising tide, the games will have to be resumed next year! The return trip was quite choppy and Jenny Ball in a Streaker was swamped but after much bailing reached MSC - well done. Peter (Boustred) in his canoe also had a rough passage but managed to cross the river by Osea without being knocked over by the waves. We all agreed it was an enjoyable picnic cruise. The second cruise was to Mill Beach. With a wind of force 0-l, sailing was slow, but with plenty of time to top up suntans. We returmed via Northey Causeway just in time for teal On the second Saturday the Sailing Club held a successful supper party and Hoe Down with music by 'Famous Potatoes' and during the following week the Cadets entertained us with their raft races. 16. WEIL'S DISEASE The national rat population is increasing and between 50 to 60% of rats carry and excrete the organism Leptospira ictero-haemorrhagiae in their urine. Infection with the organism causes an illness which has been known to result in death of 10% of cases. There has been a recent increase in the incidence of the disease - 133 cases were notified in 1988 compared with amily 68 in 1987 and 32 in 1986. Formerly occuring mainly among sewage or abbatoir workers and miners, recent records show that the majority of fatalities are now related to water activities. In 1989 there have been 19 deaths of which no fewer than 13 were associated with water users. The nature of leisure water activity means that the average age of this at-risk group is fairly young with most cases occuring in the 13 - 42 age group. ABOUT THE ILLNESS The organism enters the human body through breaks in the skin such as cuts, blisters and abrasions or via the lining of the nose, throat or alimentary tract. The incubation period is 7 - 13 days and the disease starts with a fever, muscular aches and pains, loss of appetite and vomiting with prostration. It is vital that the doctor be told of any water-borne activity as the symptans are easily confused with those of flu and if the patient has a 'clean' occupation the possibility of Weil's Disease may be overlooked in the early stages. Subsequent bruising of the skin, sore eyes, nose bleeds and jaundice may occur. The fever lasts about five days and may be followed by significant deterioration. Laboratory testing of blood will confirm the diagnosis but this may take undue time — in an ordinary hospital. Send samples direct to: The Leptospirosis Reference Unit, Public Health Laboratory, County Hospital, Hereford, HR1 2ER. Tel. [redacted] here they will be tested within 24 hours. Treatment is usually by Penicillin Antibiotic. RATS AND THE ILLNESS The rat is a creature of the water's edge. The leptospira organism is passed in urine and, while it does not live long in dry conditions, can survive for same time in water. Salt water soon kills off the organism but there is a significant risk in tidal waters such as lower parts of the Thames and other rivers. The risk increases upstream and is greatest in canals, ponds or areas of slowly draining water. There is a significant risk to users of river banks or reservoir edges. WATER USERS Sailors, boardsailors, canoeists, oarsmen, swimmers or Fisherman are at risk in any area with a population of rats. Any skin wound or blister, old or new, may be infected if immersed in water polluted with the organism. GENERAL CARE Handrails, steps and walkways should be checked for gaps, nails or rough edges that may Cause minor wounds. ALL MEMBERS: Every effort must be made to see that food residues are removed fram the Clubhouse, boat and trailer parks or picnic areas. A happy well-nourished rat will produce more rats. Wear shoes to protect the feet from cuts. Don't allow water to collect inside your dinghy, it may be wet but it may not all be water! (Ed's note: The same caution also necessary with pools of water collected on the outside of boat covers i.e. don't let it come into contact with any wounds.) Cruiser Owners: Don't think it is solely a dinghy sailor's problem. If you ever have to come ashore clutching at the jetty from your tender, you too are at risk. Waterproof surgical plasters of an adequate size should be used to cover old skin wounds before going afloat or to the dinghy park. Such protection will also apply to club workingparties when members may be clearing old structures or other hazards. Every sailing club should have available to members at all times a supply of clean fresh water to wash wounds and a shower for those who may have fallen into suspect water.

2s COMMODORE'S NOTES As the Sailing Programme draws to aclose it is time to start to think about the future. This begins with the election of next year's Cammittee at the Annual General Meeting and there is a nomination form elsewhere in this issue of Navigans. The only restrictions that apply are that the Canmmodore, Secretary and Treasurer must be Ordinary Members and that the Canmodore, along with the Vice and Rear Commodores, must have served at least one year in the last three on the Main Cammittee before being elected to these positions. Under the Constitution and Rules of the Club the Main Cammittee can, via Rule 10.7, make nominations for any position and increasingly over the last few years, these have been the only naminations. Whilst this helps with continuity, it should not exclude others fram seeking nomination. Early next year I will attempt to give an indication of those people serving on all the Cammittees who may be intending to retire, so that others can came forward. You will see fram the nanination form that very few of the positions are elected if you compare the list with the Cammittee in the front of the Year Book. Again, volunteers are always required to fill these positions and if you are interested, please contact the relevant Sub Cammittee Chairman. Regarding this year, I an pleased to say that members have came forward to fill all the positions. There are however a number of other positions to be filled by election, namely, the Fleet Captains and the Dinghy and Cruiser Representatives on the Clubhouse and Social Committees. These are elected at your Fleet Meetings, so do consider volunteering and attend the meetings. I hope that the dates of these meetings will be published in Navigans. Winter Tasks Over the winter there is a considerable amount of work to be carried out, ranging from erecting the Tractor Shed and Tender Rack through refurbishing the Entrance Hall, redecorating the Galley and Bar, to work to replace the old sewage-system covers and remove the trees to increase the size of the dinghy park, and same work on the road; these activities will be arranged on a Fleet basis as last year, when we made a tremendous improvement in the site. In addition to these, there are a number of items which will be carried out using professional help, which includes an electric shower in the Ladies' Changing Roan, and an updating of all the radios to allow us to use Channel M2. Beyond these activities, the Main Cammittee have made a definite committment to a second Rescue Boat and the Sailing Sub Cammittee are producing a proposal so that we can approach the MASC for the funds. At the same time we will be asking the MASC to replace the water pipe. Finally, next summer a series of working parties will be needed to start work on the Cruiser Park drainage. Obviously the costs of all these schemes are much less if we, the Members, carry out as much work as possible, but it does require help fram everyone and not just a dedicated few. I ask you all to contact your Fleet Captains during November and arrange to help however you can. If there are any Members who are able to lay bricks or can carry out same carpentry or electrical work, could they please contact Chris Davies as soon as possible to assist with the winter work. Finally can I remind you all that the tickets for the Laying Up Supper on Saturday lith November are now available and the Annual General Meeting is on Sunday 19 November. N.T. P.D. BLACK, HON SECRETARY SOLO FLEET NEWS Our Open Meeting went off very well, thanks to a steady force 4-5 all day and the efficient management of the Cat Fleet - our thanks to all who helped. The entry of 18 was perhaps a little disappointing, but they were certainly offered a hard day's sailing with really good beats - not normally a feature of the courses at Stansgate. It was a day for the heavy weather stars, especially the morning race which had wind against tide, creating the usual short chop which is so difficult to deal with in aw Solo. Overall the leading positions were: lst Alan Burrell (Halfway YC) 2nd Malcolm Gandy 3rd Dave Nixson 4th Roger Smith 5th John Salmon 6th equal - Ron Greygoose, Colin Willsmore. The last Eastern Area event of the year provided a complete contrast, sailed as it was almost entirely in a force 1 on Fishers Green pond. The three races nevertheless demanded plenty of concentration from the entry of about 16. Malcolm Gandy managed to win two of them to take the event and, in doing so, wrapped up the Eastern Area Series - well done, Malcolm. Other Marconi finishing positions at Fishers were: John Salmon 3rd, Janet Keeble 5th, Roger Smith 8th. I propose to hold the Fleet AGM this year at my place - [redacted], Billericay, on Friday 3rd November, so please put a note in your diaries and try to keep that evening free. I'll provide more details later. I will definitely be standing down as Fleet Captain this time so urgently need your naminations for next year. John Salmon, 0277 [redacted]

N.J. JAMES Many old friends in our Club were saddened to hear of the death of Norman (Jimmy) James, Jimmy had not enjoyed good health for several years and passed away on 14th September. He had a long association with Marconi's, at Baddow and then at Witham, with the Marconi Microelectronic Company. With his family he sailed a GP 14 for many years and more lately enjoyed cruising in his Centaur "SONYA" which unfortunately he had to sell because of his health. Jimmy was a very popular Club member, always willing to help. He will be missed very much by his fellow mariners, and we send our condolences to Peggy and his sons Roger, Peter and Nigel.
